1931-02-17.text: Sydney, N.S.W., Feb. 22. (P)- Dame Nellie Melba, Australian diva who is critically ill here, was gradually sinking tonight.

New Delhi, India, Feb. 17.—(A.P.)—For four hours this afternoon Mahatma Gandhi, gaunt leader of India’s restless millions, and Viceroy Lord Irwin, representative of the British empire, met in one of the strangest peace conferences history has ever witnessed. Neither would say much about what they had talked over but they let it be understood that their meeting had been mutually satisfactory and that they would continue their talk tomorrow. Viceroy Lord Irwin hoped in the negotiations to persuade Gandhi to call off the civil disobedience campaign and collaborate in the working out of a federation and dominion status for India in pursuance of plans evolved at the Indian round table conference.

New Delhi, India, Feb. 16.—(AP)—Peace in India now rests in the hands of Mahatma Gandhi, Lord Irwin, the viceroy said today, for the government is ready to concede most of his demands, if he will agree to call off his civil disobedience campaign and give some evidence of a “change of heart toward the government.” Lord Irwin has set aside all of tomorrow and the next day for conferences with the picturesque little man who is leading India’s campaign for independence, and today he spent several hours talking to three influential Indian delegates to the recent round table conference in London. Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru, who is credited with having broken down Gandhi’s resistance to the point of arranging a personal talk with the viceroy, gave Lord Irwin his own ideas of the situation in a meeting also attended by Srimivasa Sastri and M. R. Jayakar. Benares, India, Feb. 16.—(AP)—Fifteen persons

HY ine Associated Press BRISBANE, Australia, Feb. 17.—Stanley Roser, an 18-year-old boy, beat off a shark which attacked him while he was swimming today. A maneater bowled him over in the water with a furious rush, but in his struggle to escape, Roser jammed a thumb in the shark’s eye and it beat a retreat. Roser walked to a hospital where doctors treated his wounds.

New Delhi, India, Feb. 17, WA The Mahatma K. Gandhi, leader of the civil disobedience movement against British rule, appeared hopeful today of an early return of peace in India. Gandhi visited the viceroy, Lord Irwin, and they talked for four hours. The civil disobedience campaign, Gandhi's demands for amnesty for all political prisoners, the London round table conference proposals for a new constitution and other issues in the controversy were discussed by the Independence leader and the representative of King George.

London, Feb. 17.--(AP)--The sum of twenty million pounds—about £100,000,000—was added today to Britain's dole fund by the House of Commons, which last night accepted recommendations of Miss Margaret Bondfield, Minister of Labor, for new unemployment loans. The new grant pushed the total of the British unemployment fund from 70,000,000 pounds (about $250,000,000) to 90,000,000 pounds (about $450,000,000). The fund is already about $235,000,000 in debt.

| WELLINGTON, New Zealand, Feb. 17 (P)—Lord Bledisloe, governor general of New Zealand, today requested that his official salary be reduced 10 per cent for the public interest. Premier Forbes gratefully accepted his offer. The governor general's salary is £5,000 ($25,000) a year with £2,500 allowances, a total of about £7,500.

MADRID, Feb. 16 (%)—King Alfonso today made the daring political gesture in an hour of crisis of inviting the enemies of his regime to help govern Spain and thereby, in the opinion of most political observers, saved the monarchy from the most menacing situation of recent history. The medium of his invitation was Jose Sanchez Guerra, a powerful political opponent of Alfonso himself, who tonight at the king’s request was working to form a ministry to replace that headed by Damaso Berenguer which resigned Saturday. The royal gesture had an immediate effect of restoring confidence. The stock exchange had one of the busiest sessions it has known for months. Values rose generally and bankers and business men expressed an optimism that has been long absent. Sanchez Guerra’s plan is a radical one, and one that if it is successful will strip the crown of much power and privilege. It contemplates

Rome, Feb. 17.—(A.P.)—A panic of spectators at the Morgana theater resulted in injuries to scores tonight when part of the roof of the theater caved in. The building was filled with a crowd of Mardi Gras carnival holiday makers. Firemen tried unsuccessfully to prevent a panic, hacking great holes in the wall as emergency exits, but the crowd stampeded. Three ambulances carried off most of the seriously injured.

MADRID, Feb. 17. (WP)—Don Jose Sanchez Guerra today abandoned his efforts to form a cabinet to succeed that of Premier General Damasso Berenguer, resigned. He advised King Alfonso to ask Melquiades Alvarez to form a new government. Alvarez is leader of the Reformist Party, which like the Constitutionalists of Sanchez Guerra, desires to call an assembly to change the 1876 constitution with restrictions on the king's power. The failure of Sanchez Guerra was a surprise inasmuch as he had announced when he left his home to go to the palace that his cabinet was completed. “Everything now depends on the King,” he had said. However, when the former premier left the palace after about half an hour with King Alfonso, he described his abandonment of efforts to form a cabinet as due to failure “to obtain the support of certain factions.” “I declined to form a government because I am a man of the ri

Shanghai, China, Feb. 17—Vernacular newspapers today said bandits and communists had slain more than 3,000 peasants along the border south of the Yangtze river between Hupeh and Kiangsi provinces. The reports were regarded here as probably exaggerated.

MADRID, Feb. 17.—Melquiades Alvarez, chief of the reformist party and one of the leaders in the demand for a new constitution in Spain, today declined King Alfonso’s offer of the premiership. Jose Antonio Sanchez Guerra, designated by King Alfonso yesterday to form a liberal government, announced after a visit to the king at noon today that he had failed in his efforts.

Berlin, Feb. 17—()—Police took steps to remove beer steins from the list of political weapons. An order made public provides that in the future beer may be served at political meetings only in paper cups. It resulted from frequent stein fights during which a number of persons were injured. The order further provides that chairs and tables must be firmly screwed to the floors and no bottles be brought into the meeting halls.

Madrid, Feb. 17.—A statement attributed to King Alfonso XIII today by General Fornells, acting undersecretary of war, was interpreted by some as indicating the king’s willingness to abdicate if his abdication would be for the good of Spain. General Fornells said that the king, after visiting General Berenguer Monday, spoke to the chiefs of bureaus of the ministry of the army and told them that he was willing to make “all sacrifices necessary for Spain's welfare.” Don Jose Sanchez Guerra today abandoned his efforts to form a cabinet to succeed that of Premier General Damaso Berenguer, resigned. He advised King Alfonso to ask Melquiades Alvarez to form a new government.

MADRID Feb 17—Censorship on Spanish newspapers was reestablished Tuesday by order of the resigned government of Premier Gen Damaso Berenguer who is continuing in office until King Alfonso solves the present crisis.

Madrid, Feb. 17.—King Alfonso XIII faced the danger of a stalemate today in his efforts to raise a new and more liberal government out of the collapse of Spain’s seven year dictatorial regime. The king, admittedly willing to make all sacrifices necessary for Spain's welfare, was carried by the rapid developments of the last three days to a point where he must choose a future course, apparently either toward republicanism or with the "right" conservatives. Don Jose Sanchez Guerra, the veteran liberal who became reconciled with the king in the present crisis, deeply disappointed the monarch when he reported he was unable to secure the support of Socialists and Republicans which was considered essential to formation of a new cabinet. The king then was forced to face the necessity of turning back to the more conservative monarchial factions for leadership or of swinging further toward the mo

MADRID Feb. 17.--INS—Due to last-minute difficulties Jose Sanches Guerra was forced to report to King Alfonso that he had failed in his efforts to form a coalition cabinet, to succeed that of Premier D'Amago. Guerra advised the king that he should call upon Melquiades Alvarez to head a new government. Alvarez is the chief of the Constitutional Reform party and considered the most liberal member of the Constituent bloc. Alvarez had informed Guerra yesterday that he and other Constituents would support Guerra in every way but that he believed inclusion of Republicans and Socialists was absolutely essential. Guerra was eloxeted with the king for some time shortly after noon today. Leaving the palace after the interview Guerra declared: "I brought to His Majesty a cabinet list which, however, did not include the names of any Republicans or Socialists. In the present extremely delicate situat

Ry The Associated Press Colon, Canal Zone, Feb. 16.—Reports were heard today that Nicaraguan insurgents had overpowered a detachment of Nicaraguan national guardsmen in the town of Gracias a Dios and captured the place, seizing its radio station. The summer fruit steamer Nicar, cruising in Nicaraguan waters, was reported to have received an urgent message from Captain Stent, commanding the guardsmen, who asked that soldiers be sent to recapture the place. Gracias a Dios is on the extreme northeastern point of Nicaragua.

1931-02-23.text: | SYDNEY, Australia, Feb. 23 (AP) — The curtain was rung down today on the life of Dame Nellie Melba, one of the purest sopranos grand opera has ever known, after weeks ebbed with a strange illness which baffled her physicians. Seventy-one years old, the famous Prima Donna for several days had fought a losing battle with a skin malady picked up in Egypt and aggravated by a long journey home from Europe before Christmas and the extreme heat of the Australian summer. Friends believed she hastened her own end with insistence upon spending Christmas in her native Australia, disregarding the advice of her physicians in Europe under whose treatment she was growing better. She became ill again aboard ship and had to enter a hospital at Sydney before proceeding to Melbourne. She was happy however, in spending almost her last hours in Melbourne, near where she was born, and from which she took he

(UP)—Dame Nellie Melba who in 1902 persuaded the London Opera house to give Caruso a trial, died today after an illness of several weeks. Death came to the opera star, one of the world’s greatest sopranos, in her 72nd year, after illness which befell her in Cairo, Egypt, and for which she consulted specialists in most parts of Europe without success. Homeward bound to her native Australia, she became seriously ill before the liner Cathay docked at Fremantle, and doctors would not permit her to land. When the Cathay touched Melbourne she was taken to a hospital and since that time has hovered between life and death. Her death marks the severance of a link between the musical worlds of today and the past two generations. Dame Nellie Melba was christened Helen Porter Mitchell. She was born at Melbourne May 19, 1861 the daughter of David Mitchell, a wealthy Scotch farmer. Her mother was of S

MELBOURNE, Australia, Feb. 23, —Dame Nellie Melba, Australian soprano, died here early today after an illness of several weeks. The famous prima donna returned to Australia several weeks ago after having contracted an illness in Egypt which responded to treatment at first but recurred after she began the journey back to Australia. She had to leave her ship and enter a hospital at Sydney but later continued to Melbourne, which she regarded as home. The illness took the form of a strange disease which baffled physicians. She was 65 years old.

NEW DELHI, India, Feb. 22.—Full power to make any decision in behalf of the All-India National Congress in his dealings with the viceroy was given to Mahatma Gandhi today by the working committee, which is the cabinet of the Congress. The action is regarded as tantamount to a vote of confidence in the ability of the little nationalist leader to obtain the maximum concessions for India from the British. It also would appear to set at rest rumors of a split in the opinions of the working committee. There had been reports that some of the moderate members disagreed with Gandhi's views and favored peace at any price. Both sides in the present peace parleys are marking time pending receipt from London of the British cabinet's views regarding Gandhi's terms for peace. The chief points in his demands are general amnesty for political prisoners, inquiry into alleged excesses by police, restorati

ROME, Feb. 23.—(UP)—At least a dozen ships have radioed or otherwise signalled their distress in the death-dealing storms of increasing violence gripping Mediterranean countries. Of these, the most important so far reported was the British 2500-ton steamer, Baron Sempill, reported sinking 112 miles south of Marseilles. The French steamer, Saint Servan, radioed that it had noted distress signals of another ship but had been unable to help because of the intensity of the storm. Sicily was virtually isolated during the storm over the weekend.

Vienna, Feb. 23.—(A.P.)—Police today announced the discovery of another plot against the life of King Zog of Albania, who missed assassination last Friday when gunmen fired at him near the Vienna opera house. The new plot was laid to Albanian political opponents of the King who, it was said, planned to attack him in Votive Park where he often walks. A flood of congratulatory telegrams on his escape last Friday poured in upon King Zog today from almost every country in the world. The senders ranged from crowned heads to humble Albanian groups. King Zog said today that he was determined to remain in Vienna and complete the cure for his malady, an indisposition brought on by smoking 150 cigarettes a day. The newspaper Wiener Stunde said today that the task of guarding the king had been made difficult because of his friendship for a Viennese music hall star, Franziska Janko, the daughter of

BERLIN—(/P)—A national petition asking President Von Hindenburg to accept the life presidency after his term of office expires in April, 1932 was advocated Monday by Arthur Mahraun, chief of the "jugdeutscher orden," a democratic political party of World War volunteers whose slogan is "Regeneration of the Fatherland." At a congress of the party held at Holzininden, Mahraun declared that all danger of civil war in Germany would be removed if Von Hindenburg, who will be 84 next year, were to accept the life presidency of his country.

LEON, Spain, Feb. 22—(AP)— An avalanche of snow and ice from the mountains overhanging this small town today uprooted massive oak trees and buried alive the family of Santiago Fernandez. Fernandez, his wife and their four young children were crushed as the avalanche obliterated their home. The slide also destroyed the only mill in the town,

| PALERMO, Sicily, Feb. 23.- A raging tempest struck towns and villages in western Sicily today, taking a toll of at least six lives. Torrential rains accompanied by winds of hurricane force caused tremendous damage, disrupting transportation and communication facilities and seriously hampering shipping. | Palermo, Messina, Catania, Taormina and their suburbs bore the full brunt of the storm. All traffic in Palermo was suspended, the lower districts of the city being entirely flooded, in some sections to a depth of seven feet. | Twenty small vessels were sunk in the harbor when the howling wind kicked up mid-ocean waves. Larger shipping, including one American vessel making Palermo a port of call, was forced to head out to sea to escape the gale’s fury. | The suburb of Uditore was flooded when a swollen river burst its levees. Streets and squares were transformed into rivers and lakes. -

MOSCOW, Feb. 23. — The Red Army today celebrated its 13th anniversary with parades, speeches and other enthusiastic evidences that it was ready to defend Russia against any invasion. The commissar of war, Vofroshilov, issued an order of the day bidding the army be on its mettle because, he said, the country was being continually threatened by “capitalistic war.” Russia stands for peace, he said, but this does not mean that the country would permit any invasion of its rights. According to government figures the Red Army numbers 562,000 which officials declare is the smallest in proportion to total population in all of Europe.

(International News Service) PARIS Feb. 21,-Thirty-five miners are dead and between 40 and 150 missing as the result of a coal damp explosion in a coal mine near Aix-La-Chapelle, according to a dispatch from Brussels today. The blast occurred on a level 1,800 feet below the surface.

1931-02-06.text: HASTINGS, N. Z., FEB. 5. (AP).—Another sharp earthquake rocked the ruins of this town at 10 o'clock last night, throwing the already frightened populace into further panic. Martial law has been declared and no one is permitted to enter the designated district without a permit lest what is left of the buildings may collapse. There has been some looting but armed sentinels were posted at various points throughout the town tonight. NO AMERICANS LISTED AMONG EARTHQUAKE CASUALTIES

NAPIER, New Zealand, Feb. 6. (UP)—Evacuation of Napier and Hastings proceeded today attended by almost every conceivable hardship and discouragement. Only one road is open and that is cracked and full of fissures. It is badly congested with hundreds of vehicles, all proceeding from the area stricken by Tuesday's earthquake and the tremors which have ceased hardly for an hour since. A number of the dazed and nerve-shattered refugees, unable to continue along the "Via Dolorosa" have fallen by the way and died where they fell. Pathetic rude crosses have been placed over shallow graves dug for them. Within the two towns the grim work of excavation of bodies of victims and identification is proceeding. In many cases the bodies are so badly crushed that recognition has been impossible and it is believed probable that a number of victims who perished in the falling hotel never will be identifie

Some Found Alive in Debris But Mostly Dead Bodies; Latest Shocks Slight. NAPIER, N. Z (Friday), Feb. 6 (P)—New Zealand's realm of ruin was under martial law today. Armed marines patrolled the streets to prevent looting and to see that nothing hampered the ceaseless toil of rescue workers seeking survivors among the wreckage left by Tuesday’s earthquake. All day yesterday a great exodus continued, the inhabitants who had escaped death fleeing from the disease which it was feared might follow upon destruction of the city's sanitary system. Communication between the razed towns of Hawkes Bay province and the outside world was reestablished. With scores of doctors, nurses and other relief workers present all that was possible was being done for the hundreds of injured but unable to be moved. There were recurrent earth shocks during the evening which served again to terrify the population, bu

AUCKLAND, N. Z., Feb. 6—New tremors shook the Napier area today while evacuation of the town, devastated by earthquake and fire, continued. The bottom of the harbor, permanently raised by the earthquake, was subjected to new earth movements and the naval sloop Veronica was grounded again. The sloop has been aground or in shallow water several times since the earth shocks began. Relief work was fully organized under government direction. Food, clothing, and medical supplies were being distributed to survivors, and complete order was maintained in Napier and Hastings, although some looting was reported from other towns in the earthquake zone. The number of dead still could only be guessed at as rescue parties attacked heaps of debris. The latest estimate was 200 known dead and 1,000 injured. Towns in the area resounded with explosions and the roar of falling brick and stone as the demoliti

SYDNEY, N. S. W., Feb. 6 (-P)— Torrential rains have flooded several towns on the north coast of New South Wales. Boats are being used to rescue people from house tops and a steamer was able to pass along the main street of Lismore. There have been no casualties thus far. Railway service has been suspended in localities.

BIRMINGHAM, Eng. and, (UP) — It was spring, the year was 1909 and T. R. Winshull was in love, He wrote his sweetheart asking her to be his bride. She rejected his proposal next day by letter. A year later, it was spring. T. R. Winshull again was in love. He proposed and was accepted. A family was reared. In 1923 Winshull died. Two years later the girl who had rejected his proposal died a spinster. A few days ago T. R. Winshull, Jr., received a letter signed “Lilly” saying she had reconsidered her decision and would marry him. Winshull stared at the letter in amazement. He did not remember proposing marriage to any girl. Then he noticed the date of the missive—March, 1909. The love letter from his father's first sweetheart had been 22 years in arriving at its destination.

LONDON, Feb. 6—(#)—Wilhjalmur Stefansson, writing in the current “Spectator,” lifts a corner of the curtain which enshrouds the death of Salomon August Andree, who “never came back from his polar balloon expedition of 1897. Andree and K. Fraenkel, whose bodies were found in the Arctic wastes last August, were overcome by the subtle fumes of carbon monoxide as they sat about a kerosene stove in their virtually airtight tent, Stefansson believes. He developed his theory from evidence discovered on White Island, where the bodies of the explorers and the remains of N. Strindberg, another member of the expedition, were found. He almost died himself of the same cause, Stefansson writes, in an Eskimo snow house on Coronation Gulf 20 years ago. “Their tent was nearly airtight,” the article says, “for it was made of balloon silk and the floor was sewn to it in one piece. It stood in a lee and in

DECISION, rendered by the Italian King Victor Emanuel in favor of France against Mexico may promote better Italian-French feeling. West in the Pacific Ocean, 870 miles west of the Mexican coast, is a little island, called by the English Clipperton Rock and by the Mexicans, La Isla De La Pasion "The Isle of the Passion." France and Mexico claimed it and agreed to let King Victor Emanuel arbitrate. Now, 22 years later, Emanuel gives the land to France, ordering Mexicans to withdraw their little body of soldiers.

LUCKNOW, United Provinces, India, Feb. 6. (AP).—Death today took from the ranks of Indian nationalists Pandit Motilal Nehru, 69, who forsook ease and affluence to lead his countrymen in a passive battle for home rule. He had been ill for several months and in January in view of his condition was released from Allahabad prison before expiration of a six months’ term imposed for his activity during the civil disobedience campaign. Mahatma Gandhi and Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, his best friends, came here directly from Yeroda prison, Poona, upon their release to be at his bedside, and day before yesterday took him by automobile to Lucknow where it was thought conditions would be more favorable to his recovery.

LUCKNOW, India. (P)—A continuous stream of silent mourners filed past the body of the Pandit Motilal Nehru Friday as the nationalist leader lay in state at the central hall here. Nehru, founder of the Swaraj (Nationalist) party, president of the All-India National Congress, and one of the most prominent leaders in the Mahatma M. K. Gandhi's campaign of civil disobedience, died at 6:40 a.m. A procession passed through the main streets later as Nehru's body was conveyed to Allahabad in a motor hearse. Cremation will take place there Saturday. Pandit is a high Indian title.

Napier, N. Z, Feb. 6 (Friday) (P)—Leaving an estimated 1,000 dead behind them, the surviving inhabitants of the New Zealand quake zone fled in great haste today as additional earth tremors continued to shake devastated Napier and nearby cities. Under martial law, the region was patrolled by armed marines to prevent looting and to see that nothing hampered the ceaseless toil of rescue workers seeking survivors among the wreckage left by Tuesday's great quake. No serious damage was done by the recurrent quakes today, but survivors were further terrified when an especially heavy shock raised the sea bed four feet at the Napier jetty.

LUCKNOW, India, Feb. 6.—(UP)—The Pandit Motilal Nehru, disciple of Mahatma Gandhi and one of the most influential of India’s national leaders, died here at 6:40 a.m. today. Nehru founded the swaraj (nationalist) party and was president of the All India National Congress. The Mahatma M. K. Gandhi motored here from Allahabad with him two days ago, in order that Nehru might receive special treatment. Motilal Nehru was 69 years old. Like other Indian leaders, he served a prison term for his activities in Gandhi's civil disobedience campaign, considered illegal by the British government. He had been ill for some time. One of Gandhi's first acts when he reached Bombay from Poona jail was to telegraph to Allahabad regarding Nehru's health. Gandhi proceeded to Allahabad from Bombay and motored immediately to the pandit’s bedside. Pandit is a high Indian title.

She rHnaLIOnNAl Ne@Wws Service) SYDNEY, Australia, Feb. 6.— Cloudbursts, floods and landslides today had caused extensive damage and much suffering in Queensland and New South Wales. It is feared that several persons have been drowned. Thousands are homeless, all they possessed in the world having been washed away by floods or carried away by resultant landslides. Brisbane, where 16 inches of rain have fallen during the past 24 hours is virtually isolated. Suburbs of that city resemble lakes. The water level of many streams in the district is from 40 to 80 feet above normal. Hundreds of acres of land are covered with 20 feet of water. Government agencies are supplying food to the homeless and destitute.
Lucknow, United Provinces, India, Feb. 6 (Friday), (4).—Pandit Moltilal Nehru, veteran Indian nationalist and friend of Mahatma Gandhi died this morning. He had been ill for some time.

NAPIER, New Zealand, Feb. 6, (Pi)—"Give me a drink," was the only remark of a boy rescued today from the ruins of the Technical school, which had imprisoned him since the earthquake Tuesday. After getting his drink of water he started to search for his parents, about whose fate he had been thinking during the three long days he lay buried in the debris.

Rome, Feb. 6.—Michele Schirru, arrested Tuesday night for possession of firearms and explosives, confessed today, police said, that he had planned an attempt on the life of Premier Mussolini. He had brought two high explosive bombs here for that purpose, police said he had told them. Bombs were found in hotel rooms which he occupied, police said. Schirru was arrested after a gunfight with police and there were rumors at the time that he had planned an attempt on Mussolini’s life but these were denied by the authorities. The police said Schirru drew a revolver while he was being searched at the police station, wounded three men and attempted suicide, inflicting a serious wound in his head. Police said Schirru was born in Sardinia and was a naturalized citizen of the United States. He will be tried by a special tribunal under the defense of the state act which provides a death penalty for

TOKYO Feb 6—(P)—The flash of a dagger in an ante-room of the Japanese house of representatives today precipitated a fight in which about a dozen persons, two of them members of the diet, were injured. Pent-up political feelings between the opposition and the government was unleashed in the ensuing melee, in which ash trays and other available objects were hurled. Police said several persons received cuts on their heads and hands. Still others were cut and bruised by crashing glass and flying clubs. A meeting of the budget committee, at which the trouble started, broke up in disorder. For two days opposition tactics had blocked budget discussions and on several occasions there had been near riots. The man who flourished the dagger was a member of the reiyukai (opposition) party but not a member of the diet. Police detained him.

The siren call of opportunity, the pot of gold at the gusher’s mouth, the glamour of klieg lights and bright sunshine inviting harried men with graying hair have set state legislative jig-saws awaiting this winter to cut out a new congressional map of the United States. Mostly it is a few of the lustier youngsters of Uncle Sam's family grown in the last ten years on the lay of changing times, making it necessary to alter the representation of 32 states in the national house of representatives. The 1930 census takers found that things had been happening in 10 years. Southern California, once a desert, had become a thickly populated part of the United States. Big Cities Grow Rapidly Detroit, New York and Chicago, where machinery groans and dollars ring, had won many another lad from the milking school. By and large the legislators don't like their job of deciding how to distribute the gain

ROME, Feb. 6—(UP)—Frustration of a plot for the assassination of Premier Mussolini was announced today by police who questioned the anarchist, Michele Schirru. The Rome Ministry said Schirru, who was arrested Tuesday after coming here on an Argentine passport and being under surveillance for months, conceived the idea of attacking the Fascist Premier and other high government officials in Paris last summer. Later he purchased bombs and explosives at Liege. He confessed to police that he came here with the idea of attacking the Premier and that he had been inclined toward Anarchy since boyhood.

| PORTO, Fed, — Vagger play broke up a budget committee meeting in the antechamber of the house of representatives today and in the ensuing melee about a dozen persons, including two members of the diet, were injured. Ash trays and other articles were thrown in the fight. | Police reported several persons suffered cuts on their heads and hands and others received bruises from clubs and cuts from crashing glass. The skirmish started when the opposition launched an effort to unseat the Minseito (majority party) ministry with attacks on Baron Shidehara, foreign minister, who has been acting head of the government since the wounding of Premier Hama-euch by an alleged fanatic several weeks ago.

ROME, Feb. 5.—(7—Discovery of high explosive bombs in the baggage of Michele Schirru, said to be a naturalized American citizen, convinced police today of the existence of what was described as an important terrorist plot. Schirru fired at policemen when he was being questioned after his arrest Tuesday night and this gave rise to wild rumors a plot against the life of Premier Mussolini had been discovered. Police promptly denied the rumors. Schirru turned an automatic pistol on three policemen and then shot himself through the head. This evening he was too weak to be questioned effectively. One of his victims, the vice commissary of police, Pasquale Clani, may die.

1931-02-14.text: London, Feb. 13,—(AP)—Nancy 'Lady Astor laid about with the rapier of her repartee in the House of Commons today, fighting the battle of temperance, but she voted with the majority in defeating a prohibition bill by 137 to 18. The bill was introduced by Edwin Scrymgeour, member for Dundee, who has spent years trying to prohibit alcoholic beverages in the United Kingdom. Lady Astor sent home telling thrusts against the liquor interests, but even so declared her intention of voting against the measure in the belief that temperance and not prohibition is the cure for whatever liquor evils there may be. The Horrible Example Both sides cited the United States, proponents of the repeal as a guiding light, and the others as a horrible example under prohibition. Lady Astor referred to the peerage as the "beerage."

Napier, N. 7.—M— Severe earth shocks, which rocked the Hawkes Bay district at noon Friday, did considerable damage in the town, already virtually destroyed by quakes of a week ago. Wallis left standing in the ruined business area fell, inflicting minor injuries on workers. All further work of clearing the town was halted. There were many narrow escapes as returning residents leaped from beneath tottering masonry. The coast to the south of the town was hidden in clouds of dust.

LONDON, Feb. 14 (.-Sir Laming-ton-Worthington Evans, Bart. secretary of state for war in two conservative cabinets, died in his sleep early today. He was 63 years old, Sir Laming-ton had a distinguished political career and was one of the mainstays in the high councils of the conservative party. He had not been well lately, but his death came unexpectedly.

LONDON, Feb. 18—(AP) The House of Commons, by a vote of 137 to 18 today rejected the bill which would have prohibited the use of alcoholic liquors as beverages throughout the United Kingdom. Lady Nancy Astor, Virginia's contribution to the British House of Commons, had members of that August body alternately laughing and gnashing, when she took the floor in debate on the bill. Lady Astor in a slashing and sometimes vitriolic speech, made it clear that she is against liquor, but did not believe in tackling the problem in the way suggested in the bill. The debate arose on the second reading of the measure introduced by Edwin Scrymgeour, prohibition member from Scotland. Lady Astor protested when the conservative, Sir William Wayland, said Americans were drinking more under prohibition than before. She said she could not vote for the bill because if she voted for prohibition she would not b

LONDON, Feb. 14.—Anthony Hall today served notice on King George to get off the throne so that Hall himself could rule Great Britain. Addressing his majesty as Mr. George Frederick Ernest Albert Windsor, Hall who asserts that he is descended from Tudor kings, set forth his claims in a ten-page clumsily-written foolscap letter, ending with the blunt order to the king to abdicate in his favor. He did say, however, that he intended to have no civil war over the succession. Hall outlined his plans for the reconstruction of Great Britain, including the redemption of the national debt of 7,630,000,000 pounds, the expenditure of 5,000,000 pounds in 20 years for the relief of the unemployed, the return to pre-war strength of British beer and the rebuilding of London to accommodate 160,000,000 inhabitants.

LONDON, Feb. 24. (GINS) - A manifesto "giving notice" to King George of England to vacate his throne and leave the country has been served by Anthony Hall, who claims direct descent from Henry VII, first of the Tudor kings, according to the Daily Herald account today. Hall, in the manifesto published by the Herald, proceeds to prove his right to the throne by a devious route. He gave his age as 51, and as his first policy change in taking over the throne promised to have beer brewed again at full strength. The newspaper quotes Hall further as saying: --- "I claim the crown. I am of the male line directly descended from the last prince to win the crown on the field of battle—Henry Tudor. "My intention is not one of civil war over this matter. You have no connection with the British royal family; you are an outsider, therefore leave the country!"

MADRID, FEB. 14. (AP).—The government of Premier General Damaso Berenguer, successor to the Primo de Rivera dictatorship, fell today, bringing to a head a crisis which appeared to be the most dangerous of any faced by King Alfonso in the course of his long reign. The King, accepting the resignation of General Berenguer and his cabinet, cancelled the parliamentary elections which were scheduled for March 1 and 15 and immediately began conferring with political leaders with a view to formation of a new cabinet. The situation which brought the fall of the cabinet developed only late last night when the Count of Romanones and other important Liberal monarchist leaders withdrew their support of the cabinet elections program.

Madrid, Feb. 14—(UP)—After years of dictatorship, martial law and rebellion, Spain appeared today to be moving toward a Republican form of government with such rapidity that the political victors themselves were uncertain what the next move in the constitutional affairs of the country would be. Within the space of a few hours the government of Premier Gen. Damaso Berenguer resigned and the king received a decree suspending the parliamentary elections scheduled for next month. The next logical development appeared to be the convocation of a constitutional assembly to draft a constitution replacing that of 1876, under which the country still is governed. The king signed the decree suspending the scheduled March elections. King Alfonso began consultations immediately after the cabinet’s resignation with leaders of the Liberal party, who forced Berenguer’s resignation, and also with the Duke

HARBIN, Manchuria, Feb. 14.— (7) —With the mercury falling as low as 45 degrees below zero, this city is experiencing one of the coldest winters in many years. More than 1,000 persons have frozen to death on the streets. In northern sections of the country, especially along the Siberian and Manchurian border, the cold has been even more severe. Although the snow is not unusually heavy for this part of the world, the intense cold has caused trains on most lines to run two and three days behind time. Several major accidents have been reported along the Chinese Eastern Railway and in one case a train left the tracks when the locomotive wheels froze and cracked. Several instances have been reported where men and women leaving cabarets in intoxicated conditions have fallen into the streets and frozen to death in a short time.

ADRID, Feb. 14.—(UP)—King Alfonso XIII accepted the resignation of the cabinet of Premier Gen. Damaso Berenguer today. The resignation of the cabinet followed the decision of the Liberal party not to collaborate in the work of the Parliament which Berenguer had planned to elect in March. Count Romanones, Liberal leader, said that his party would keep its promise to participate in the elections, but that the Liberals would withdraw from Parliament unless a constitutional convention was called. Socialists and Republicans had announced their decision to boycott the elections. Count Romanones, it was understood, informed King Alfonso that it was impossible to disregard this attitude on the part of important political elements. It was expected that a concentration government would be formed to convoke a constitutional convention. Opponents of the government's election plans held that the cons

| MADRID, FAD. 14—(A)—(SATURDAY)—(4)—Count Romanones, Liberal Monarchist leader, announced after a midnight interview with Premier Damasco Berenguer, the premier had told him his cabinet would resign today, in view of the grave situation of Spain both economically and politically. Count Romanones said he told the premier he and the Marquis of Albucemas, another powerful Liberal leader, would participate in the March elections solely that they might ask the dissolution of parliament and the convocation of a constitutional convention. The Liberal Monarchists have hitherto supported the government’s election program and the decision of the two leaders represented a complete change in attitude. The expected resignation of the ministry, Count Romanones said, would give King Alfonso a free hand to call a concentration cabinet of the leaders of all the Monarchist parties. This cabinet would be

Madrid, Feb. 14.—(L N. S.)—The government of Spain, unsettled since King Alfonso dissolved parliament and sponsored a military dictatorship in 1923, entered upon an entirely new phase today when Premier Damaso Berenguer and his cabinet resigned from office. The action marked the end of his directory rule in this country and the way for a succession of events which are expected to decide the fate of the Spanish monarchy. The resignation resulted from Premier Berenguer’s realization that the forthcoming general elections would fail to create a representative Cortes, owing to the non-participation of the majority of political parties. Demands Dissolution. The final blow to the Berenguer regime was given in a statement by Count de Romanones, former premier and liberal monarchist, following a midnight conference with the cabinet. Count de Romanones clarified his position by stating he would p

By United Press MADRID, Feb. 14——Count Romanones telephoned to Cartagena today and asked Admiral Aznar, captain general of the navy, to come to Madrid. It was believed possible that the admiral would be asked to form a new cabinet.

1931-01-03.text: LONDON, Jan. 2—(4)—General astonishment has been aroused in Great Britain by the departure of Miss Amy Johnson, 23-year-old aviator, on a long lone flight across snow-covered northern Eurasia to Peiping, China. Leaving Hendon airdrome yesterday forenoon, she stopped at Lympne momentarily and proceeded to Liege, Belgium, for the night. She expects to continue to Berlin, then to Moscow, where, equipping her plane with skis, she will fly across barren Byark and to Peiping. In addition to general fear for her safety in view of the extreme hazards of such a journey, her friends were represented today as feeling considerable anxiety on account of her health. The Daily Express said she was in ill health and had become a neurotic from the strain of her flight to Australia. The Soviet embassy in London told the Daily Herald that such a flight as she contemplated would be difficult and she must be

Summoned tonight, negotiations be- tween the employers’ and weavers’ representatives broke down on the question of “more looms per weaver” demanded by the employers. Since leaders of the workers already have declared they will call out employees from any mill where this system is worked on Monday, the outlook was considered black tonight. Pin Hopes on Meeting. Cardiff, Wales, Jan. 2. (7) — In little chapels scattered through the grimy valleys of South Wales, men and women spent today praying that some way may be found to end the dispute between masters and men which sent 140,000 coal miners into idleness yesterday. They pinned their hopes on a meeting tomorrow of the coal conciliation board from which might come a compromise ending the strike, few days more of which would bring misery and want to tens of thousands. The women knew that theirs would be the heaviest burden. They knew alread

Manchester, Eng., Jan. 2.—A great stoppage of work in the Lancashire cotton industry, affecting 200,000 men, tonight threatened to add to the gloom into which the new year has already been plunged by the coal dispute in South Wales. At a special meeting between members of the Cotton Spinners and Manufacturers Association and the Weavers’ Amalgamation, hurriedly summoned tonight, negotiations between the employers’ and weavers’ representatives broke down on the question of “more looms per weaver” demanded by the employers. Since leaders of the workers already have declared they will call out employees from any mill where this system is worked on Monday, the outlook was considered black tonight.

Vancouver, B. C., Jan. 2.—-(4)— The Vancouver Province today said a “very interesting and stupendous plan is being discussed in London, New York, Washington and Ottawa for the rehabilitation of silver and the general reorganization of oriental trade and markets. “Generally,” the Province states, “the plan is to call together the five or six leading war lords of China, who presently are fighting among themselves. The project is to ‘sell’ the Chinese leaders the idea that everyone would be infinitely better off if the Chinese armies were turned into industrial units, carrying out great public works. Loan Suggested “If a semblance of peace can thus be attained, then Britain and the United States would jointly arrange a loan of a thousand million dollars to be spent in opening China by railways and highways and by lending support to various schemes to bring about an era of orderly civilizati

London, Jan. 3 — The London Daily Express featured an announcement today that it will start the serial publication of a book called “The Strange Death of President Harding,” commencing next Monday. The editor of the Daily Express said he was unaware of any State Department negotiations to suppress it.

Carlisle, Scotland, Jan. 3,—Many persons were feared killed and today when the Edinburgh to London express became derailed and crashed into an embankment on the outskirts of Carlisle. Three coaches were telescoped by the crash. All available doctors and nurses were rushed to the scene. The derailed train was the noon express from Edinburgh. Packed with travelers planning a weekend in London, the engine left the rails and ploughed down the embankment, dragging two coaches and a dining car with it.

PARIS, Jan. 2.—(AP)—Marshal Joffre, deep in a coma from which his physicians did not expect him to awake, remained alive today, one of them indicated, through injections of serum. Dr. Boulin, meeting newspaper men outside the hospital of St. Jean De Dieu, said: “The final coma which will take the marshal can be foreseen from a half to three-quarters of an hour in advance by acceleration of the pulse, which has been 140 since yesterday. “The patient remains unconscious. Heavy doses of a serum are being injected which should permit the es, to pass today and perhaps At 11 a.m. yesterday the old soldier, whose 79th birthday is only a few days away, lapsed into a deep unconsciousness which was described by those present as much more like sleep than the apparently final stage of an illness which the marshal has had with all the obstinacy of his being. Since then he lay perfectly still, an arm

| Paris, Jan. 2.—Marshal Joffre’s life ebbed slowly away tonight as he lay in the coma into which he sank yesterday morning, but the sturdy heart beat on and his doctors could only await the inevitable end. His wound was healing where they amputated his leg, there were no complications, but the old soldier was growing weaker every hour. Can't Last The doctors said they had been administering stimulants at intervals for hours but that this could not go on indefinitely. Already it had lasted much longer than they had expected.

PARIS, Jan. 3 (AP)—Marshal Joffre will be buried in a national funeral as elaborate as that tendered his illustrious colleague, Marshal Foch, but his body will not lie in state under the Arc de Triomphe, for the Marshal himself had said he did not wish to be the cause of his troops and the people of Paris risking their health in the Paris winter to do him honor. Throughout Paris and all of France today the flags over public buildings fluttered at half staff.

| COLOGNE, Germany, Jan. 3. (P)— Miss Amy Johnson, British girl aviator, who took off from here for Berlin at 11:05 a. m. today on the next stage of her flight from England to Peiping, China. Her route lies over Russia, Siberia and Mongolia and is particularly hazardous at this time of the year.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 3—The British gunboat Mantis, on patrol duty in the Yangtze Kiang, was attacked today by 800 insurgent troops who opened a heavy fire upon her. The Mantis replied with great effect, inflicting many casualties. There were no casualties aboard the Mantis.

BERLIN, Jan. 3 (AP)—Miss Amy Johnson, British woman flier, landed at Tempelhof airdrome near here at 5:34 p. m., today after a flight from Cologne. She is attempting to fly from England to Peiping, China. Miss Johnson drifted clear off her course northward to Leubz, near Parchim, in Mecklenburgh-Schwerin, where she was compelled to make a forced landing. After ascertaining her whereabouts she again took off and reached Berlin without incident.
GLARUS, Switzerland, Jan. 3. — A party of 15 German skiers was swept away by an avalanche on a mountain slope, near Elm. Thirteen of the party were killed and two were rescued.

PARIS, Jan. 3 (UP).—Joseph Jacques Cesare Joffre, marshal of France and commander-in-chief of her forces in the World War, died today at the age of 78 years. The end came at 8:23 a.m., an official bulletin said. Joffre’s condition took a critical turn shortly after 7 o’clock this morning, when members of his general staff were summoned to the hospital. Doctors said then that he was still breathing, although his pulse beat was imperceptible. The cause of death was given as complete exhaustion of heart, body and resources due to the effects of gangrene which followed arteriosclerosis.
ROM, Jan. 3.—The squadron of twelve Italian seaplanes which are preparing at Bolama, Portuguese Guiana, for a trans-Atlantic flight to Rio De Janeiro, will take off Monday for Port Natal, Brazil.

PARIS, Jan. 3--Marshall Joseph Jacques Casaire Joffre, hero of the Marne and commander-in-chief of the French army during the first two years of the war, died at the clinic of St. Jean De Dieu at 3:25 a.m. eastern standard time, today. Captain Saint Sernin of the Marshal's headquarters staff made the announcement to the assembled journalists in the vestibule of the clinic. “At the warrior’s bedside in his final moments were Madam Joffre and the immediate family; as well. In leaving the death chamber shortly after, Dr. Leriche, Joffre's chief physician, declared that the marshal passed away without regaining consciousness. “When the amputation was performed on Dec. 19, the marshal was completely lucid, although in great agony,” Dr. Leriche said. “He fell into a coma on the 26th of December at 8 p.m.” “He regained consciousness for five and 19 minute periods intermittently. He died painles

1931-02-26.text: Wellington, New Zealand, Feb. 26,—(AP)—More than 180 persons were killed in the Ba and Singatoka districts of the Fiji islands in the worst hurricane and flood there in recent years, members of the crew of a government ship reported on their arrival at Suva, Fiji islands, today. The hurricane, which occurred a few days ago, was reported to have blown a train off the rails at Lautoka, causing many casualties. The lighthouse at Nadi was blown away. The hurricane was felt along only a narrow strip of territory, outside of which the country was unaffected.

| MELBOURNE, Feb. 26. — (UP) — Dame Nellie Melba, famous Australian singer, whose voice was heard throughout the world, was buried today in the most impressive funeral service in Melbourne's history. The entire city was hushed as the funeral procession passed through the city’s streets. Prior to burial, thousands filed past the flag-draped coffin lying in state at the Scottish church.

Melbourne, Australia, Feb. 26.— | ()—The body of Dame Nellie Melba was laid to rest today by the side of that of her father in the cemetery of the little village of Lilydale, near the home she loved. The usually busy streets of Melbourne were hushed and lined with sorrowing crowds when the casket was taken on a farm cart from the Presbyterian church, where thousands had filed past the bier, paying their last respects to the famous singer. The church, where the diva as a girl sang in the choir, was full to overflowing for the funeral service, which was attended by representatives of federal and state governments and of the world of music and art. Dame Nellie Melba died Monday evening after a strange lingering illness, designated in a posthumous diagnosis as paratyphoid.

Naples, Italy, Feb. 26.—(AP)—The southwestern Italian coast was ravaged today by a storm which has raged over Sicily for the past four or five days. Shipping was hard hit and some loss of life ashore was feared. The coastal cattle boat, Schiatfino, which was loading cattle here, was left in a sinking condition after being struck by a giant wave. A smaller fishing craft capsized off the shore of Catania and three of its crew were lost.

OLDENBURG, Germany, Feb. 24. (AP)—The former Grandduke Friedrich August of Oldenburg died today at the age of 78. The Grandduke abdicated Nov. 11, 1918, when a body of revolutionary sailors from Wilhelmshaven told him that the time for royalty in Germany had passed.

1931-01-13.text: LONDON, Jan. 13. (AP)—A combination of characteristics of the American and British parliamentary system is the plan of the Indian round table conference, which adjourns Monday, for a future government for India. The plan, evolved by the federal committee of the conference after weeks of labor, was presented substantially to the meeting yesterday by Lord Chancellor Sankey. It virtually outlines a dominion status for India, but must be accepted by parliament before it can become effective. There are to be two legislative houses, the upper one of which Lord Sankey called the “Senate.” It is to have probably 100 members, who will hold office for overlapping terms, so that its entire membership never will be new. The lower house, either a house of representatives or chamber, will have 250 members, elected for five years after the manner of members of the British House of Commons at a general

Horta, Azores, Jan. 12. ()—Hope that the transatlantic “payload” aviators, Mrs. Beryl Hart and Lieutenant William S. MacLaren, were still alive was virtually abandoned tonight. Not a word or a sign of them had been received since they took off from Hamilton, Bermuda, at 11:15 a.m., (e.s.t.) Saturday for Horta on the second lap of their flight in the monoplane Tradewind from New York to Paris. Strong winds and high seas have prevailed since that time and it was feared that had they been forced down their frail machine could have withstood the seas only a few minutes. They had expected to take 21 hours for the flight and were due at 8:15 a.m., (e.s.t.) Sunday morning. Tonight, indicative of the fear that they were lost, gasoline supplies which had been kept on a scow in the harbor in readiness for refueling were withdrawn. There was still a possibility they had been forced to come down nea
MOSCOW, Jan. 14. — Amy Johnson, British aviatrix, left for Warsaw to fly back to London. She has abandoned her solo flight across Siberia to Peking.

TOKYO, Jan. 18—-(AP)—Reports of the movement of Russian troops toward the western frontier of Manchuria reached official circles here today. The military movement was described as being due to Moscow's belief China may not abide by the Khabarovsk agreement of 1929 giving Russia virtual control of the Chinese Eastern Railway, which connects Vladivostok with the Trans-Siberian Railway by crossing Manchuria. Manchurian troops also were reported concentrating near the Russian frontier. Neither of these reports could be confirmed.

1931-02-18.text: NEW DELHI, India. — (P) — Mahatma Gandhi and Lord Irwin, the viceroy of India, talked together for three hours Wednesday afternoon, seeking a way out of India's political difficulties. Gandhi appeared cheerful as he left the viceregal palace, remarking “the issues are still in the clouds. I am not coming back tomorrow.” The Mahatma will consult with other leaders of the Indian Congress party and within the next few days will resume his conversations with the viceroy.

New Delhi, India, Feb. 17. — Mahatma Gandhi and the Viceroy of India, the two men who personify the clashing principles at the bottom of all of India’s troubles, talked over their differences for four hours today and when Gandhi left the vice regal palace he said he was satisfied, even optimistic. Neither said much about what had passed between them. But it was obvious from Gandhi's cheerful manner that the meeting had been satisfactory to him. The conditions of a settlement outlined by the viceroy yesterday to some of his intimates, included the granting of nearly all demands if he will call off the civil disobedience campaign and cooperate in working out a constitution — Macdonald's declaration at the end of the London round table conference.

Melbourne, Australia. Feb. 18. 1—Relatives of Dame Nellie Melba were summoned to her bedside today when the famous opera singer lost strength after an illness of several weeks. Melba was unable to leave her steamer when she arrived in Australia from England, suffering, it was said, from a skin disease.

2 - MADRID, Feb. 17 (#)—A new political crisis, in which loomed the threat of a military dictatorship, was thrust upon Spain today with the failure of Jose Antonio Sanchez Guerra to form a government on a basis of liberal constitutional revision. Sanchez Guerra, designated by King Alfonso yesterday to get together a cabinet, went to the palace at noon today and informed the king that he had been unable to secure the collaboration of the Republicans and Socialists, radical Left groups, and would have to renounce his task. He advised the king to call upon Melquiades Alvarez, another advocate of constitutional revision to limit the powers of the throne, and leader of the “Reformist” group of the Spanish Conservative party. Alvarez, if anything, would be regarded as more radical than Sanchez Guerra, whose designation by the king yesterday was regarded by Monarchists as a surrender to the Ext

Madrid, Spain, Feb. 18—/P— After four days of political turmoil and uncertainty, Spain today had a new monarchist cabinet, avoiding revolution on the one hand and dictatorship on the other. Either of those possibilities had seemed imminent but now it is believed that the tense atmosphere of the past week will be cleared and that the situation is once more tranquil, at least for the time being. The fundamental causes of all the trouble of the past year still exist however, and opposition to the monarchy probably will be renewed when the time is right. Admiral Juan Bautista Aznar, the oldest officer in the Spanish navy and generally regarded as a neutral in politics succeeded where Jose Sanchez Guerra and Melquiades Alvarez had failed. This afternoon he brought a new cabinet to the royal palace and its members were sworn in before the king. It includes General Berenguer, the admiral’s pred

MADRID (U.P) — Admiral Juan Bautista Aznar Y Cabanas became premier of Spain Wednesday, taking the oath of office at the head of a monarchical concentration government. After more than four days of the most serious government crisis during the reign of King Alfonso XIII, the 70-year-old captain general of the navy was suddenly called to the premiership to safeguard the throne against threats of republican upheaval and demands for far-reaching restrictions on the monarch. Within less than three hours Admiral Aznar completed the task which the most influential liberal politicians in Spain had failed to accomplish. The monarchical concentration cabinet will work for parliamentary government as well as a constitutional convention to revise the constitution of 1876, but without such stringent restrictions on the king’s power as proposed by the constitutionalists and liberals who failed to for
ISTANBUL, Feb. 18--(4)—Seven peasants were buried alive in a snow avalanche in the mountains of Eastern Turkey, near Malatia, rescuers finding the bodies. Others are feared lost in the blizzard.

Tokio, Feb. 18 (UP)—Three Japanese naval aviators were killed and the auditorium of an agricultural school was destroyed when a naval seaplane caught fire and crashed in Shizuoka prefecture today. The plane was acting as an attacker in practical exercises when it suddenly burst into flames. It fell directly on the school auditorium igniting the structure.

Rome, Italy, Feb. 17.—The crash of the ceiling of the Morgana theatre here and the stampede of the holiday crowd from the darkened building during the showing of a picture today led to more or less serious injuries to 13 persons and slighter hurts to dozens. Panic seized the crowd which filled the house during the celebration of a mardi gras half holiday. Shrieks and groans came from those dashing wildly for the exits. And then above the pandemonium rose the strains of the orchestra, which tried to quiet the confusion by playing royal and fascist airs. Firemen opened all emergency exits and then hacked other openings through which others escaped. The theatre, which combines a playhouse and motion picture house, was dark when the ceiling suddenly tumbled down on the startled men, women, and children. In a minute the crowd had left their seats and was rushing towards the exits and trying t

MADRID, Feb. 18—Dr. Julio Wais, finance minister in the government of former Premier Damaso Berenguer, announced this morning that a new coalition monarchist government would be formed later today and would be sworn in this afternoon. Dr. Wais’ announcement followed an early morning interview with King Alfonso after representatives of conservative monarchist parties had conferred with General Berenguer for four hours in the ministry of war last night and agreed to support the king.

Madrid, Feb. 18—(INS)—Determined to continue his reign as absolute monarch of Spain, King Alfonso XIII today defied his implacable foes and placed the government of his country in the hands of a royalist group headed by Admiral Juan Bautista Aznar as premier. Admiral Aznar’s cabinet took over the reins of government from the cabinet of General D’Amaso Berenguer this afternoon, after taking the oath of allegiance to the king at the royal palace shortly after noon. Thus ended, at least for the time being, the period of political uncertainty which has existed in Spain since last Saturday when General Berenguer resigned, and which led to reports of possible revolutionary movements, another military dictatorship and even abdication by the king. Clever Politician. In solving the crisis as he did, King Alfonso once again proved himself the most astute politician of them all. Before calling upon
Tokio, Feb. 18, W.e)—Admiral Gentaro Yanashita, high military councillor of Japan, died here today.

ENSCHEDE, Holland, Feb. 18— Somebody broke into the biggest movie theatre in town last night, stole the film, "All Quiet on the Western Front," and burned it in the backyard. Enschede is not far from the German border and hundreds of Germans have crossed the frontier every day to see the picture which is barred in Germany.

PARIS, Feb. — Findings isn’t keepings in Paris. On the contrary, keeping is stealing. The average Parisian hastens to the police with discovered property because there are penalties for not doing so and there is a reward to be paid out of tax on the rightful owner when a lost article is restored.

TOKYO, Feb. 18. Two officers and two pilots and one petty officer were burned to death today when a plane belonging to the Yokosuka naval aviation station burst into flames in midair and crashed on top of the Fujieda agricultural school in Shizuoka prefecture. The plane and school were burned.

1931-02-03.text: AUCKLAND, N. Z., FEB. 3. (AP).—An earthquake and fire leveled the city of Napier, N. Z., today, leaving a casualty list reported at 100 dead and 1,000 injured and wrecked four nearby towns, causing an undetermined number of fatalities and injuries. Napier was still ablaze and virtually helpless tonight, the quake having cut off its water supply. Its stunned populace stood by, unable to count its dead and without effective means of fighting the fire. Dynamite was resorted to in an attempt to check the flames. The first shock came shortly before 11 a. m., shaking a large portion of the coastal region of Hawkes Bay province, of which Napier is the capital. Hastings, a town fifteen miles from Napier, reported 21 dead and 100 injured. The towns of Waikawa and Waipukurau also suffered. Fire from the Napier blaze caused the shutting off of oil tanks at Port Ahuriri. All points reported the casu

London, Feb. 3—The former Helen Vivien Gould, American heiress who as the youthful bride of the fifth Baron Decies dazzled English society, died here at dawn today of a heart attack which developed from jaundice. She was 39 years old and had been ill three weeks. Death came in a London nursing home. Besides her husband, who has had a famous career in the army, she left three children, a son and two daughters. The granddaughter of Jay Gould, whose railroad manipulations made him a money king of the post-Civil War period, Lady Decies came to be known in England for the spectacles she sometimes presented society, her penchant for the unexpected and as a lavish charming hostess.

Auckland, New Zealand, Feb. 4.—(Wednesday)—The broadly curved eastern coast of North Island, which was rocked near Hawks Bay by a devastating earthquake early Tuesday, was shaken again at midnight by new tremors which were less violent. The new tremors, which occurred at intervals, hampered the feverish work of rescue in the stricken district around Napier, where semi-official advices reported 100 dead, and Hastings, where The earthquake which caused a twisting or shifting of certain undersea regions along the coast and was reported to have raised the harbor floor at Napier 138 feet and wrecked most of the business buildings at Napier and Hastings. Tidal waves and fire added to the many millions of dollars of damage. At Hastings 16 employees were still trapped in a store building which was demolished. One man was extricated uninjured after nine hours of work, but the new tremors hindered

WELLINGTON, N. Z., Feb. 4.—(@)—Three towns were in ruins today, more than 100 persons were dead and upwards of 1,000 injured, as the result of one of the most terrible earthquakes that ever struck New Zealand. It began on North Island early yesterday, bringing stone and brick buildings toppling about the heads of their occupants and pedestrians in the streets, and setting fire to hundreds of frame structures. Then the water supply, wrecked by the shocks, gave out and the firemen were helpless, none. In a series of recurring shocks, the seaport of Napier was laid waste, the flourishing town of Hastings 12 miles away was devastated and buildings came tumbling down by the dozen in the town of Wairoa. The shocks were still continuing today and the population was stunned and helpless in the face of the disaster. Oil tanks exploded and spread flaming horror through Napier. In that city alone t

WELLINGTON, New Zealand. Feb. 3.—A terrific earthquake which rocked Napier, a city of 14,348 population on the west coast of North Island, at 8:51 o'clock this morning reports of great loss of life. Messages broadcast by his majesty's sloop Veronica said that a great toll was feared and that some deaths were certain, although it gave no figure. The ship’s messages indicated that nearly every stone building in the town was destroyed. Fires were raging in the center of the city. A man who witnessed the quake in Napier rushed to Dannevirke, an island town about 70 miles southwest of the stricken city, and telephoned to Wellington that the loss of life must have been considerable. He said he saw long lines of casualties in the town, which looked as if it had undergone a great bombardment. All the large buildings in the center of the town were razed and the post office was largely in ruins. T

CHATHAM, Eng., Feb. 3.—(AP)— Six men were injured, one critically, when an explosion of undetermined origin wrecked the internal combustion engine of the submarine V-1, one of the largest undersea boats in the British navy, today. She had left Sheerness for a trial run after reconditioning and had gone 20 miles on the surface to the Thames estuary when the blast occurred.

The damage was summarized as follows: Napier, east coast town with a population of over 11,000, reported practically razed; fire followed earthquake; high tumbling into sea; general hospital reported buried in landslide; harbor bottom believed raised permanently; ships fled to open sea to escape being stranded in suddenly decreasing water. Hastings, a few miles inland, southwest of Napier, officially stated twenty-one won; Gisborne, on the east coast, about 100 miles north of Napier, almost every building damaged, fatalities undetermined.
