AUCKLAND (WP) — Semi-official wireless advices received Tuesday said 100 persons had been killed at Napier in the earthquake which devastated that district. About 1,000 others were injured.

Wellington, N. Z., Feb. 3. (P)— Heavy loss of life which probably will run into the hundreds was caused by a terrific earthquake which struck North Island, New Zealand, early today. The business area of the town of Hastings, 12 miles southwest of Napier, was devastated by the quake and a conflagration which followed. Several persons were killed in the collapse of the Roach building, and five women died when an apartment house fell in about them. At Hastings the death toll will probably be more than 100. The known dead there numbered 21. Smaller communities suffered proportionately. Hospital Collapses. Napier, a city of about 15,000 on Hawkes Bay, was believed to have (Continued on Page Five.)

WELLINGTON, Feb. 3 — At least 126 persons were known to have lost their lives and more than 1,000 were injured in a disastrous earthquake which devastated the city of Napier and rocked all of North Island, New Zealand, yesterday. A check-up of the casualties almost twenty-four hours after the tremblor, which was followed by tidal waves and landslides, occurred, showed more than 100 dead in Napier, ten known dead in Hastings and several others in various cities of the island. Care of the injured is seriously hampered by the fact that all the nurses attached to the city's chief hospital are understood to have been killed when their three-story home adjoining the hospital collapsed with the hospital. According to other dispatches to the evening newspapers here, thousands of frightened inhabitants of towns like Hawke Bay are packing the beaches. Food is being distributed to them from small b

LONDON, Feb. 3.—Lady Decies, the former Helen Vivien Gould, daughter of the late George Jay Gould of New York, died here today following a brief illness. She had been suffering from heart trouble for the past few weeks but her condition did not arouse any anxiety until yesterday when she was transferred from her home to a London nursing home. Last night it was announced that she was dangerously ill. The end came today when her heart suddenly collapsed. Lady Decies is survived by her husband, the fifth Baron Decies, one son and two daughters. Lord Decies was former press censor for Ireland and aide to the Duke of Connaught. They were married in 1911. Lady Decies was only 38 years old. At the time of her marriage to Lord Decies in New York she was just 19. She was the fourth child of the late George Jay Gould.

AUCKLAND, New Zealand, Feb. 3 4UP)—The town of Napier, on North Island, New Zealand, was in ruins today, devastated by a terrific earthquake, landslides, fire and a tidal wave. It was estimated that 100 persons were killed by the earthquake at Hastings, inland and a few miles southwest of Napier. The loss of life at Napier was still undetermined, but it was feared that it would be high. Part of a cliff 390 feet high at Napier fell into the sea, carrying with it many dwellings. A private hospital was buried in a landslide and it was feared that nurses and patients were crushed. Part of the Napier public hospital was wrecked. Many nurses and patients were reported missing. Fire broke out in the doomed city and was fed by broken oil tanks. The steamship Northumberland, in Napier Bay, reported by wireless that the entire town back of the promenade appeared to be in flames as landslides occur

Wellington, New Zealand, Feb. 3. (Tuesday) — A violent earthquake which struck the city of Napier at 8:51 a.m. today knocked down many buildings, started numerous fires and apparently caused thousands to be homeless. The destruction was particularly severe in the neighborhood of Napier, where oil tanks were set afire and many houses collapsed. The shocks were recorded in Riverview observatory here, lasting two hours. They were considered the worst since June 17, 1929, when great damage was done in the Karamea region, on the west coast of South Island. Landslides extended for miles and the region was cut off from the outside world, while the ocean bed at the White Cliffs of Karamea was reported to have risen nearly 100 feet over a distance of about a mile. Hundreds of homes in outlying districts were destroyed then and in some places entire towns were evacuated. The quake was felt over th

CHATHAM, England, Feb. 3. — (INS) — One member of the crew was badly burned and others suffered from shock following an explosion aboard the British submarine X-1 during trials in the Thames estuary today. The X-1 was able to proceed to the Chatham naval base under her own power after the blast occurred.

By Associated Press. London, Feb. 1 - One man was seriously burned and several others injured today in an explosion on the submarine XN-J, during maneuvers in the Thames estuary. The Admiralty said it believed the explosion was not serious. Details are scant.

MMmUNEMIEEN, Turkey, Feb. 20. (AP) —The bodies of 28 Turkish moslem reactionaries swung from gibbets in the cold Balkan wind today in a storm warning from the republic that the days of the caliphate have passed forever. Singly and in some cases by groups, the condemned men, convicted of leading an abortive revolutionary movement here Dec. 23, were led at dawn from their cells to the gallows, where gypsy hangmen, western caps oddly topping baggy Turkish trousers and scarlet sashes, swung them aloft. Because of the martial law which has been in effect since the revolt, citizens were kept in their homes until 8 a.m. and there were almost no witnesses to the executions beyond a few officials. An occasional scream could be heard from women peeping from behind shuttered windows, however, and with the advance of day, shuddering crowds passed the gruesome scene. Perhaps the only cheerful place i

Menemen, Turkey, Dec. 3 (UP)— Bodies of 28 dervishes convicted of plotting a religious revolt swung from 28 gallows here today, pronounced guilty of a crime against the state. They were hanged at dawn. The bodies will swing in public places until tomorrow. Four death sentences have been commuted by the national assembly. The prisoners were brought from their cells where they spent the night weeping and praying, turned over to soldiers, and marched down the streets to their respective gallows in a cold rain. Several youths collapsed before they reached the gallows but the soldiers dragged them through the streets. The older men, bearded sheiks, walked solemnly and upright to their places of execution.

Las Palmas, Canary Islands, Feb. 3—After several attempts to get into the air in continuation of its flight across the Atlantic, officers of the DO-X, giant German seaplane, had suspended their flight today until tomorrow. The plane taxied yesterday from near Los Palmas to Bahia, Gando but even there the water was too rough today for the take-off.

LAS PALMAS, Canary Islands, Feb. 3—The German flying boat, DO-X flight to Cape Verde Islands was postponed today due to temporary motor trouble. The Do-X started maneuvers for departure on its flight, but the motor trouble forced the delay. The trouble was repaired at 8:26 A.M., which officials considered too late to permit the ship, which is at Gando Bay, 25 miles from Las Palmas, to reach Cape Verde before dusk. Later, the right pontoon of the DO-X was damaged when the plane was returning from Gando Bay to Las Palmas, navigating on the surface of the water. Officials said the extent of damage was uncertain, but that the date of departure was indefinite until it was determined how much time would be required to repair the ship.

By The Associated Press. Madrid, Spain, Feb. 2.—The giant German seaplane DO-X lay anchored in Gando bay near Las Palmas, Canary Islands, tonight, preparing to hop off for the Cape Verde islands early tomorrow morning should weather and ocean conditions be favorable. Messages received from Las Palmas indicated, however, that a choppy sea might cause difficulties in the takeoff with a heavy load of gasoline, oil and crew. For the flight to the Cape Verde islands, the second leg of a projected journey to Rio de Janeiro, the big flying boat was taking on an additional 1500 gallons of gasoline.

VIENNA, Feb. 3—(?)—A rocket experiment which its author hoped might eventually lead to a trip to the moon has ended with the premature explosion of the rocket on top of Mount Redorta with injuries to three persons. The rocket was the work of Dr. Darwin Lyon, New York scientist, who had designed it to carry instruments into the stratosphere to determine the density, composition and temperature of that medium at an altitude of about 93 miles. Mount Redorta, 10,000 feet high, is in the Italian Alps.

Istanbul, Turkey.— (7) —Twenty-eight religious reactionaries, convicted of participation in the abortive revolutionary outbreak of December at Minemen, were hanged there at dawn Tuesday; Four of the 32 religious reactionaries scheduled to mount the gallows were not hanged. The Angora parliament Monday night commuted the sentences of two and two others died of heart attacks in their cells.

BERLIN, (UP) Participation by the United States Navy airship Los Angeles in maneuvers off Panama constitutes a violation of the treaty of Versailles, the newspaper Lokal Anzeiger said Tuesday. A dispatch from the newspaper's correspondent in Paris declared that the treaty forbids the use of the Los Angeles for military purposes, and that although the United States obtained permission in the present circumstances from Britain, France, Italy and Japan, the American government did not elicit agreement from other Versailles signatories. “The procedure is a pretty specimen of the victorious powers' respect for allegedly sacred treaties,” Lokal Anzeiger said.

1931-01-04.text: NORTH BEACH AIRPORT, L. I., Jan. 3. U.P)—Mrs. Beryl Hart and Capt. William S. Maclaren left here today in a Bellanca seaplane on a two-stop flight for Paris. The first goal of the fliers was Bermuda, some 700 miles to the southwest. From there they planned to hop to the Azores. The purpose of the flight, they said, was to demonstrate the feasibility of round trip air transportation between America and Europe over the Southern route. Dr. James H. Kimball, meteorologist of the government Weather Bureau here, predicted favorable weather for the first leg of the flight. Capt. Maclaren was at the controls of the plane as it soared away from North Beach Airport at 5:50 a. m. It was still dark when the craft, after circling the bay once, headed southeastward—a dim white blur in the faint moonlight. Capt. Maclaren said he and Mrs. Hart expected to arrive in Bermuda in eight hours. The “Tradewind

LONDON, Jan 4 (Sunday) — Princess Louise, oldest sister of King George and British Princess Royal, was stated in an official bulletin early today to be showing increased weakness. Although she has been seriously ill for some months, this is the first recent indication of a recurrence of the heart trouble from which she has suffered for some time. While the physicians gave no further information about the princess's condition, issuance of a bulletin at the unusual hour—12:45 a.m.—was accepted generally as ominous. Princess Louise will be 64 years old February 20. She is slightly more than two years older than her brother, King George. Her husband, the late Duke of Fyfe, died in 1912, leaving her with two daughters, both of whom are married.

(By ‘The Associated Press) London, Jan. 3—Industrial troubles in two major industries make this a gloomy week end for Britain. Today a miners’ conference broke down at Cardiff and in Lancashire it appeared that nothing could stop a threatened strike of 200,000 men in the cotton industry. The miners had hoped for some sort of compromise with the owners, but this afternoon their spokesman said they would have to turn to the government. They were going to try for a conference with Ramsay MacDonald on Monday, It looked as though they would suggest once more that the government take over the pits and run the industry at least temporarily, assuring employment to miners who would face great necessity in a strike. Two miners have been idle since New Year's Day when they stopped work automatically at the expiration of a temporary agreement on wages and working hours. They want retention of the ol

PARIS, Jan. 3 (AP)—Death came today to Marshal Joffre, last of the chief French military leaders of the great war, after a fortnight’s illness in which it was necessary to amputate his left leg. The Marshal would have been 79 years old tomorrow. The end was peaceful. Three members of his family, Mme. Joffre, his son-in-law, M. Lafile, and his brother, Ferdinand, General Issaly, his chief of staff, Colonel Desmazes of his staff, his doctors and a few others were present. He died without coming out from the coma which closed over him at noon Thursday, his life gradually ebbing since. The announcement was made at 8:30 a.m. A member of his military household, Captain Saint Cernin, pale with emotion, emerged from the hospital and in a husky voice telling newspapermen: “The Marshal is dead, gentlemen.” He displayed a bulletin signed by the physicians, Professor Leriche and Drs. Boulin and Font

The world, no less than France itself, tonight mourned the passing of Marshal Joseph Jacques Joffre, saviour of Paris in 1914, who died at 8:23 a.m., after a long and grim struggle with arteritis. His country, plunged in grief, was to honor by a great national funeral the memory of one of the most illustrious soldiers of her history. Death Comes Calmly Marshal Joffre—the “Papa” Joffre of the French Poilu and of all his countrymen, passed away peacefully.

Paris, Jan. 3, (UP)—Marshal Joseph Joffre, a great soldier who had never lost a battle during 78 years of his life, surrendered to death today after a fight which his doctors said would go down in medical history as miraculous. The end came at 8:23 a. m., just as the fading tinkle of the chapel bell at the hospital of Saint Jean de Dieu died out. The bell had summoned the monks to the hospital to mass, and in sombre black smocks, with their hoods turned down around their necks, they gathered to pray for the soul of the Hero of the Marne. Candlelight fell upon the narrow windows of the chapel, mingling with the sun’s rays that filtered through the stained glass, to give a mystical and mediaeval setting to the scene. Madame Joffre Present, In the marshal’s simply furnished room, Madame Joffre, his daughter Madame Laffaille, his staff officers and doctors, and a few monks were gathered at t

PARIS, Jan. 3.— (U.P) — The body of Marshal Joseph Jacques Joffre lay tonight within the monastic halls of the Hospital Saint Jean de Dieu, where his life ended at dawn, just as the mellow tones of the chapel bell calling the monks to mass died away. While the nation which once had entrusted him with its military security and gloried in the battle of the Marne, planned final honors in the manner in which “Papa” Joffre had requested, condolences from kings and presidents and veteran soldiers in all parts of the world were received by the government and Mme. Joffre. A death watch was kept tonight by Mme. Joffre, Mile. De Baye, a family friend, and members of the marshal's staff. It was learned that one of Joffre’s last instructions to his wife forbade the making of a death mask, post-death photographs or sculptures. In accordance with the wishes of Mme. Joffre, who stood at the marshal's b

GENEVA, Jan. 3.—(INS)—Representatives of the principal governments of the world agreed to hold a general disarmament conference here on March 1, 1932, it was learned today from a reliable source. The conclave will be held under the presidency of Edouard Benes.

Paris, Jan. 3—(A.P.)—Mary McCormick has decided to marry Prince Serge Mdvani when his divorce from Pola Negri becomes final, the American opera singer told close friends today on her arrival from New York to fulfill engagements at the Opera Comique. Rumors of Miss McCormick’s engagement to the prince have been frequent, but she had never before admitted to her friends here that she had finally made up her mind. Tonight she said: “I am thinking about cancelling all my European engagements and taking a boat back home. I am giving up my career in Europe and I have decided to get married.”

Paris, Jan. 3—(A.P.)—A bomb exploded tonight on the Champs Elysees beside the famous restaurant, Des Ambassadeurs, making a terrific blast that was heard all over Paris, but injuring no one. A large hole was burst in the wall of the restaurant, which was closed, and much glass was shattered. Crowds in a theater next door, where George Milton, famous French comedian, was playing in "Miami," became greatly excited, and the great Saturday night throng which collected outside, as it was only 10 p.m., added to the confusion. Police could advance no motive for the placing of the bomb except that someone with criminal intent wished to get rid of it before it exploded in his hands, presumably having intended originally to place it elsewhere. Bits of shell were found nearby and some theories were heard that the explosive had been constructed from such a missile.

1931-03-04.text: New Delhi, India—Mahatma Gandhi, Indian nationalist leader, and Viceroy Lord Irwin at high noon Wednesday signed a truce which ends the nationalist civil disobedience campaign and secures nationalist cooperation in working out a qualified dominion status for India. The truce culminated negotiations of weeks which reached fulfillment in an agreement at 1:30 a.m. Shortly afterward Gandhi left the viceregal palace in a drenching rain to inform the nationalist working committee at Old Delhi. While the committee voted unanimous approval of the terms Gandhi curled up in sleep on a straw mat. On awakening he had his head and face shaved, donned a spotless white homespun chaddar and loin cloth and set out for his meeting with the viceroy. Amnesty Is Granted In return for abandonment of the civil disobedience campaign which (Continued on Page 13.)

NEW DELHI, India, March 4.—(AP)—The civil disobedience movement ended today after almost a year of turmoil, suffering and conflict among the 20,000,000 natives of the Indian sub-continent. The Mahatma M. K. Gandhi, a slight, emaciated man whose power sprang from the adoration of millions who call him “The Great Soul and Lord Krishna,” whose authority is derived from the crown, signed a truce ending the uprising against British rule. The momentous peace agreement was reached just two weeks after Gandhi and the viceroy held their first conversations here. The negotiations were interrupted several times by marked divergencies, but during the last few days both sides showed a willingness to make concessions which made a settlement possible. The truce was regarded as the climax of the campaign waged by Gandhi since 1909 when, as a young barrister, he went to London and laid his views on India

(Associated Press.) Peace at last has come to India, racked for a year by a civil disobedience movement which defied all the authority of the British, filled the jails of the country and was responsible for millions of dollars of economic loss. After nine hours of almost continuous discussion, lasting until 1:30 a.m. Wednesday, Mahatma Gandhi and Viceroy Lord Irwin agreed upon formulas for settlement of all points in the dispute. A formal agreement will be drawn up later, when the little nationalist leader goes for a final talk with the viceroy. Its contents will then be made known. It is known that the viceroy gave tacit agreement to the important contention of the nationalists that Indians have the right to make their own salt. Proves Good Negotiator. That the puny Gandhi could have borne almost the entire burden and responsibility of this conference has amazed even his sternest Englis

NEW DELHI. India, March 4. (Wednesday) — Peace dawned for distracted India this morning after a year of civil disobedience activities that had torn Great Britain’s Asiatic domain by strife. Viceroy Lord Irwin, representing the British government, and Mahatma Gandhi, half-naked little chieftain of the Indian nationalists, reached an agreement at 11:30 this morning after Gandhi yesterday had won from Lord Irwin tacit agreement that Indians along the coast had the right to make their own salt from seawater instead of buying it from the government monopoly. This was one of the principal points for which the nationalists had fought in a year of civil resistance, and with accord on this matter it was felt one of the most serious obstacles to restoration of peace in India had been overcome. Iowa City, Mar. 4—(A.P.)— Chairman H. B. Carroll of the legislative committee investigating the University of Iowa administration announced this afternoon that the committee had taken over the handling of the university business office. He stated in response to a question this morning from Emmet Tinley, attorney for the board of education, that the committee had been watching since Monday night to prevent removal of the records. "It is not the intention of the committee or of any member to interfere with the operation of this great institution," Carroll said. Doran, Tinley Argue, "There is no claim, is there, that the institution has suffered?" asked Senator I. H. Doran of Tinley, referring to the latter's contention that business had been held up yesterday. "I'll make that later," Tinley replied. ROME, March 4. (AP) — It was learned on good authority today that the British-Franco-Italian naval accord gives France a global tonnage of 670,000 and Italy 441,000 as of 1936. The French quota includes 85,000 tons of obsolete ships and the Italians 5,000 tons. This gives France an efficient tonnage of 586,000 and Italy 436,000, leaving France a superiority of 150,000 tons. It is pointed out here, however, that the Italian claim to parity has not been sacrificed since the accord is only a temporary measure. It does not hold Italy to agreement beyond 1936. It was learned also that the accord establishes a naval holiday and until the end of 1931 no new units are to be laid down although units under construction may be completed.

1931-01-22.text: LONDON, Jan. 21—The MacDonald government was defeated in the House of Commons today on an amendment to the education bill, but Prime Minister MacDonald said no vital principle was involved. Thus the government will not be obliged to resign. LONDON, Jan. 21.—The MacDonald government was defeated today in the House of Commons by 282 to 249 on an amendment to the education bill.

Windsor, Ont., Jan. 22.—(AP)—(By the Canadian Press)—The report presented to Congress by the law enforcement commission, stressing the claim that the Canadian anti-export law has failed to reduce the flow of liquor to the United States, is to have an echo at the next session of the House of Commons. Col. Sidney C. Robinson, M. P. for Essex and sponsor of a motion now on the order paper at Ottawa, calling for abandonment of the export ban and a return to legalized exporting, said today he would comment “in emphatic words” on the Wickersham commission's admission. Raymond D. Morand, M. P. for Essex East, said he would support Colonel Robinson's stand. Colonel Robinson recalled that when United States officials paved the way for negotiations with Canada, which resulted in the Mackenzie King government introducing legislation which ended legal export of liquor, the claim was made that this s

LONDON, Jan. 22. (AP).—Although defeated in the House of Commons considering the issue at stake in the amendment of minor character. The vote was 282 to 249. The government accepted the amendment, which was forced by one of its own members, John Scurr, a Roman Catholic, and later passed the amended bill on its third and final reading by a vote of 256 to 238. Most of the liberals abstained in the second vote. The bill provides for raising the age at which children may leave school from 14 to 15 years, with an allowance of five shillings to be made to needy parents whom the law affects. The Scurr amendment authorized a government appropriation to equalize the additional burden that the law would impose on the religious, or non-provided schools.
Chryston, Lancashire, England, Jan. 22 UP)—Five miners were killed and several were injured in an explosion at the Augengeich Colliery today.

LONDON, Jan. 22 —(P)— With only three dissenting votes the lower house of the Canterbury convocation of the Church of England today gave its approval to faith healing and asked that it be given the official sanction of the church. The approval took the form of a petition to the Archbishop of Canterbury, asking "him to appoint a joint commission to frame a provisional service for unction by the imposition of hands, this service to be used until a permanent and fully authorized form could be issued under synodical sanction.

London, Jan. 21.—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's labor government was defeated by 33 votes in a division on the controversial education bill in the House of Commons tonight, but some hours later carried the bill victoriously through third reading by 256 votes against 238—a government majority of 18. Now the measure goes to the House of Lords. The defeat had no immediate consequence, for immediately after the division Mr. MacDonald announced to a wildly excited house that no big question of general principle was involved and that the government would carry on. The defeat came mainly as the result of the intrusion of a religious controversy into politics, for the division in which the government found itself outvoted, 282 to 249, was taken on an amendment to the education bill, moved by John Scurry, a Roman Catholic laborite. This amendment called for the passage of an act giving financi

LONDON, Jan. 22.—- (UP) —An epidemic of influenza, said by medical authorities to be seasonal and not of a serious character, swept Great Britain and several parts of Europe today. Britain suffered the heaviest death toll. The average number of deaths weekly in the British Isles was estimated at 100. The epidemic grew more severe in London, where there were 38 deaths last week, or double the number of the previous week. Troops quartered at Aldershot were attacked by the invisible enemy Sunday. Two hundred men had been confined to hospitals today. Officials of the ministry of health worked night and day to combat the spread of the epidemic and the public was advised by the press on the best way of escaping the in-

VIENNA, Jan. 22 (AP)--Reports from Constanta on the Black Sea today said 50 persons had been drowned when the steamship Javaria buckled amidships and sank with 36 of the crew and 16 passengers during a gale.

Geneva, Jan. 21.—(AP)—Charges of “menaces, acts of terrorism and bloody violence” were laid before the council of the League of Nations today by Julius Curtius, German foreign minister, in a formal protest at Polish treatment of German minorities in Upper Silesia. German-Polish relations growing out of the minorities question are regarded in Geneva as one of the greatest threats to the peace of postwar Europe. It has been feared for weeks that the debate begun today will set off international antagonisms of far-reaching consequences. Herr Curtius charged that not only had Germans been mistreated but that other racial minorities, particularly Ukrainians, had suffered during the November election period. Not only were they robbed of their electoral rights, but they were threatened in menacing letters and made victims of other methods of intimidation and abuse, he said. He asked that steps

Madrid Jan. 22 (AP) —Disorders broke out among students in the University of Madrid today. Student leaders in fiery addresses demanded the establishment of a republic in Spain. Despite the continuation of martial law which was proclaimed during recent revolutionary attempts, about 3,000 student members of the university scholars federation struck as a protest against the government.

Shanghai, Jan. 22—(UP)—Baroness Paulittle Depidoll, wife of Baron Charles Depidoll of Luxembourg, died today at a local hospital. Physicians attributed her death to poison taken last Saturday. The Baron in a formal statement said he had been estranged from Baroness Depidoll since last October. Local newspapers described the Baroness’ death as terminating “one of Shanghai's most discussed love triangles.” The Baroness also was reported to have taken poison while aboard the Maru while en route here. Sir Frederick Whyte, adviser to Nanking government, summoned a physician immediately after the boat docked at Shanghai. Lady Whyte was believed to be in San Francisco for the purpose of placing her son in a school there. Baron Depidoll has been representative in China for the Metallurgique at Luxembourg since 1928. The Baroness took the poison after Sir Frederick returned from Hawaii.

MOSCOW, Jan. 22.—Soviet Russia is threatened with the greatest war in history, Commissar of War Voroshilov said in an address to the Congress of Communist Youths. The Soviet Union, he declared, must organize the masses not only for the purpose of defending the country against inevitable intervention, but for victory over “the country which first draws the sword against us.” Three million young communists are in the congress of youths, he said, and 200,000 of them are in the army. He urged the entire membership to begin intensive training for the defense of the state. “Our country,” said he, “is a socialistic island surrounded by capitalist enemies. These are difficult times and we must not forget the external factors all about us. The danger of attack is constantly growing and it is obvious that the international bourgeoisie are preparing to march against us.” He quoted the German Genera

The Hague, Jan. 22.—(2)—Mme. Anna Pavlowa, the famous dancer, was in a critical condition today as a result of an attack of pleurisy. She contracted a chill when forced to remain for some time on a railroad track after an accident while she was en route from France to The Hague.

Tokyo, Jan. 22.—(Thursday)—(AP)—Baron Kijuro Shidehara, acting premier, told the 59th session of the diet today that Japan was still watching the American immigration law with keen interest. This law excludes Japanese and Chinese from the regular immigration quotas, admitting them only as students and in other special classes, and long has been a sore spot with oriental nations. Peace Talk “Our friendly relations with the nations of Europe and America,” said the acting premier in convening the diet this morning, “are entirely satisfactory and will, I am convinced, continue to grow in strength. “On the question of the United States immigration law, which for the past seven years has been weighing heavily on popular sentiment in this country, there is no longer any doubt that our position: (Continued on Page 10) |

1931-01-12.text: BOMBAY, India, Jan. 12.—Serious disorders broke out again today for the first time in recent weeks of the civil disobedience movement. Police clashed repeatedly with independence volunteers and members of the Congress who attempted to enforce a hartal or strike in protest against the execution of four men charged with the murder of a policeman at Sholapur. About 150 persons were injured, at least 25 of them seriously.

ALICE SPRINGS, Northern Territory, Australia, Jan. 12.—()—Two aviators lost in the Central Australian desert for more than two weeks were brought here today by rescuers with a story of how they had lived on malted milk tablets, boiled grass and even tadpoles now and then while they wandered toward civilization through a trackless wild. They are Captain W. L. Ptemburgh and S. J. Hambre, who started out for some mining properties last December and were forced down in the desert on Dec. 20. A searching plane located them on Saturday and a rescue party in automobiles went out to get them. They were weak and exhausted today but otherwise uninjured.

HORTA, Azores (UP)—A strong “northeaster” bringing stormy weather and vicious winds whipped over the Azores Monday while an apparently hopeless watch was kept for a man and a woman who had challenged the Atlantic on a flight of 2,000 miles from Bermuda to the Azores. Anxiety that had mounted during the hours in which Mrs. Beryl Hart and Lieut. William S. MacLaren were not heard from in their white seaplane Tradewind turned to a faint hope that they might have missed their mark, a small group of islands in the ocean and continued to the safety of the European coast. But no word of their progress reached Paris, their ultimate destination, and ships east of the Azores had not reported sighting their plane. The Tradewind left Hamilton, Bermuda, at 11:15 a.m., Saturday. The fliers were 24 hours overdue here at 7 a.m. Monday. Unless they landed at sea and were picked up by a ship without wirel

Shanghai, Jan. 10.—(P)—Hundreds of persons died in a snow and dust storm which subsided tonight after raging two days southward from Mongolia’s deserts to the Yangtse valley. The storm laid an icy siege over all north China; hundreds of thousands were suffering acutely in temperatures averaging 15 degrees below zero. Large numbers continued to freeze to death among the poverty stricken populace.

Shanghai—(—Winter, in this part of the world the harbinger of death and intense suffering, Monday gripped virtually all of North China, Manchuria, Siberia, Korea and Japan. It paralyzed communications, crippled railroads and took an undetermined toll of human life and property. China, from the Yangtse river northward, lay under a mantle of ice and snow, while frigid blasts from the north added to the depth of the white blanket with a mixture of snow and sand from the barren steppes of Mongolia. It was feared thousands had perished from the intense cold in northern China alone, dispatches describing the finding of scores of frozen bodies in the streets of large cities. The fate of western China, much of which was isolated owing to disrupted communications, was uncertain. Many cities of north central and northeastern China reported below zero weather and at Harbin, Manchuria, the thermomet

PHANGHAL, Jan. 11 — Sub-zero weather, spreading death and destruction, gripped virtually all of China north of the Yangtse river today. A vast blanket of snow and ice reached from the sea westward as far as Kansu province and from the Yangtse northward into the barren wastes of Mongolia, when the blizzard came. Fragmentary reports of the storm, which raged fiercely for three days, trickled in over crippled communications. No estimate of the dead was available, but it was feared the toll would run into the thousands. The local weather office described the blizzard as the most severe of many years. Bodies in Streets. Scores of frozen bodies were picked up in the streets of Peiping and Tientsin, Chihli province. Hundreds of others perished in surrounding areas, their wretched, fireless hovels providing scant protection from the biting blasts. Even in the vicinity of Peiping and Tientsin, la

(BY THE ASSOCIATED PRESS) Horta, Azores, Jan. 12.—The cold expanses of the Eastern Atlantic, lashed by a mid-winter storm, apparently have swallowed another adventurous man and woman who dared to fly from New York to Paris. Early this morning, not a word had been heard nor a sign seen of Mrs. Beryl Hart, flying widow, and Lieut. William S. Mactaren, her navigator, more than 12 hours overdue here from Hamilton, Bermuda, on the third lap of a Trans-Atlantic air crossing with a payload of freight. The American fliers left Bermuda at 11:15 a.m. (e.s.t.) Saturday and were due to end the (2,045-mile hop in Horta at 8:30 Sunday morning. Rockets flashed through the dark and stormy sky in attempts to pierce a heavy cloud-bank which hemmed in this island city. (By The Associated Press) Tokyo, Jan. 12.—Five persons were killed and 70 or 80 injured as part of a passenger train jumped the track and fell into a river while crossing a bridge near Kochi at 4 o’clock this morning.

Vienna, Jan. 12, (PF) - One hundred and twenty men and women skiers broke legs, arms, ankles or fingers Sunday around Vienna and the courtyard of an emergency hospital here resembled in some ways a first aid station behind a battle line. Hundreds of other injuries were reported throughout Austria. Ice crust forming over the snowfields accounted for the extraordinary number of accidents.

TOKYO, Jan. 12.—(A)—The death toll of a blizzard which swept a large portion of the Far East over the week-end, today it was estimated, took the lives of 30 Japanese, including 200 fishermen whose boats were swamped off Somagun. In the Moji region six froze to death. A thousand houses were unroofed and several were killed by collapsing houses in the Echigo district.

TOKIO, Jan. 12.—A fast express train, en route from Shimonoseki to Tokio, plunged into the river at Hiroshima today, killing six persons and injuring 50, it was announced officially. Many of the victims were trapped while they slept. Tangled wreckage made rescue work difficult.

PLYMOUTH, ENGLAND, Feb 4 (UP)—A royal air force plane was wrecked in Plymouth Saturday and eight of the 12 men aboard were drowned. Another man critically injured in the crash, died later, making a death toll of nine. Three men were in a hospital critically injured. The plane crashed when the pilot, apparently confused by bright sunlight on the water, misjudged the landing surface. An explosion wrecked the craft, which sank and trapped the men in the submerged cabin from which only four were able to escape. One of the survivors was an officer. The demolished plane was a R. A. F. Blackburn-Irish flying boat, a tri-motored craft which carried a complement of 12 including four officers, led by wing commander C. G. Tucker. Tucker was killed. Returning From Practice The plane was returning from aerial firing practice just before noon. It glided gracefully toward the water, eye witnesses said,

Plymouth, Eng., Feb. 4.—(AP)— Nine men in the crew of a Royal Air Force seaplane were feared lost today when the ship went into a dive while maneuvering over Plymouth Sound, struck the water with great force and was wrecked by an explosion. As she struck, she heeled over on one side and sank immediately. When rescuers went out in small boats, they picked up two officers and one of the crew, all injured. Commander Tucker, Flying Officer Wood and several enlisted men were missing. Divers recovered one of the bodies this afternoon. The cause of the accident was not immediately determined.

Large numbers of persons were still prisoners of toppled buildings. Many were believed dead, but it was hoped a few would be found alive. WELLINGTON, N. Z., (Wednesday), Feb. 4—Three towns were in ruins today, more than 100 persons were dead and upwards of 1,000 injured, as the result of one of the most terrible earthquakes that ever struck New Zealand. It began on North Island early yesterday morning, bringing stone and brick buildings toppling about the heads of their occupants and pedestrians in the streets and setting fire to hundreds of frame structures. Auckland, New Zealand, Feb. 5.—(Thursday)—The extent of disaster caused by Tuesday’s earthquake was indicated today by the first reports of organized relief forces which invaded the ruined cities of the Hawkes Bay region. With the death toll in three of the stricken cities placed at about 431 and with other regions unreported, a general order was issued for evacuation of the flourishing city of Napier, famous resort town on the eastern coast of North Island. The evacuation was ordered carried out within two days due to the breakdown of sewage facilities and the fear of authorities that an epidemic would start unless the inhabitants leave at once. It was arranged to evacuate 5,000 women and children immediately. New tremors, preceded by a deep booming noise, were felt last night. Feb. 4 -- (UP) — New Zealand rushed aid to quake, tidal wave and dire survivors at Napier and adjacent towns today while reports indicated the death toll would run into hundreds. The latest estimate placed the dead at Napier alone at 300. Twenty-six were known dead at Hastings. The injured already totaled thousands. The open air dressing station erected at Napier had accounted for 600 serious injuries. Fires still were raging at Napier at 7 P.M. today. Many victims were incinerated. Seventeen bodies had been recovered from the ruins of the hospital and the nurses’ home. Attendants worked heroically to remove patients before the hospital collapsed. One patient was undergoing an operation which was completed in the open air. A temporary hospital was established on the race course, which was described as a sh

WELLINGTON, New Zealand, Feb. 4 (Wednesday) (AP —At least five towns in the Hawke's Bay province of North Island lay broken and burning today while the earth still rocked with the continuing shocks of the earthquake that brought wholesale death and desolation to a peaceful countryside. There were known to be 125 dead in Napier and Hastings and the final figure, it was feared, would be several times that number. In Napier alone there were 1000 injured. The quake began yesterday morning and its violence brought public buildings, houses, hospitals, stores and homes down that were previously standing.

WELLINGTON, Feb. 5—Thursday)—(INS)—Based on reliable reports received here up to 1 o'clock this morning it is estimated that Tuesday's disastrous earthquake in the Hawkes Bay province of North Island took a toll of at least 640 lives. Police in Napier, which is a veritable shambles of dead and dying, estimate 500 are dead there. Hastings, twenty miles southwest of Napier, will probably have a death roll of 100. Thirty-one are known to be dead in Taradale, near Napier. Two priests and seven students of a Catholic seminary were killed in Green Meadows, practically a suburb of Napier.

' CHRISTCHURCH, N. Z., Feb. 4 (UP)—The Napier district was struck by another severe earth shock at 8:40 p. m. Tuesday, it was reported here, adding to the panic and horror of survivors. It was reported that every chimney and water main between Napier and Waipukurau, a distance of about 50 miles, was broken. The earth shocks also were felt on South Island, although they were mild.

BY ALFRED BARALIN (Copyright, by The Associated Press) AUCKLAND, New Zealand, Feb. 3. — A terrifying earthquake and fire had reduced the beautiful seaport city of "sunny" Napier to a shambles today, wrecked nearby towns and resulted in loss of more than 100 lives and injuries to upwards of a thousand persons. Secure in the general belief the region was immune from seismic disturbances, the populace of Napier was stunned by the severest quake in New Zealand’s history. Recurring shocks wrecked stone buildings, broke the water supply system and placed the city of 20,000 at the mercy of fire that started as frame structures collapsed. Buildings were dynamited in an effort to halt the flames. It was shortly before noon yesterday when the first jolt was felt up and down the coastal region stretching back from beautiful Hawkes Bay, on which Napier, capital of Hawkes Bay province, is located. (International News Service) BOMBAY, Feb. 4. — Mahatma Gandhi, leader of the campaign of civil disobedience against British rule in India, today made a definite offer to seek peace with the British Government. India's Holy Man wrote a letter to Lord Irwin, the viceroy, urging him to institute an inquiry into six specific instances of alleged police excesses against Indian nationalists since the start of the civil disobedience campaign. Gandhi asserted in his letter that he would interpret the viceroy’s favorable reply to his request as a genuine gesture of peace, and in that case he would exert all his influence to persuade the all-India Congress, representing the Nationalists, to accept the offer of the British Government of eventual qualified dominion status for India. The annual meeting of the all-India Congress has been fixed provisionally for April 6. The viceroy's reply is awaited

(By United Press) AUCKLAND, N. Z., Feb. 4.—The death toll in the New Zealand earthquake mounted rapidly today as rescue forces made their way through the stricken Hawkes Bay region. The most definite figures were: Town—Estimated no. of dead, Napier 300. Hastings 80 to 100. Tardale 31. Total 411 to 431. There were scores of persons still buried in debris of wrecked towns and several villages known to be devastated but as yet without any definite estimate of casualties. The toll was expected to be increased. The injured and homeless were counted in thousands.

WELLINGTON, New Zealand, Feb. 3-(AP)--E. C. Weston, manager of the Christchurch company, who was in a department store at Hastings, North Island, when yesterday's earthquake struck, told of the disaster when he reached here today. "I had just completed my business in the store," he said, "when I felt the preliminary tremors. A young girl clerk ran into my arms and I tried to pacify her, telling her it would all be over in a second. "A heavy shock came on the heels of the first movement and a great steel pillar fell across the girl's body, crushing her against the counter. She screamed but the pillar was so heavy that I could not budge her and she was dead in a moment. "It came to me that I had escaped by inches, I managed to crawl on my hands and knees from under the wreckage. "Everywhere people were panic-stricken and there were screams for help coming from all sides."

Bombay, India, Feb. 4.—(2)—On the eve of peace parleys with delegates returning from the round table conference, the Congress party headquarters announced today that its president and members of its war council would publicly manufacture salt in the great Maidan square tomorrow. This is in direct defiance of the law and it is the offense for which Mahatma Gandhi was imprisoned last May. The gesture of civil disobedience is certain to result in the arrest of all those who engage in it and the authorities are prepared for trouble.

London, Feb. 3.-- (AP) -- The MacDonald labor government won an easy victory in the House of Commons tonight, carrying the electoral reform bill on second reading by a majority of 65 votes. Most of the liberals in the House of Commons voted with the laborites and thus upset the conservative attack.

Las Palmas, Canary Islands—(7)— Crippled by giant waves in Bahia Gando, several miles from here, the DO-X, German twelve-motored seaplane, appeared today to have been thwarted in its transatlantic flight project for at least two weeks. Some doubt existed here as to the extent of injuries sustained by the plane yesterday morning as it attempted to take off for Porto Praia, Cape Verde Islands, en route to Rio de Janeiro, but it was understood that both motors and superstructure were damaged. An urgent message has been sent to Lisbon to the Dornier engineer, M. Bernier, to proceed at once to the Canary Islands to aid in the repairs to the plane. He is leaving for Cadiz to catch a ship to Las Palmas. He inferred before his departure that repairs might take several weeks since parts would have to be imported from Germany. Captain Christiansen attempted yesterday morning to taxi here from Bahi

Las Palmas, Canary Islands, Feb. 8. ()—The giant German seaplane DO-X lay at Gando bay near here tonight while mechanics attempted to repair damage suffered when a big wave struck the ship as she was taxiing for a take-off this morning. Experts here believed it would be at least fifteen days before the plane could resume the flight to Porta Praia, Cape Verde islands, the second leg of a projected journey to Brazil. The part damaged was the understructure. One report indicated another complication through the faulty functioning of two of the twelve motors. Captain Friedrich Christiansen attempted to taxi from Gando bay to Las Palmas today but after a short cruise over the rough waters he decided to return to Gando bay.

LAS PALMAS, Canary Islands, Feb. 4.—Continuation of the bad luck which has dogged the DO-X ever since she left Altenrhein, Switzerland three months ago to attempt a flight across the Atlantic, today held the giant million dollar German flying boat at Gando Bay, near here. - While attempting a takeoff for the Cape Verde Islands in rough seas yesterday morning several braces and supports of the ship were bent and strained. Repair parts will have to be brought from Germany and prospects of a continuation of the flight before March—are remote.

Las Palmas, Canary Islands, Feb. 4 (UP)—The departure of the flying boat DO-X for Cape Verde on the next leg of its proposed flight to South America was dependent today upon the repairing of one of the ship’s pontoons, and appeared indefinite. The pontoon was damaged yesterday when the DO-X was returning to Las Palmas from Gando Bay. Weather on the bay was favorable for a takeoff but Captain Friedrick Christiansen postponed the starting for a day.

Menemen, Turkey. Feb. 3 (7)— Awed residents of this old Turkish town remained indoors today or hurried in frightened groups past the principal corners where swung from gibbits the bodies of 28 men, branded as traitors to Turkey. The 28 were hanged just as dawn broke, for their part in the abortive attempt to restore the Caliphate, December 23. The condemned men were sent to the exact places in the town where each had taken part in the revolt and there they were executed by baggy-trousered gypsy hangmen. All day long the bodies swung in the wind, for the order of execution prescribed that they must not be cut down until they had served from dawn to dark as an example for other religious reactionaries.

Paris--P:—After 22 years, the king of Italy, Victor Emanuel, agreed upon by France and Mexico as an arbiter to determine ownership of tiny, desolate Clipperton rock, Pacific ocean island, has found against Mexico and awarded the island to France. His decision, filed yesterday at the Quai D'Orsay, rules that the Mexican government, which has kept a small garrison of men there since 1897, must quit the island and surrender sovereignty to the French government. Clipperton rock lies 870 miles off the west coast of Mexico in latitude 10 north, and its sole importance, it appears now, is that eventually it might be used as a seaplane base. It is of coral structure, and low except for one point, 170 feet high. It encloses a lagoon.
Paris — Vice Admiral Dominique Gauchet, 64, who commanded the allied Mediterranean fleet during the World War, died Tuesday night.

The work begun at London will be continued without interruption, he said, and the new Indian constitution will be passed through the British parliament as soon as it is completed. This pronouncement of British policy pledged liberation to India’s 50,000 political prisoners if “civil quiet is proclaimed and assured” in India. In a long declaration of British government policy, the weight of government support was pledged to the findings of the committees of the round table conference which has been laboring in London for two months. LONDON, Jan. 19.—(AP)—Ramsay MacDonald, beginning his long awaited pronouncement on British policy in India, today told delegates to the Indian round table conference that he accepted the idea of an all-Indian federation at the desire of the round table delegates. He read a declaration by the government deciding to transfer full responsibility for the government of India to the federal and provincial legislatures. The work of negotiations for the future Indian government will be continued without interruption, he said, but details of the structure are still to be decided on. “It is a great achievement,” he said, “both for India and Great Britain. We are grateful to you.” The Indians, said the prime minister, must settle their own communal disputes, for Britain is ‘neither pro-Hindu, pro-Moslem, nor pro-any section of the Indian population. “The attitude of the British government,” he tol

[United Press Staff Correspondent] LONDON—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, delivering the labor government’s declaration of policy to the India round table conference today, announced readiness to grant amnesty to the thousands of political prisoners in India if civil order were assured. The round table conference, which convened on Nov. 12 in an attempt to form a basis for a new Indian constitution, ended at 4:20 p.m. without having achieved its full purpose but with a record which was generally described as “a successful failure.” 50,000 in Jails There are more than 50,000 political prisoners in India. The prime minister expressed sympathy for the political prisoners and the followers of the imprisoned Mahatma M. K. Gandhi in the Indian civil disobedience campaign. MANCHESTER, England, Jan 19.—Two Royal Air Force officers were killed and nine persons were injured today when a Royal Air Force bombing plane crashed at the airdrome at Worthydown.

London, Jan. 18.—(4?)—With re-assembling of parliament on Tuesday, Great Britain’s labor government will face a series of tests, any one of which it is believed in some quarters may result in the overthrow of the government. The battle is expected to start Wednesday over the government’s education bill, now in committee stage.

London, Jan. 15.—(AP)—Joy over settlement of the South Wales coal strike was mixed with gloom tonight over a shutdown in the cotton industry affecting 250,000 weavers. The shutdown occurred at noon yesterday at Lancashire as a result of a lockout declared by the employers after a strike in the Burnley area against a system of having each weaver tend more looms than customary. No Settlement in Sight Most of the employees affected are women and girls, no immediate settlement of the dispute was indicated and grave fears were entertained that the whole cotton industry employing a half million workers might be brought to a standstill within the next few days.

Silver Belt A. P. Leased Wire: CARDIFF, Wales, Jan. 19—South Wales miners who have been on strike since January 1 returned in full force to the pits today, victorious in their demand that reduction of the working day to seven and one-half hours be not attended with a decrease in wages, although making balancing concessions. Skeleton crews resumed work Saturday and Sunday after consummation of an agreement between owners and miners Thursday. One hundred fifty thousand workers were affected by the strike.

SANTANDER, Spain, Jan. 19 (#) After an exciting trip from Paris, the Prince of Wales and his youngest brother, Prince George, were en route today aboard the liner Oropesa on an 18,000-mile journey which will culminate with their inauguration of the British trade exhibition in Buenos Aires in March. The prince’s trouble began late Saturday night when their train was held up 30 miles below Bordeaux by the derailment of a northbound train from the Spanish frontier. Awakened by the halt, both watched the work of clearing the track. French railroad officials at Bayonne sent a special train north to pick them up and carry them to Hendaye. There, already four hours late, they transferred to motor cars, beginning a dangerous ride over sloppy mountain roads to Santander, watering place of the Spanish kings. At Bilbao the automobile occupied by the Prince of Wales careened into that which Prince G

ISTANBUL, Turkey, Jan. 18.—Fourteen persons were killed in a fire today in a building containing commercial offices and a motion picture supply store. Ten girls were seriously injured. Of the 14 persons who lost their lives, seven succumbed to burns, three were asphyxiated and four died in jumping out windows. The building was in the Galata quarter.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 19.—(UP)— G. W. Brophy, former Phoenix, Ariz., flying instructor, will take off from here on his proposed flight to Manila tomorrow or Wednesday instead of this morning as first planned, he announced today. Workmen were busy installing an additional 50-gallon gasoline tank and small open cockpits to his plane, the Phoenix. He will carry no radio. Mrs. Brophy, his wife, also an expert aviator, expressed regret that she was not to accompany him on the journey. She has been a regular visitor at the flying field to witness and supervise preparations.

. PARIS, Jan. 19 (AP) — The French government plans to fix the price of high grade wheat at $2 a bushel, the Associated Press was informed at the ministry of agriculture today. A bill to that effect has already been prepared and Minister of Agriculture Victor Boret is confident that it will be passed by parliament, it was said. Even at $2 a bushel, taking into consideration high costs of production, French farmers will just about break even, in the opinion of the minister. Under the proposed measure, some of the lower grades of wheat will command a lower price than $2, but the higher grades, such as Manitoba hard, will bring the top price. The ministry of agriculture estimates that the increase in the price of bread to meet the new wheat price will be about one cent a pound.

Santander, Spain.—The prince of Wales and his brother George rose at dawn Sunday to watch a big derrick clear the track for the royal train which was taking them to the coast for embarkation on their South American tour. The princes left their Pullman car when their train was suddenly halted between Ichoux and Lugos, 30 miles southwest of Bordeaux, and they learned an express train had been wrecked ahead of them. No one was injured in the derailment, however. Exhibiting much the same curiosity that impels an American pedestrian to watch a steam shovel, the royal pair pulled on their clothes and piled out with the rest of their party to watch the wrecking crew at work. After several hours a special train brought the party to Santander, where they embarked on the liner Oropesa, which will take them to South America on their sailorman's tour for Great Britain.

) Paris, Jan. 19-()—The cabinet today decided to issue a decree ordering special certificates for all foreign wheat entering France. The decree resulted from allegations that foreign wheat has been entering France in excess of the official quotes which last year was fixed at 19 per cent of the total wheat necessary for consumption in France. This year's quota has not yet been fixed. Another cabinet decree which has been drafted would obligate all exporters to the government regarding the use of wheat. Nothing was said about price fixing although it has been generally expected that the price would be set at a little less than $2.92 a bushel.
Madrid, Jan. 19.—(4)—Four thousand members of the printing crafts went on strike today for shorter hours and a twenty cents increase in the daily wage. Newspapers were exempted by the union.

1931-01-08.text: MELBOURNE, AUSTRALIA, JAN. 8. (AP).—Six men were killed, one is missing and three were injured in the huge tidal wave which swept the coast of New Guinea on December 24, the administrator of that territory reported today. The great wall of water from 25 to 50 feet high swept along the coast for forty miles and rolled 300 yards inland, he said.

LONDON, Jan. 8.—(4)—One hundred ships from all ports of the world were held in British ports today by a heavy fog. The Mersey was shrouded and many boats anchored there feared to move. At Manchester a fog of intensity unknown for a generation has persisted for five days. Bronchitis and pneumonia have accounted for many deaths, traffic on land has been greatly impeded. There have been many accidents and injuries.

Ripon—A)— A volunteer fireman Edward Kopplin, 55, is dead and damage of $55,000 was estimated by school officials as the result of a fire that destroyed Smith Hall at Ripon College. Kopplin, driver of a city fire truck, fell dead apparently from heart disease as the truck careened into a curb at the scene of the fire. About 50 members of Delta Sigma Psi fraternity were made homeless by the fire and two of their number were injured slightly as they attempted to retrieve their belongings from the burning building. Bruno Anderson and George Cunningham, football stars, were the injured students.

Paris, Jan. (.—(@)— the body of Marshal Joffre, hero of the Marne, rested today in Les Invalides, hall of French immortals, whose massive dome shelters the bodies of Napoleon and Foch. Two million Parisians braved freezing weather to stand outside Notre Dame and along the route to Les Invalides for hours while the funeral cortege, in sombre ceremony, proceeded from the cathedral to the temporary resting place of the man who saved France from the invader in 1914. PARIS, Jan. 6. (AP)—Frenchmen today gazed for the last time on the familiar, beloved features of “Papa” Joffre, Marshal of France, hero of the Marne, and commander of the French armies in the first two years of the World War. Sixty-five thousand persons were estimated to have filed by the catafalque in the chapel of the Ecole Militaire from 9 a.m. yesterday to 11 p.m. last night and it was believed that many more would view the body today. There can be no extension of the time for doing homage at the dead Marshal’s bier beyond 9 o’clock tonight, for at that time the body will be removed to the cathedral of Notre Dame for the last requiem of the church. (Continued on Page 5)

Paris, France—France, in a final tribute of love and respect to the “Savior” of Paris, gave Marshal Joffre Wednesday a national funeral which in its grandeur reminded of that “day of ashes” when the body of Napoleon Bonaparte was brought back from St. Helena. Wednesday night the body of the victor of the Marne lay, like that of Napoleon, under the great dome of the Invalides, in a disused sacristy of the Chapel of St. Louis, dedicated to the old crusader king. It was placed there so that Madame Joffre might pray beside her soldier husband in silence. Some months from now the body will be transferred to “Chestnut Grove,” the marshal’s country home, where it will be entombed in a mausoleum like that of Washington at Mt. Vernon. Church and state united to make the last rites of France’s loved soldier a full expression of the republic’s gratitude and respect. Thousands of French people fille

ROME, Jan. 8. (UP)—Tragedy dimmed the rejoicing of the Italian people over the South Atlantic flight of General Italo Balbo's seaplane squadron today. Officials announced that five aviators were killed in two accidents that marred the beginning of the flight from Bolama, Portuguese Guinea, approximately 1900 miles over the ocean to Natal, Brazil. Two pilots, two mechanics and one wireless operator were killed. The first accident occurred when the airplane piloted by Captain Enea Silvio Recagno was forced to descend. First Sergeant Louis Fois was killed when the heavily loaded plane struck the water. The left float of the seaplane was damaged. Captain Recagno, Lieutenant Renato Abbriata and Radio Operator Sergeant Mario Mancini were not injured, officials said. The seaplane remained afloat and the four survivors were rescued. The machine later was towed to Bolama. The accident that cost t

- Rome, Jan. 7 (4’)—Ten Italian sea-planes sailed gloriously in a flight from the west African coast to Brazil yesterday, but left behind them tragedy, with five aviators killed, three others injured and four ships disabled. An official announcement of the casualties, withheld by the government until the home folk were in bed, that their rejoicing might not be marred, cleared up the confusion that has existed since the planes left Bolama, Portuguese Guinea. Twelve planes were due to start originally. Two crashed at or near the takeoff. Two replacement ships set off and later were forced to alight in mid-ocean, although without injury to the occupants. Captain Recagno lifted his ship off the water at the takeoff but it fell. Sergeant Luigi Fol, the mechanic, was killed as it crumpled. The two pilots, both officers, and the radio operator were injured. A second plane carrying Captain Luigi

Berlin, Jan. 8—(#)—Thomas L. Chadbourne of the Cuban-American sugar delegation today announced that he had negotiated an agreement by which the German sugar interests will “participate in a world pact for control of sugar production. The German delegation, it was learned, agreed to accept a quota permitting exportation of 350,000 tons in the fiscal year 1931-32; and 300,000 tons each in 1932-33 and the two following years.

(International News Service) ROME, Jan. 8.—The Italian Government revealed today that five aviators were killed and three seriously injured in the crash of two of the twelve trans-Atlantic seaplanes which started from Bolama in Portuguese Guinea for South America Tuesday, under command of General Italo Balbo. The official report on the tragedy, of which there had been rumors since yesterday, was given out 48 hours after the accidents in order to soften the blow to the Italian people, who gave themselves over to unbounded rejoicing when ten of the machines spanned the hazardous 1,860 miles to Natal, Brazil, in 17 hours and 15 minutes. According to the government's account of the tragedy, twelve double-pontoon seaplanes lined up in four squadrons of three machines each for their start under a full moon, (Continued On Page Two)

ROME, Jan. 8.—A stern warning to the Christian world to take heed of its mad pace and turn back into the paths of divine law was pronounced today by Pope Pius XI in his eagerly awaited encyclical on marriage. The document explained with evident regret that since even among the faithful pernicious mistakes were being made and "depraved and perverted customs acquired," the Vatican deemed it necessary to raise its voice to warn its flocks away from these poisoned pastures. Scores of divorces. The encyclical in its entirety harks back to the fundamental marriage law elaborately put forth in the encyclical of Leo XIII which refutes divorce and emphasizes that only by continence within the married state can families be limited without transgressing the divine law. ROME, Jan. 8—Birth control theories were condemned in an encyclical addressed by Pope Pius XI to Roman Catholic bishops Thursday. The reference to contraceptive methods appeared clearly aimed at the resolutions of the recent Lambeth conference of Anglican bishops in London, who admitted the advisability of birth control under certain circumstances. A Mortal Sin The encyclical said that an act impeding procreation is an offense against God and a mortal sin. "The destruction of an unborn child is murder," the encyclical added. The encyclical quoted Saint Augustine, recalling his statement that "the wife was a mere mistress and the man was the wife's paramour." All relations except conjugal were condemned in the encyclical, which said that any third party was inadmissible. Several Subjects The encyclical, dated Dec 31, contained 16,000 words. Vienna, Jan. 7.---(4?)—Members of the Austrian Heimwehr and some soldiers of the regular army tonight joined with masses of fascists who surged riotously through the streets in protest against the American motion picture film “All Quiet on the Western Front.” Disorders increased rapidly after police blocked all the bridges leading across the Danube to the Jewish quarter. Despite the mobilization of 2,000 officers, the National Socialists ran riot in many parts of the Austrian capital. Precautions were taken to protect Jewish residents since all fascist protests against the film both here and in Germany have been directed against Jews as well as the alleged pacifist sentiments of the picture. The theater where the picture was shown tonight is in the Jewish quarter, across the river. BERLIN, Jan. 8—(AP)—The efforts of Thomas L. Chadbourne of the Cuban-American sugar delegation, to obtain an international sugar agreement for the limitation of production and export met with success when representatives of German producers today accepted his offer for export limitation. The acceptance is subject to the ratification of the German sugar industry but it was said in responsible circles there was little doubt that this would be forthcoming. Mr. Chadbourne's proposals for the German quota were 500,000 tons for the fiscal year 1930-31; 350,000 tons for 1931-32, and 306,000 tons for each of the following three years. Efforts to secure a satisfactory limitation agreement were begun at Amsterdam early in December when Cuban and Javanese producers’ representatives reached a provisional accord. At Brussels later a similar accord was negotiated between the Cuban-Javanese group and E

By RICHARD D. McMILLAN PARIS, Jan. 71—(UP)—The people of Paris bade goodbye to Marshal Joffre today in state funeral ceremonies as solemnly impressive as those for any man of the generation. The body of the old soldier lay in a tent at the Invalides tonight, its temporary resting place until a mausoleum has been constructed at the Joffre estate outside Paris. There, at a spot overlooking the river Seine, the hero of the Marne will find his final resting place. Malmed trench privates marched bareheaded along with princes, generals and statesmen, behind the gun carriage carrying the marshal’s body in the funeral procession from the historic old grey walls of the Cathedral of Notre Dame, where funeral services were held, past the statue of Joan of Arc to the Invalides. 1931-02-16.text: New Delhi, India, Feb. 16.—(#)— The peace of India will be at stake when Mahatma Gandhi reaches here from Allahabad to confer with Vice-roy Lord Irwin as “man to man” on the problems facing the country. The nationalist leader is expected either tomorrow or Wednesday. If the conversation is satisfactory Gandhi is expected to confer with others of the working committee of all India National Congress and call off the civil disobedience campaign. Steps then will be taken to work out a federation dominion status under plans evolved at the London conference, The Viceroy’s invitation was telegraphed to Gandhi, who at Allahabad was observing his weekly day of silence. He left tonight by train for New Delhi, The invitation was arranged by mutual friends, Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru and M. R. Jayakar, both of whom came here last week to confer with the Viceroy. The two men were members of the London rou

New Delhi, India, Feb. 16. (P)— Viceroy Lord Irwin said today that the government is ready to grant general amnesty to political prisoners in India, and to consider withdrawal of the present laws against congress party activities, if Mahatma Gandhi will call off his civil disobedience campaign and give evidence of ‘a change of heart’ toward the government. He told this to Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru, Srimivasa Sastri and M. R. Jayakar, round table conference delegates, with whom he had a long talk this afternoon, preliminary to an interview with Gandhi tomorrow or Wednesday.
Sydney, N. S. W., Feb. 15.—(P) Dame Nellie Melba, 72, who has been ill since early in November was described today as being in a dangerous condition.

(U. BP. Staff Correspondent.) London, Feb. 16.—(UP)—King Alfonso XIII of Spain, Europe's longest reigning monarch of the oldest dynasty, faces the gravest situation of his reign, a crisis which threatens the stability of the Spanish throne and which may eventually result in the alteration of the king’s constitutional responsibilities toward the state. Hitherto Europe's most popular ruler, Alfonso is facing a storm of criticism and is now definitely on the defensive against a rising tide of demands for the summoning of a constitutional convention, to which he is strongly opposed. “In the present temper of the country a constitutional convention would be almost certain to limit the king's power drastically and reduce him to the position of a figurehead, similar to the other constitutional monarchs of Europe. There might be an attempt to force the king’s abdication, and leaders of several p

LONDON, Feb. 16—(PF)— Words never formed by human lips and spoken by a voice that never existed were heard last night in the London office of an American film company. It was a synthetic recipe invented by the young Englishman E. A. Humphriss, who, the Express said, found it possible to reproduce word sounds by copying the impressions from the sound track of a talkie film. He chose the words, “all of a tremble,” and by analyzing the “peaks and valleys” of the sound track was able to dissect them into their various sounds. Afterward drawing them separately on cardboard strips and joining the strips together to form the words, he photographed them on a celluloid film which when run through a talkie projector reproduced the words in a deep bass tone. Humphriss said the job took one hundred hours.

MANCHESTER, Eng., Feb. 16. (P) —Between 250,000 and 30,000 Lancashire cotton mill workers returned to the factories today ending a strike of nearly a month's duration. Agreement was reached last Friday between the workers and the employers’ demand to institute a “more looms per weaver” system. Although the system gave the workers somewhat better pay they attacked it as throwing other men out of work. Because of the depressed state of the industry, it was not expected that more than 50 to 60 per cent of the workers would find jobs today but reports of revival of trade in India gave considerable hope.

Canton, China, Feb. 16 (One hundred persons drowned in the Pearl River south of here today. A steamer with 500 aboard struck a rock and sank. Those aboard had been celebrating the Chinese New Year.

MADRID, Feb. 16.—(UP)—Don Jose Sanchez Guerra, who has been premier, exile and revolutionary leader, was commissioned by King Alfonso today to solve the governmental crisis by formation of a new cabinet. The choice of Sanchez Guerra, whose 1929 revolt plot against the Primo de Rivera dictatorship failed chiefly because a leaky boat delayed his arrival at Valencia, was made after the King had failed to persuade several Monarchist leaders to succeed the resigned General Damaso Berenguer. Sanchez Guerra is leader of the constitutionalist party, and he has consistently demanded the calling of an assembly to change the constitution of 1876. If he succeeds in forming a cabinet it was considered certain that it would bring about a change in the entire Spanish political system, probably with far-reaching restrictions on the throne. Although Sanchez Guerra is a monarchist of the left wing, he lon

MADRID. UP. King Alfonso conferred with political leaders to form a new cabinet on which may depend the peace of the country and possibly the fate of the throne itself. Considerable difficulty is being experienced in reconciling the conflicting ideologies of the political factions and in obtaining the co-operation of discordant party leaders toward finding a successor to Premier Berenguer, who resigned. The political turmoil may be only increased unless the king succeeds in harmonizing the opposing factions. However, if he does bring them to an agreement by putting some “lefts” in the new government, he will give power to those forces which are openly opposed to the existence of the monarchy. Numerous political meetings which had been scheduled for Sunday in Madrid and elsewhere were suspended by police to prevent possible disorders. The crowds packed the streets around the meeting place
(By United Press) Tokio, Feb. 16—Itaru Matsumuro, Privy Councilor of Japan and former Minister of Justice, died here today.

Baden, Germany, June 16 (F)— The engagement of Prince Berthold Baden, son of the last imperial chancellor, and Princess Theodora, niece of former King Constantine of Greece, was announced today. Prince Berthold's father, Prince Maximilian Baden, died at Constance in 1998. Princess Theodora is the daughter of Prince Andrew of Greece and Princess Alice Mountbatten.

MADRID, Feb. 16. (INS)—King Alfonso XIII bowed to the will of a majority of the country's political leaders today when he accepted the complete formula of Jose Sanchez Guerra, former premier and ex-rebel, for the solution of the country’s constitutional crisis. The formula provides immediate election of a constituent cortes, authorized to decide whether Spain shall continue to be a monarchy or become a republic. Until this decision is made Guerra will hold practically autocratic power in Spain. The announcement of the king's acceptance of Guerra’s program did not state definitely that he will take a vacation in the meantime, but the program means practically that.
