1931-03-13.text: London, March 13,—(A.P.)—The British government is extending an invitation to Mahatma Gandhi, leader of the Indian nationalists, to come to London shortly and participate in further negotiations looking toward granting qualified dominion status to India. Concluding debate on India in the House of Commons last night, J. Ramsey MacDonald, Prime Minister, announced that a second round table conference would be convened in London in the fall, and that prior to that time the federal structure committee of the first conference would meet here. The Prime Minister's announcement was made after the attitude of the opposition parties toward India had been considerably clarified by Stanley Baldwin, Conservative leader, who repledged himself and his workers for striving by every possible means to work out a solution of India’s problems.

POINT BARROW, Mich., March 13.—UP)—Two airplanes bringing a new supply of antitoxin for this diphtheria-stricken village were awaited anxiously today. Joe Crosson and S. E. Robbins, Alaska airmen, left Fairbanks yesterday with the serum. Crosson landed here last Sunday with a quantity of antitoxin, which soon was exhausted. Several new cases have been reported since then, four virulent cases yesterday.

MAESTOG, Wales, March 13 —(— Vernon Hartshorn, lord privy seal since 1930 and formerly president of the South Wales Miners Federation dropped dead at his home here today. The Rt. Hon. Vernon Hartshorn, lord privy seal since 1930, and M. P. from the Ogmore division of Glamorgan-shire since 1918, was fifty-nine years old. He was postmaster-general in 1924, a member of the Indian reforms commission from 1927 to 1930; served on the coal trade organization committee and also on the coal controllers’ advisory committee, and was president of the South Wales Miners’ Federation.

| LONDON, March 13 na — Ramsay MacDonald's government escaped defeat by only five votes in the House of Commons today on a motion to reduce a supplementary estimate of £14,000 (about $70,000) for salaries and expenses of the mines department. Many Laborites voted with the opposition on the motion, which was defeated 173 to 167.

CAIRO, Egypt, March 13 (/)—Excavations on the site of the ancient city of Hermopolis have uncovered several statuettes of Toth, god of writing and science, and a number of Egyptian and Roman sarcophagi.

SHANGHAI—(?)—Two hundred persons were believed drowned when the heavily loaded Chinese passenger steamer Pa Chi blew up and sank in the Yangtse Kiang seventy miles from here. Among the 500 passengers aboard the vessel were a hundred Chinese soldiers who were thought to have thrown their cigarette stubs into the cargo, principally cotton. An explosion followed, spreading fire in the hold. Most of those on the boat jumped over the side where a revenue cruiser was able to pick up a few survivors.

By The Associated Press. NICE, France, March 12.—Long hours of merciless questioning today failed to shake the story of Mrs. Fred G. Nixon-Nirdlinger that when she shot and killed her husband, the Philadelphia theatrical magnate last night, she killed in self-defense. “Do you regret your act?” the police asked her. “If I hadn’t killed him, then he would have killed me,” she said. Friends of Nixon-Nirdlinger and his wife, who was Miss Charlotte Nash of St. Louis, said that he undoubtedly loved his wife very much but was most jealous. Yesterday he engaged detectives to trail her, explaining that he did not intend to use any information he might get against her but simply wanted to know what she was doing. His body is being held at the morgue and while she is being held by police no formal charges have been filed.

NICE, France, March 12--(AP) A story of her husband’s nagging jealousy, which he climaxed with an attempt to strangle her, was told police today by Mrs. Fred G. Nixon-Nirdlinger, who, at midnight, shot and killed the Philadelphia theatrical magnate. Mrs. Nixon-Nirdlinger, who was “Miss St. Louis” and runner-up in the 1923 Atlantic City beauty pageant, was arrested, pending a complete investigation. In substantiation of her plea of self-defense, she exhibited red marks on her throat, which she said were caused by her husband's fingers as he attempted to end a jealous quarrel by choking her to death. The slain theatre man was 54 years old, his wife 26; they were married in 1925, and had two small children. Mrs. Nixon-Nirdlinger told police she was sitting in their apartment last evening when her husband asked her what she was doing. She answered that she was studying Italian. “Because you

SHANGHAI, March 12. (AP)—Seven gunboats comprising the United States Yangtze river patrol have been the targets of not less than thirty-seven bandit attacks since last July, American naval authorities here revealed today. During the same period armed American guards aboard commercial vessels were attacked eighty-seven times. Not once did the roving bands of river shore brigands, with their ancient, rusty, muzzle-loading cannon, succeed in inflicting serious damage on the gunboats patrolling the miles of the Yangtze between Nanking, capital of China, and Chungking, deep in the interior. Scores of bandits fell dead before the fire of machine guns and three-inch rifles manned by American bluejackets. Countless others were wounded, but an accurate check of the dead and injured never was made because surviving brigands invariably carried off the victims.

Nice, France, March 12.—Mrs. Fred G. Nixon-Nirdlinger, dimpled "Miss St. Louis" of an Atlantic City beauty contest eight years ago, waited anxiously in her prison cell tonight while police checked on her story that she acted in self-defense when she shot and killed her husband, a Philadelphia theatre magnate, in their Riviera apartment. Police Physician Peadeleu examined bruises on the 26-year-old beauty’s arms and neck, which she said were inflicted by her husband in an effort to choke her during a jealous quarrel last night. The doctor made a written report saying "the arms and neck showed signs that the woman had been roughly handled." Police found in the Nixon-Nirdlinger apartment a bullet which had pierced the bedroom door at an angle, and this tended further to substantiate the young wife's story that she had fired from her bed. Paris, Nov. 27 (Friday).—The Chamber of Deputies voted confidence in the government by 325 to 240 this morning after a lengthy debate in which the foreign policy of Premier Laval and his trip to the United States were exhaustively discussed. In the course of the debate the Premier declared his government had refused to entertain any proposal linking German private debts with the program of the Bank for International Settlements committee which is to examine Germany's capacity to pay reparations under the Young plan.

, Tokyo, Mar. 3—(/P)— Japan's tiniest bit of royalty was christened Yori Atsuko today on the seventh day after the princess’ birth and shortly thereafter, in strict accordance with time-honored rites, Emperor Hirohito had duly reported the name to the spirits of the imperial ancestors. The name was chosen from the ancient Japanese scriptures, Yori meaning obedience to heaven and Atsuko meaning generosity to those on earth. Princess Yori is the fourth daughter born to their imperial majesties, Emperor Hirohito and Empress Nagako. The sovereign is without a direct male heir to succeed him on the throne of the line unbroken for ages eternal. The name Yori Atsuko was chosen by the Princess’ father. Early this morning the infant was given a ceremonial bath in a newly wrought tub of Hinoki (cypress) wood. Several ladies of the court were in attendance. In a special chamber adjoining the bathro

By United Press BERLIN, March 13.—Eleven persons were stabbed and beaten at Spandau, near Berlin, today during a fight between Fascists and Communists at the Unemployed Labor Exchange. Fourteen Nazis, or Fascists, were arrested.

Nice, France, Mar. 13.—Police investigation of the death of Fred G. Nixon-Nirdlinger indicated today that his widow, the former Charlotte Nash of St. Louis, who admitted shooting her husband, might never face trial for the killing. As police were re-enacting the shooting at the home of the couple on the Promenade des Anglais, it appeared likely that the traditional French attitude toward 'crime passionnel' would come to the aid of the girl who won second honors in the 1924 Atlantic City beauty pageant. Preliminary investigation was said to bear out her contention that she shot in self-defense. It was pointed out that the police had partly verified Mrs. Nixon-Nirdlinger's story by determining the angle at which a bullet found in the wall of the room had been fired. She said she fired the first shot from the bed while her husband was choking her. Doctors said that the bruises on her neck i

| HAMBURG, Germany, Mar, 13 (AP) — Fifteen hundred persons were arrested by police here last night in what was probably the largest political raid ever staged in Germany. Of the 1,500 about 1,200 will be prosecuted for disturbing the peace. Police learned that communists had forged a considerable number of tickets for a meeting of fascists. They waited until about 4,000 persons were in the meeting hall, then closed the doors and conducted a two hour examination of the admission cards to detect the forgeries.

SHANGHAI, March 13—(AP) Additional reports on the sinking of the coastwise steamer, Pachi, indicated today that 262 lives had been lost Wednesday night. The remainder of the 722 persons aboard were saved. First reports gave the death toll at 200 and the number rescued at 180. All who perished were Chinese.

Shanghai, March 12 (®)--More than 200 Chinese perished when the burning Chinese coastal steamer Pachi exploded and sank 60 miles north of the mouth of the Yangtze River last night. A revenue cruiser and native boats picked up 180 of the approximately 400 persons aboard. Those rescued had leaped into the sea from the flaming vessel. The explosion occurred when some of the 100 Chinese soldiers aboard threw cigar stubs into the cotton cargo. Flames whirled through the hold, and a second explosion followed. The cruiser, patrolling near the Pachi, steamed to her aid when she was seen afire, but before the cruiser arrived an explosion killed many passengers on the Pachi's fore deck. Those left aboard the Pachi were drowned, as the vessel sank quickly.
BERLIN, March 13—The former chancellor, Dr. Herman Mueller, who is in here, was said today to be in a serious condition although he spent a quiet night.

Shanghai, March 13.---A sister of General Holung, notorious Communist, led 3,000 Chinese bandits into a fierce battle Friday and met defeat. The woman directed her forces to attack the town of Lachin. As the feminine warrior was crossing the Hupeh-Hunan border, she was met by government troops of the Forty-eighth division under General Hsu Yuan-Chan. In the fighting that followed there were many casualties and the invaders were finally routed.

SHANGHAI, CHINA, (U.P)—An army of 3,000 bandits led by a woman—sister of the communist general Ho-Lung—was defeated today by government troops. The woman led her forces into the battle when they encountered government troops which were protecting the town of Lachih.

1931-03-20.text: LONDON, March 20. — (UP) — Lloyd's correspondent at Alexandria relayed a wireless message today saying the Italian warship Porto Corsini was in distress 30 miles south of Sheduan island. The Lloyd's dispatch said the British steamer City of Dunkirk and the British motor vessel Ortina Shell were proceeding immediately to aid the Porto Corsini. Available atlases do not list a Sheduan island. The island of Shad-Wan is in the Red Sea, near the Gulf of Suez.

LONDON—(#)—Captain A. T. Doff Cooper, husband of Lady Diana Manners, will sit for St. George's division of Mayfair in parliament, having won a bye-election Thursday from Sir Ernest Petter, 17,242 to 11,532. His victory was a vindication of the policies of Stanley Baldwin, conservative leader, and a rejection of the insurgent conservative platform of the Beaverbrook and Rothermere press, which took Sir Ernest's part. Liberals and laborites were not represented, the seat being traditionally conservative. The election campaign was marked by unusual animosities. The servant vote in this section of Mayfair outnumbers the vote of the masters.

LUCKNOW, United Provinces, India — (#) — A Moslem landlord in the Mochi district sent a dead calf to one of his Hindu tenants who was behind in his rent. The Hindu and his friends, who regard any cow as sacred, were infuriated and, going to the landlord’s house, dragged him out and killed him with blows from sticks and scythes. They burned his house and went to other Moslem homes and did likewise. The entire adult male Mohammedan population of Mochi, consisting of seven men, were murdered. The Hindus spared only the women and children. Timely arrival of British troops terminated the massacre, which was spreading to the area adjacent to the village, where five others had been killed.

PISA, ITALY, Mar. 19—(4)—Col. Umberto Maddalena, famous Italian flier and finder of the dirigible Italia survivors, Lieut. Fausto Cecconi and Mechanic Sergeant Damonte were killed today when their seaplane fell into the sea. Maddalena discovered General Umberto Nobile and a group of other survivors of the Italia in 1928 near Spitzbergen and dropped medicine and supplies to them on the ice after the Italian airship had been wrecked on its north pole flight. He and Lieutenant Cecconi formerly held world air records for distance and duration flights and both had recently returned from the Latin-American flight of Air Minister Italo Balbo on which Maddalena was adjutant.

PISA, Italy, March 19.—Three heroes of Italian aviation who would have taken part this summer in a projected group flight from Orbetello, Italy, to New York, plunged to their death today in the sea near here. The dead are: COL. UMBERTO MADDALENA, who in 1925 first sighted Gen. Nobile and the stranded crew of the dirigible Italia. CAPT. FAUSTO CECCONI, former co-holder with Maddalena of the world records for non-refueling endurance and distance flights. SECOND LIEUT. GIUSEPPE DAMONTE, commended with Maddalena and Cecconi on the recent Italian air squadron flight across the South Atlantic to Brazil. The three met death together today as they flew from Sesto Calende to Rome in preparation for an effort to regain the distance and endurance records over a closed circuit, held by Maddalena and Cecconi from last June until less than three weeks ago. Col. Maddalena was piloting the Savoia-Marche

PARIS, March 20.--(UP)—The Paris-Bordeaux express train was derailed at Estampes, 35 miles from Paris, last night in an accident which cost the lives of 9 persons, one of whom died of heart trouble. The accident was one of the most unusual on record. The restaurant and baggage car side-swiped a local train. Then another car of the express was derailed 50 yards further along the track, while still another car was derailed and turned over 760 yards further along. The local train, as well as the express, was seriously damaged, but it carried no passengers.

Shanghai, March 20.—()—(Friday)—Unconfirmed waterfront reports today said 250 persons drowned when the French steamer Chankiang struck a rock and sank in the China Sea off Amoy March 16. The Chankiang carried 300 passengers and crew. Of these, reports said, only 50 were saved. Wireless messages were garbled and reports of the loss of lives may be greatly exaggerated.

PISA, Italy. March 20.—(AP)—A variable propeller of a type which Col. Umberto Maddalena always favored, was blamed today for the disaster which yesterday took the lives of Maddalena and two companions, Capt. Cecconi and Lieut. Damonte. None of the bodies has been recovered. An inquest commission found that the propeller had broken, cutting the fuselage in two when the plane was several thousand feet in the air. The propeller was Maddalena’s specialty. He believed it enabled him to take off with heavier loads of fuel than with an ordinary propeller.

He Goes Down Venice Canal in Triumphal Procession. Venice, Italy, March 19.—(4)—Down the Grand Canal of Venice came Charlie Chaplin this afternoon in a triumphal procession reminiscent of the Pied Piper of Hamlin. Big boats, little boats, motor boats, row boats, steam boats, ferry boats and gondolas tagged along behind his motor launch, Charlie bowed and waved to throngs which filled the windows of famous old palaces along the banks.

TOKYO, March 19 (#)—Opposition to the government of Premier Hamaguchi culminated Thursday in street fighting in which eleven demonstrators and several policemen were injured. Carrying banners reading “dissolve the corrupt diet,” and “overthrow the reactionary Hamaguchi cabinet,” the paraders attacked with sticks police who barred their way to the diet building. The six thousand policemen guarding the parliamentary building charged into the crowd and arrested 140 of the demonstrators. Premier Hamaguchi, severely shot November 14 by a misguided patriot, only recently resumed direction of his government.

1931-01-29.text: LONDON, Jan. 29, (#) — Safely past the most formidable obstacle placed in its path in months, Premier Ramsay MacDonald's labor government today appeared assured of power at least until the presence of the new cabinet next April. The labor members, singing Auld Lang Syne, ganged into the government lobby of the Commons just before midnight last night and repulsed with a 27 majority a conservative attack on the trade dispute act, up for its second hearing. The vote was 227 to 250, Sir John Simon and seven fellow liberals voting with the Tories. A government defeat would have meant resignation. A few minutes later, abstaining Liberals voted with the government to defeat a second motion of Stanley Baldwin, Conservative leader, which would have sent the bill to a committee of the whole instead of a small Standing committee. The vote was 306 to 244. After the members flocked back into the Hous

LONDON, Jan. 8 UEP TEENS atatiie minister Ramsay MacDonald's Labor government fought off two conservative attacks late tonight with the aid of the Liberal party and thus remains in office whereas defeat probably would have meant its immediate resignation. Both victories were on motions offered by Stanley Baldwin, leader of the Conservatives and former premier, against the hotly-contested trades dispute bill. The first was to reject the bill on second reading and this, with most of the Liberals abstaining, brought a vote of 277 against 250, or a margin of 27 for the Labor government. Sir John Simon and a few other Liberals who are opposing the measure in all its stages voted with the Conservatives but with the majority of the balance-of-power party abstaining the administration had sufficient strength to weather one of the most dangerous crises in its more than 19 months of life.
Cork, Irish Free State—(#)—The department of health Thursday closed all the national schools because of an epidemic of influenza. There have been few deaths.

London — (*) — In the Russian church where her body had lain in state since it was brought from Holland, Wednesday, funeral services were held today for Anna Pavlova, the greatest dancer of her age. The rites of the Russian church occupied two and a half hours, beginning with the impressive holy liturgy. In the great congregation were the Russian consul-general, many other figures of international prominence, and several of the dancer’s pupils. The body was cremated at Golders Green, Thursday afternoon.

Ottawa, Jan. 28.—Brig. Gen. Benedict Crowell, assistant secretary of war in the Wilson cabinet, believes Alfred E. Smith of New York is the logical democratic presidential candidate in 1932. General Crowell came to Ottawa today to visit Col. Hanford MacNider, United States minister. The general, an executive of the National Association Against the 18th Amendment, said there had recently been “a great shift in American public opinion against prohibition.”

PARIS, Jan. 29—(P)—Winter tempests lashed many parts of France today while dispatches from the Franco-Italian Alps reported a growing toll of death from avalanches and storms. Heavy snows fell in Southeastern France. According to reports from Chambery, 21 Italian soldiers have been killed by avalanches in the Haute Maurienne section of the Alps during the last few days. Constant snow and the danger of further avalanches hindered rescue workers. Some of the men killed had been dispatched to search for missing comrades. Only five bodies had been recovered today. Forty inches of snow impeded train service near the Italian frontier. Only passenger trains were running, and these were hours behind schedule. Telephone service was disrupted in the region. Three men sent to relieve marooned telephone workers were caught in an avalanche, but were dug out by rescuers.

MADRID, Jan. 29 (AP) — Every university in Spain was closed today by a general strike of students. Police reserves were on duty at all of them. The strike was described as a movement by radical students against the government and for a republic. Martial law continues in Madrid and Saragossa while the censorship has suppressed all details of the strike.

PARIS, Jan. 20—Nelson Morris, Chicago millionaire who for a long time has been trying to keep his actress wife, Jane Aubert, off the stage, filed a suit in Paris courts today against the Frano Film company for $16,000 damages. Morris alleges his wife did a song and dance number for the film company since the court's decision denied her the right to appear on the stage without his permission. He says also in the act his wife was dressed in a costume "offensive to conjugal decency." The case will be heard in the civil tribunal Feb.

Rome —(M)— Italian newspapers incensed at a speech attributed to General Smedley D. Butler of the United States marines, in which he was reported to have made remarks derogatory to Premier Mussolini, Thursday printed editorials characterizing the speech as impudent, insolent and ridiculous. La Tribuna in a headline uses the word “insolent and ridiculous,” declaring in an editorial, “this is not the first time General Butler has created incidents for his government with his impudent, fantastic

1931-01-27.text: POONA, India, Jan. 26—(AP)—Mahatma Gandhi, frail 61-year-old leader of the Indian nationalists, was released from prison shortly after 11 o'clock tonight. They took him out the back way secretly, bundled him into a closed automobile with drawn curtains and drove to a small railway station about ten miles from Poona, where the authorities put him on a train for Bombay.

(Copyright, 1931, by Associated Press) Bombay, Jan. 27.—(4—Tumultuous multitudes surrounded Mahatma Gandhi upon his arrival from Yeroda prison today and gave him one of the greatest ovations of his strange career. Only after hours of cheering and acclamation such as few men have known could he break away, pleading with them: "If you love me, go home. Go home and spin yarn and bring it to me. Copyright 1931, By Associated Press Poona, India, Jan. 27.--(Tuesday)—- India’s mystic agitator, Mahatma Gandhi, was spirited out of Yeroda prison’s gaunt walls in a remarkable midnight drama and astounded his British warders by telling them he soon would be back. It lacked one hour of 12 o'clock last night when he was hustled out the back gate of the penitentiary and placed in a motor car which sped through the darkness of the Poona hills and deposited him on a Bombay train at a point ten miles distant. But before he left, the bent little nationalist leader startled officials with these words: “I expect to be back here within two months. I am not at all happy at the thought of entering again the whirlpool of life in the outside world, with its overwhelming suffering, sorrow and sordidness. LONDON, Jan. 26.—(P)—Premier Ramsay MacDonald warned the House of Commons today that unless Great Britain is willing to continue peaceful negotiations for the settlement of the Indian problem, British soldiers must be prepared to subdue by force not only the Indian masses but also the spirit of the times. Mr. MacDonald said that by a policy of repression Great Britain would obtain neither credit nor success. A great proportion of the masses, he said, were women and children, and the task would develop into one of repression of the entire Indian population. “If we are prepared,” he said, “to stage for the whole world the failure of our political genius and at the same time provide a spectacle which will bring our name and fame very low indeed, then refuse to allow us to go on. “But if, on the other hand, you want to bind India to you by bonds of confidence and make her happy within your e

LONDON, Jan. 27 (#)—Developments in parliament today were believed generally to point to a government victory when the ministry’s trades dispute bill comes up for its second reading tomorrow. So strong has opposition to the measure grown that the prospective division has been regarded with the utmost apprehension by the government. The chief Liberal whip told a party meeting last night that the majority of the Liberals had agreed to abide by the official Liberal decision to abstain from voting and that fewer than twelve Liberals would vote against the government. A motion of censure of the government offered by the orthodox Liberal following criticizes the government on its unemployment record. The motion of censure forestalls a Conservative motion which has been in the offing for weeks. It is generally believed that David Lloyd George, the Liberal leader, has neither wish nor hope for h

Bombay, India, Jan. 27.— Mahatma Gandhi, released last night from the British prison, urged the authorities to liberate thousands of Nationalists still in jail, emphasizing the necessity for a general political amnesty if peace is to be restored in India. Tumultuous multitudes surrounded Gandhi upon his arrival here. They gave him one of the greatest ovations of his strange career. The women garlanded him with flowers and entwined his neck with thousands of yards of material which resembles American ticker tape. Outside the house in which he will stay crowds prostrated themselves before the mystical leader in adoration and worshipped him as if he were a god.

BOMBAY, India, Jan. 27. (UP)— Mahatma M. K. Gandhi, returning to leadership of the Indian independence movement after eight months as a “pampered prisoner” today declared himself anxious for “peace with honor.” “Speaking for myself I am anxious for peace if it can be had with honor,” the thin little spiritual and political leader of millions of Indians said shortly after his arrival at Bombay where tens of thousands of admirers welcomed him, “but even if I stood alone I could be no party to any peace which does not satisfactorily solve three questions: salt, foreign cloth and liquor.” “The reprehensible ordinances invoked by the viceroy, Lord Irwin, must be withdrawn in recognition of the elementary rights of Indians before the civil disobedience can end,” the Mahatma said.

SOTODBY, 200018, Jah. ci. (iar) - Mahatma Gandhi served notice on Great Britain today that regardless of progress in the establishment of self-government in India, a Congress including a campaign of civil disobedience will continue unabated. The Nationalist boycott of foreign cloth, the party’s refusal to pay taxes and its picketing of liquor, drug and cloth shops will go on. The Mahatma, idol of millions, issued this first concrete statement of the policy of his party as he sat Hindu fashion on a stone floor here, surrounded by newspaper men. It was the first statement of the kind since his release from the prison at Poona last night. Gandhi emphatically endorsed immediate measures for India’s full independence as outlined in a resolution by the Congress party last year. “We can suspend judgment on Prime Minister MacDonald’s statement of policy at the round table conference in London,”

Gandhi, leader of the Indian Nationalists, served notice on Great Britain today that his efforts in behalf of Indian independence cannot cease. Greeted by thousands of his followers on his arrival here from Poona, the 61-year old ascetic announced that his campaign of civil disobedience against British rule would continue “until all political prisoners have been released and all repressive ordinances cancelled.” Urges Continuance Gandhi declared that the Indian Nationalist movement was no longer controllable by a few “front rank leaders.” “It has become broad-based,” he said, “and the large numbers of local leaders thrown into prison alone are able to deliver the goods.” He urged continuance of civil disobedience pending discus

Gandhi appeared before tens of thousands of hysterical followers last night at the esplanade Maidan, where he was caught like a tiny shadow in a swirling mass that quickly got beyond control of the congress officials. The crowd—estimated at 200,000, with thousands more unable to crowd into the esplanade—raised such a tumult that none but the wizened little mahatma could control them. Gandhi raised his hands before the throng and they began dispersing, shouting joyously. Gandhi was received with deep reverence and wild acclaim when he arrived here by train today. The frail Indian, clad in the usual loin cloth, received garlands from many of his followers. A poor woman entered his railway carriage and prostrated herself at his feet. Gandhi helped lift her up, and signalled to the immense crowd of his admirers to allow him to leave the train. In

Bombay, Jan. 27 (UP)—Mahatma M. K. Gandhi, Indian nationalist leader, who was released from prison at Poona today, was received with deep reverence and wild acclaim when he arrived here by train. The frail Indian, clad in the usual loin cloth, received garlands from many of his followers along the route. Gandhi insisted on spinning during the latter part of his train journey. At various suburban stations outside Bombay he smiled at the hundreds who were on the platform to get a glimpse of him, but he never ceased spinning, a symbol of the development of Indian national industry. In a talk with interviewers, Gandhi made an appeal for the release of 50,000 political prisoners arrested during his civil obedience campaign. One Moslem was killed and 50 persons were injured in fighting between Moslems and Hindus coincident with the release from prison of Mahatma Gandhi. Police fired on the mob

BOMBAY, Jan. 27 (4#)—Mahatma Gandhi has learned to like prison. After several hours on the train from Chinchwad to Bombay Gandhi, who had been very quiet, turned to the Associated Press correspondent, the only newspaperman allowed to accompany him, and said: "I don't like the commotion and tumult of the outer world. "That is why prison, despite its isolation and loneliness, gives one the joys of peace, calm meditation and inner serenity."

DOORN, Holland, Jan. 27. (AP). —His once imperial majesty, William Hohenzollern, today celebrated his seventy-second birthday quietly at Doorn house in the Dutch village of his exile. Many messages of congratulation came from Germany and a number from American friends. Here, where the former Kaiser lives like a country squire, he worked as usual in his Rosarium, digging and chopping wood like one of his Dutch laborers. His daily constitutional through the village was part of his birthday routine. Most of his family were present except Prince Oscar, who has been operated upon and is recuperating in a Berlin hospital.

PARIS, Jan. 27, (AP)—Premier Pierre Laval took the new French cabinet to the Elysee Palace this forenoon and presented the members to President Doumergue. After the presentation, they were sworn in and left to begin work on the ministerial declaration on which they will seek a vote of confidence in the Chamber of Deputies probably Friday.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 27—(UP)— Dispatches received here today said that G. W. Brophy, aviator who had been missing was safe at Hunghsai. It was believed that he became lost in a snow storm while flying from Foochow to Canton. He was long overdue at the latter city. Brophy was on a lap of his proposed flight from Shanghai to Manila when he disappeared.

PARIS, Jan. 27 — Senator Pierre Laval presented a new cabinet to President Gaston Doumergue today. It was formed with the support of Ex-Premier Tardieu, and contains ten members of the Tardieu government which was overthrown in December. Tardieu holds the post of Minister of Agriculture in the new cabinet. His influence in aiding Laval to form a cabinet was obvious, for Laval failed in the same task during the pre-Christmas crisis. Laval announced the completion of a cabinet early today and then went to his home, worn out by 48 hours of almost unbroken political conferences. He was pleased at his success, but disappointed that the attitude of the radical socialists, who declined to support him, caused him to form a more conservative combination than he had intended.

Paris, Jan. 27—(Tuesday)—(— Pierre Laval, who has been working several days to assemble a new French cabinet, succeeded definitely in lining up his ministries at 1:30 o'clock Tuesday morning. Laval—who incidentally is only 47 years old and thus probably the youngest premier France has ever seen—formed his cabinet only after tortuous negotiations. It leans to the right even more than did the last Tardien ministry, defections among the radicals having made “the republican reconciliation” ministry desired by the new premier impossible. Laval will present his ministers to President Gaston Doumergue Tuesday morning and they will get to work without delay. Observers believe that their chances for survival are slight and that the country soon will go through another period of premier hunting.
Doorn, Holland, Jan. 27—Wilhelm Hohenzollern, who abdicated his title of Kaiser when he left Germany in 1918, observed his 72nd birthday in simple fashion today at Doorn House.

ZURICH, Switzerland, Jan. 27. (AP)—M. V. Bianchi, Italian consul general here, was shot three times today by a former Italian soldier named Bassi, whom Bianchi had declined to give financial aid. Bianchi was wounded in the chest, the stomach, and one hand.

DOORN, Holland, Jan. 27. (AP) — Former Kaiser Wilhelm celebrated his 72nd birthday today, but grippe which gets prince as well as commoner cast a shadow over the anniversary as some of his closest relatives were unable to attend. Only former Crown Prince Friedrich Wilhelm with his second son, Louis Ferdinand, Prince Adalbert, and Prince August Wilhelm, with his son, Alexander, were able to felicitate the former emperor personally at his place of exile. The other Hohenzollerns, including the former Kaiser’s only daughter, Princess Victoria, his only sister, Princess Margaret of Hesse, former Crown Princess Cecile, and Princess Adelbert, all of whom regularly attended in other years, were prevented from coming to Doorn by the illness, which is raging in many parts of Germany. Princess Oscar still is suffering from the after-effects of an appendicitis operation.

HAMBURG, Germany, Jan. 27.— Fifty policemen joined with fascists to do battle with 200 communists who attempted to interrupt a fascist meeting here last night. One person was killed in the shooting which accompanied the fracas and three police and two communists were seriously wounded. Three fascists were slightly injured while seventeen communists suffered from knife thrusts.

THE HAGUE, Jan. 27 (UP) — Memorial services were held here today for Mme. Anna Pavlova, the Russian ballerina, who died here last week. The body will be sent to London tonight where it will lie in state before cremation.

PARIS, Jan. 27.—Senator Pierre Laval, son of a country butcher, and at 47 one of the youngest men to reach the head of the French government, today completed a ministry of the Right and immediately began formulation of a declaration of policy on which he will face the chamber of deputies probably Thursday or Friday. The political complexion of the new government, which does not come into official being until given a vote of confidence by the chamber, is much like that of Andre Tardieu, who resigned in December. Radical Socialists refused to participate. The new ministry lists Tardieu in the portfolio of agriculture, where he may handle the growing wheat problem. Aristide Briand is back at the Quai D’Orsay. Politicians generally today were doubtful of the cabinet’s chances of survival in the first test of strength in the chamber.

1931-01-23.text: New Delhi, India, Jan. 23—Viceroy Lord Irwin, it was understood here today, already has made a decision to release Mahatma Gandhi, imprisoned nationalist leader. Only the details of his removal from Yeroda prison, Poona, so as to avoid a public demonstration remain to be arranged. The Mahatma was arrested last May 4 more than a month after he had led a group of all-India national congress volunteers from Allahabad down to the sea at Dandi where they manufactured salt in defiance of British law.

New Delhi, India, Jan. 28 — An announcement by Viceroy Lord Irwin of the release from prison of Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru and other leaders of the All-India National Congress was expected momentarily today. A defense of general amnesty for 50,000 political prisoners was expected to follow the release of Congress executives, although consultation with provincial governments would be necessary before wholesale releases begin. Hot Springs, Ark., Jan. 23. -- Ban Johnson, former president of the American League, entered St. Joseph's Hospital today to undergo an operation for amputation of a toe.

London, Jan. 23 (UP)—The renewal of menacing attacks on the cabinet of Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald, coupled with the economic depression and growth of unemployment, can cause serious discussion in some quarters today of the possibility of a "constitutional dictatorship." Political sources which look at the fear of such a system in England have considered, however, some other manner of radical alteration in the Parliamentary machinery. Meanwhile, coincident with the defeat of the cabinet on the school attendance bill and uncertainty regarding the trade dispute bill crisis, there has been a deliberate effort in the last two days to center attention of the nation on proposals for a virtual dictatorship. GRANADA, Spain, May 16 — Four persons were killed and ten injured during the night at nearby Atarfe when residents of the little town attempted to defend their church against incendiarism. Word was spread about Atarfe that a band of anti-church demonstrators were coming to burn their church, after having destroyed the convent at Santa Fe, and they gathered on the outskirts of the village to repel them. They attempted to stop an automobile filled with men coming from the direction of Santa Fe, firing at it. Those in the car fired back at them, killing three of the townsmen as the car careened off to the side and ran into a wall. The chauffeur was killed. Those riding in the automobile told authorities investigating the affair that they had had nothing to do with the attack on the Santa Fe convent, which was damaged but not destroyed, and that they had fired at the townsmen thinking them t

The Hague, Jan. 23.—()——Death today stilled forever the dainty fragile form of Anna Pavlova, whose dancing stirred millions, civilized man and savage alike. She would have been 46 years old January 31. Pneumonia and influenza, contracted early this week after she had been held for hours by a railroad accident in a waiting train at Dijon, France, rang down the curtain upon a life which for 35 years she devoted to depicting in rhythmic movement the beauty she saw around her. With her at the end were her husband and accompanist, Victor D’Andre, two Dutch physicians, and her own Russian doctor, Professor Valerski, who yesterday resorted to a pulmonary operation in a vain attempt to save her life. Death interrupted her plans to interpret for occidentals what she had found of grace and beauty in a recent visit to Japan, China, and Asiatic countries. Upon completion of this project she intended

PARIS, Jan. 28 (AP) — For the seventh time in the life of the present parliament President Gaston Doumergue today cast about for strong steady hands to take the reins of the French government and hold them against the straining of the badly teamed parties of the chamber of deputies. Conferences were begun with presidents of the chamber and senate and parliamentary committees for a premier-designate to succeed Theodore Stegg, whose ministry fell in the chamber last night, 293 to 283, after a life of 40 days. His was the 85th government of the third republic. The defeat came on a question of confidence posed after interpellation on the efforts of the ministry of agriculture, headed by Victor Boret, to fix the price of wheat in France at about $2 a bushel.

| THE HAGUE, (UP).—Anna Pavlova, world famous dancer acclaimed as one of the greatest artists of her time, died here at the Hotel Des Indes early Friday. She was stricken with pleurisy Tuesday. Pavlova would have been 46 years old on January 31. She contracted a chill en route to The Hague when she was forced to remain in the open air for a long time due to a railroad wreck near Dijon, France. She was ill when she arrived here. Pavlova's rise in the dancing world brought her the same position that was accorded in the theater to the great Sarah Bernhardt. Her triumph in America was sensational. Her engagements included not only the usual “star” presentations in the opera houses of great cities but also performances in small towns, in amusement halls and small vaudeville houses where the name of a European actress was scarcely known. PARIS, Jan. 23. (Pj)—The French chamber of deputies overthrew the government of Premier Theodore Steeg, 293 votes to 283, serving notice that France will not pay two dollars per bushel for wheat while it is 80 cents in Chicago and 60 cents in Winnipeg. The government had sought to stabilize the price at two dollars.

The Hague, Jan. 23 (Friday) (P) Mme. Anna Pavlova, 45, considered the world’s greatest ballerina, died early today after a three-day illness from influenza and pleurisy. The dancer fell ill January 20 after she had come here on tour from Paris and at first it was believed that she merely was suffering from the grippe as the result of a slight cold contracted in Paris. Later the combination of pleurisy and influenza developed, which was complicated by a weakness of the heart. Geneva, Jan. 22.—(U.R)—The world disarmament conference will be convened Feb. 2, 1932, the council of the league of nations decided today after deliberations on the most favorable date for calling the long-awaited meeting for reduction and limitation of war materials. The chairman of the conference will be announced at the May sessions of the council.

Berlin, Pan. 23. — An official announcement at Odessa said that 54 passengers were drowned when a steamer foundered in the Black Sea during a storm, the Moscow correspondent of the newspaper Zeitung Am Mittag reported today. “The report said that 17 fishing boats were missing after the storm, and that warships were searching for them.

MADRID, Jan. 22. (#)—Students at the University of Madrid declared a strike today as a protest against the Berenguer government, boycotted their classes and gathered to hear speakers who demanded establishment of a republic in Spain. The monarchy was denounced at meetings in the university buildings and many professors joined 3,000 student members of the university scholars’ federation in the strike. One of them asserted that since Spain had no constitution there was no reason for him to lecture his classes on political law.

Chancellor Bruening, arriving here today for a conference with Saxon industrialists, was greeted at the railway station by crowds of unemployed who shouted, “down with him,” and milled around his automobile until mounted police dispersed them. The crowd gathered again in front of his hotel but was driven off without serious disorder.

PARIS, Jan. 22.—(UP)—The brief and tumultuous career of the government headed by Premier Theodore Steeg came to an abrupt end today when the cabinet was defeated in the chamber of deputies on its farm relief program. France, for the twentieth time since the World War, was without a government. The vote of 293 to 283 was announced amid the wildest excitement among deputies of the right and center groups, and complete silence on the left. The slim majority of 10 votes for the opposition was sufficient, and members of the cabinet, led by Premier Steeg, at once proceeded with the routine of drawing up a formal letter of resignation. (Continued on Page 2, Col. 2.)

PARIS, (UP).—The French political crisis, carried over from the holidays by agreement among the enemies of ex-Premier Theodore Steeg, confronted President Gaston Doumergue and political leaders in a more menacing form than ever Friday. The president requested Steeg, whose government was overthrown on its wheat policy in the chamber of deputies by a vote of 293 to 283 Thursday, to continue in office temporarily while efforts were hastened to form a new ministry. Doumergue exhausted his supply of possible premiers before Steeg formed a cabinet in December, after it had been intimated in well-informed quarters that the president would resort to dissolution of parliament and new elections unless political parties settled their differences. 1931-01-18.text: MANCHESTER, England, Jan. 17 (P)—Lancashire cotton mills were closed today against 250,000 weavers, whose representatives have refused to accept a “more looms per weaver” system inaugurated by the mill owners. The lockout brought England face to face with an even more serious labor crisis than represented by the South Wales coal mine strike on the same day that the Wales coal strike officially ends, allowing 150,000 miners there to go back to work. In addition to the weavers, 250,000 spinners and members of the various finishing trades also will be laid off shortly, since without the weavers there will be no work for them to do. This will bring the number affected by the Lancashire lockout to about half a million.

MANCHESTER, Eng. Jan. 17— Lancashire cotton spinning mill owners made good their threat of a lockout today when 700,000 looms stopped operating promptly at noon, putting 200,000 operatives out of work. The mill owners had threatened last night to put the lockout into effect today if the workers did not meet certain of the operators’ demands. The chief one of which was operation of eight looms by each individual. Workers refused. No further negotiations were arranged.

LONDON, Jan. 17—Dispatches to the Evening News from Calcutta today said four persons had been killed and twenty others injured in rioting at Jhalda in the Bihar province of Bengal. The reports said police used guns to defend themselves against a mob which refused to disperse.

Cardiff, Wales, Jan. 17.—(AP)—By a vote of 169 to 72 the Wales miners’ union tonight voted to accept the terms of a provisional settlement reached with the mine owners last Thursday and to go back to work on Monday. This ends the strike which began on January 1 and affected 150,000 men.

| WARSAW, POLAND, JAN. 17. (AP).—Orders to hunt down and destroy every American apple in Poland went out to all cities and larger towns of Poland today. | The health authorities some time ago prohibited the sale of apples from America alleging they had been sprayed with arsenic but despite the prohibition there was evidence that the American apples still continued to penetrate the market, hence the extermination order.

AMSTERDAM, Holland—A destructive storm ravaged Holland Saturday. Telegraph and telephone lines were badly damaged. Shipping and other traffic was disrupted and several floods were reported in various sections of the country.

Paris, Jan. 17.—(UP)—The Prince of Wales and Prince George left tonight for Santander, where they will board the S.S. Oropesa en route to Central and South America. The two princes, who arrived here yesterday from London by airplane, abandoned air travel until they reach South America. They left Paris at 8:40 p.m. on an overnight train bound for the famous Spanish coastal resort where King Alfonso has his summer residence. From Santander, the Oropesa will go to Vigo and, after leaving the European coast, strike out across the Atlantic for Bermuda, where it is scheduled to arrive January 27. The two princes will spend only about ten hours in Bermuda.

1931-02-20.text: By The Associated Press. LONDON, Feb. 20.—High winds with accompanying rain, sleet and snow, lashed a large part of Europe today, disrupting traffic and in many places hampering communications. A heavy choking fog which spread over England cleared today and residents of the southern counties were comparatively comfortable, but Spain, France, Belgium, Northern Italy, Germany and Scandinavia were hard hit. High seas caused a number of shipping accidents. There were 456 deaths from influenza in the larger cities of England during the week, an increase of 125 over the week before.

LONDON, Feb. 19, (#) — A shy little man with eloquent feet was ‘England's greatest hero today. It was Charlie Chaplin, of course, coming home for the second time since he left his London attic to seek his fortune twenty years ago. Ever since it became known that he was returning, the newspapers have maintained a barrage about him and today they followed him with bulletins from his ship to London. A tremendous welcome began the moment he stepped off the boat at Plymouth and it continued as the boat train sped through the countryside on a schedule the movie fans knew by heart.

CROYDON, AIRDROME, ENGLAND, (U.P)—The Hon. Mrs. Victor Bruce, ending her 20,000 mile airplane trip around the world, announced today that she hoped to ‘make a trans-Atlantic flight to South America within the next few weeks. “I would like to help British aviation by flying to Buenos Aires during the British Trade Exhibition, which opens March 14,” Mrs. Bruce said. “The sea flight involved is only 1,250 miles. I would not mind that.” Mrs. Bruce visited 23 countries and three continents. She started her trip from Beston Air Park, Middlesex, on Sept. 25, 1930, seven weeks after she learned to fly. Mrs. Bruce holds 17 world motor records for women.

London, Feb. 19, (4°)—Charlie Chaplin hopes for quiet days during his visit to England, he told reporters today, but if his first day was a sample he will play the lead in a long mob scene. The little comedian landed at Plymouth this morning on the second visit he has made to his homeland in 20 years, and from the moment the Mauretania cast anchor until he reached his London hotel, and even then, he was besieged by crowds. All this was very well, Charlie said in the privacy of his royal suite which the hotel had reserved for him, but he wanted to walk about unknown in the streets he knew as a poor youth. He even hinted that he might don a disguise.

LONDON, Feb. 13.--Capt Malcolm Campbell, who returned home today after establishing a new automobile speed record in the United States, has been made a knight by King George, it was announced this afternoon.

LONDON, Feb. 20, — England welcomed home two popular heroes today, one a king of speed and the other the most famous exponent of pantomime, Captain Malcolm Campbell and Charlie Chaplin. Captain Campbell, who set a world land speed record in his Bluebird racing automobile at Daytona Beach, did not live up to his speed reputation when he arrived at Southampton so late that a banquet in his honor was held without him. The liner Mauretania ran aground off West Drambles and remained stuck in the mud for three and a half hours. Chaplin disembarked from the Mauretania at Plymouth glad to reach his native land and get off the liner that had kept him sea-sick during the Atlantic crossing. Chaplin said he still was using the same cane and the weird pair of shoes with which he began his career in moving pictures, and which have helped him to make millions of cinema-goers laugh.

LONDON, Feb. 20—(2)—Charlie Chaplin slipped out a side door of his hotel today and set off down Pall Mall for a quiet walk, incognito, so to speak. Before he had gone 50 yards a street sweeper spied him, flung his hat in the air and cried, “Wot cheer, Charlie old boy.” Instinctively Chaplin waved back and in a moment he was the center of a crowd in the middle of Trafalgar Square. He escaped in a cab.

LONDON, Feb. 19. (AP) — Much of Europe today was in the grip of winter weather with extremely low temperatures and considerable snow. In some of the northern districts highway traffic was greatly impeded by drifts. A northeasterly gale raised dangerous seas in the North Sea and about the eastern and southeastern coasts of England - though the British Isles escaped the extremities of the continental weather.

CROYDON, Eng., Feb. 20, (#)— Mrs. Victor Bruce, British woman aviator, came down here in her Bluebird plane from Lympne airdrome this afternoon, completing a trip around the world by sea and air. Frederick Montague, under secretary of state for air, and a group of other notables were here to meet her. In the flight from Lympne she was escorted by several planes whose pilots included Amy Johnson, Winifred Spooner and Squadron Leader Ridley.

Madrid, Feb. 19. (4)—Spain’s new cabinet, headed by Premier Juan Bautista Aznar, in his first official meeting tonight decided on the calling of elections and the establishment of a constitutional government as soon as possible. Other important policies are a plan to give administrative independence to the Catalonian district and another to better the status of the peseta, Spanish monetary unit. As the first important matter the cabinet will fix dates for municipal, provincial and parliamentary elections in their respective order, the government promising complete sincerity in all. Then the ministry will turn its attention to improving the value of the peseta, will revise some of the repressive acts decreed under the seven-year dictatorship of Primo de Rivera, and will present a bill in the new parliament for administrative independence of Catalonia.
