BERNE, SWITZERLAND, FEB. 20. (AP).—A family of seven, including two children, was believed to have perished near Grisons today when an avalanche hurtling down the mountainside crushed a house and buried the debris under 20 feet of snow. Two bodies were recovered, but at mid-afternoon five persons were believed still buried.

PARIS, Feb. 20.—(AP)—Mrs. Charles A. Levine, wife of the American aviation enthusiast and former junk dealer, today took up residence in Paris preparatory to obtaining a divorce. In a published statement she said that former Magistrate Henry M. R. Goodman of New York, who came to Europe aboard the Roman, which also carried Mrs. Levine, would act as her attorney.

MADRID, Feb. 19.—(4)—Limited revision and modernization of the Spanish constitution of 1876 is expected from the new government of Premier Juan Bautista Aznar, whose monarchist ministry meets this evening in first formal session. “We shall call municipal elections first,” Admiral Aznar said, “Then we shall have balloting for provincial deputations and finally parliamentary elections.” The parliament probably will be brought together several months from now, but will not have the power of “constituent cortes” demanded by the republicans and parties of the left. They wished it to decide if Spain should continue a monarchy or should become a republic. The premier said, “Reforms of certain clauses of the constitution of 1876” would be asked but he did not indicate which clauses he re-

BY THE ASSOCIATED PRESS, Genoa, Italy, Feb. 19.—General Italo Balbo, returning in triumph from his recent flight to Brazil, hinted tonight that he plans to lead a formation flight to New York. Genoa was a riot of bunting and cheering crowds when the steamer Conte Rosso warped into the dock and Balbo, followed by his 43 companions on the Brazil flight, marched through lanes of the black shirt militia to the city hall where Mayor Broccardi gave him the key to the city.

MADRID, Feb. 20 (AP)—To decide whether to call a general strike as a protest against the new monarchist government of Premier Admiral Juan Aznar Y. Cabanas, the executive committee of the Socialist party and the General Labor Union will meet tomorrow. The committee is to choose between postponement of the strike attempt until the government's program is further developed and ordering it immediately. If the latter course is chosen it will constitute the first test of the new government's ability to maintain order. General strikes heretofore in Spain have caused serious disorder. The new government has announced that while it intends to do its utmost to preserve popular liberties, it will resort to iron-fisted methods if necessary to preserve public order. The strike of taxicab and motor transport operators in Madrid which has been called for tonight was ordered postponed at noon pending t

Madrid, Spain, Feb. 20.—(AP)— Taken by surprise at the monarchist union which has permitted formation of a government under Premier Admiral Juan Aznar y Cabanas, socialists, republicans and other radical elements were believed to be marking time before renewing active opposition to the throne. Although Spain continues tranquil, there were reports that the socialist and labor leaders were planning a general strike, withholding action temporarily in order to witness the governmental program in full swing. A meeting of the socialists and general workers’ union has been called for tomorrow to formulate a program. Two linotype operators who broke a strike called by that group yesterday were badly beaten by a group of strikers last night. Police broke up a demonstration of 200 strikers in front of the residence of Dr. Jose Maria Albinana, nationalist party leader. Catalonia, turbulent south Sp

SANTANDER, Spain, Feb. 20.—(®)—Rain fell today in Santander, Biscay, port of northern Spain, for the sixty-third consecutive day. It was mixed with snow and hail and provided thoroughly miserable weather for inhabitants of this district, who would like very much to see the sun shine again. A terrific storm has raged for many hours at sea and the movement of ships has been greatly impeded. Trains have been delayed and some are not arriving at their destination at all. Leon dispatches say intense cold prevails there, with snow five feet deep in nearby localities. Heavy snow has blocked highways about Bilbao. Considerable rain and snow have fallen about Logrono.

1931-01-30.text: | WHITEHAVEN, Cumberland, Eng., Jan. 30. (AP) — Twenty-eight coal miners are known to have been killed in an explosion which buried them in the deep Haig pit here yesterday. The total was computed by mine officials who issued a casualty list at noon. Sixteen bodies had been recovered at that hour. All the others had been located and were being brought out as quickly as possible. Twenty-five miners were brought out alive. Twelve of them are in serious condition in a hospital. The mine owners said a number of men caught on the fringe of the explosion turned back into the gas-filled passages and rescued some of the injured. But for them the death toll would have been higher. The cause of the accident has not been determined.

LONDON, Jan. 30—(AP)—Birth of a new faction within the ranks of the Conservative party was seen today as the probable result of disagreement on Indian policy between Stanley Baldwin and the outspoken Winston Churchill. From correspondence between the two Conservative leaders just published, it appears that Churchill, while his "warm personal friendship" for Baldwin is undiminished, thinks it best that he abstain from meetings of the party's business committee—or was council—which is composed of the inner few and includes chiefly, former cabinet ministers. Baldwin, while equally warm in his personal remarks, accepts Churchill's view that he should cease attending the cabinet meetings.

By The Associated Press. Ottawa, Canada, Jan. 29. — Premier Bennet entrained for Washington at 3:30 o'clock this afternoon. The United States minister to Canada, Col. Hansore MacNider, boarded the same train for the United States capitol.

London, Jan. 29.—(4?)—Princess Beatrice, daughter of one queen and mother of another, lay gravely ill at Kensington palace tonight but her aged face was lighted with a smile of happiness. For her daughter, Queen Victoria of Spain, arrived today to tend her. A slight improvement in the princess’ condition was noted in a bulletin issued tonight.

London, Jan. 30—(INS)—Many prominent persons, including several members of European royal families, are stricken today with grippe, influenza and allied ailments. The epidemic is sweeping all Europe. The list of sufferers includes the following: London: Princess Beatrice, aunt of King George and mother of the Queen of Spain, suffering from acute bronchitis, whose condition is considered serious. The Marquess of Reading, former Viceroy of India and wartime ambassador to the United States, confined to his house with an attack of influenza. Evelyn Laye, British musical comedy and talkie star, suffering from bronchitis. Madrid: Princess Isabella, aunt of King Alfonso, recovering from an attack of grippe. Sofia: Queen Joanna, formerly Princess Yolanda of Italy, suffering from influenza. Her condition is considered serious but not grave. Prince Cyril, brother of King Boris, recovering from an

By The Associated Press. Madrid, Spain, Jan. 29.—Rioting by republican students flared in Spain today, adding uneasiness to a political situation already muddled by the refusal of all parties except the extreme right monarchists to participate in the March 1 parliamentary elections.

BERNE, Switzerland, Jan. 30.—(P)—Three English women, whose names were not learned, and a Swiss guide were buried in an avalanche near Eggishorn on Wednesday, word received here today said. There were a party of six tourists and three guides. Rescue parties found two women and two guides near Riederalp. The bodies of the others have not been recovered.

Rome—Apology by the United States for allegedly derogatory remarks made by Maj. Gen. Smedley D. Butler about Premier Mussolini appeared Thursday night to have closed what might have developed into an unpleasant incident. While the premier was described as being naturally somewhat annoyed, official circles said he considered that Butler’s views were those of only one American general and not of the American people. The promptness of the official American apology completely satisfied Il Duce, it was said, and the evening papers did not even comment on the affair. But morning papers, issued before the apology became known, were incensed. La Tribuna described the marine officer's remarks as insolent, impudent and ridiculous.

RIS, Jan. 30.—(UP)—The affairs of King Carol and Princess Helen of Roumania were the subject of renewed rumors today in the chancellories, where it was said the Princess had insisted that Parliament consider what was described as a “bill of rights” for queens. Dramatic sources said came from Bucharest, related that the princess, on advice of her lawyers, had presented an ultimatum to the king in which she insisted upon complete separation and the custody of her son, Crown Prince Michael. It was recalled that the king, after failing in efforts toward reconciliation with Princess Helene, who even refused to accept the title of queen, placed Michael in military school over her protests. Princess Helene was said to be convinced that Carol's sworn reform upon his return from exile in a Normandy chateau, which he shared with auburn-haired Mme. Macda Lupescu, has its loopholes. She has professe

ROME, Jan. 30.- The annoyance of Premier Mussolini at remarks of Major General Smedley D. Butler describing him as a hit and run driver and of a war-like nature was said in official circles today to have been assuaged by an official apology from the American government. The Duce was represented as considering now that General Butler's views were those of only one American general and not of the American people. His attitude has calmed somewhat a rising tide of popular indignation and appears to have closed what might have been an unpleasant incident.

1931-02-21.text: LONDON, Feb. 21. — King George today conferred a knighthood on Captain Malcolm Campbell, the world's motor car speed king. The knighthood was in recognition of Campbell's accomplishment at Daytona Beach, Fla., where he set a world speed record by driving 245.73 miles an hour in his car, “Blue Bird II,” Feb. 5. The ceremony in which the racing driver, who came home to England from his conquests in America as a popular conquering hero, was at Buckingham Palace.

LONDON, Feb. 21. (W.P)—Twenty-five were killed, 14 were injured and three are missing in a mine blast at Eschweiler, it was officially announced today. The explosion was caused by black-damp, preliminary investigation revealed. Eschweiler is near Aix La Chapelle, on the German-Belgian border.

LONDON, Feb. 21, (/)—Captain Malcolm Campbell walked into Buckingham Palace this morning, spent 40 minutes with King George, and came out Sir Malcolm Campbell, his majesty having bestowed upon him the accolade of knighthood. The honor was in recognition of the captain’s feat of driving an automobile 246 miles an hour on the sands of Daytona Beach, Fla, on Feb. 5.

LONDON, Feb. 21.—One of Scotland Yard’s greatest chiefs, Sir Edward R. Henry, who brought fingerprints to their great importance in criminology, was mourned today by London “Bobby” and skilled detective alike. He died during the night at the age of 80. Sir Edward began his studies of fingerprints while a member of the Indian civil service many years ago and continued research during the years he was with Scotland Yard. He established that there was only one chance in 640,000,000,000 of two fingerprints being identical.

LONDON, Feb. 20. (P) Avalanches in the Alps today were reported to have taken 15 lives, including nine Sularen. At two separate places today. Advices from Berne, Switzerland, said a family of seven, including two children, were thought to have perished in an avalanche that hurtled down the mountainside, crushing and partly carrying away the Post hotel in Lukmanier pass in the canton of Grisons.

London, Feb. 21 WPi—Bodies of 14 dead and 14 injured have been recovered from the pit of a mine wrecked in a mine damp explosion at Eschweller, near Aix la Chapelle. The fate of 13 others known to be below the surface was unknown. More than 30 others believed to have been below when the blast snuffed out the lives of their companions escaped.

New York, Feb. 20 (4)—The stock market boiled up briskly today, sending share prices to fresh high levels for 1931. There were bright spots in the day's business news, particularly a report showing a cheering pickup in building contracts, but in addition, bulls used an old-time, and of late rather neglected expedient to blow up the speculative fires—merger talk. Since the market boiled over on Tuesday, it had merely simmered until today, when trading swelled to 3,800,000 shares, the largest for a rising market since the bear stampede early last week. Progress was rather uneven, such a traditional leader as United States Steel common ending the day with a loss of 37 cents at $147.87 a share, after reaching a new top for 1931 at $149. Rails and coppers also held back, but utility, communication, motor and chemical issues were bid up vigorously. Net gains of $1 or $4 were numerous, while a

VIENNA, Feb. 21.—(AP)—Precautions for the safety of King Zog I, 36, self-made monarch of Albania, were redoubled today as police investigated an unsuccessful attempt against his life as he left the opera last night. The king’s adjutant, Maj. Topolai, received one of the twelve bullets intended for the monarch and was killed instantly. Another bullet wounded an Albanian court official, M. Lipozova, in the hip. The two assassins, who gave their names as Asiz Cami and Nadk Tielezi, were captured by chauffeurs of other cars standing behind the royal vehicle. They were badly manhandled. Questioning brought no other explanation than they had acted through political motives. A blood feud exists among the Albanian mountaineers against the king and there have been frequent attempts to kill him. He rarely emerges from his palace at Tirana without clouding his movements. He came to Vienna last mont

WARSAW, Poland, Feb. 29. — Brutal truth in the remote village of Zagajniki has proved stranger than the fiction which has laughed away a preposterous when Henry Rostworowski, Polish dramatist, wrote it as a play. Andrew Cygan, as this real life drama goes, came home to that little town after 18 years of hard work and thrifty living in America. Late in the night, according to the story the villagers tell, he knocked at the door of the cottage where his aged parents lived. His mother let him in, but the only light in the single room came from a fire on the hearth. It was too faint for the old eyes of his parents to recognize their son. He decided to pose as a stranger. Late into the night he sat with the old folks beside the fire and told them of the wonders of the new world, showing them a wallet bulging with money. A look of grim understanding passed between the old man and his wife, and

| VIENNA, Feb. 10.—King Zog of Albania, one of the most closely guarded monarchs of Europe, whose life has been plotted against many times, was fired at tonight by would-be assassins, but escaped injury. The king was leaving the Vienna Opera house, surrounded by his staff, when several shots were fired into the group. The bullets missed the king but his adjutant, Major Topolai, fell dead and a court officer, M. Lipozova, was wounded in the leg. According to one report, King Zog owed his life to Major Topolai, who saw the assassins take aim and dashed in front of his royal master. He received the bullets intended for the king in his own breast.

VIENNA, Austria, Feb. 21. (U.P.)— A nation-wide search was under way today for the assassins who fired upon King Zog of Albania as he was leaving the opera with his royal party last night, killing the king's aide-de-camp and critically wounding his court chamberlain. The slain aide was Major A. Topalai and the chamberlain, expected to die, is Mehmed Bey Libuhova, credited with being the brains of the Zog regime. The party was in the arcade of the theater when the assailants opened fire. In the short battle which followed, the King and his henchmen “shot it out” with their attackers, during a score or more shots in the crowded arcade.

VIENNA, Austria, Feb. 20 (UP)—King Zog of Albania narrowly escaped with his life Friday night when assassins opened fire on him as he left the opera, killing his aide de camp and critically wounding his court chamberlain. The king escaped unscathed from the fusillade of bullets which crashed through the arcade to the opera house. The slain aide was Maj. A. Tope. The wounded court chamberlain, Mehmed Bey Libuhova, is regarded as the "brains" of the Zog regime in Albania. His condition was reported to be critical. King Zog and members of his entourage returned the fire of the assassins. The Albanian consul in Vienna, a member of the entourage, emptied his pistol, firing six shots at the assailants. In the brief battle, a score of shots were fired in the crowded confines of the arcade. The gunmen fired from 10 to 15 rounds and fled. They were overpowered by two policemen and a chemist's gua

Y Associated Press, Berlin, Feb. 20.- Dr. Wilhelm Kuelz, who was president of the League of Nations in 1927 and minister of the Interior in the Hans Luther cabinet of 1927, grappled with a would-be assassin in the main lobby of the Reichstag today after the man had sent three bullets past his head. The assailant, who told police he represented the "Bavarian protestors organization," was soon noticed in the lobby as Dr. Kuelz came in from the street. Without warning, he whipped out a pistol and began firing. Three shots rang through the lobby, bringing attendants and police on the run. When they arrived, Dr. Kuelz was struggling with the man in an effort to disarm him. There was a stiff fight, but police overpowered him and detained him for examination as to his sanity. Dr. Kuelz, who is now a member of the Reichstag for Leipzig, could not explain the attack on him other than that the man

Vienna, Feb. 20. — (P) — An attempt was made tonight to assassinate King Zog of Albania as he was leaving the opera house. The king was not hurt but a member of his staff was killed. Two men fired a number of shots at the king. Both assailants were captured by the police. King Zog has been in Vienna for the past few weeks under the care of physicians.

1931-02-28.text: NEW DELHI, India, Feb. 28 U™. The working committee of the Indian Congress party today voted to reject the viceroy’s proposals for a compromise settlement of the party's demands. It was said that all hope of a settlement of the differences between the Congress and the government over the status of India had been virtually abandoned by the Congress party tonight.

New Delhi, India, Feb. 27—Mahatma Gandhi and the viceroy of India, Lord Irwin, had a long conference today and after its conclusion it was understood they had failed to agree on 2 vital points of the pending peace negotiations. After the meeting, Gandhi said the talks "might be resumed." This was taken to mean that it would be necessary to refer the subject matter of the conversation to the British government for a decision.

LONDON (UP)—Staid and dignified London “went Hollywood” Friday night when Charles Spencer Chaplin appeared in person at the premiere of his latest film, “City Lights.” The only thing missing from the brilliant first night was the Hollywood weather. London retained all of its typical winter rains for the opening. But there were immense crowds, titled persons, celebrities, flood lights, limousines, and full dress as members of all classes of the city gathered inside and outside the Dominion Theatre. George Bernard Shaw, Lady Astor, many peers and peeresses and British notables by the score gave Chaplin’s picture an enthusiastic welcome. The greatest ovation of the evening, however, was accorded the comedian himself when he appeared on the stage for a curtain speech after the presentation of the film. As he moved toward the wings, the comedian suddenly went into his famous Chaplin walk. The

LONDON, Feb. 27.—After thirty years, Miss Emily Payne of Temple, Texas, has traced three brothers now living in England. For three decades she had sought Joseph, Sydney, and George Payne, succeeding at last through the joint efforts of the American and British post office service.

By The Associated Press, New Delhi, India, Feb. 27.--Negotiations which began so hopefully between Mahatma Gandhi and the Viceroy of India apparently have reached a point where the two men can go no further as individuals, and Gandhi tonight sat cross-legged in a circle of members of the Congress Working Committee, talking over with them the things he has discussed with the Viceroy. Gandhi and Lord Irwin talked for three hours today, and although neither would say what they had discussed, it was understood that they had failed to agree on certain outstanding demands in the Mahatma’s program.

London. Feb. 28—(AP)—George Bernard Shaw, whose critical blast has withered more than one theatrical flower, was carried away by Charlie Chaplin’s latest movie when it opened here last night. “The little fellow is a genius,” he was quoted as saying, “now I know what comedy really means.” Not all the newspaper critics agreed that the new opus is Charlie's best effort to date, but the usually sedate London Times devoted nearly a column to its review, describing the comedian’s performance as “masterly.” The Manchester Guardian also gave it a column, asserting that “no one but Chaplin is as good as Chaplin.”

NEW DELHI, India, Feb. 28 (3 —Negotiations between Viceroy Lord Irwin and Mahatma Gandhi to bring about relaxation of the civil disobedience campaign reached an impasse today as opposition developed within the national working committee to some of the viceroy’s proposals. The point at issue is Lord Irwin's refusal to sanction an inquiry into alleged police abuses which Gandhi has requested, the viceroy citing official statements of restraint of police in the face of insults and abuse from mobs. Two other major differences which remain unsettled concern the rights to picket shops and to manufacture salt. In view of these differences it was believed today that Lord Irwin would find it necessary to confer further by cable with London. He. Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru, and M. R. Jayakar met this morning in a further attempt to smooth over the difficulties, while the working committee meets again th

ROME, Feb. 28 (A. P.)—Great Britain and Italy today reached an accord in principle for the settlement of all naval problems left pending by the London conference of last year. The accord will be submitted to the French foreign minister, Aristide Briand, in Paris tomorrow, and if he accepts it a five-

LE BOURGET, France, Jan. 16. (AP) The Prince of Wales and his brother, Prince George, landed here this afternoon after a flight from the Hendon airport, England, on the first stage of their 18,000-mile journey to South America. The little moth plane came down to a perfect landing in rather poor flying weather with low visibility, threatening clouds and some fog. The trip from London had taken two hours and eighteen minutes.

ROME, Feb. 28.—British and Italian officials conferring here on Franco-Italian naval problems reached an agreement in principle on questions left outstanding at the London Naval Conference, it was announced officially today. British Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson and First Lord of the Admiralty A. V. Alexander will proceed to Paris this afternoon to submit the agreement to the French government. The agreement then will be submitted to the governments of the United States, Great Britain, Japan, and the British Dominions represented at the London Naval Conference.

| Paris, Feb. 28 (UP) — A new scheme of naval limitations whereby world powers will be asked to limit their construction to 25,000 ton warships will be proposed by France, Britain and Italy, the United Press learned at the foreign offices today. The limitations scheme confirmation was coincident with the announcement that Italy had agreed in principle to the Franco-British proposal entailing adhesion to the London naval treaty and giving up the claim for naval parity with France. British Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson, Foreign Minister Aristide Briand, and other officials, will confer here when the British delegates return from Rome. They are expected to decide whether the new scheme of limitations will be submitted to the United States and Japan immediately or held until the League of Nations world disarmament conference meets at Geneva. An enormous saving is expected to result from

ROME, Feb. 28 (P).—The Italian government this morning accepted proposals advanced by Great Britain which will permit its full adhesion to the London naval treaty. The proposals previously had been accepted by the French government. Adhesion of the two governments to the London treaty, reached at the conclusion of the naval conference almost a year ago, will make that pact a five-power instrument instead of a three-power treaty as it is now. Negotiations which brought the Italian acceptance were carried on by Arthur Henderson, foreign secretary, and A. V. Alexander, first Lord of the Admiralty for Great Britain, and Dino Gianni, foreign minister, and Rear Admiral Siriana for Italy. Premier Mussolini himself carried on part of the conversations for Italy. Parity Postponed. The proposal advanced by Great Britain, some reports said, specify (Continued on Page 12)

1931-02-19.text: (By Associated Press) St. Just, Eng., Feb. 19:—All hands of a crew of 29 were saved from the Greek steamer Theotokos which sank after a collision with an unidentified steamer off Lands End last night.

NEW DELHI, India, Feb. 18.--- (AP)—Mahatma Gandhi and the Viceroy of India had another three-hour conference today, their second, then adjourned further conferences so that both could consult their associates on questions which had been propounded by both sides. Neither discussed the matters they had talked about and no definite date was announced for resumption of their conversations but it was believed that there would be another meeting on Friday or Saturday.

Madrid, Feb. 18.—(4)—Spain tonight had a new government, peacefully formed, and was looking forward to a period of calm after the political turmoil of the last five days. Admiral Juan Bautista Asenar, staunch royalist and political neutral, heads the ministry formed today by King Alfonso in a successful effort to head off another military dictatorship like that of Miguel Primo de Rivera. People Quiet The king called for no participation by left, socialist and republican elements, and their attitude remained problematical tonight. The public generally, however, seemed to be waiting quietly until the program and policies of the new government could be formulated and put into effect. The cabinet which replaces that of Damaso Berenguer, which resigned last Saturday, because of widespread opposition to Premier Berenguer’s plan for parliamentary elections in March, includes Berenguer himself,

CHERBOURG, France, Feb. 19. —(UP)— Capt. Malcolm Campbell, who recently set a new world’s automobile speed record at Daytona Beach, was raised to the knighthood today by King George of England. The British vice consul communicated the king's desire to Campbell while the speed driver was still aboard the steamship Mauretania off Cherbourg.

MADRID, Feb. 19,—Spain’s new cabinet headed by Admiral Juan Bautista Aznar y Cabanas met today to prepare a ministerial declaration outlining a new political era after eight years of government without a parliament. The confusion which followed the resignation of Premier Gen. Damaso Berenguer after a year as a dictator was resolved at least temporarily when the 70-year-old admiral obeyed the order of King Alfonso XIII to form a government.

HENDAYE, Spanish Frontier, Feb 19. (AP).—Reports were current along the frontier today that King Alfonso of Spain had purchased a chateau at Talence, near Bordeaux, France, for use in an emergency which might have caused him to leave the country over which he rules. While the general feeling here was that Alfonso never would run away from events in Spain, it was commented in Petite Gironde, a widely known Bordeaux paper, that “for Alfonso it is all or nothing. Each time he plays a card or makes a move he is justified in thinking of Charles I, Louis XVI, or Nicholas II.”

Paris, Feb. 19.—The French naval budget totaling 2,856,511,533 francs (about $114,260,461) was passed by the chamber of deputies early today after the legislators had been reminded that “Italy is rushing construction.” Marine Minister Charles Dumont declared “the navy is the guarantee of French security and colonial integrity. Therefore, we need a modern navy.” Recent efforts of Great Britain to persuade France to delay her building program appeared wiped out by the chamber’s decision. The only determined stand against the huge naval appropriation, exceeding that of last year by about $5,320,000, came from the Socialists who attempted to clip about $1,606,000,000 from the budget. The socialist amendment was rejected, 450 votes to 100.

Hendaye, France, Feb. 18 (A’)-—A report flashed along the Franco-Spanish frontier tonight that Alfonso XIII of Spain had, through a “straw man,” purchased a chateau at Talence, near Bordeaux. This was interpreted here to mean that the king was prepared to take refuge in France should need arise, but the general feeling is that he would never “run away.” Instead, say those who know the Spanish monarch best, he likely would retire to the chateau voluntarily to permit free functioning of the constituent assembly which his new cabinet is said to have promised and which would decide whether Spain is to become a republic, like her numerous offspring in the Americas or to be converted into a “democratic” monarchy similar to that of England. In the meantime Alfonso, in naming what liberals call the “anodyne” Admiral Aznar as his prime minister, is deemed along this friendly frontier to have made

Genoa, Feb. 19. —(P)— General Italo Balbo, who led a squadron of airplanes from Italy to Brazil, came home in triumph today aboard the steamer Conte Rosso. He and his forty-seven companions were greeted by a wildly cheering crowd. The heroes of the first flight across the Atlantic in group formation received a tremendous welcome. Fifty-six aviators left Oxbetello, Italy, last December but only 48 are returning. Four died when their ship crashed and four others made a forced landing shortly after the flight started.

| MADRID, Feb. 18. —U, P)—King Alfonso XIII breathed easier this evening than he had in five days, his realm governed once more by a monarchist cabinet, believed to be opposed to left wing demands that powers of the crown be restricted. Strange political bed-fellows were in the new ministry, organized by Admiral Juan Bautista Aznar y Cabanas. Admiral Aznar, supporter of the throne named by the king to form a cabinet, succeeded in three hours. The cabinet was approved by King Alfonso and, with the exception of two ministers, was sworn in without further ceremony. It includes, strangely enough, General Damaso Berenguer, erstwhile premier, as minister of war, and both Count Romanones and the Marquis de Alhucemas, liberal monarchists. These two men were almost entirely responsible for the downfall of the Berenguer dictatorial ministry last Saturday, after a year in office—yet today all are s

1931-01-28.text: (Copyright 1931, By The Associated Press) Bombay, British India, Jan. 27.— ‘Mahatma Gandhi, toothless, shriveled wraith of a man, sat cross-legged on a stone floor today, serving notice on the British empire that India’s campaign of civil disobedience would continue unabated, while outside a frantic crowd, mad for a glimpse of him, struggled so furiously that a woman was crushed to death. Thirty-one others were injured in the crush. Naked but for a homespun loin cloth, he leaned against a hay mattress in the center of a circle of newspaper men, an expression of deep melancholy on his ascetic face, but an almost spiritual light in his eyes. “We can suspend judgment on Prime Minister MacDonald’s statement to the round table conference at London,” he said, “but we cannot suspend the activities of the Indian congress and of the approaching peace talks with delegates returning from the round

BOMBAY, Jan. 28. (/P)—Leaving behind him a message to India’s nationalist millions that their fight for independence must go on, Mahatma Gandhi today speeded by train toward Allahabad, a Central Indian city, where are gathered most of the nationalist working committee. At Allahabad, India’s “City of God,” located on the sacred Ganges, he will visit the bedside of one of his dearest friends, the aged Pandit Motilal Nehru, father of Jawaharlal Nehru, president of the All India National Congress, and discuss with him Britain's offer of an eventual qualified dominion status for India. He faces in Allahabad, when he arrives there tonight, a welcome probably as enthusiastic and frenzied as that which tens and hundreds of thousands gave him here yesterday upon his arrival from eight months in Yeroda prison. In the crush, which centered about his frail 96-pound body one woman was trampled to dea

London—Britain’s second labor government, approaching its third year, Wednesday faced a critical commons vote with confidence that its master politician, J. Ramsay MacDonald, had maneuvered the ministry to another victory. The promised abstention of the rank and file of the liberal party from voting in the division on the second reading of the trades dispute bill made it pretty certain that the government would be upheld by a majority of from 15 to 30 votes. A dozen explanations were current today in the parliamentary lobbies for the prospective ministerial victory in what a week ago appeared to offer a probability of government overthrow. The simplest and most plausible of these was that David Lloyd George, liberal leader, considered that, however bad a labor ministry, it was to be preferred to a conservative government and would lend his aid in keeping the labor government in power unt

London, Today.— (AP)— Physicians attending Princess Beatrice, 74 year old aunt of King George, who is suffering from a broken arm and acute bronchitis, regard her condition as “not without anxiety.” Queen Victoria, of Spain, her daughter, is hurrying to London to be at her bedside. The physicians said the broken arm of the Princess was making satisfactory progress, but that danger lay in the bronchitis. The medical bulletin issued this morning said: “Her Royal Highness, the Princess Beatrice, has had a fairly restful night. Her general condition remains unchanged.”

Silver Belt A. P. Leased Wire BERLIN, Jan. 2.—A violent earthquake shock was felt this morning at Hindenburg in upper Silesia and through the Kattowitz district. Damage was believed to have been comparatively slight.

MADRID, Spain, Jan. 27, (hy) — Riots and student strikes in six Spanish universities today caused the closing of one of the schools and resulted in an extra session of the cabinet to deal with the situation. At Granada 200 medical and law students clashed with members of monarchial organizations, stoned the organizations’ headquarters and the police station and refused to attend classes. The university was closed to prevent further disorders and five students were arrested and later released. One policeman was injured.

PARIS, Jan. 27 (®) — Premier Pierre Laval’s day-old cabinet sat up late tonight polishing off the declaration of policy with which it will make its first test of strength in the Chamber of Deputies on Friday. “Although the ministry was admitted to differ little from that of Andre Tardieu which was overthrown in December, observers thought that it leaned a little more to moderate opinion in the Chamber and would be a little stronger in the Senate. M. Laval’s inclusion of Blaise Diagne, 68-year-old colored deputy from Senegal, was generally approved, and because of its appeal to sentiment favoring assimilation of the colonies, was considered to add strength to the combination.

Vienna, Jan. 28.—(l)—King Zog of Albania arrived here today to consult specialists about a throat ailment from which he has suffered for considerable time. His trip to Vienna marked the first journey of the self-proclaimed monarch beyond the boundaries of his little kingdom. The ailment has been considered serious, according to reports from Tirana in recent months. Various specialists have visited in the Albanian capital in the past to examine the king but have not given him the required relief. The trouble was said to be due to his habit of smoking several packages of cigarettes a day and to the restricted activities of the king since he decided to abandon the presidency of the republic of Albania for the throne.

BARDONECCHIA, Italy, Jan. Jan. 27. (A)—Six Italian frontier guards were killed and several others were injured today by an avalanche which overwhelmed a patrol in the mountains near here. The accident, second of its kind within a week, occurred in the almost impossible Alpine heights between this city and the French town of Chambery.

By International News Service, | LONDON, March 30—Because he feared that his thirty-year-old automobile might fall into unkindly hands, Dr. Francis Pearse today decided to bury it with all honors in a plot of ground near a cemetery. Up until three years ago he drove the car regularly.

NICE, France, March 30.—(AP)—Her nerve bolstered by brandy, Mrs. David Townsend, former Broadway “Follies” girl, drove her car off a 200-foot precipice near here and found in death the rest that life denied her. While she drank she scribbled a note to her husband, reputedly wealthy Wall Street broker, which read: “Please take care of my mother. Pay 4,000 francs to Wally.” Another paragraph which referred to the possibility of her going back to the stage was undecipherable. When she did not appear at a party Saturday evening which she had planned, friends sought her, but their search was unavailing until Sunday morning when police saw her car crushed on the rocks below one of the sharpest precipices on the Riviera. Her husband, identifying the body, was prostrated. He could think of no reason, he said, why she should have ended her life, other than that she had suffered a sudden neurasthe

Shanghai, China, March 30— 2p--- Word has been received here by the St. Columban’s mission of the death Mar. 5, of Father Superior Tierney of the Kiencheng mission while a captive of Chinese communities. While details of his death were not learned, the bandits frequently had said they would kill him if ransom of $40,000 were not immediately forthcoming. In a letter which he contrived to smuggle through his captors some weeks ago he wrote he was failing and that he was quite resigned to die. Father Tierney, superior of St. Columban’s mission at Kiencheng, a small interior city located southeast of Nanchang in the south China province of Kiangsi, was captured last November 17.

Turin, Italy, March 30—(A.P)— Reports were current here today that a bomb had exploded in the Piazzetta Pasello near the royal palace where the Crown Prince Humbert and his bride Marie Jose, princess of the Belgians, live. Officials denied any knowledge of such an affair. The infernal machine was said to have been in a box of explosives, close to the wing of the building occupied by the royal apartment, the royal armory and the prefecture seat of the provincial government.

BERLIN, March 30—(UP)—The communist members of the Reichstag petitioned Speaker Paul Loebe today to reconvene parliament immediately for the purpose of rescinding the dictatorial decree issued by President Paul Von Hindenburg and Chancellor Heinrich Bruening for suppression of political violence in Germany. The fascists and nationalists likewise have expressed their desire for reconvocation of the Reichstag in an effort to force withdrawal of the decree, which enforces drastic penalties and regulations to prevent disturbance.

PARIS, March 29 — Aristide Briand’s senate speech yesterday in which he declared he would continue to the bitter end protesting against the proposed Austro-German customs accord was interpreted today by the semiofficial newspaper Le Temps, as a warning to Berlin and Vienna. “It must be understood,” the newspaper said, “that the entire French nation supports the government in any diplomatic action calculated to thwart this customs union - which would compromise Austrian independence and create a dangerous situation in central Europe.”

BERLIN, March 30.—(INS)—Forty-eight hours after President Paul von Hindenburg invoked the dictatorial clause of the constitution to curb radical activities, he was confronted with an acute labor crisis from two sections of Germany today. Wage contracts with 300,000 miners in the Ruhr district and 200,000 metal workers in northwest Germany were cancelled. Grave labor conflicts were feared as a result.

ROME, Mar. 30. (AP) — The world grain conference, which for four days has been trying to solve the problem of the international wheat surplus, ended its general sessions this afternoon and dissolved into several committees which met to investigate special phases of the difficulties. Practically all of the delegates who attended the conference received appointments on the special committees and it was said that these would continue working until probably Wednesday. Thus far the conference is hopelessly divided. It seems certain that further conferences will have to be held before anything like a solution can be achieved. The European countries along the Danube still maintain the necessity of a preferential tariff system which would mean a virtual boycott against non-European wheat. In retaliation, the great wheat growing countries of the world have threatened to revoke their most-favored

ROME.- Repeal of prohibition laws in the United States to partly reduce the world wheat surplus was suggested Monday when the International wheat conference continued its meeting here. Englebert Dolfus, Austrian minister of agriculture, said that while he had no intention of entering into the internal affairs of another state, if the United States abolished prohibition part of the land now used to raise wheat could be cultivated to raise barley for the making of beer. This would automatically effect a proportional reduction in the American wheat crop and decrease the world output, Dolfuss said.

1931-01-07.text: | London, Jan. 7.--(AP)--Britons, accustomed to iron-handed discipline aboard the ships of His Majesty’s navy, were astonished today at reports of widely extended insubordination at the naval yard at Devonport. Sailing orders of the submarine depot ship Lucia were countermanded. Thirty of her crew were arrested Sunday after a demonstration in protest at curtailment of Christmas leaves. | The Plymouth correspondent of the Daily Mail asserted in a dispatch to his paper that such startling revelations had come from investigation of the Lucia incident that movements of several other ships on spring maneuvers had been canceled. The ships held at Devonport navy yard, the dispatch said, included the cruiser Norfolk, whose captain, C. B. Pickett, is a member of the court trying the Lucia offenders, and all submarines of the “L” class, of which the Lucia is the parent ship. The Daily Mail reporte

VRCrOUrR, NOTIAEMOCRIANG, Si h- —(P)—Her head bashed in and her body virtually roasted, pretty Evelyn Foster, 28, was found semi-conscious beside the smoking ruins of her automobile on the frost-bound moors near here last night. In a moment of lucidity before she died today she told her father that a stranger had accosted her Tuesday night, asking her for a lift to Newcastle, saying that he had come from Scotland. About 14 miles from Newcastle the stranger ordered the girl to halt the car. He then clubbed her over the head, tossing her on the back seat and setting fire to the automobile which he shoved over a cliff. Miss Foster told her father that she fought off unconsciousness while the car bounced down the valley, flaming furiously. When the automobile struck a boulder and halted, she was able to drag herself from it. She did not know how long she lay unconscious before a bus driver d
LONDON.—The German steamer Carl sank after a collision with the Swedish steamer Themis in Swinemunde harbor today, Lloyd’s at Stettin reported. Casualties were unknown.

PARIS (A.P.)—France mourned her “savior,” Marshal Joseph Joffre, with all the splendor due one of the generation's outstanding heroes as the old soldier's funeral procession passed through the streets of Paris from Notre Dame cathedral to the Invalides Wednesday. Joffre's body was placed in a circular sacristy inside a square tent, draped with black and violet, at the Invalides. Battle flags were arranged in the formation of mounting guard. A Napoleonic bronze stood in each of the four corners around the marshal's resting place. Princes, generals and statesmen whose names are famous throughout the world marched in the procession with maimed privates who served in the trenches. The marshal’s body was carried on a gun carriage while ex-soldiers and men and women who lost relatives in the World War knelt in pious tribute. A million persons lined the route followed by the cortege in a journe

(By The Associated Press) Paris, Jan. 7—France paid homage to the still form of Marshal Joffre as it lay banked by flowers on a catafalque in the chapel of the Ecole Militaire. Last night in a plain oak coffin which will never be opened again, the Marshal's body lay in the cathedral of Notre Dame. On the coffin was the simple inscription, “Joseph Joffre, Marshal of France, 1852-1931.” This morning at 9 o'clock after funeral services in the cathedral, an impressive cortege escorted the body to the Invalides, where it will repose in a vault for several months before being buried in its final resting place at Louveciennes. Thousands still stood outside (Continued on page three)

I. N. S. Staff Correspondent PARIS, Jan. 7.—In majestic manner enriched by the presence of representatives from Governments in many parts of the world, France said farewell today to Marshal Joseph Jacques Cesaire Joffre, the cooper’s son from the hillsides of the Pyrenees who became the hero of the Marne and the nation’s idol. As a last token of appreciation for a life of unstinted devotion and service to his country, France bestowed upon him the highest final honor it can offer—a national funeral. The church bells of Paris tolled forth the opening memorial service at the Cathedral of Notre Dame at 9 a.m. (4 a.m. Eastern Standard Time). A hush settled over the city in the morning, and solid banks of humanity waited in silence along the route to Les Invalides, where the body will rest in a special vault until removed to Louveciennes, home of the Joffre family. Paris—All the pomp and ceremony of republican France was summoned Wednesday to pay final honor to Marshal Joffre. Sorrowing multitudes gathered from dawn to witness the progress of the cortege from Notre Dame to Les Invalides, where the marshal’s body finds a temporary resting place not far from the tomb of Napoleon. The gates of the great cathedral were thrown open at 8 a.m. and within a few minutes the vast nave was filled by more than 10,000 persons. Roofs of nearby buildings were packed hours before the passage of the cortege. Traffic was halted. Infantry standing elbow to elbow took positions along the entire three miles from Notre Dame to Les Invalides. Military bands with drums and trumpets hung with crepe were stationed at intervals of 1,000 yards. Arrival of President Doumergue was the signal for the beginning of the requiem service at Notre Dame where the body of the marshal wa

Moscow, Jan. 7—Christmas was celebrated according to the old Russian calendar in Orthodox churches today while atheists held lectures denouncing religion and Christmas services were burlesqued in theaters and other amusement places. Workers joined atheists in demonstrating their contempt for Christmas celebrations.

Rome, Jan. 7, U.A—Two of the Italian seaplanes en route from Bolama to Natal were forced to land in mid-ocean without harm to their crews, it was announced officially today. The seaplane piloted by Capt. Donadelli was unable to proceed after its water supply was exhausted through leakage. The nature of the trouble encountered by the machine piloted by Capt. Balstracchi has not been ascertained. The official announcement did not give the present whereabouts of the crews of the two machines, but it was presumed that they landed near an Italian war vessel and were picked up. Bolama, Portuguese Guinea, Jan. 7, U.B—One of the Italian seaplanes which left here for Natal was destroyed by fire and sunk, and another machine was damaged badly when the two machines collided after the take off, it was learned here today. The mechanic of the damaged seaplane was reported missing today, when news of t

| Moscow — Today is the Russian Orthodox Christmas but it was not celebrated with the enthusiasm of former years because the Soviet campaign aimed against all religious festivals is keeping the people out of the churches. Many churches held services this morning but their congregations were slim. Millions of workers who used to observe this holiday at least as a day of rest voted this year to stay on the job and censured all those who took a day off. The so-called anti-religious museums were crowded and the theaters offered special programs under the auspices of the Atheists society. There were no Christmas trees and no toys. The children went to school just as though it were an ordinary day.

1931-01-05.text: London, Jan. 4,--(fP)—The princess royal, eldest sister of King George, died this afternoon at the age of 63. Though she was known to have been an invalid many years, the first intimation to reach the public that her condition had become critical was in the form of a bulletin issued early today from her residence in Portman Square, saying she was showing signs of increasing weakness. Though Princess Louise Victoria Alexandra Dagmar—to give her her full name—was of such a retiring disposition she sometimes was called ‘Her Royal Shyness’ she was greatly loved by all who got to know her. She was the most democratic of royal ladies and on many occasions took rides in buses, the other occupants of which were ignorant (Continued on Page 2?)

LONDON, Jan. 5 (P)—All Britain today mourned one of the most democratic of its royal family, Louise, Princess Royal, nicknamed “Her Royal Shyness,” who died in her sleep yesterday of heart disease. King George, at Sandringham, was notified of her death, the Lord Chamberlain immediately ordering a period of four weeks full mourning for the British court and two additional weeks of half mourning. The Princess Royal, who was the eldest sister of the king, was 63 years old, a year and eight months younger than her imperial brother. Her death was not unexpected. She had had recurrent attacks of the heart trouble, and in 1925 she suffered from a serious gastric hemorrhage, although until recently she had been in somewhat better health. Her physicians at midnight Saturday announced an increased weakness in her condition. Although shy and resentful of the ostentation which accompanies the royal

LONDON (UP)—The royal courts of Britain and Norway mourned Monday the death of the Princess Royal, the sister of King George of England and Queen Maud of Norway, who died in her sleep here Sunday. The Princess Royal, who would have been 64 years old next month, had been in failing health for several years. Signs of increasing weakness from heart trouble brought her daughters, Princess Arthur of Connaught and Lady Maud Carnegie to her bedside. King George ordered six weeks mourning at the British court after his sister's death. A similar period of mourning was ordered at the Norwegian court. The title of Princess Royal is not hereditary and can only be conferred by the king. It was not believed in court circles that it would be conferred upon anyone for a considerable period of time. PLYMOUTH, Eng. Jan. 5-17, two members of the crew of Lucia, submarine depot were “lodged in naval barracks” today after what is believed to have been a demonstration in first curtailed Christmas. An investigation by the authorities is under way, the 42 crew members have been replaced so that the Inez may join the Atlantic fleet maneuvers. Officers of the ship and of the Devonport Naval Station would make no comment regarding the affair other than that "it was being investigated and that it was not a mutiny."

(By The Associated Press) London, Jan. 5.—South Wales coal miners today asked the MacDonald government to step in as arbitrator in the labor dispute which tied up the South Wales mines and threw 140,000 men out of work. Ramsay MacDonald was expected to take part in the conference before it ended. The miners want the government to induce the mine owners to accept the recommendation of the National Industrial Board of Adjustment of the 45-hour week without reduction in wages. The owners were invited to present their side of the case tomorrow. The miners will remain here to meet the owners if a joint conference seems warranted.

Plymouth, England, Jan. 4 (P)— This town and the adjoining naval port of Devonport buzzed tonight with rumors that mutiny had broken out aboard the submarine depot ship Lucia, now in the Devonport dockyard. Forty-two members of the Lucia’s crew were reported to have been lodged in the naval barracks and others were sent to take their places... Officials admitted some trouble aboard, but declared it did not amount to mutiny.

Paris, Jan. 5—(U. P.)—The body of Marshal Joseph Joffre lay in state on a simple military camp cot at the Chapel of Saint Louis today, while thousands of Frenchmen, many of them weeping, filed reverently past the bier. Joffre's head rested on a white cushion. His face, hollowed and worn by suffering, was hardly recognizable. A blue tunic covered his legs, hiding the amputation above his left knee, which was kept secret at the Marshal's wish for eight days while he fought against the poison of gangrene. Many of his countrymen had walked outside the chapel since daylight to pay homage to the great soldier of France. In the Marshal’s crossed hands rested a silver crucifix. A military medal was the only decoration on the famous black tunic he wore at the battle of the Marne, when he gained the nation’s acclaim and love as the hero of a decisive battle. There was weeping as the thousands, crushed close together outside the Ecole Militaire until nine o'clock, lined up to take their final glance at the body of Marshal Joffre, laid out on a camp bed in the chapel of the old military academy. Three women—the widow, Madame LaFilet and Mademoiselle DeBaye—maintained vigil tonight over the body of Joseph Jaques Cesaire Joffre. To them he had been husband, stepfather and personal friend. Just outside in full dress uniform, members of the dead soldier's staff kept guard of honor. Tomorrow and Tuesday hundreds of thousands are expected to file past and Wednesday millions of Frenchmen probably will line the boulevards of Paris and fill Notre Dame Cathedral to pay last homage to Marshal Joffre, victor of the Marne and savior of France. ROME, JAN. 4—(4)—A reiteration of the strict Catholic doctrine regarding marriage is expected in the encyclical which Pope Pius will issue this week. Far from making concessions to modern trends, it is understood the encyclical will hark back to the first principles of the church—restating Catholicism’s utter disapproval of divorce and emphasizing the doctrine that only by continence within the married state can families be limited without transgressing the Divine law. This restatement, it was generally assumed, would be the Pope's answer to the Episcopal Bishops' qualified admission of birth control in certain cases, emanating from the Lambeth conference in London last summer. Mixed marriages, those between Catholics and non-Catholics, are also expected to be the subject of special comment. It is generally taken for granted the Pope will re-emphasize that Bishops before granting dispens

Warsaw, Poland, Jan. 5—Despite a mishap 60 miles north of here when she smashed the undercarriage of her plane in making a forced landing late yesterday, Miss Amy Johnson, British woman aviator, was understood today to intend continuing her much opposed flight to Peiping, China. Leaving Berlin shortly before noon, the pretty 23 year old girl was driven by the wind to the north of her objective, Warsaw, when she turned about she ran into a heavy fog bank and finally made a forced landing at the village of Amelin, near Krasnosielk. She was not injured. While the plane is being repaired she accepted the hospitality of the Catholic priest at Krasnosielk, who invited her to spend the night at his house. Her failure to arrive in a reasonable length of time had excited considerable fear for her safety here and word had been broadcast for all policemen throughout Poland to be on the lookout.

Briandon, France, Jan. 5 (UP)—Alpine avalanches took a toll of 11 lives over the weekend. Six Frenchmen died when they were engulfed in an Alps pass under a snowslide estimated at 35 feet high. Four young skiers vanished in an attempt to scale a cliff. Two Paris students, also on skis, were overtaken by an avalanche but one escaped.

Warsaw. Jan. 4, (P).—Amy Johnson, the 23-year-old flier who left England New Year's Day on a project flight to Peiping, was driven by fog to a forced landing late today at the village of Amelin, near Krasnosielk, about 60 miles north of here. She was uninjured but the undercarriage of her machine was smashed in the rough landing. Miss Johnson, who last summer flew from England to Australia in 19 days, left Berlin for Warsaw at 10:27 a.m. today in the face of unfavorable weather. Atmospheric conditions were so bad she was driven northward from the German capital and missed Warsaw entirely. Then, before she could get back on her course, a heavy wave of fog engulfed her and she was forced to come down.

* Rome, Jan. 5.—(UP)—Twelve Italian seaplanes led by Minister of Air Gen. Italo Balbo were expected to leave Bolama, Portuguese Guinea, tonight on the long and dangerous flight across the South Atlantic to Natal, Brazil. Unofficial sources said that the four squadrons of three machines each would take off in the light of a full moon, if weather conditions permitted. The air ministry issued a weather forecast over the projected route, indicating that Balbo and his companions would soon be started on their long transatlantic venture. Rome, Jan. 5.—(UP)—Favorable weather prevailed along the route of the 12 Italian seaplanes now at Bolama are scheduled to follow across the South Atlantic Ocean to Brazil and it appeared certain the trans-ocean voyage would start tonight in the light of a full moon.

MADRID. Jan. 4 (By Telephone to London).—Six persons were injured slightly today as mounted police charged to break up a demonstration by 250 persons in Puerta del Sol, the principal square of Madrid. The manifestation, in which mainly railway workers and students participated, was the first such in the Spanish capital since martial law was proclaimed after two attempts at military revolt last month. The trouble began when a group of discontented railway men attempted to visit political prisoners and were refused admittance to the jail because the law limits such a visiting party to eight persons. Later in the afternoon the same group, augmented by other workers and students, attempted to parade through Puerta del Sol, shouting protests against the government. Mounted police scattered them with sabres, but the incident caused intense excitement in Madrid.

LONDON, Mar. 28. P)—The death of Arnold Bennett, 63, considered one of the greatest novelists of the post-Victorian era, was mourned today throughout Britain. Bennett died last night after a month’s illness. Death was due to typhoid fever. He appeared somewhat improved Wednesday after a blood transfusion but became unconscious yesterday. A few friends were at the bedside when he died. Bennett was born at Hanley, Staffordshire. He married a French woman, but a legal separation was effected in 1922.

Lendon, March 28—(A.P.)—Although Emilio Scala will actually receive less than a half a million dollars, instead of a potential million and three-quarters as a result of winning with his ticket on the Irish hospital sweepstakes yesterday, he will be thoroughly satisfied as soon as he actually gets the money in his hands, he said today. "When that happens," said the Italian proprietor of a humble coffee house in Battersea, "I will know that I am a really rich man and that it isn't all a wonderful dream." It developed today that Scala actually retained only one-quarter of his ticket for himself and his relatives in Italy, selling a three-quarters share in it to a firm of bookmakers for slightly more than $50,000. Although he did not get to bed until 3 o'clock this morning as a result of the excitement yesterday, he was up again at 5 and had opened his shop at the same time as usual. "I was

Nice, France, March 29.—(AP)— Peggy Davis, 37, former Broadway show girl, gave the Riviera a new tragedy last night when she drove her automobile over a steep cliff in the vicinity of the Vanderbilt estate, and dropped 200 feet to her death. The former actress was the wife of an Australian, David Townsend, who is well known in Wall Street circles. She drove the car to her hotel near the cliff, where she scribbled a note as she drank two brandies. Leaving the note with the proprietor of the hotel, she jumped into the automobile and plunged over the edge of the cliff. The note, addressed to her husband, asked his pardon for her act, and beseeched him to take good care of her 1-year-old daughter. Police have been unable to find a motive for her suicide, as apparently her marital life had been happy.

Berlin, Mar. 28—(A.P.)—Millions of German citizens tonight were studying, in their evening newspapers, one of the most far-reaching decrees ever promulgated in the young German republic. It was “Father” Hindenburg’s ukase for squelching disorder. “Those who read radical papers didn’t know but that this might be the last issue of their paper for some time, for amid the drastic provisions of the decree is one empowering the authorities to suppress for as long as eight weeks, if it were found necessary. Those who belonged to such organizations as Adolf Hitler's brown shirts or the Communist red front did not know whether they could meet with their brethren again, for under the new decree, their organizations may be dispersed with the stroke of a pen. Furthermore, under the decree such fundamental rights as freedom of the press, the inviolability of personal liberty, secrecy of postal, teleg

ROME, Mar. 28—(AP)—Russia threw her gauntlet down at the world grain conference this afternoon. In a defiant speech, Abraham Kissin, Soviet delegate, declared that far from reducing her wheat production, his country would increase it this year and that instead of giving up her policy of so-called "dumping" she intended to increase her wheat exports in order to pay for her imports which now exceed $500,000,000 a year. Kissin sharply criticized the speech of Argentine Ambassador Perez, made to the conference yesterday, declaring it only could have been made by a man devoid of a sense of humor and proportion. Perez, speaking for the larger wheat growing countries outside of Europe, condemned the European proposal for a system of preferential tariffs and a virtual European boycott against foreign wheat. Berlin, March 28—(A.P.)—Large national economic units, particularly the United States and Soviet Russia, were pictured today in reports of an address of Dr. Karl Renner, former Austrian chancellor, as having made the projected economic union of Austria and Germany necessary. Dr. Renner, speaking before the Austro-German people’s union, said that the economic unity of the United States had long challenged the existence of disunited tariff-ridden Europe, while recently Soviet Russia had risen as a new great rationalized and unified trade force. “Caught between these two economic giants,” he continued, “the individual nations of Europe soon will be helpless dwarfs, unless Europe acts to make economic Pan-Europe a reality. Germany and Austria have taken the first step. It only remains for other nations to join them.” On the other hand, Vienna dispatches today said some Austrian economic expe

1931-03-17.text: BOMBAY, India, Mar. 17 — Mahatma Gandhi, accustomed to adulation and worship, and commanding the respect even of his British antagonists, last night heard jeers, hoots, hisses and catcalls from a labor audience which he was about to address. Communists taunted him with failure to provide for release of labor agitators in his face with Lord Irwin which led to abandonment of the civil disobedience campaign, and charged him with betraying the workers. “Down with Gandhi,” they shouted. “Down with the national congress! Down with British imperialism.” They tore down the Nationalist flag on the platform where Gandhi sat, amazed and bewildered, and replaced it with a flaming red banner. Nationalist volunteers fought with the communists for a few minutes and replaced the red flag with the nationalist emblem. Gandhi then pleaded that he had done his best for the labor agitators. Dublin, Irish Free State, Mar. 17.—Residents of the Saorstat and kindred souls in the northern counties today celebrated Saint Patrick's day with nationwide religious ceremonies, civic programs, sporting contests, and feasts and dancing which may last until tomorrow morning. An eleventh hour legislative omission prevented drowning the Shamrock in good Irish whiskey, but for those who did not live too far away there was a prospect of a trip over into Ulster where restrictions closing public houses on Saint Patrick's day do not hold. A resolution which would have repealed the restrictions, now nearly a decade ago, was on the calendar of the Dáil and should have been passed on late yesterday afternoon, in time for today's celebrations, but for some reason it was left off the listing of the day’s events and cannot come up until Wednesday. BY WILLIAM T. COSGRAVE President, Irish Free State DUBLIN, March 17.—(UP)—St. Patrick’s day, 1931, finds our young state enjoying peace and progress,— After less than a decade of years in control of her own affairs she has recently been elected a mem- ber of the council of the League of Nations. Her minister-plenipoten- tiaries have been received in the Vatican state, in the United States, France and Germany, and the min- isters of those states have been appointed to represent their re- spective governments in her capi- tal. Her credit is well maintained at home and abroad. National se- currencies are steady at a premium, and compare most favorably in Wall Street with those of the strongest nations of the world. The development of our tourist traffic has been taken in hand by the Irish Tourist Association. Rail- ways, omnibuses and hotels are combining to develop the amenities of travel.

London, March 17.—(#)—The Labor government today blamed lax party discipline for a defeat in the commons last night on a minor clause of the electoral reform bill, 246 to 262. The defeat brought cries of “Resign! Resign!” The ministry will not resign, but steps will be taken to ensure members being in their seats for future divisions. Absence of sixteen unpaired labor members last night may be called officially to the attention of their constituencies. The presence of the sixteen would have prevented the government defeat, but it would not have prevented a break between Sir John Simon, insurgent liberal, and his party leader, David Lloyd George, who thus was unable to throw his entire party to the support of the government. CALCUTTA, India, March 16. (UP)—Douglas Fairbanks, the noted movie actor, was almost mobbed by Indian admirers on his arrival here today from Rangoon. In the stampede an auto in which the actor was being driven to his hotel struck and injured an Anglo-Indian boy.

CARDIFF, Wales, March 17. (#)— Five thousand coal miners of South Wales quit work today in protest against a wage cut of 14 cents a day awarded recently by the chairman of a joint conciliation board. It was feared that when the delegates resumed their conference next week they would vote definitely for a policy of abandoning their tools.

Dublin, Irish Free State, March 14—(4)—There will be no (legal) drowning of the shamrock in good Irish whiskey in the Free State on St. Patrick's day, for the dail "forgot" to act on a measure permitting saloons to function tomorrow. Drowning of the shamrock is an old Irish custom which means pretty much what it says. In the old days it was a St. Patrick’s rite, but in 1924 the dry leaders in southern Ireland pushed through a law closing public houses on March 17 in loyalty to the patron saint. By some mischance the bill was omitted from the day's program and now it cannot be reached until next Wednesday. London, March 16.—Wedgwood Benn, secretary for India, told the House of Commons today that as a result of the Irwin-Gandhi agreement, 14,335 political prisoners—13,927 men and 408 women—had been released up to last Friday, March 13.

Bombay, India, March 16 (#)— Mahatma Gandhi, before whom millions of Indians prostrated themselves, was hooted, jeered, hissed by Communists tonight when he tried to make a speech here. “Down with him, down with the Congress and British imperialism,” the Communists shouted as the gentle little man climbed a platform in the center of the tremendous crowd. He seemed in a daze as the Communists rushed the platform, ripping a Congress party flag from its staff. This had never happened to him before in a lifetime of peaceful fighting for Indian independence. A Communist clambered on the platform and harangued the crowd, abusing Gandhi for “betraying the workers” by failure to provide for the release from prison of labor agitators under his truce with the viceroy. There was utmost confusion as Gandhi’s men hauled the speaker down, tore from his hands the red flag which he would have placed at

LONDON. Mar. 17.—(#)—Philip Snowden, chancellor of the exchequer, who was operated on yesterday for a bladder ailment, was said today to be doing as well as could be expected. “The doctors are very pleased with Dr. Snowden's condition,” Mrs. Snowden said.

Mansfield, O., March 17 (U.P) — Millard Lea Rahberts, of Portsmouth who was arrested here on a robbery charge, had been identified today as one of the three alleged bandits who held up a bus of the Blue and Grey lines near Portsmouth, Feb. 27, and robbed passengers of approximately $600. The driver of the bus, Charles Steele, of Columbus, identified Rahberts. Steele was forced to stop the bus when two passengers pointed pistols at him. They took money and jewelry from other passengers and escaped in an automobile driven by an accomplice.

(By The Associated Press) LONDON, March 16.—Ramsay MacDonald's government was defeated by four votes in the House of Commons tonight on a clause of the electoral reforms bill abolishing university constituencies. It will not resign. The House voted 246 to 242 to reject the clause. The division came a few hours after the government had won a majority of only 10 votes against an amendment to this same clause exempting Queen's University, Belfast, from its provisions.

By The Associated Press. Pisa, Italy, March 16.—Cardinal Pietro Maffi, 73, twice a papal possibility, died here tonight. Pietro Maffi, archbishop of Pisa, was a man of science and of letters, a close friend of the royal family and one of the outstanding figures in the Catholic hierarchy. With Cardinal Gasparri, former papal secretary of state, he shared the honor of wearing the "collar of the annunziata," the highest gift of the crown and a distinction which entitled him to be styled "cousin" of the king. This honor was conferred on him shortly after he had performed the marriage ceremony of Prince Humbert of Piedmont, heir to the throne, and Princess Marie Jose of Belgium in January last year. He was born in a village of Pavia on October 12, 1858, a year and some months after Pope Pius XI was born.

ROME, March 17. (AP)—The Roman Catholic world today mourned Pietro Cardinal Maffi, Archbishop of Pisa, who died last night at 73 after a life spent in science, letters and the church. The end came peacefully after a lingering illness. The Pope, acting for the second time within a few weeks on behalf of the dying cardinal, sent his benediction.

PISA, Italy, March 17—Pietro Cardinal Maffi, one of the most prominent members of the sacred college, died today at the age of 73. The death of the Cardinal, who was considered for the papacy upon two occasions, was caused by heart trouble and pneumonia. The news was communicated to Pope Pius and King Victor Emmanuel, a long close friend of the cardinal. Cardinal Maffi, who was archbishop of Pisa, was famous as a mathematician and astronomer, and was widely known for his book "The Map of the Skies: Through the Camera." He was decorated with the Collar of Annunciation, the highest decoration of Italy, on the same day he officiated at the wedding of Crown Prince Humbert and Princess Marie Jose of Belgium. He was the first cardinal to receive the honor since 1870, and thereby became a "cousin" of the king. Cardinal Maffi was an opponent of the fascist government when it was established by P

CANTON, March 17. (AP).—Seventy-three officers of the Chinese army were executed here today after discovery of a communist plot to start mutiny in the troops at Swatow. A hundred other officers and soldiers are awaiting sentence. The central government stated in connection with the executions that it was having considerable trouble with red activity and influences, which have obtained a strong hold throughout the country. Ten days ago a division of government troops stationed on the Peking-Hankow railroad mutinied because they believed that their disbandment was imminent, and tore the tracks up in their neighborhood. They joined Red forces in ravaging the surrounding country.

Rome, March 17—(AP)—Police of four countries hunted today for a dozen members of an alleged international confidence gang revealed with the arrest of Mr. and Mrs. Charles L. Spencer of Albany, N. Y., and Leo L. Davidson, native of Kansas City, Mo., charged with a $35,000 swindle. Davidson hanged himself yesterday in his cell with a noose made from his underclothes. Police of England, Germany and Belgium who were notified of the arrests were asked to round up companions of Davidson and the Spencers. Spencer was said to have operated in Brussels, London and Berlin. Mrs. Spencer was released today but remained under police observation. A British Army Colonel B. B. Paymaster caused the arrest yesterday of Davidson and the Spencers. Authorities withheld his name but said he told them Davidson sold him $35,000 worth of fake stock. An investigation of Spencer’s marriage license will determine w

| VIENNA, Austria, March 16—(4)—Charlie Chaplin had a half hour of comparative peace tonight but he earned it. When a crowd of more fans mobbed him at Prater amusement park he climbed into the gondola of a Ferris wheel and rode around for 30 minutes.

Vienna—Some of Vienna's Charlie Chaplin fans fell through automobile tops today in their eagerness to get a look at the film comedian when he reached Vienna by train from Berlin. A crushing crowd was at the railway station and some of the throng climbed onto the tops of motor cars parked around the station, breaking through when they craned their necks.

1931-03-11.text: LONDON, MAR. 11. (AP).—The terms of the British-Franco-Italian naval accord transferring the London naval pact into a virtual five-power agreement were made public today in the form of a memorandum by Arthur Henderson, the foreign secretary. Its terms covered three outstanding considerations in the armament situation—technical problems of European naval power are swept away; renewal of an armaments race, such as led to the World War, has, it is hoped, been prevented; success of the world disarmament conference at Geneva is brought measurably closer. The agreement is based on the principle of continuance of the present Franco-Italian tonnage ratio until 1936, filling a gap in the London treaty by bringing the French and Italian fleets within the effective operation of the pact signed at St. James Palace last spring. More important than its technical aspect, however, may be the rapid subst

The ships will be armed with guns not to exceed 12 inches in caliber. The agreement permits France to build the proposed 29,333 ton “super-cruiser,” for which plans already have been drawn up by the naval ministry at Paris. The official memorandum, which embodied the terms of the accord in an annex, specified that, subject to decisions of the forthcoming 1932 world disarmament conference, the tonnage of French submarines in commission would not exceed 81,989 tons up to December 31, 1936. London—AP—There was no sign Wednesday of a break in the bitter winter weather which has gripped most of Europe since last week. France, Germany, Austria and the British Isles continued to experience exceptional low temperatures and heavy snowfalls. Although some places in England reported higher temperatures, others recorded temperatures of below zero Fahrenheit. Renewed snowstorms thickened the already heavy blanket of snow. France is experiencing the coldest late winter in many years. Temperatures vary from 14 to 26 Fahrenheit. Snowfalls have been particularly heavy in Normandy, Brittany, Alsace and Savoy where enormous avalanches have blocked a number of roads.

London, March 11 (UP)—The terms of the Franco-Italian naval limitations accord were made public today in an official memorandum revealing that both countries had agreed not to build more than two capital ships each of maximum tonnage of 23,333 tons before December 31, 1936. The ships will be armed with guns not to exceed 12 inches in calibre. The agreement permits France to build the proposed 23,333 ton “super-cruiser” for which plans already have been drawn up by the navy ministry in Paris. The official memorandum which embodied the terms of the accord specified that, subject to the decision of the forthcoming 1932 world disarmament conference, the tonnage of French submarines in commission would not exceed 81,989 tons up to December 31, 1936.
