Paris, March 11.— (AP) — Dispatches from Barcelona, Spain, today said the new republican catalanist party there had published a declaration expressing Catalonia’s aspiration to full autonomy and consecration to the principle of self-determination. The declaration proclaims complete separation from civil and ecclesiastical powers so far as the schools are concerned. The right to use of the Catalonian language, a guarantee of protection for private property honestly acquired, the right of workmen to sufficient pay, and insurance against illness, old age and unemployment. “The new party,” the proclamation reads, “erects a republic of democracy and catalanism in their general principles. On the twenty-second of March we will accomplish various public acts to inaugurate our activities.”

TURIN, Italy, March 11—-(UP)— Professor Lacchinin of the Pino Torinese observatory announced today the discovery, through astral photography, of traces of a new planet in the solar system. The new planet was named provisionally Ba.

Madrid, March 11.—(4)—Inquiries made in well-informed sources in Barcelona today regarding reports published abroad of the proclamation of a republic at Barcelona brought the statement that nothing was known there of such a development. Barcelona was reported to be quiet and considerable surprise was expressed to the reports abroad. Paris, March 11. (#) —Dispatches from Barcelona, Spain, today said the new Republican Catalanist party there had published a declaration expressing Catalonia’s aspiration to full autonomy and consecration to the principle of self-determination. The declaration proclaims complete separation from civil and ecclesiastical powers so far as schools are concerned, the right to use the Catalonian language, a guarantee of protection for private property honestly acquired, the right of workmen to sufficient pay, and insurance against illness, old age and unemployment.

Paris, Mar. 11 — Renewal of harmony among the five naval powers of the world is regarded in France as the most important achievement of the Franco-British-Italian naval accord. A spokesman for the foreign office said today that the agreement among these three nations is the sole guarantee for the success of the 1932 disarmament conference upon which the world has staked so much. Aristide Briand’s next move will be to submit to the French parliament the London naval treaty of 1930 which, it is expected, now will be ratified almost unanimously.
MUNICH, Bavaria, Mar. 11—() — Ink bottles and ash trays were used as missiles by Fascist members of the city parliament in an attack on People's Party deputies during debate last night.

1931-03-26.text: Nelson, B. C., March 23, (?)— itch powder has come to vex the Doukhobors, Seven Doukhobor women sat sunning themselves on a fence near Thrum. Spring had come, and the sunning was thorough, for the Doukhobors, a religious sect, are champions of the nude. Police, reporting the matter today, said the women were near the highway and railway. Officers told the Doukhobors to seek shelter and put on some clothes. The law met resistance; whereupon the constables unlimbered a unique contraption and sprayed the women with itch powder. The official report of Staff Sergeant Stephenson said the officers ‘dusted the Doukhobors with itch powder.’ “Finally,” continues the sergeant’s report, “after much dusting of itch powder and by force, the women were sent into their homes.”

London, March 26.—(U. P.)—David Lloyd George, Liberal party leader, announced in the course of a speech at Caxton Hall today that he favored “giving the Labor government another chance” with the understanding that Prime Minister J. Ramsay Macdonald’s cabinet will be ousted if it fails “to retrieve the situation.” Lloyd George warned that defeat of the government is inevitable “if the affairs of the nation are handled nervelessly and without vision or courage.” Lloyd George said the Liberal party which holds the balance of power in the House of Commons, would precipitate the defeat of the cabinet if “we are convinced there will be no improvement.” Unless the government leaders avoid reaction “they are headed for disaster” and will bring down with them “the whole force of progress” Lloyd George said in outlining the aims of the Liberal party. If the government fails in the future, the Libe

DUBLIN, Irish Free State—The condition of Tim Healy, veteran Irish statesman and first governor-general of the Irish Free State, who has been ill for some time, took a grave turn for the worse this afternoon. His son, who is an attorney and was arguing a case in court, was summoned to the bedside.

ROME, March 25. (P)—Two more arrests in connection with plots against the life of Premier Benito Mussolini were announced today by Italian secret police “Ovra.” Authorities said the men arrested were members of a bombing gang headed by Michele Schirru, a naturalized American citizen, who was arrested February 3, and is awaiting trial. Police did not disclose what preparations had been made in the conspiracy against the premier by the two newly-arrested men, Ersilio Belloni and Luigi Delfin. It was said they planned the execution of criminal acts, but were taken into custody March 4.

PARIS, March 26 (AP)—The Italo-French-British naval treaty conference ended today without any announcement of what decision had been reached by the representatives of the three countries on the final details of the treaty. It was understood, however, that the points discussed and solutions suggested must be referred to British naval experts in London.

MADRID, March 28. (UP)—Flying the red flag of rebellion students clashed with police at the San Carlos medical school today, resulting in the death of two persons and serious injury to 14. The students barricaded themselves within the school buildings and battled authorities with bullets and stones. Using pistols at first, the police were forced to resort to rifle fire to quell the uprising. About 40 were slightly hurt. After four hours of intermittent firing the students abandoned their fortress and fled through a rear door into the streets. They were not detained by the civil guards although later several were arrested. The government is studying the possibility of closing the university if trouble continues.

Rome, March 26 — Representatives of forty-six nations assembled here today to study methods for meeting the world wheat crisis. Premier Mussolini inaugurated the wheat conference at the International Institute of Agriculture. The United States was represented by an observer, Croes Simpson. The Italian government took the initiative to deal with a situation that has few recent parallels in the history of wheat production. No fewer than seventy-four nations, dominions and autonomous territories received invitations for today's meeting. Among the nations represented were Germany, Argentina, Bulgaria, France, England, Ireland, Australia, Canada, South Africa, British India, Greece, Mexico, Uruguay, Russia, Hungary, Poland, Switzerland and Czechoslovakia. Participating as observers are representatives of the League of Nations, the International Labor Bureau, the International Chamber of Comme

| PARIS, March 26 (CP) — The Austro-German customs pact will be submitted to the council of the League of Nations for its judgment, it was agreed today by Foreign Minister Arthur Henderson of Great Britain and Aristide Briand, no matter what attitude Germany and Austria may take. His information was contained in a statement to the press today by a spokesman for the French government, following a meeting between Henderson and Briand.

Berlin, March 4 (47) Chancellor Bruening today told Sir Horace Rumbold, the British ambassador, that the projected customs union between Germany and Austria is entirely within the bounds of the Geneva protocol of April 1922 and that, in his opinion, there is no reason for taking the agreement before the League of Nations council. If other governments want to examine its legal aspects, he said, Germany and Austria will not object and there is no reason for them to fear the outcome of such an examination. The proposed accord is purely an economic matter, Bruening said, and the German government considers it inadmissible to submit the agreement to examination from a political viewpoint. Herr Bruening told the ambassador, but it will probably be two or three months before the agreement is concluded. Sir Horace had come with a formal inquiry as to Germany’s intentions, at the direction of Art

PARIS, March 25.—(4)—Stiff and sore from a boar hunt on horseback, Charlie Chaplin said today he had cancelled his trip to Aintree to watch the running of the Grand National. “I feel that the mere sight of the horses going over the jumps will hurt every bone in my body,” he said.

MADRID, March 26.—(%)—Police guards on the streets of Madrid were doubled today in an effort to prevent further disturbances such as the student riots of yesterday when two persons were killed and thirty injured, several seriously. Twelve of the injured were civil guards and police officers. A government statement said that order would be maintained at all costs and denied that the students, who have been responsible for the disorders, represented a grave political problem. Many observers, however, felt that the government and the monarchy, in view of the prevailing open hostility of anti-Monarchist elements, was facing a serious situation.

1931-02-10.text: LONDON, Feb. 10. (AP) — An ominous picture of the next war waged by airplanes equipped with poison gas to wipe out non-combatant populations was drawn today by Arthur Henderson, British foreign secretary. Speaking before 3,000 persons at Queen’s Hall in the first of a series of addresses intended to mold public opinion in preparation for the forthcoming International disarmament conference, the labor minister pleaded for support of his government’s hope of substantial arms reductions.

LONDON, (AP)—The governor of New Zealand today cabled the dominion secretary that known deaths in the earthquake there last week so far number 212 and the injured 954, but the casualty list still is imminent.

LONDON, Feb. 9—()—King George today appointed the Earl of Bessborough, a distinguished Irish peer, to be governor-general of Canada succeeding Lord Willingdon, who has been named vice-roy of India. The announcement caused surprise, for Lord Bessborough's name had not hitherto been mentioned in connection with the post. The date of his departure for Canada was not announced.

Plymouth, £n7., Feb. 10. (AP). — “Lawrence of Arabia” that romantic figure who is now known as plain aircraftsman. Show appeared today as one of the heroes of the recent disaster here when nine men were killed in the plunge of a ‘staplane. At the court of inquiry Shaw turned up as one of the principal witnesses and it was revealed that he played a prominent role in the rescue of members of the plane's crew who escaped death in the crash. Because of his military achievement in Arabia Colonel Thomas E. Lawrence might have held a high government position, but in 1927 he suddenly decided to end the brilliant career he had begun and had his name legally changed to Thomas Edward Shaw. He was assigned as an enlisted man to the air service. Today he flitted in and out of the session of inquiry, which was private, with every attempt to escape publicity. Few details of his rescue work leaked from

LONDON, Feb. 9—(AP)—The MacDonald labor government tonight obtained a majority of 45 votes in carrying the agricultural marketing bill on second reading by 258 against 213 votes. The bulk of the liberal party voted with the laborites, assuring their victory in the division. It was the second time within a week that Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald had beaten his conservative opposition with the aid of the liberals.

TOKIO, Feb. 10.—(UP)—Forty-two persons were believed drowned when the Japanese liner Kikusui Maru sank after colliding with the French liner Porthos at 7:40 p.m. yesterday. The collision occurred in Akashi channel near Kobe, during a dense fog and blizzard. The Kikusui Maru sank almost immediately after the crash. Fifty-two were rescued and landed at Tokio. The Kikusui Maru plies between ports of the Inland Sea. The Porthos was leaving Kobe en route to Shanghai when the boats collided. All those reported missing were Japanese. The blizzard held responsible for the wreck is general throughout Japan. Snow storms were exceptionally severe in Tokio.

By ERICK KEYERS (United Press Staff Correspondent) BERLIN, Feb. 10.—The chief opposition parties, led by the 107 Fascist deputies, declared a boycott on the Reichstag today and evacuated the chamber in a body a few minutes prior to the foreign policy declaration of Dr. Julius Curtius. The foreign minister, who had been prepared to meet attacks of the opposition, read his speech indirectly demanding revision of the Versailles Treaty to a chamber dominated by pro-government deputies. Curtius announced Germany has no intention of destroying the Young reparations plan because international law binds her to the plan. “However, we never guaranteed our ability to fulfill the reparations obligations,” he said. “There has been a thorough revolution of world economic relations since the Hague reparations conference but the spirit of international co-operation is scarcely noticeable yet.” The Fasci

Berlin, Feb. 10—Reminding the world that Germany never guaranteed her ability to fulfill the Young Plan, Julius Curtius, the foreign minister, today told the Reichstag that the nation is determined nevertheless to live up to its provisions as long as possible and to try to change it only by legal means. In his first appearance before the parliament since he returned from the League of Nations discussions at Geneva, he outlined in detail the German foreign policy and described the world disarmament conference called for next February as the ‘touchstone of the efficacy of the League of Nations.’

BERLIN, Feb. 10. U.P)—The Fascist Party deputies, 107 strong, walked dramatically out of the Reichstag today with a threat that they would “not return until it is necessary to defend the nation against the treacherous attack of parliament.” The Fascists, angered by the parliamentary reforms forced through by the cabinet to prevent obstructionist tactics, were joined in their walkout by the Nationalist and Landvolk deputies.

1) Berlin, Feb. 10—(IWS)—Angered over the passage of a measure depriving them of their department, the fascists are withdrawing from the Reichstag. It is understood the Hitlerites plan to open their own assembly at Weimar in Thuringia, where a fascist government is in power. The fascists immediately resigned all their parliamentary offices, Stoehr surrendering his vice-presidential chair. Stoehr and Axel von Freytag-Loringhoven, a member of the Nationalist party, concurred in announcing the launching of a "bitterest life and death country-wide fight against the government and the Reichstag." On behalf of the communists, Deputy Stoecker announced his party would not join the exodus, which he characterized as a "swindle maneuver." The communists will retain their Reichstag seats, he said. The announcement, believed unprecedented in German parliamentary history, was followed by the formal e
ROME, Feb. 10. — The newspaper Giornale d’Italia reported today that Pope Pius would probably call a consistory for the creation of new cardinals immediately after Easter.

1931-01-31.text: Hastings, Eng. —-(UP) — Fire which some residents regarded as fulfillment of an ancient curse, destroyed part of the historic Battle Abbey today, with the loss of many valuable relics and tapestries from the days of the Normans. The fire, from which 120 girls in the Abbey school at the Town of Battle Abbey marched in safety, burned a banner of William the Conqueror valued at $50,000 and also destroyed one of the oldest examples of Norman architecture in England, where a high altar was built over the spot where the last Saxon king, Harold, was slain. Natives recalled an ancient curse which repeatedly has figured in the history of the Abbey. When Henry VIII seized the abbeys and monasteries throughout England, he gave Battle Abbey to Sir Henry Brown, who celebrated with a great feast. Amidst the revelry there was a thunderous knock on the door and a shrouded monk entered, pointing at Sir H

Manchester, England, Jan. 30. — Ge Churchill, fighting conservative, tonight followed up his break with party leaders over the Indian question by predicting “a terrible catastrophe” in India as an outcome of the government's policy. This policy, as outlined by Premier Ramsay MacDonald, looked to a “safeguarded” dominion status for India. The conservative leader, Stanley Baldwin, in a speech in parliament, virtually accepted the general principle and this led to Churchill's withdrawal from the inner circles of the party's leadership.

PARIS, Jan. 31 (AP) — Pierre Laval, son of a country butcher and one of the youngest men ever to reach the head of the French government, was established in office today by two votes of confidence, which surpassed the hope of even his fondest friends. His supporters saw in the two majorities, 54 on the first vote, and 51 on a ballot rejecting an opposition amendment to the original question of confidence, in the seventh in the life of the present parliament, would hold on until a new president is elected in June to succeed M. Doumergue. In winning his chamber victory after reading of the ministerial declaration, Premier Laval, who is 47 and always wears a white tie, proved almost as great a spellbinder as his mentor, Aristide Briand, a leading candidate in the race for the presidency to succeed M. Doumergue. Modest, persuasive and sincere, his appeal to rise above politics and work for t

(By Associated Press) ISTANBUL, Turkey, Jan. 31—Thirty-seven persons accused of attempting to foment a holy war in Turkey were condemned to death today by a military court. The sentence of five were commuted to 24 years hard labor. The other 32 will be hanged tomorrow in the public square.

PARIS, Jan. 30.—Pierre Laval, a butcher's son and one of the youngest of France’s prime ministers, was confirmed as the head of the government by the Chamber of Deputies in two test votes tonight. The youthful prime minister staked his life of his ministry on a laconic resolution expressing approval of the ministerial declaration which he had read earlier in the day—and in which he asked for peace among the political groups so he might carry on the country’s business without the interruptions of political bickering. He was accorded a vote of 312 to 258 and immediately raised the question of confidence anew by demanding the rejection of an amendment which had been offered to the original motion.

Istanbul, Turkey, Jan. 31.—(AP)—Sheik Essad, 96-year-old leader of a holy war which flamed and died in a day last December, dropped dead in his cell today when told he was to be hanged for treason. He would not have gone to the gallows, for the parliament was ready to commute the sentence to a long prison term. Military court which recently condemned several other leaders in the movement today passed sentence of execution on 37 more of the accused, including the old sheik’s son, Ali, himself 63 years old. Five of the condemned, all of them over 65, were reprieved when their sentences were commuted to 24 years at hard labor. The other 32 will be hanged tomorrow in the public square at Menemen.

Paris——Dierre Laval, one of the youngest premiers France ever has had, made his bow to the chamber of deputies Friday afternoon with a plea that the warring political blocs bury the hatchet and give the government a chance to carry out its policies of peace and reconstruction. His government, the ministerial declaration said, “stands for methodical and patient organization of world peace in collaboration with all nations sincerely holding the same viewpoint, regardless of treaties.” There was a general expectation that the chamber would endorse Laval's program and vote him a grant of power. Debate on this first declaration of the new government was to take place this evening. “The government,” Laval's declaration said, “will pursue a policy of better understanding among the nations, without losing sight of the national security. “The government also has decided to continue the national d

Shanghai, Jan. 31.—(A.P.)—Chinese press dispatches today said Nationalist government troops had surprised 8,000 bandits in southwest Honan province, killing 1,000 and rescuing 600 of their captives who were held for ransom. The dispatches said the brigands were moving the captives into the mountains when attacked. The escaping outlaws fled.

(By Associated Press) SESTO CALINDA, Italy, Jan. 31. —The Italian aviator Passaleva today claimed the world’s record for altitude with a useful load of 2,000 kilograms (4,400 pounds). He reached a height of 6,500 meters (21,363 feet). The previous record was held by the pilot Antonini, also an Italian, with an altitude of 6,262 meters (20,433 feet).

SHANGHAI, Jan. 31.—(4)—Chinese press dispatches today said nationalist government troops had surprised 3,000 bandits in southwest Henan province, killing 1,000 and rescuing 3090 of their captives who were held for ransom. The dispatches said the brigands were moving the captives into the mountains when attacked. The escaping outlaws fled. The Rev. Bert Nelson, an American missionary, and the Rev. K. N. Tvedt, a Norwegian, who have been held by bandits since last October, have been taken to Hwang Shihkang near Anhuihupeh. This information came to the American legation today in a message from the Rev. C. C. Skinsnes, of the Lutheran United mission at Hunan. Both are in good health, despite the hardships they have endured, the message said.

LAS PALMAS, (Canary Islands, Jan. 31.— The DO-X, world’s largest heavier-than-air plane, carrying a total of nineteen persons, passengers and crew, arrived here from Lisbon, Portugal, this afternoon at 10:50 a. m. (Eastern Standard Time.) With its arrival here the big ship had safely completed the first leg of the flight which is to carry it from Portugal to New York, via the South Atlantic and Brazil.

ARICOIA, Italy, Jan. 31. — (2) — Latin blood, Italian nights, dark eyes and the strains of mandolins got themselves so tangled up here that I took a company of carabineers to put them right again. Teresa Palombi was altogether too beautiful for one small village, one hundred youths thought so. And they proceeded to do their best to tell the fair one. One hundred mandolins tinkled under her window. One hundred throats warbled, “O Sole Mio,” into the moonlit night. One hundred knives were ready to leap at the throats of ninety-nine hated rivals. The lady was eighteen and she loved it. That is she loved it until all the boys began to compare notes. They found she'd told them all that each was “the only one.” It took a company of wide-hatted carabineers to arrest one hundred young men thirsting for each other’s blood. Now they're all in jail, all but those in the hospital. Teresa weeps alone

SHANGHAI, Jan. 30.—(7)—Barbaric cruelties inflicted by Reds upon government troops defeated with heavy losses in Kiangsi province were related today in Chinese press dispatches from Nanchang. General Chang Hwei-Tsai, commander of 12,000 government troops in Southern Kiangsi whom the Communists recently disarmed, was reported tortured to death by his captors when the government failed to send the Reds $2,000,000 Mexican ($480,000 gold) for release. The story of torture was brought to Nanchang by one of three brigadier generals with the captured army. The two other brigadiers suffered Chang's fate.

1931-03-23.text: LEIGHTON BUZZARD, England, March 22.--(4)--Three passengers and three of the train crew were killed today when the Royal Scot Express, one of the finest and fastest trains in the world, left the rails near here and piled up along the track. One of the dead was Sir George Saltmarsh, grain expert, who was vice chairman of the allied wheat purchasing commission in 1915 and 1916. The engineer, the fireman and a dining car steward were killed and nine other passengers were seriously injured. The cause of the accident was not immediately determined. The accident, which occurred at 12:15 p.m., caused great excitement in this peaceful countryside, 38 miles from London. Tangled wreckage blocked all traffic. There was no fire. The “Royal Scot” is one of the fastest trains in the world and about a month ago averaged 90 miles per hour for a 299-mile run.

London, March 22.—The life of the Labor government as well as the fate of many national and empire issues may be profoundly affected by the British political drama which will be unfolded this week. Indian negotiations and international problems, particularly in reference to world-wide disarmament, are only a few of the questions involved. Never in modern times has the political confusion been greater in this country than at present. A major crisis exists as a result of the fine balance of parties in Parliament and internal party dissension over policies and personalities. The Laborites have their own worries with Sir Oswald Mosley forming a “new party” on the right and the Maxtonites on the left wing causing even more real trouble. But Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's troubles are small compared with those of leaders of the older parties, such as David Lloyd George and Stanley Baldwin.

LEIGHTON BUZZARD, Eng. March 23.—(UP)—Relief crews and doctors labored throughout the night to remove injured and dead from the wreckage of three coaches of the Royal Scot Express, which was derailed at the station here yesterday with a loss of at least six lives. It was feared that more of the wounded might die. The train was one of the fastest in the world and was making about 76 miles an hour when it fouled a switch. Two coaches were telescoped, another was turned over and wrecked and every car on the train was derailed. About 60 persons were injured, most of them slightly. The engineer and fireman were killed. One of the passengers killed was Sir George Saltmarsh, an authority on wheat, who had just returned from Australia.

MELBOURNE, Australia, March 22.—An intensive search was made today for an airplane of the National Airways, carrying six passengers and a pilot, which has been missing between Melbourne and Sydney since yesterday. Five planes made a fruitless search today and considerable anxiety was expressed over the absence of the plane. It was last seen about 3:30 P.M. yesterday at Wagaratta, 145 miles north of here. The search will be continued on a wider scale tomorrow. Among those who will join in looking for the missing plane is Wing Commander Charles Kingsford-Smith, famous Australian flier.

NEW DELHI, Mar. 22.—(AP)—“Come walk with me at four o'clock in the morning and I will answer all your questions,” Mahatma Gandhi said, when asked for an interview. And so, with several hundred admirers trotting behind and settling a rapid pace, the nationalist leader, despite his frail physique and more than 62 years, discussed the affairs of his country as he walked for five miles among the crumbling monuments and seared forts of old Delhi’s forgotten empires. “War will never be exterminated by any agency until men and nations become more spiritual and adopt the principle of brotherhood and concord rather than antagonism, competition and superiority of brute force,” Gandhi declared. “You in the west do not recognize the power of spiritual things, but some day you will and then you will be free from war, crimes of violence and things that go with these evils. The west is too materialisti

NEW DELHI, India, March 22—(P)—Mahatma Gandhi today turned down an invitation to ride in an airplane with John E. Pratt and Ross Hadley, American aviators who arrived here today on a round-the-world flight. “If I must soar into the heavens,” Gandhi told them, “I prefer to do it through the natural process of transmigration after I leave this earth.”

BERLIN, March 28. (AP)— Foreign Minister Curtius today received successively the French, British and Italian Ambassadors to explain the intentions of Germany and Austria in agreeing to a virtual customs union. During the next few days, it was announced, the foreign minister will see the ministers of all states bordering upon Germany and Austria to offer similar explanations. In foreign office circles confidence prevailed that Curtius can satisfactorily allay any fear that the proposed union might be in contravention of existing treaties or protocols. VIENNA, Mar. 23. (AP) Austria today answered protests against her proposed customs union with Germany with an invitation to other European countries to join them in an abolition of customs barriers. A formal protest by diplomatic representatives of France, Italy, and Czechoslovakia drew from Dr. Johann Schober, foreign minister and vice-chan

(By The Associated Press) Paris, Mar. 25--The Havas News Agency says today that a decree naming Charles Chaplin a chevalier of the Legion of Honor will be issued soon by the foreign office. LAKOTA CAFE OPEN TUESDAY

Berlin, March 23—(4)—Development of a 200-horse power “vest pocket” motor weighing only 14 pounds, which is expected to revolutionize long-distance airplane flying, has been accomplished by Paul Heylandt, a German expert on liquid gases. With Max Valier the inventor last year surprised the world with a rocket-motor propelled by recoil through igniting liquid air mixed with gasoline. Herr Heylandt will arrive in New York for a visit soon. By improving and enlarging his rocket-motor, which originally weighed seven pounds and then yielded 35 to 40 horsepower, Heylandt now feels he has a motor that surpasses any gasoline motor for economy, simplicity and safety. “By May or June we will be able to demonstrate that a continuous stream of propulsive energy can be created by our invention, which is superior to powder rockets where the stream is sporadic,” he said. “We are concerned this year wit

MADRID, March 23.—()—Riot- ing broke out around the city hall and inside the council chamber today, when during a meeting of the city council Alderman Garcia Cortes, formerly a socialist and now a liberal, opposed a measure for an increase of pay for municipal employees. Clerks, porters, and all classes of city hall employees stormed into the council chamber, shouting for more money and “down with Garcia Cortes.” On the outside, shouting street cleaners and other employees packed the plaza. When Alderman Cortes left the city hall the crowd attacked him. Police dispersed the rioters without injury or arrest.

| Paris, March 23. — Thirteen years ago today the great German gun, the “Big Bertha,” fired for the first time on Paris from Laon, a distance of 75 miles, and Parisians today observed the anniversary of one of the blackest days of the war by carrying flowers to Saint Gervais, the church in which 75 women and children were killed and 80 hurt by a shell of the big gun on Good Friday afternoon, 1918. The first of the seven German “Paris guns” was set up in the forest of Laon early in March, 1918, and for several weeks the gun crew fired blank shells to get used to the great artillery piece. Finally, on the night of March 22, the German High Command ordered the gun fired the next day and on March 23 seven shells were dropped on Paris at intervals of 15 minutes. The first hit in front of the East Railroad Station where troops were embarking. The public blamed air bombs, although the skies wer

PARIS, March 23.—(#)—The French cabinet approved today the movement initiated by Aristide Briand to attempt to determine whether the Austro-German economic accord involved any infringement of the independence of Austria. Briand explained that the ministers of various European powers interested have requested information on the proposed treaty from Vienna.

VIENNA, Mar. 23 (P)—Quick to resent a collaboration which they feel may bear the seed of dread “Mittel Europa,” France, Italy and Czechoslovakia have made formal protest at a projected Austro-German treaty of customs union. Diplomatic representatives of the three countries in a Sunday call upon Dr. Johann Schober, foreign minister, informed him that the conclusion of such a union would infringe the Geneva protocol of Oct. 4, 1922. This protocol is that in which Austria, obtaining a loan from the former allied countries, reiterated its agreement to preserve its independence. Dr. Schober is understood to have attempted to show them that the pact in no way compromised the protocol and did not impair Austrian independence. Vienna's Answer VIENNA, Mar. 23 (UP)—Austria today answered protests against her proposed customs union with Germany with an invitation to other European countries to join

PARIS—Charlie Chaplin was the guest today of Aristide Briand at a small informal luncheon at the foreign office. Lord Tyrrell, the British ambassador, was there and also Minister of Justice Leon Berard who decorated Chaplin in 1921 with the Purple Rosette, making him "Officer of the Academy."

Tokyo, Japan—(By the Canadian Press)—Mlle. Alexandra Tolstoy, daughter of the Russian Novelist Count Leo Tolstoy, who has reportedly sought permission from the Canadian government to enter the Dominion, says now that she has been ordered by the Soviet government to return to Russia. “I have no intention of doing so,” she commented. “The Soviet government is oppressing primary school education of the Yasnaya Polyana system, so cherished by my father, and is permitting terrorism against religion, dear to my father and myself. I have accepted an invitation from the Doukhobors in Canada to go there and edit their newspapers, and I hope to spend the rest of my life in Canada.” Mlle. Tolstoy has not yet received from the Canadian government the permit for which she has applied, the obstacle to which is her inability to produce a passport from Russia.

MADRID, March 22. - (4) ~ Two dozen beggars, many of them blind, were selected today for the annual ceremony in which the king and queen, aided by Spain's grandees, humbly anoint their feet. Bishop Zion, chief chaplain of the palace, selected 12 men and 13 women from several hundred candidates for the ceremony, which will take place at the palace on Holy Thursday, April 2. King Alfonso and Queen Victoria will be seated on their thrones when the unfortunates are brought before them. Their majesties will then descend and anoint the feet of their poor subjects. Each supplicant will receive a basket of food and new clothes.

PARIS, March 23 (P)—Richard Halliburton, author and lecturer, hopped off today on the second lap of a projected round the world flight. Accompanied by the American pilot Moye Stephens, he left for Lyons, Perpignan, Barcelona and Fez.

1931-03-21.text: .PLYMOUTH, England, July 28 “Pi—The submarine Nautilus, in which Sir Hubert Wilkins plans to cross the North Pole under the ice, left today for Bergen, Norway, en route to the Arctic. Hundreds of Americans witnessed the departure of Sir Hubert, in his little craft as she passed alongside the Mauretania, just in from New York. Passengers aboard the liner cheered lustily.

New Delhi, India—(?)—Departing from his traditional attitude of non-cooperation with the government, Mahatma Gandhi today joined what might be termed a miniature round table conference which is to pave the way for the second round table conference to be held in London soon. Attired only in his loin cloth, which cost about a shilling, he sat at a massive walnut table in the sumptuous viceroy’s palace with blue-blooded Indian princes clad in resplendent silk and gold robes, stunning turbans and glistening jewels around him. At his right sat Viceroy Lord Irwin, who a year ago had him thrown in jail for his challenge to the British crown. Today's conference with the congress of Indian princes, which has been in session at New Delhi for several days, is for the purpose of preliminary work to the second round table conference at London and to measure the possibilities of cooperation between th

Glasgow, Scotland—#—The inbound Canadian Pacific liner Montclare ran aground Saturday afternoon on the Arran side of Little Cambrae Island, in the Firth of Clyde, in a dense fog. Six tugs were sent from Greenock to the liner’s assistance. The Montclare developed a dangerous list as the tide receded and lifeboats were lowered to carry the passengers ashore. The tugs which went to the scene picked up 200 passengers who had been landed on the rocky island. It was feared the Montclare had a bad hole. It struck a hidden reef.

BERLIN, March 20,—(AP)—Hermann Mueller, twice chancellor of the German Republic and one of the leaders of the revolution in November, 1918, died tonight after a prolonged illness. The political leader's wife and two daughters were at his bedside when he died at 10:45 p.m. The 54-year-old statesman had been in a coma for hours and his physicians had given up hope for recovery. Herr Mueller, who headed the sixth and nineteenth post-revolution German Cabinets, underwent an operation on Saturday for removal of a bladder abscess and gallstones after several days of acuteness. His condition improved somewhat, reviving hopes he might recover, but he suffered a relapse Monday night and steadily became worse. He became so weak yesterday that blood transfusions were resorted to. Inflammations of the right lung set in and he was conscious only momentarily since yesterday. Despite his robust appeara

BERLIN, March 21. (AP).—The band which, unflinching, wrote the principal German signature to the treaty of Versailles, was stilled today in death. Succumbing to a long illness, Dr. Hermann Mueller, twice German chancellor and one of the two or three most influential men of German postwar politics, passed away last night. He was 54 years old. He was in a comatose condition for several hours preceding the end which was brought about by thrombosis of the liver, complicated by pneumonia. A bladder operation last Saturday failed to aid him. Dr. Mueller first was a German chancellor for three months in 1920. He came to power the second time in June, 1928, remaining in office until March, 1930, when the present chancellor, Dr. Bruening, succeeded him.

Terness of good dissension was brought once more into sharp relief today when the Reichstag and the Prussian Diet met to pay tribute to former Chancellor Hermann Mueller. His death last night removed another statesman who personified the policy of conciliation and treaty settlement. The convened at noon with many members garbed in black out of respect to the former chancellor, but the National Socialists, the Nationalists and even the were absent from the chamber as President Loebe began the session with a eulogy to his comrade. In the Diet only one Communist was present, and he refused to stand when other members rose in token of respect for Hermann Mueller.

BERLIN, Mar, 21.—P—Germany today mourned the death of Hermann Mueller, former coalition government chancellor who gained world recognition as one of the German statesmen who signed the treaty of Versailles. Mueller, one of the leading power war statesmen in republican Germany, died last night after a fight which developed into pneumonia. His condition had been steadily worse following an operation last Saturday. It was believed that Mueller was the most influential moderate leader in the Social Democratic Party. It was believed that his death probably would be felt at once in the party's policies, as radicals are urging stricter advance of the socialist platform.

1931-03-07.text: LONDON, Mar. 7 (AP) — Wild storms which lashed the eastern Atlantic into a turbulent fury, today disrupted shipping as far north as Iceland and as far south as northern Africa. J. P. Morgan’s yacht, the Corsair, upon which the Archbishop of Canterbury, convalescing after an attack of neuralgia, is accompanying the financier to Palestine, had to put in at Gibraltar to escape the gale. The Ile de France and President Harding were many hours late on the way to Cherbourg because of the storm. The President Harding developed propeller trouble and may have to be drydocked. A northeasterly gale whipped up high waves in the North Sea and broke over defenses on the southeast coast of England, flooding a large section of the sparsely inhabited flat country known as Romney Marsh.

London, March 7.—(AP)—Philip Snowden, British chancellor of the exchequer who has been ill for several days with influenza, was understood today to be in a more serious condition than was at first supposed. His advisers have called in Sir John Thomson-Walker, a Harley Street surgeon. An official bulletin will be issued this afternoon as soon as Sir John has seen Mr. Snowden.

LONDON, Mar. 7—(7)—With the date for presentation of his 1931 budget only a short way ahead, Philip Snowden, 67, chancellor of the exchequer, is confined to bed with an illness which probably will not permit him to leave his home for several weeks.
LONDON, March 7 (7) — A Reuter’s dispatch from Belgrade said at least fifteen persons were drowned today in a steamer collision on the River Danube.

London, March 6.—(AP)— A wild scene of cheers, boos and free-for-all fights marked a mass meeting at Albert Hall tonight at which a so-called “Soviet Slave” appealed to British friends of Russia to do all in their power to end what he described as terrible conditions in the convict camps of north Russia. The mass meeting was called by the great Trades Defense Union. More than 50 scuffles and fist fights occurred and there was much shouting of “Long Live the Soviets!” Many of the disturbers were thrown bodily into the streets after they hurled derision at Winston Churchill, Lord Brentford and other speakers. LONDON, March 7.—A 15-mile-an-hour easterly gale, the worst experienced this year, swept the English Channel today, forcing many ships to seek refuge in various ports and inundating a large area of land in proximity to the coast. Authorities at Southampton stated that the United States Lines vessel President Harding developed propeller trouble en route to New York from Hamburg and asked that a crew of divers be held in readiness here. The liner’s message, although not giving the exact nature of her trouble, requested immediate examination of her screws on docking here.

Vienna —(P)— Widespread destruction in South Serbia from two earthquake shocks this morning was reported in dispatches from Balkan cities today. Residents and public buildings in many towns, notably Demir, Kapia and Valandovo were shaken down. The shocks drove large sections of the population panic-stricken into the open. There was only one known fatality, but it was feared there were others. In the Valandovo region, a mountain slide swept a shepherd and 200 sheep to death. At Guevgueli, the first shock split the post office in two. The Athens express was held up because of the quakes, which tore up the roadbed.

Tokyo, March 7—(A.P.)—The arrival of a new princess at the imperial palace today caused all Japan to celebrate, and while her birth left the emperor still without a male heir to succeed him on the throne, any feeling of disappointment among the people was well concealed. The royal baby was born at 12:02 p.m. and is the fourth daughter borne by Empress Nagako. Since only male descendants of the Japanese emperors may occupy the throne, Prince Chichibu, younger brother of Emperor Hirohito, remains as the heir presumptive of the oldest unbroken royal line in the world. The line was established in 660 B.C., and Hirohito is the 124th emperor. News of the birth was broadcast by radio throughout the nation and by a single blast of sirens in Tokyo and other larger cities. Newspapers issued extras and the rising sun flag, national emblem, was hoisted in many places. The new princess, who weighed 7

PARIS, Mar. 7. (AP)—French rivers, swollen by heavy rain and snow during the past week, have flooded a large area and today were doing considerable damage. The Seine was rising steadily and had a threatening aspect because of the tremendous volume of water rushing into it from tributaries. At Paris the Seine has risen more than 11 inches since yesterday. The waters have invaded the Ile St. Louis, and in the suburbs have transformed many streets into sluggish brooks.

Paris, March 6, — (4) — Several suburbs of Paris were under water tonight and with the Seine river still rising, conditions were more precarious than in the disastrous floods of last December. A light snow fell throughout the day. The meteorological bureau expects a further rise of the Seine. So far Paris itself has been immune from damage.

Vienna, March 7—(INS)—Many Serbians were reported killed today in an earthquake that shook the southeastern part of Yugoslavia during the night, advice from Belgrade stated. ‘The town of Delmir Kapu was said to be entirely destroyed,

ROME, March 7.—(AP)—It was said on excellent authority here today that the Italo-Franco-British naval accord would be signed at London Tuesday by the ambassadors of the three countries, as well as by the ambassadors of the United States and Japan. PARIS, March 7.—(AP)—The foreign office announced today that the text of the British-Franco-Italian naval accord will be made public Wednesday at 1 p. m., Paris time, in Paris, London, Rome, Washington and Tokyo.

Parla, Mar. 7—(P)—France tomorrow will count noses, Throughout the country census takers will rap on front doors and ask for return of blanks which were left several days ago to be filled out. An unofficial count in 1929 placed the population at 41,140,600. All the blanks will be collected in one day. Voyagers will be tabulated in hotels, The census is taken every five years.

TOKIO, Mar. 7.--A daughter, fourth child of the Nipponese reigning house, was born today to the Empress of Japan. Although the entire country had hoped and prayed for an heir apparent, the broadcasting of the happy event gave occasion for nationwide rejoicing. Thousands of the Mikado’s subjects flocked to the royal palace immediately after announcement of the princess's birth, to kneel and bow in reverence before its gates and pray for the well-being of mother and child.

1931-03-03.text: New Delhi, March 3 (4)—Mahatma Gandhi and Sir George Schuster, Indian finance minister, conferring today at the Vice-Regal Palace, reached an agreement on the salt question, one of the outstanding problems in the way of abandonment of the civil disobedience campaign. Almost exactly a year ago the Indian Nationalists, led by Gandhi, initiated a campaign of violation of the salt laws, which provide for a British monopoly. Throughout current negotiations for calling off the civil campaign, Gandhi has contended that the Indian people be empowered to make their own salt. It was understood the agreement provides that people living on the seacoast will be allowed to manufacture and sell salt, which will be regarded as nature's gift to them.

MELBOURNE, Australia, Mar. 8 (AP) — Millions of mice suddenly have invaded the Nullarbor plains along the trans-Australian railway. The station master at Loongana today reported that miles of the country served by the railway were infested with the rodents. While he was attending a passenger train thousands entered his office and soon began eating a roll of pound notes. He said that every house in the district had been invaded by the pests which were attacking even the furniture and the bedding.

New Delhi, India, March 2.—(4)—All signs indicated tonight that Mahatma Gandhi and Viceroy Lord Irwin would sign a truce tomorrow, thus bringing an era of peace to distracted India. The strife and bitterness which have torn the country intermittently for twenty years—and especially the last year—costing thousands of lives, millions of dollars and untold misery, will, it is believed, cease at last. Rebels Face a Task. Gandhi and his host of nationalist rebels will be free to devote themselves to the task of constructing a new and united India. This turn of events, following indications Saturday that there was little hope for the viceroy and Gandhi agreeing, tonight was regarded as the most momentous period in India’s history since Great Britain took possession of the great peninsula 150 years ago. Things looked black Saturday after the working committee of the All-India Nationalist Congre

NEW DELHI, India, Mar. 3 (UP) — An agreement permitting natives along the sea coast to gather, manufacture and sell salt was reached today by Mahatma Gandhi and Schuster who are negotiating for a settlement of the civil disobedience movement. The salt law previously had forced natives to buy salt from British interests holding a monopoly. The agreement brought the negotiators nearer the expected peace agreement.

NEW DELHI, India, March 3.-- (UP)-- A truce in the Indian civil disobedience movement apparently was at hand tonight with only one outstanding question to be settled. The unsettled question, which was the subject of consultations which the Mahatma Gandhi continued to conduct, concerned return of confiscated property of volunteers in the independence movement and reinstatement of dismissed government servants.

(United Press Staff Correspondent) PARIS, Mar. 2—The naval accord reached last week at Paris and Rome was “merely the prelude to the rapid ending of all Franco-Italian problems,” Foreign Minister Aristide Briand said today in debating the foreign affairs budget in the chamber of deputies. Briand described the accord as another move toward world disarmament. “The naval accord represents another step in the general direction of total world disarmament,” Briand said. “Italy must be praised for her unselfish role. “The conclusion of a naval agreement is merely a prelude to the rapid ending of all Franco-Italian problems, including the thirty-year discussion of the status of Italians in Tunisia and of the African colonial frontiers.” The Franco-Italian controversy in northern Africa has been a serious one in the past, particularly in connection with claims of Italy that she was not treated ju

PARIS, March 2 UP—With a tripartite naval agreement reached among France, Great Britain and Italy, and approved today by the French cabinet, the next development tonight appeared to be that another five-power parley now may be necessary. Although it is admitted that the modifications to existing naval treaties caused by yesterday’s three-power accord do not affect directly the vital interests of the United States and Japan—other powers which attended the London naval conference last spring—the Associated Press was informed tonight of the likelihood of the five power meeting. This was laid to the supposition it may be difficult to incorporate the modifications without a formal meeting of all the powers which signed the Washington treaty of 1920. Nevertheless, all circles are confident the United States and Japan will accept the new accord.

MOSCOW, Mar. 2 (AP) — Fourteen leaders of the Russian Social Democratic party today began detailed confessions on the witness stand after pleading guilty yesterday to plotting overthrow of the Soviet government by means of sabotage and foreign intervention. There seemed little interest in the proceedings and there were many vacant seats in the courtroom. This was attributed partly to the dry program outlined by the famous Soviet prosecutor, N. B. Krilenko, who spent most of the session examining the defendants on the organization of the Social Democratic party. Examination He conducted the examination in five parts: First, organization, second, activities of the party in foreign countries, third, the connection with other counter-revolutionary organizations, fourth, sabotage, fifth, documentary evidence. The defendants today all wore earphones and listened intently to Krilenko’s question

Berlin, Mar, 3—(AP)—The Bruening government weathered another storm in the Reichstag today defeating a communist motion of non-confidence in Martin Schiele, minister of agriculture, 311 to 60. The vote was taken shortly after the Reichstag convened. The communists took the position that the government's farm policy was harmful to labor.

PARIS, March 3 (4)—No country emerged victor in the naval accord arrived at over the week-end by France, Great Britain and Italy, Aristide Briand, French foreign minister, told the chamber of deputies today. “Every country made the necessary sacrifices,” he declared. “That is the best praise I can give it.” The details of the agreement have not yet been published, pending their study by the Washington and Tokyo governments. “It is a satisfactory accord,” Mr. Briand said, “and when you know all of its details you will be convinced that it is satisfactory.”

(Oey S488 MHOUCIALOG FTES. j Paris, Mar. 3—Foreign Minister Aristide Briand told the chamber of deputies today that Soviet Russia has the most formidable army in the world. Replying to charges by Marcel Cachin, communist deputy, that France was inimical to Soviet Russia and was harboring a “white army,” he declared the charges “both unjust and ridiculous.” “The French government,” he said, “has no knowledge of such organizations and it is stupid to talk about a white army existing in Paris while Russia herself has the most formidable army which exists in the world.”

1931-03-02.text: Lopdon, Mar. 2—(4)—The greater part of Europe and the British Isles were under snow today. A biting wind piled the white blanket high in places and in others swept the ground bare. Bitter cold prevailed. Extreme winter conditions prevailed over most of the continent from Urria to France. Sheep farmers suffered severe losses of stock. The gale which accompanied the snow raised dangerous seas in the channel and North Sea which claimed several victims. Sixteen were believed to have perished near Fraserburgh, Scotland, when a Dutch trawler turned over offshore and conditions were too bad to attempt a rescue. One body was washed ashore.

LONDON, March 2—Northern Europe looked for an abatement today of violent weather that caused numerous deaths in storms and blizzards and harassed shipping during the weekend. The entire crew of 16 aboard a Dutch fishing trawler from Ymulden was believed drowned off Reshearty, Scotland. The trawler was seen wallowing, bottom up in tremendous seas. Assistance was impossible although the ship was not far from shore. One body was washed up on the beach. Three fishermen were drowned in Seaton Sluice, Northumberland, when their boat capsized. Violent gales in the Irish Sea and the English Channel handicapped continental steamers and kept smaller boats in port. The gale reached 70 miles an hour in the Irish Sea. Heavy snow storms were general in the British Isles. Four inches of snow was recorded in many parts of the London area. Heavy blizzards were reported in Denmark. Several towns were floo

NEW DELHI, India, Mar. 2 — Mahatma Gandhi, exhausted and hoarse from his long conversation last night with the viceroy, was more cheerful today than at any time since the two men began their over-the-table conversations regarding Indian policies. The tide has turned, he said, expressing hope that developments at

An Aberdeenshire crew of twelve men was reported missing. Three men fishing from a motorboat off the Northumberland coast drowned when their boat capsized during a blizzard.

DELHI, India, Mar, 1—After six hours of heart-to-heart talk, Mahatma Gandhi, the late Nationalist leader, and the Viceroy of India tonight managed to prevent India’s political peace ship from foundering. After it had appeared negotiations to calm the country's turmoil of political affairs were doomed to failure, the little half-clad leader emerged smiling from his long talk with Lord Irwin and announced the conference would be continued Tuesday. Reject Viceroy’s Offer. Last night it had appeared not power on earth could adjust the disagreement after the working committee of the all-India national congress had rejected the Viceroy’s offer for a compromise settlement. It is understood the Viceroy’s action in reopening the discussions with Gandhi has caused a split in his executive council, some members of which have threatened to resign if Lord Irwin capitulates to Nationalist demands. London, March 2—(A.P)—The strange tale of a wife writing love letters for her husband to his bigamous wife because he could neither read nor write, was on record in Old Bailey court here today. In 1926 William George Chapman married Miss Venetia Stephenson. Four years later he also married Ethel Frances Talbot without the formality of divorcing his first wife. “Best love forever, until we return to ashes,” said one of the letters Talbot received during the courtship. The two women, it developed, had been good friends and when wife No. 2 learned that wife No. 1 had written her husband's love notes, she collapsed in the courtroom. Chapman pleaded guilty and was sentenced to nine months’ imprisonment on a bigamy charge.

MANSFIELD, March 2 — Three grocery store robberies and two holdups in which the victims were kidnapped and ‘taken for a ride’ were believed solved today with the arrest of three men. The prisoners were identified by Robert Forsythe as the bandits who forced him into their auto and stripped him of his clothing after driving to a lonely section of the country. Eugene Weyrick and Frank Roth were victims of similar holdups. Police believe also that the trio is responsible for three grocery store robberies last week.

Paris, March 4. — The French cabinet today decided that the tri-partite naval agreement reached last week by Great Britain, Italy and France was “satisfactory” it was announced after a meeting of the ministers, presided over by President Doumergue. Thus France's adherence to the arrangement which must now be submitted to the United States, Japan and the British dominions was virtually assured. The point which seemingly created the greatest interest was that one which some newspapers alleged would ask the United States and Japan to agree not to build capital ships larger than 23,000 or 26,000 tons, whereas the maximum fixed by the Washington treaty and unchanged by the London document was 35,000 for battleships.

Franco-Italian naval race, one of the most serious threats to the peace of post-war Europe, appeared today to have been eliminated with definite agreement of Great Britain, France and Italy on a naval relationship to be maintained during the next five years. The terms of the agreement were withheld pending transmission to Washington and Tokyo, but it was understood today that they were constructed around the actual needs of France and Italy until 1986, rather than on the basis of specifying a proportion between the navies. The agreement, if acceptable to the United States and Japan—and there was no doubt here on that score—will broaden the London naval treaty, which never was more than a three power pact in its important phases, to a five power instrument, limiting until 1986 the navies and naval construction programs of the great maritime nations of the world. ISTANBUL, Turkey, Mar. 2. (AP) — Leon Trotsky, Russian revolutionary leader who for more than a year has been a man without a country, has been burned out of house and home. The villa which he has occupied during his exile on Prinkipo Island, in the Sea of Marmora, took fire before dawn yesterday and burned to the ground before Trotsky and his wife, both of whom are ill with malaria, could rescue more than a few of their possessions. Trotsky was not able to save even a suit of clothes, but he did preserve some valuable letters from Lenin. Material for a book which he has been writing was lost as was his valuable library of hundreds of books. He managed to save a manuscript of a history of the Russian revolution which is about to be published.

PARIS, March 1.—An agreement on limitation of naval armaments which involves modifications of last year’s London naval treaty was concluded in Paris this evening by France, Britain and Italy. The text of the agreement will be cabled immediately to Washington and Tokyo, as both the United States and Japan were signatories to the London naval pact. It also will be sent to Canada and other British dominions which participated in the London conference. The accord which was reached by foreign and naval ministers of France, Britain and Italy, will be submitted to the respective governments with a recommendation that it be approved. Briand announced the details of the agreement would be published (Continued same page, 9 Column 1.)

Paris, March 2 (UP)—The naval accord reached between France, Italy, and Great Britain regulating construction until 1936 and avoiding a building race between France and Italy was approved today by the council of ministers. The accord will be submitted to parliament as soon as the United States and Japan adhere to the clause limiting the construction of future warships to 25,000 tons or less. "I am very well satisfied with the conclusion of the accord," Premier Pierre Laval told the United Press. "It will have much to do with our future relations with Italy." It was understood that the accord might be summed up as a modification of the Washington naval treaty. The totals of tonnage allotted to capital ships at Washington and incorporated in the London naval treaty will need to be rearranged.
