ISTANBUL, Turkey, March 2— Part of Leon Trotsky’s valuable library and an unfinished book upon which the exiled Soviet leader was working were destroyed by fire which damaged Trotsky's residence on Prinkipo island near here. Trotsky and his family were forced to leave the house in their night clothes, Trotsky's correspondence with Nikolai Lenin was not damaged. The fire originated in a faulty flue. Trotsky’s neighbors attempted to fight the fire with buckets of water but could not curb the flames. The large white wooden villa in which Trotsky has lived since his exile was gutted and only a shell of the structure remained. Fire fighters arrived from the mainland but were too late to save the interior of the house.

PARIS, March 2.—(UP)—March brought the winter’s worst storm today. An area extending from Russia to Central Italy was whipped by snow, wind and rain. Snow covered most of the British Isles and half of France. Many mountain villages were isolated. According to reports received here, two thirds of Italy was in the grip of the storm. Railroads were blocked in Denmark and Russia and trains were delayed in Germany, Holland, Belgium and France. Twenty fishing ships were reported missing in the North Sea and the English Channel.

ISTANBUL, Turkey, March 1.—(™—The villa occupied by Leon Trotsky on Prinkipo island in the Sea of Marmora burned to the ground this morning. The exiled Soviet leader, who has been ill with malaria, and his wife, who has been ill, were uninjured, but their private possessions, including material for a book the exile had been writing, were destroyed.

Berlin, March 2.—(UP)— A 15-horsepower, 2-cylinder automobile said to be the smallest yet produced—was one of the sensations at the Berlin automobile exhibition today, and German manufacturers already are thinking of invading the American market with it. The car is more diminutive than the Austin and stands a little over four feet high. Its makers claim it can do 60 miles to a gallon of gasoline and are particularly enthusiastic about the cabriolet model which has a rumble seat.

Parts, March 1. (4)--March entered France like a roaring lion today, bringing a severe snowstorm to Paris and vicinity. It was accompanied by thunder and lightning. Violent northeasterly gales lashed the Atlantic seaboard. Near Caen the valley of the Auge River was flooded for 30 square miles.

PARIS, March 2. (®) — The red ribbon of a knight of the Legion of Honor may blossom in Charlie Chaplin’s buttonhole next week-end when the comedian visits Paris. It was reported from 2 reliable sources today that the foreign office sees no impediment to the decoration and it was expected that the ministry of fine arts would shortly make a formal request for it. Charlie received the purple rosette of an officer of public instruction in 1921 on the occasion of his Paris visit when he appeared in a charity gala for the benefit of the devastated regions.

Tokio, March 2 (UP)—the birth of a fourth child and possible imperial heir to Empress Nagako is expected about the 15th of the month. The imperial household obviously is hopeful that the child will be a boy and heir to the throne, eventually succeeding his father, Emperor Hirohito, as 125th emperor in an "unbroken line" descended from the sun goddess, Amaterasu Omikami.
GENOA, Italy, March 2.—(4)— Heavy seas lifted the Italian schooner Luisa Madre and flung it against a breakwater. It was impossible to launch boats and the crew of six is believed lost.

Moscow, March 1,—(AP)—A counter-revolutionary trial opened this evening. All the actors were present, including 14 gloomy and mostly bewhiskered defendants; five judges, one of them a woman; the fiery prosecutor, N. B. Krilenko, and two defense counsel. But although the stage properties were the same as the recent dramatic engineers’ trial—except for motion picture cameras—great interest appeared absent. Before the indictments were ready, Krilenko said he intended to call six witnesses, including Professor Leonide Ramsin and Victor Laichey, two of the eight engineers who were sentenced to death but received commutations to 10 years imprisonment, and M. Kondriatiev. The last named was one of the leaders in a group of food speculators of whom 48 were shot last September. Guilt Admitted While all the 14 defendants are alleged to have confessed to manipulating the Russian social democratic p

1931-04-02.text: LONDON, (UP)—Twenty-three passengers aboard the French liner Florida, which collided with the aircraft carrier Glorious off Gibraltar yesterday, are missing and believed dead, the foreign office announced today. One passenger was known dead, the announcement said, and 15 were injured, two seriously.

London, April 2 (UP)—Lady Jean Doyle, widow of Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, told the United Press today that she had received a written message from her husband who died July 7 last. She said it was “the first time a message has been received from my husband in his own handwriting since his death.” Lady Doyle said the handwriting in the message from the famous spiritualist and creator of Sherlock Holmes was “100 per cent evidence of his psychic powers.” “My son and I were sitting with a famous photographic medium before us hoping that my husband would be able to show himself or the plate by us,” Lady Doyle told the United Press. “No hand but my own touched the plate from beginning to end including the development of the negative. “We developed the negative ourselves. In addition to my husband’s face which was shown on the plate as it appeared over the shoulder of my son, there was, to our ama

London, April 1. (AP)—Several of the crew of the French liner Florida were killed today when that vessel collided with the British aircraft carrier Glorious, sixty miles east of Gibraltar. An announcement by the British admiralty said the bodies had been left in the Florida, which was taken in tow by the Glorious. Others in the crew were seriously injured. All were transferred with the passengers to the man-of-war. So far as could be ascertained tonight none of the passengers were killed or injured. The commander-in-chief of the British Mediterranean fleet was proceeding to H.M.S. Queen Elizabeth to join the Florida off Malaga at daylight.

(International News Service) LONDON, April 1.—In a report to the British Admiralty, the commandant of the British carrier Glorious stated that twenty-three emigrant passengers of the French liner Florida were found to be missing following a collision between the two vessels. The report stated they were probably killed when the two ships crashed in a dense fog sixty miles east of Gibraltar. Most of the French liner’s passengers were Italians and Syrians. Seventeen planes from the Glorious’ complement were in the air at the time of the collision. Four passengers from the Florida who were thrown into the water by the impact were rescued and taken to Malaga by the airmen. The Florida was beached at the first opportunity, but the Glorious was found seaworthy and proceeded to Gibraltar. The foreign office announced that one of the Florida’s passengers was known to be dead and two seriously and

Malaga, Spain, April 2 — The French consul here reported today that thirty persons had been killed and five seriously injured when the French liner Florida collided with the British aircraft carrier Glorious during a fog in the Mediterranean yesterday. The dead and injured are all steerage passengers, Italian, Spanish, French, or Greek returning to Europe from the Argentine. Passengers of the first and second classes escaped unhurt... The Florida, badly damaged in the bow, was brought to Malaga this morning accompanied by a British gunboat and five British destroyers. Both the Florida and the Glorious are now at Malaga, the Glorious bringing with her all first and second class passengers and injured steerage passengers of the Florida. The dead and injured of the Florida will be transferred to the Glorious and then put ashore.

| PARIS, April 2. (®)—Pola Negri, moving picture actress, was granted a divorce by the French courts today from Prince Serge Mdivani. | She sailed yesterday for America. | Before sailing Mme. Negri said “I am going to make my first talkie. I want to be free and stay free.” _ Prince Serge, a member of the former Russian nobility, and Pola Negri were married at Serraincourt, France, in 1927. She sued for a decree in October, 1930. Prince Serge is a brother of Prince David Mdivani, husband of Mae Murray. Miss Mary McCormic, opera singer, told friends in Paris last January that she and Prince Serge would be married as soon as the decree was granted. The latter confirmed this in Los Angeles on March 19. In announcing her intention, Miss McCormic said “I am giving up my career in Europe and I have decided to get married.” The wedding date has not been announced,

Berlin, April 2. — The Fascist party of Adolf Hitler — recently become one of the most powerful political organizations in Germany — was split today by a rebellion of part of its Berlin and east German forces. Captain Walter Stennes, who had been dismissed by Hitler, led the rebellion, which seriously threatened to disrupt the military-like organization of the Fascist storm detachments. Hitler's dismissal on Wednesday of Stennes, who was in command of the Berlin and eastern German storm troops, aroused partisans of the ousted lieutenant and led to the revolt movement.

Paris, April 2.—Pola Negri, film actress, was divorced today in the Seine Tribunal from the second of her wedded husbands, Prince Serge Mdivani. The divorce was granted on the grounds that the Prince abandoned his wife.

ROME, April 2—(#)—The world grain conference ended today without having arrived at any concrete plan for dealing with the world surplus of wheat. The conference, which agreed to meet again next year, however, left a series of recommendations for international collaboration in producing, selling and buying wheat. The delegates of the larger non-European wheat exporting companies, however, agreed to hold a conference of their own at London April 18. George Howard Ferguson, Canadian high commissioner at London, who will preside at the London meeting, emphasized today that the meeting would have no connection with the world grain conference, the international institute of agriculture, or the League of Nations.

Malaga, Spain, (UP) — Thirty steerage passengers were killed in the collision between the French liner Florida and the British aircraft carrier Glorious, the captain of the Florida announced today. The captain gave the list of missing persons as 17 Italians, four Poles, three Yugoslavs, five Syrians and Turks, and one Spaniard. One injured passenger died after being taken aboard the Glorious. Seven bodies had been recovered from the wrecked steerage quarters of the Florida. The passengers were killed when the force of the collision threw quantities of cargo upon them. Six injured persons were placed in a hospital here. Estimates of the total number of injured ranged between 20 and 30.
Warsaw, Poland. Apr. 5 A military plane flying over Warsaw today crashed into a square near the war office, killing aviation officers Zebroukt and Liwlowski, the two occupants.

Berlin, April 2 (UP)—The “beginning of the end” of violent Fascism was seen in responsible government circles today as a result of the rebellion within the ranks of the extremist party led by Adolf Hitler. The defection of a strong faction of the Fascist party under the leadership of Captain Walter Stennes was held likely to split the political organization and result in the transformation of the Hitlerite movement into a legal nationalist party. It was considered probable that Hitler would retain leadership of the party but at the cost of disbanding the bulk of his “storm troops.”

1931-02-01.text: Las Palmas, Canary Islands, Jan. 31. Carrying 19 men and 180,000 pieces of mail, the Dornier DO-X, largest airplane in the world, today successfully completed the first leg of its long-delayed flight from Lisbon to New York by way of South America. She left the Tagus harbor at Lisbon at 8:08 a.m., the roar of her American motors echoed in the cheers of the crowds which lined the waterfront. She arrived here, 715 miles from her starting point, at 3:10 p.m. after an uneventful voyage. Preparations were begun immediately for the next stage of the flight—to Cape Verde, 845 miles away. Tonight the mechanics began filtering into the huge tanks of the flying boat the 4,160 gallons of gasoline which it is estimated will be required on the hop to the Cape Verde islands. Captain Christiansen said that he expected to be able to take off at dawn.

1931-01-01.text: CARDIFF, Wales, Jan. 1—(AP)— New Year's day dawned bleak and cheerless in the great South Wales coal mining area with 150,000 miners thrown out of work by a general strike edict which became effective at midnight. Simultaneously with an order by the miners federation for its members not to report for work today, the owners issued directions for the mines to be locked to all workers who refused to accept the owners’ terms. Unless new negotiations which the South Wales conciliation board hopes to open Saturday between owners and workers are successful, the 150,000 miners and their families, estimated to number more than half a million persons, face hardship and suffering. It has been suggested that the government, if it cannot force an agreement, may declare a state of emergency and take over the pits temporarily. Representatives of the ministry of the mines made a last minute effort to wa

CARDIFF, Wales, Dec. 31—(AP)—A general strike in the great South Wales coal mine area, involving approximately 150,000 workers, was ordered tonight by officials of the miners' federation (effective at midnight). The decision of the miners’ leaders came after an evening of hurried conferences. Directly affected are the 150,000 miners who work in the area with their families, while a spread of the situation to other British coal fields is possible. Even as the South Wales meetings were being held, mine leaders in the Bristol area were debating stopping work tomorrow.

| By The Associated Press. LONDON, Jan. 1.—Europe stepped blithely into the new year today, forgetting for the moment the national disasters, cabinet crises, economic woes and sundry other burdens of misfortune which made a nuisance of 1930. From London, where the majestic tones of Big Ben above the parliament buildings tolled the hour of midnight, to remote hamlets where the whistles of trawlers or the gaiety of villagers bore tidings that a new leaf was turned, the countries of the old world frolicked. In the capital of the British empire lords and ladies choked the streets along 'arries and arriets, drinking, laughing and making merry in general, while the same spirit reigned everywhere under the Union Jack. Germans dined on fatted carp, the traditional New Year’s platter decoration, washing it down with flagons of beer and munching Berliner pfankuchen—a sort of doughnut which guarant

LONDON, Dec. 31—(AP)—Unless millions of British radio fans were "disgusted" tonight, they probably soon will be shelving "fancy that" and other exclamatory expressions for "sho-sho!" For Amos and Andy, the blackfaced pair familiar to American dial twisters, were heard in Great Britain tonight for the first time. Reception was excellent and officials of the British Broadcasting Corporation estimated that a potential audience of 12,000,000 was available to hear the pair dissect the King’s English, across the Atlantic.

London, Jan. 1. — Miss Amy Johnson, noted British flier, left on a flight to Peking today in her Gypsy Moth plane. She expected to stop at Berlin tonight. Tomorrow Miss Johnson planned to reach Warsaw, proceeding to Moscow Saturday and thence to Samara, Omsk and along the route of the trans-Siberian railroad to Irkutsk, and Chita. From there she will cross the Gobi desert. She was flying alone.

PERTH, Australia, Jan. 1—A triple murder and suicide at a prominent farmer’s home here has left the community gaping this New Year's Day. Victor McCaskell, farmer, reported having found his wife and child battered to death and the hired man hanging on his premises. Police were not satisfied with his explanation and asked for his arrest. McCaskell thereupon placed a stick of dynamite in his mouth and blew his head off.

Hendon, England, Jan. Miss Amy Johnston, 23, aviation aviatrix, took off at 10:40 a. m. today on the first lap of a projected flight to Peking, China. Miss Johnston is the only woman ever to have flown alone from England to Australia. She will equip her plane with skiing at Moscow.

Hendon, England—{2}—Miss Amy Johnston, British 28-year-old aviatrix, took off at 10:40 a.m. today on the first lap of 2 projected flights to Peiping, China. Her start was delayed by fog. The first stop was to be Lympne, to clear the customs, and from there to Berlin. She planned to be at Moscow on the third day out, proceeding from there across Asiatic Russia and Mongolia to Peiping. Miss Johnston, who is the only woman ever to have flown alone from England to Australia, has planned the trip for about two months. Much of the route is uncharted and may have many dangers. The plane will be equipped with skis at Moscow.

London, Dec. 31.—(4)—The London naval treaty, born of the five-power conference last spring, at last is in full force with the deposit at the foreign office today of the ratification by the Irish Free State. The treaty is really a trilateral one, for France and Italy have not yet agreed on the proportional tonnage each shall have, and have therefore not adhered. In recent weeks, however, there have been indications the long drawn-out conversations between the two powers may shortly bear a fruitful result. Advices from Rome today indicated the prolongation of the 'naval holiday' between the two countries and said direct negotiations would be resumed toward the middle of January. | Washington. Dec. 31,—()—As a gesture of good will on New Year's day, President Hoover tomorrow will issue a proclamation putting into effect the London naval treaty. Paris, Jan. 1.—(P)—Marshal Joffre, fighting his epic battle against death, sank into a coma at noon today and reports that he had died flashed across the world, but the Spartan soldier lived on and the reports were officially denied. At 4:30 o'clock this afternoon the Marshal's physicians disclosed that he had been unconscious since eleven o'clock this morning. Respiration was 35, their bulletin said, and the pulse 140.

PARIS, Dec. 31. ()—Lingering on as the old year ebbed away, Marshal Joffre sank into a state of semi-consciousness today, then rallied enough to drink some milk before he fell into a sound sleep. As night fell his doctors issued a bulletin announcing his breathing was regular and his temperature only a little above normal. They said, however, it might be necessary to issue another bulletin tonight, and this was interpreted as their guarded way of saying the marshal might not live to see the dawn. Only three visitors were admitted to the sick room in the hospital of St. Jean de Dieu and one of those was Jean Fabry, a former aide, who took the general's wasted hand. Marshal Joffre looked up at him and said, "My dear Fabry." That was all.

(By United Press Jan. 1—Marshal Joseph Joffre's condition became critical and put an official bulletin announcing that the veteran soldier was still alive. The courage with which the hero of the Marne has held to life became gravely ill last night, and most of his close friends feared he was losing ground. Death Rumored: A false rumor of the death of Joffre was circulated in Paris and abroad. The baseless rumor was announced on the alleged 'official' news, prompting Premier Theodore Steeg to go to the hospital 'to salute the hero.' The capital was confused by the false reports, recalling that a similarly false report of the death of the late Georges Clemenceau, war-time premier, was circulated in Paris and abroad some hours before the 'real' death actually occurred. Correspondents in touch with the hospital authorities were informed that Joffre was in a critical condition, but still figh

Paris, France, Dec. 31—While jazz bands crooned and whistles blared the Parisians’ welcome of 1931, a gray woman tonight kept silent watch beside the hospital bed of the man France loves as “Papa” Joffre. She is La Maréchale, wife of the aged marshal, who has stood beside him the last 30 years. Tall, gaunt and militant in her determination, she has watched beside the marshal’s bed in the hospital Saint Jean De Dieu since his leg was amputated above the knee eleven days ago. Tonight her watch was shared by hundreds outside. In the narrow Rue Oudinot, drenched with rain and swept by wind, men and women shivered en masse, praying for the life of “Papa” Joffre. Taxis tooted and gendarmes shouted, but the watchers clung to the curb and prayed.

United Press Staff Correspondent Paris, Dec. 31—(UP)—Marshal Joseph Joffre, given up two days ago as on the verge of death, sat up in bed today and tried to gulp his warm milk when a nurse fed him. Dr. Rene Fontaine, leaving the Marshal's bedroom at 10 p.m. declared there was no danger of his dying tonight. He said Joffre demanded a barber, who shaved him. He then drank more milk. The old soldier was improved, but the doctors attending him refused to be optimistic. His condition remained critical, with the crisis, or series of crises, passed. At 7 p.m. he said: "I feel better," and ate lightly. His pulse was more regular than in the past. Pulse 110, temperature 98.4 Fahrenheit. The state of the amputation was satisfactory. The unique report was signed by Dr. Riche, Dr. Raoul Boulanger.

1931-01-21.text: PARIS—(/)—The French-Italian naval construction truce, agreed upon last year after the two countries failed to adhere to the principal sections of the London naval treaty, was said to have ended. Rome dispatches stated that Italy is prepared from now, independent of its normal construction program, to build gun for gun with France.

MUNICH, Germany, Jan. 21. (AP) Seven of the eight Bavarian constables who were buried in an avalanche near here yesterday were found dead under the snow today. The eighth was still alive but severely injured.

ROME, Jan. 20 (Official sources say that Italy is prepared to build gun-for-gun with France in naval construction this year, since they assert that there appears to be little hope for renewing the construction truce which expired last month. This, it is said, is independent of Italy’s normal program. The suspended 1830 program provides for twenty-nine craft—twenty-two submarines and seven other units—and this will be started with the laying of the keels in a few months. France is said here to have completed her old naval program, and hereafter anything that she builds will be duplicated by Italy. PARIS, Jan. 20 (#)—The naval truce between France and Italy has come definitely to an end. It was learned in official quarters tonight and both countries now are free to engage in whatever warship building they wish. So far as French official circles are aware, the hopes for pourparlers between

MOSCOW, Jan. 20.—The Soviet press today turned shafts of ridicule against the American Congressman Hamilton Fish, Jr., in long editorials denouncing his recent report to the Congress of the United States on his investigation of communist activities in that country. The newspaper Izvestia calls the report a “skyscraper of insolence,” and the newspaper Pravda says of it, “Of all anti-Soviet documents in the recent past, the Fish report is the most impudent, insolent and ridiculous. It is ninety pages of absurdity based on forged documents.”

Bremen, Germany 1° — Max Schmeling, German boxer, sailed aboard the Europa today with his trainer, Max Machon, for New York. Schmeling said that he intended to go in training immediately for a series of exhibition bouts in Baltimore and 48 other American southern and southwestern cities, and Havana. “Whichever way my fight with Stribling turns out,” he said, “I shall come back to Germany even if I have to go out again in September to meet Carnera.” Denver—Regis College, a Jesuit institution, has discarded intercollegiate football. A decision to abandon the game was reached by the athletic board of control last night. Chicago—Art Shires, self-styled passed through on his way to Milwaukee to discuss his 1901 contract with the Brewers of the American Association baseball league. He said he would also sign for a short theatrical engagement.

1931-03-08.text: London, March 7.—(A. P.)—All the prize fights of recent years in Ames Hall put together have not produced so much good scrapping as developed when the Trades Defense Union exhibited a purported "soviet slave" in a mass meeting called to protest Russian economic methods last night. The "slave" voiced an appeal for freedom for the men, women and children working in Russian timber camps, from which he said he escaped a few months ago. Running fights continued between spectators and a crowd of interrupters during the two-hour meeting. The disturbers were ejected. The disturbance began when Winston Churchill and Lord Brentford, formerly Sir William Joynson Hicks, both former conservative ministers, started addressing the meeting. Both were heckled. Lord Brentford said treatment of women in the prison camps was such that he dared not reveal it in a mixed audience. The "soviet slave," whose nam

LONDON, March 7.—(UP)—The worst gale since 1917 swept the British Isles today as Britain received her share of 10,000,000 tons of air rushing from the northern to the southern hemisphere and creating weather havoc throughout the world. “This transference of air occurs every season between January and July,” Sir Napier Shaw, famous British meteorologist, said. “It is not surprising that it does not always cross the equator without immense friction.” The portion of the “friction” received by Britain caused immense damage and discomfort on sea and land. Huge seas in the English Channel sent all shipping rushing for shelter. The Thames rose rapidly and reached its most dangerous state since the disastrous floods of 1928. The river overflowed at Putney and Wandsworth. The south coast was ravaged by waves which swept over the seawall for many miles and flooded many towns and villages. Littlest

LONDON, March 10 (UP), P. Morgan's yacht Corsair, upon which the Archbishop of Canterbury has been invited to join the American financier on a Mediterranean cruise, was forced to seek shelter at Gibraltar during a heavy storm, the Exchange Telegraph company said today. The British cruiser Centaur was slightly damaged, the Exchange report said, by heavy seas. Several ships of the British Atlantic fleet now at Gibraltar got up steam and prepared to put out to the open sea.

AVAIYU, MATCH 5, WU.F)—A GIRL was born to the Empress Nagako at the Imperial Maternity Villa today, her fourth daughter, leaving the Japanese empire without a male heir apparent. The baby was born at 12:02 p.m., the imperial child weighed 3.365 grammes (7.4 pounds) and was 49 centimeters (19.25 inches) in height. Mother and daughter were reported doing well. The Empress entered the Maternity Villa at 9:50 a.m. She passed her 28th birthday in retirement yesterday. Two of her daughters, Teru and Taka, are living, in addition to the baby born today. The other girl born to the imperial couple died in infancy. For the fourth time the hope of all Japan for an heir to the throne was unfulfilled.

Tokyo, March 7. (AP)—Japan sang praises today to a new member of the imperial family, born to Emperor Hirohito and Empress Nagako at 12:02 p.m., but Prince Chichibu, the emperor's younger brother, continued to be the heir presumptive of the oldest unbroken royal line in the world. Birth of the little princess, the fourth daughter born to the imperial couple, was heralded throughout the empire by the national radiocasting system with broadcasting of the national anthem. In Tokyo citizens were apprised of the event by the municipal sirens while the official Gazette, the government organ, issued one of its rare “extras.” 3 Ceremonies Performed. Rome, March 7, (#)—The formality of signing the naval accord between Great Britain, France and Italy is taking almost as long to arrange as the negotiations out of which the agreement came. It had been understood here today that the ceremony of signing would take place in London next Tuesday, but in official quarters tonight, it was said that the signing had been postponed until the United States and Japan had examined the text. The situation as it was understood here tonight is that publication of the agreement, originally set for last Monday, is still unsettled, but dispatches from London and Paris said the text would be published on Wednesday simultaneously in all the capitals concerned. The agreement, it is understood, has not been even initiated by the men who write its terms, because the British delegates prefer to await the approval of Washington, Tokyo, and the British dominions.
VIENNA, March 17,—(4)—Earthquakes in South Serbia wrought extensive damage today, but caused only one death. The worst quake in its history shook Mirovitz, the principal sufferer, levelling 15

1931-02-09.text: WELLINGTON, New Zealand, Feb. 9—(AP)—Residents of the devastated Hawkes Bay district were terrified and driven from their temporary shelters by a new series of violent tremors today. The quakes felled many buildings not wholly destroyed in last week's tremors and toppled piles of masonry, battered the beaches, forcing the panic stricken inhabitants to higher ground. Napier, Hastings and the Wairoa district especially felt the shocks. The face of a bluff overlooking Napier was sheared off by a landslide. There were no casualties. Residents are living in tents and other temporary shelters. Communication lanes have been interrupted.

LONDON, Feb. 9, UPA mother of four children, who was sentenced to hang for having murdered the fourth baby, has given birth to twins in the hospital of Holloway prison. The woman is Mrs. Olive Catherine Wise, who once was married and bore three children legitimately to her husband. They were separated and she bore a fourth child to another man. He deserted her and she attempted desperately to feed the four hungry mouths. She even chopped wood and hawked it through the streets but finally gave up the struggle, placed the baby in an oven and turned on the gas. British law takes no cognizance of exceptional circumstances or temporary insanity in murder cases and she was condemned to hang. A storm of public indignation followed and her sentence was commuted.
By United Press LONDON, Feb. 9—The Earl of Beauchamp was appointed today as governor general of Canada, succeeding Lord Willingdon, who has been named viceroy of India.

London, Feb. 9. (4) — King George today appointed the Earl of Bessborough, a distinguished Irish peer, to be governor-general of Canada succeeding Lord Willingdon, who has been named viceroy of India. Lord Bessborough is the ninth Earl of that name and comes of a distinguished family which gave to Ireland and Great Britain many noted soldiers, parliamentarians and lawyers.

Wellington, New Zealand, Feb. 8. Heavy earthquake shocks again rocked the Napier and Hastings section of the Hawks Bay district, which was the scene of last Tuesday's disastrous quake in which many persons were killed. Today's tremors started at 2 p.m. The face of a bluff overlooking Napier was sheared by further landslides. Heavy breakers swept the beaches and forced the terrified inhabitants, encamped about the town, to flee from the shoreline to higher ground. The number of deaths in the recent severe earthquakes in Napier was placed at 103 today after further reconstruction and search of the ruins had been completed.

This placed the spot about 180 miles north by west of Corvo Island, the northernmost and smallest of the Azores group. LONDON, Feb. 9.--(UP)--Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald told the House of Commons today the government was not considering any proposal to summon an international round table conference on the subject of inter-allied debts and war reparations. MacDonald's statement was in reply to a question asked by Commander J. M. Kenworthy, who sought to bring the question of a readjustment of war debts, which recently has aroused wide comment in unofficial circles, to the House of Commons.

By sant wants eee TOKYO, Feb. 10—Sixty-nine persons were feared lost today in a collision between the French steamer Porthos and the Japanese Kikusut Maru in the harbor during a heavy snowstorm yesterday. The Japanese vessel sank quickly and the Porthos, after picking up 2 of her complement, returned to port with small damage.

MADRID, Feb. 8.— After more than seven years of dictatorship, constitutional guarantees were restored to Spanish subjects today by a royal proclamation which calls for parliamentary elections in March. The guarantees and parliamentary elections were suspended by the dictatorship of the late Primo De Rivera September 23, 1923. General Damasco Berenguer, who succeeded Primo De Rivera as dictator more than a year ago, had continued the suspension during the past year, which saw a series of labor, political and radical disturbances in the country. Today's action of King Alfonso was seen in certain quarters as a testimony of complete confidence in Berenguer’s work. Press censorship will not be raised officially until tomorrow because the law forbids Sunday newspaper work.

MOSCOW, Feb. & (*) — Employment of hundreds of thousands of women in industries to overcome the present shortage of labor, is being considered by the government of the Soviet Union. With thousands of jobs for which there are no takers, the country today has the greatest shortage of labor in its history. Millions of women are inactive and it is believed the problem can be solved by pressing them into service. The children would be cared for by the state while their mothers are working. “The problem of attracting hundreds of thousands of women to industrial labor is acute,” said an official announcement. “In order to solve this problem as painlessly as possible the government, together with trade unions and other social organizations, has collaborated a number of measures directed toward freeing women from domestic work and securing children with the necessary care while the mothers are at

Moscow, Feb. 9 — Hundreds of thousands of Russian women, who during 1930 played an increased role in the socialization of Soviet Russia, are to be enlisted as workers in a further effort to solve the union's serious labor shortage. With thousands of jobs open and no takers, the government is completing plans to fill vacancies with women, providing nursery facilities for children who will be brought up under the care of the state. An official announcement states: An Acute Problem, “The problem of attracting hundreds of thousands of women to industrial labor is acute. PARIS, Feb. 8—(AP)—Dueling, which was thought to have been eradicated in France since the Armistice, was revived today when Horace De Carbuccia, managing editor of a weekly publication, met Henri Danjou, a journalist, with pistols on the field of honor. Neither was injured, De Carbuccia firing in the air while Danjou’s bullet missed his adversary. They were not reconciled after the duel. De Carbuccia, a Corsican, objected to certain articles written by Danjou, which the former held to be derogatory to Corsica.

1931-03-27.text: Dublin, Irish Free State, March 27.—(#)—The Saorstat today mourned Timothy Michael Healy, Irish parliamentarian extraordinary and its first Governor General, who died in the night after a three weeks illness. He was 75 years old. The end had been foreseen for several days, although he was ill with what was thought to be only a bad cold for some time before the seriousness of his malady, a bronchial affection, was appreciated. He took a turn for the worse yesterday morning and his son was summoned to his bedside. Death came at 7:50 P. M. As a member of parliament for what is now the Saorstat, Healy founded a tradition of his own, the “Irish Nights” in which he would sit back with his silk hat tipped over his nose, pretending not to listen to debate. Suddenly he would arise, obtain the floor and make a speech of vitriol coated with honeyed Irish words. He withdrew from the House of Commons

LONDON, March 27 (A. P.)—C. C. Woods, 32, Buffalo, New York, won approximately $886,360 in the Irish hospital sweepstakes at today’s grand national at Aintree with his ticket on Greeaac, which placed second. His ticket had cost him about $2.50. The other two big prizes in the sweepstakes went to Emilio Scala, London cafe owner, who had the ticket on the winning horse, “Grakle,” and to George Dyamond of Cape Town, South Africa, who won third place with his ticket on Annandale. Scala's prize is approximately $1,772,720 and Dyamond’s approximately $590,905. Scala must divide his prize of more than one and three-quarters millions, however, as he sold part of his ticket before the race. It was unknown whether Woods or Dyamond retained full rights in their tickets. The fourth place ticket of Rhyticere, the holder of which just missed stepping into the leisure class, was held by the caretaker o

Dublin, Irish Free State, March 26 (P).—Timothy Michael Healy, over whose bittersweet sallies in the House of Commons old timers still chuckle, died today at the age of 75. He was the first governor of the Irish Free State, but he will be remembered longer as one of the most brilliant Parliamentary speakers who ever galvanized the House of Commons into action. In the old days before the Free State got a Parliament of its own he used to sit in his corner of the House his silk hat tipped down over his nose, pretending not to listen. Then he would get up on his feet and begin one of those characteristic speeches in which the vitriol of his sarcasm was overlaid with the honey of his Irish humor.

London, Mar. 25 — After listening to David Lloyd George urge “a policy of cooperation, not frustration,” the Liberal candidates’ association deferred the vote today on the question of general support of the MacDonald government. Stanley Baldwin, conservative leader, asked today that the debate on the vote of censure be deferred until after the Easter holidays and the proposal was agreed to by Prime Minister MacDonald. Parliament reassembles after Easter on April 14, but the date for the debate has not yet been fixed. Premier MacDonald already has indicated that, if defeated on this vote the government probably will resign or recommend a general election.

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Mar. 26—Timothy Healy, veteran Irish statesman and first governor of the Irish Free State, died here at 7:50 p. m. this evening. “Tim” Healy, as he was known not only in Ireland but throughout the world, was 76 years old. He had been ill for some time but throughout his sickness his doctors were reticent about reporting his progress. It was believed at first that he was suffering from a very bad cold.

LONDON, March 27.—It’s a hundred to five that your next child won’t be a twin and you can take out an insurance policy against it being a twin with a premium of five per cent. Douglas Cox, London insurance broker, is an authority on insurance against twins. He takes the view that his policy is one of the most logical, from an insurance man’s point of view. For five pounds premium, paid six months prior to the expectant birth, a policy is issuable paying 109 pounds in the event twins are born. Both children must live 24 hours under the provision of the policy. Some premiums depending upon the frequency of twins in the ancestors of the prospective parents, might be three pounds.

LONDON, Mar. 27. U.P)—An Italian who came to London thirty years ago and pushed an ice cream cart through the streets became a millionaire today when Grakle won the Grand National Steeplechase at Aintree. Clayton C. Woods, 248 Carl Street, Buffalo, N. Y., won the second prize, worth about $803,360. Emmilio Scala, proprietor with his brother of a coffee shop in Southwest London, held Grakle’s ticket in the Irish Sweepstake. The first horse home won approximately $1,772,700 for the lucky ticket holder. Scala shared his fortune with forty relatives. He is the father of four children. His wife was ill when the family received the news that they had drawn Grakle in the

THE WEATHER—Rain tonight, turning to snow Saturday; colder in south portion tonight; much colder Saturday. —— 0 FORMER BRITISH AUTHOR NEAR DEATH London, Mar. 27.—(UP)—Arnold Bennett lapsed into unconsciousness at 6 p. m. and was in a highly critical condition; the famous writer is ill of typhoid. LONDON, March 27.—The condition of Arnold Bennett, noted English author, who is suffering from typhoid fever, was regarded as extremely grave today. He has lapsed into unconsciousness.

PARIS, March 27—(UP)—Charlie Chaplin was decorated today as a Knight of the Legion of Honor, in recognition of his artistry. The decoration was awarded at the foreign office, by Philippe Berthelot, general secretary of foreign affairs.

TOKYO, March 27. (AP) — The volcano Yakegadake in Nagano Prefecture began to erupt today after an inactive period of several years. The eruption was accompanied by a loud report and tongues of flames. Then a shower of ashes aroused villagers and farmers for miles around. Nagano is a silk center and farmers feared damage to mulberry trees now beginning to bud. The foliage of these trees produces food for silk worms. Slight earthquakes were felt in the northern part of Nagano a few hours after the eruption. The shocks also were felt here. The meaning of Yakegadake is “boiling mountain.”

Rome, March 20.—(1)—The “bread baskets of the world” battled Thursday afternoon against a proposed European boycott on imported wheat. Presenting a united front against the boycott proposal, made by an executive committee of the world wheat conference Wednesday, delegates of Canada, South Africa, India and Australia and two representatives of United States wheat growers decided Thursday to oppose strenuously any agreement by European countries for special tariffs which would militate against overseas exporters. The delegates agreed to hold over the heads of the Balkan countries the threat that, if they joined the boycott, pressure would be used to secure the abrogation of existing most favored nation treaties giving privileges to those countries. The Europeans expected to present their views at Friday's meeting with Rumanian Minister of Agriculture Madgeara leading the fight. The world's

Paris, Mar. 26. (4?).—The French Chamber of Deputies struck a blow in the Austro-German tariff accord tangle today when its customs committee proposed a general European customs agreement, edging out Germany and Austria, as a counter move. The proposal was made contingent on whether or not Germany and Austria actually carry out their proposed arrangement.

Paris, March 26.—(AP)— Striking at the Austro-German trade accord, the customs committee of the chamber of deputies proposed today a general customs agreement among all European nations except Austria and Germany. Meanwhile, Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson told the Associated Press the British and French governments were agreed the contemplated treaty should be submitted to the League of Nations to determine whether it violates the Geneva protocol under which France, Italy and Czecho-Slovakia guaranteed a loan to Austria. French Plan Contingent on actual execution of the German-Austro treaty, the French customs committee advocated the erection of a general tariff wall against the contracting nations and the renunciation of existing treaties between France and both of them.

1931-02-05.text: (BY THE ASSOCIATED PRESS) NAPIER, New Zealand, Feb. 1 (Thursday) The bodies of fifty-seven victims, killed when Tuesday's earthquake virtually wiped this bustling seaport from the map, had been identified today, while more than 1,000 injured, several hundred of them in a critical condition, had been treated. No official estimate of the number of dead had been attempted, but popular belief and the unofficial estimates of relief workers placed it at more than 500 and possibly as many as 1,000 for Napier, Hastings and other towns of Hawkes Bay province in the earthquake affected zone. All efforts were spent today in aiding the injured, searching the ruins for still living victims and preparing for a general evacuation of the city before disease can follow in the footsteps of disaster. The expression “wiped from the map” may be used advisedly, for not only have the man-made structures of Nap

AUCKLAND, N. Z., Feb. 5.—(U.P.) —A total of almost 200 bodies have been recovered from the earthquake wrecked region of Hawkes Bay, officials reported today. Fifty bodies previously were buried and the rest were placed in a common grave where services were combined with a religious service for unidentified dead.

PLYMOUTH, Eng. Feb. 4—A giant seaplane of the Royal Air Force, while engaged in practice, plunged into the waters of Batte Bay today with a loss of nine lives and injuries to two. One man escaped unhurt. The surface of the smooth bay, which was bright as a mirror, apparently caused the pilot to misjudge his distance above the water in landing. The craft dived full tilt into the water and before it could level out disappeared below the surface. A loud explosion was heard as the plane struck with terrific force. It brought small craft in the nearby waters to the rescue. The plane overturned and only the pontoons were visible. All except four of those in the plane were trapped in the submerged body. Divers were sent down in an effort to recover the bodies of the missing, among whom was Wing Commander C. G. Tucker, who had a splendid war record. After the accident, Flying Officer F. K. Wood

- BOMBAY, India, Feb. 5.—Renewal of the salt making campaign of the Indian nationalists in a public square here today led to the arrest of the five members of the working committee of the All India National Congress. It was the 22nd successive war council of the congress here to go to jail. The twenty-third war council promptly took its place at the salt deposits.

LONDON, Feb. 5.—(AP)—Disturbing reports that Ramsay MacDonald, British prime minister, had suffered a breakdown in health and would take an immediate vacation to recuperate were discredited at Ten Downing Street today. The prime minister, despite an all-night session of the House of Commons, was at his desk this morning. His presence was not required in all of last night’s debate which kept the Commons members on their benches for 17 hours and it did not greatly interrupt his schedule. Authoritative statements were made that he was in no danger of a breakdown in health and that his doctors had not advised a few days of complete rest, as reported generally here last night.

London, Feb. 5. (INS)—The British air ministry to-day ordered a complete inquiry into the flying accident in Plymouth Harbor yesterday when an R. A. F. tri-motored all-metal flying boat dived into the water and exploded, killing nine and injuring three. Eye witnesses of yesterday's accident said the pilot of the bomber was apparently trying to come down on the water when the accident occurred. The plane was returning to its Plymouth base after bombing practice. Bright sunlight dazzled the pilot, who apparently did not realize he was so close to the water. One wing touched the water and the next instant there was a violent explosion. London, Feb. 5. (INS)—Martial law has been declared at Hastings, New Zealand, one of the two cities razed by Tuesday's earthquake, according to a Central News dispatch from Auckland. This action was taken to prevent looting. Sunday has been declared a day of

LONDON, Feb. 1.—Martial law has been declared at Hastings, New Zealand, one of the two cities razed by Tuesday's earthquake, according to a Central News dispatch from Auckland. This action was taken to prevent looting. Sunday has been declared a day of mourning throughout all of New Zealand for earthquake victims. A sharp quake rocked Gisborne, 100 miles northeast of Napier, late tonight, sending most of that city’s 11,000 inhabitants scurrying to the streets. Little damage was done. According to a message to the Evening News from Christchurch, martial law has also been declared in Napier where marines are patrolling the streets to prevent looting. Desperate hungry men and women are ransacking the ruins of the city in search of food.

London, Feb. 5 —(UP)—Scotsmen stood in line and waited their turn to contribute to charity today. Londoners gasped to see the Scotch myth exploded. The occasion was the opening of an exhibition of Scottish antiques and historical relics. Proceeds went to charity. Scotch lads and lassies saw the chair in which Bonnie Prince Charlie sat as a boy. Kilted Scots filed past such relics as the rosary of Mary Queen of Scots, the first Bible printed in Scotland, and the hunting flask of the famous sheep thief, John Armstrong. Exhibits were loaned by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, Hugh (Continued on Page 2)

I. N.S. Staff Correspondents Wellington, Feb. 5.—While recurrent tremors continued to rock the Hawke Bay district, hundreds of rescue workers today were counting the dead and caring for the injured in Napier and Hastings, the two cities razed by Tuesday’s violent earthquake. Red Cross officials on the job estimate the death toll will probably total between 700 and 1,000. Napier and Hastings are being completely evacuated in an effort to prevent the outbreak of disease and pestilence. Hundreds of injured have been brought to Wellington to be cared for. Others have been sent to Auckland while the remainder are being treated as well as possible in emergency dressing stations erected in the stricken area. While relief work in Napier, Hastings, Taradale and Green Meadows is well in hand, there is still doubt as to the fate of many island towns and villages where communications were cut by the

* U8 tailed ress.) PLYMOUTH, Eng, Feb. 5,--The bodies of Wing Commander, C. G. Tucker, and one aircraftsman had been recovered Thursday from the wreck of a Royal Air Force sea- plane which fell into the harbor here Wednesday. Eight men were drowned and one other died of in- juries. The others were injured severely.

ROME, Feb. 5. (AP)—Alarming rumors of disturbances involving the home of Premier Mussolini, Villa Torlonia, were officially and emphatically denied today and their source apparently revealed as in a fight Tuesday morning between two men and police near the famous Trevi Fountain. It was reported here that a man had been arrested near the fountain after a revolver battle with police in which one policeman was wounded. The man was found carrying a bomb. Another man with him escaped. The name of the arrested man was understood to be Michele Schirro. The incident gave rise to rumors that the arrest had been made outside the Duce's home.

MENEMEN, Turkey, Feb. 4 ()— Town criers were beating tom-toms through all the villages of Smyrna province tonight to warn the inhabitants not to give shelter to a man who fled to freedom from the arms of official death. Twenty-eight men convicted of treason were led out to die on as many gallows in Menemen yesterday, but a 28-year-old villager named Hussein broke from the grasp of his Gypsy hangman. Mashing through a cordon of soldiers he disappeared in the dark, untouched by the bullets they sent after him. The town criers in all villages were ordered to warn citizens that anyone sheltering the fugitive would be hanged beside him as soon as he was found.

1931-02-02.text: London, Feb. 2. — — Ireland, northern England and Scotland were in the grip of a vicious winter storm and a 60-mile-an-hour wind today while many ships in the Irish Sea battled high winds and waves and were forced to ask for assistance. Three persons were killed by the storm in northern England. Many heads of livestock were missing. Communication and transport services were disrupted by heavy snows forming drifts from four to six feet deep. Passengers on the omnibus route between Glasgow and Cupar were stranded throughout the night in a blizzard. The coast road near Antrim was blocked by three landslides. Hundreds of tons of earth fell before the force of the gale on the Isle of Man, flooding the railway between Douglas and Peel and necessitating conveyance of passengers by omnibus. Northern England and Scotland experienced the wildest weather in years over the weekend. Snow, sleet and h

MANCHESTER, Eng. Feb. 2.— Winston Churchill celebrated his withdrawal from the conservative "shadow cabinet" by condemning the labor government and the Indian nationalist party in an unusually bitter speech here. Churchill’s attack on the way Prime Minister Ramsey MacDonald and his colleagues handled the Indian situation was one of the most drastic launched against any British government for years. Politicians regarded Churchill's remarks as the opening of his own private campaign against the proposals of the Indian round table conference and considered his speech of possibly far-reaching importance. The former conservative minister, who still is one of the most influential men in the party, opened his attack with his usual vigor, but surprised his audience with the extent to which it was carried. "The government is preparing to hand rule in India to comparatively small and utterly misre

Tipton, Feb. 9--(AP)—The county Board of Supervisors has ruled that a man who doesn’t know the difference between a wolf and a police dog isn't entitled to any bounty. The hide Henry Kroh of Lowden turned in with a request for a $10 bounty was that of a police dog, they said. They refused to pay.

Sydney, Australia — () — Mrs. Katerina Rehua, a Maori woman whose husband has been out of work for nine months, entered an endurance swimming contest here Sunday to earn enough money to buy food for her four children, one of which is only nine weeks old. She swam 47 hours and 52 minutes, but she finished second to Mercedes Gleitze, who kept up the grind for 23 minutes longer. Her prize was $500 and Miss Gleitze contributed another $500 from her winnings of $1,500. Mrs. Rehua and her husband said they had spent their last shilling for carfare to the pool where the marathon was conducted.

The Dornier flying boat DO-X at Las Palmas, Canary Islands, today awaited a final tuning of her 12 motors before beginning a 900-mile flight south to St. Vincent, in the Cape Verde Islands. Trouble in one of the giant sky ship’s motors prevented departure early today. One engine had to be dismantled before mechanics could pronounce the ship in perfect running trim. The human cargo on board totals nineteen; thirteen make up the crew, the others being passengers. The monster of the air is pictured above as she gracefully skims through the air under command of Captain Friedrich Christiansen (lower left), master of the ship. Lieutenant C. H. Schildhauer (right)

Las Palmas, Canary Islands, Feb. 2—Butting its way through a choppy sea without attempting to take off, the German flying boat DO-X steamed out of the harbor under its own power this morning and cruised 12 miles to Gando Bay, from which it will continue its projected trans-Atlantic flight tomorrow if the weather is favorable. She dropped her anchor in a sheltered cove and waited the arrival of a barge bringing nearly a thousand gallons of fuel, more than enough to carry her to the Cape Verde Islands, the next stop on her way to Brazil.

LAS PALMAS, CANARY ISLANDS, Feb. 2—(#)—The DO-X, twelve motored German seaplane, today delayed until tomorrow its take-off for the Cape Verde Islands, whence it will proceed across the Atlantic to Natal, Rio De Janeiro and New York. Continued bad weather and rough seas made the postponement necessary. The big seaplane lifted its anchor early in the morning and left the harbor, radioing that it was proceeding to Gande Bay, 12 miles south of Puerto Lalua, where it could take off easier than on the bay. The DO-X came here Saturday after a seven hour flight from Lisbon. Bad weather forced postponement of the next hop to the Cape Verde Islands Sunday. Meanwhile, the ship has been refueled with more than 4,000 gallons of petrol for the 845 mile flight to Port Praia. The crew remained aboard the vessel last night, refusing invitations to ceremonies in the city.

LAS PALMAS, Canary Islands, Feb. 1.—(#)—The German seaplane DO-X postponed the second leg of its flight to Brazil until tomorrow because of rough seas, cloudiness and generally unfavorable weather conditions. The giant passenger flying boat, which arrived here yesterday from Lisbon with 19 persons aboard, probably will take off at 7 a.m. tomorrow for the 845-mile hop to the Cape Verde islands, if flying conditions improve. This flight had been scheduled for today. After the 12 American motors of the plane had been tested today the DO-X was refueled and her officers piloted her to an anchorage in the bay. There she will remain until tomorrow. A large crowd watched today's maneuvers. The airship made the 715-mile jump from Lisbon in a little more than seven hours.

BRUSSELS -— (4) — Industrial sulphurous fumes which combined with the fog to make an acid which ate at the lung cells of those breathing the mixture were blamed today for the death of more than 60 persons in the Meuse Valley in early December. The newspaper Nation Belge said that the inquest which has been sitting at Liege had found the deaths had occurred from inhalation of a sulphurous anhydride. While the toxic fumes are perennial in the industrial district, it is only rarely that such extreme fog conditions as occurred at this time make them dangerous. The report of the inquest is only provisional and states the first finding, that is, that the fogs contained sulphurous anhydride. A supplementary report to be published shortly is expected to state the exact source of the noxious fumes, which are regarded generally as having come from industrial plants around Engis.

Rome, Feb. 1.—(AP)—The Italian foreign office, which last week was quoted as saying that Premier Mussolini never had met Cornelius Vanderbilt, Jr., said today it did not mean the premier had not met Vanderbilt but merely that he had not driven with him. This was in connection with the affair which has caused Major General Smedley D. Butler of the United States marines to be summoned for court martial, as Butler is accused of implying that Mussolini was a hit-and-run driver and is said to have based his account on the story of a motor car ride Vanderbilt took with the premier. Merely Routine “Vanderbilt had an audience with Premier Mussolini about five years ago,” said a foreign office statement, “but it merely was a brief audience such as hundreds of foreigners have been granted. “We wish to reiterate emphatically that Vanderbilt never has been driven in an automobile by Premier Mussolin

ROME, Feb 2. (P)—Cornelius Vanderbilt, Jr, American mentioned in the recent “Butler incident,” was given an audience by Premier Benito Mussolini in 1926, it was revealed at the Foreign Office today. The audience was not regarded as important, officials said, and no record of it was found in a preliminary examination of the files. It was pointed out that there was no record of Vanderbilt having ridden in a motor car with Mussolini. Officials said that if Vanderbilt had ridden with Mussolini in 1926 he would have been the first American so honored, and the fact would have been recorded and remembered. Vanderbilt was mentioned in reports received here as having told the story that Mussolini ran over and killed a child while driving his automobile. Gen. Smedley Butler's remarks about Il Duce were said to have been the result of the story.

LAS PALMAS, Canary Islands, Feb. 2—(AP)—The DO-X, 12-motored German seaplane, today delayed until tomorrow its takeoff for the Cape Verde islands, whence it will proceed across the Atlantic to Natal, Rio De Janeiro and New York. Continued bad weather and rough seas made the postponement necessary.

1931-03-09.text: London — () — Bitter winter weather, which swept most of Europe over the weekend, closed in on London and southern England Monday with temperatures very low, a high wind drove a heavy snow before it today with indications that it would continue. Elsewhere in Britain the storm abated, leaving eastern Scotland deep in the year’s worst snow. Some sheep farmers lost half the lamb yield. Northeastern England also was under a thick white blanket with the most bitter weather of the winter prevailing. Northern France, Germany, Belgium, Scandinavia, Austria and Poland all were affected by the unusual cold. Snowdrifts blocked highways and delayed trains. Where it was warmer swollen rivers threatened serious flooding. Snow continued for 46 hours straight in Vienna. The river Seine at Paris was one foot above alarm level yesterday. It is not expected to go much higher, Rivers of Burgundy and southea

Calcutta, India, March 9.—A new outburst against the leadership of the Mahatma M. K. Gandhi in the nationalist congress party and against his peace truce with the British government occurred today at a meeting of extremists. J. M. Sen Gupta, former mayor of Calcutta and one of the most prominent Bengal independence leaders, was received with jeers and hostile shouts when he addressed a conference of Bengal students.

Ottawa, Ont... March 8. (7)—W. D. Herridge, K. C., whose appointment as Canadian minister to the United States was announced last night by Premier R. B. Bennett, will take up his duties in Washington as soon as he can set his private affairs in order. Herridge, a prominent Ottawa lawyer drawn into politics through his friendship with Premier Bennett, will succeed Hon. Vincent Massey, who resigned a year ago to become Canadian high commissioner to London, a post now held by Howard Ferguson, former premier of Ontario. Herridge, who accompanied Premier Bennett on his campaign tour which resulted in the overthrow of the Mackenzie King government, is a son of the late Rev. W. T. Herridge, former moderator of the Canadian Presbyterian general assembly.

LONDON, March 9.—(UP)—A heavy snow storm struck London at noon today after the coldest night recorded here in 14 years. The storm followed a weekend of bitter weather in all parts of the British Isles, earthquakes in Macedonia and strange weather elsewhere. Blizzards raged throughout England and Scotland. Shipping was disrupted in the English channel and the North Sea and lifeboats were kept busy assisting distressed vessels to shelter. The steam trawler Lochiong was wrecked on the Fifeshire coast. The crew of 10 men was rescued. The city streets were covered with snow which melted in the morning but was replaced by a heavier blanket at noon. Traffic proceeded slowly through slippery streets and the underground system was crowded with thousands of workers who sought to avoid delay in bus and tramway traffic. The snow storm in London was the heaviest recorded in 20 years. Scores of horses

New Delhi, India, March 8. (2) — Under the terms of the recent agreement between Viceroy Lord Irwin and Mahatma Gandhi, 24,000 non-violent political prisoners will be given their freedom this week, to begin the task of carrying out the Nationalist leader's pledges of peace. The first group of those who were arrested for their effort to liberate India from British domination was set free yesterday in various jails throughout the country. Five thousand others will start home tomorrow.

Stoke-On-Trent, England, March 8. — Lady Cynthia Mosley, chief aide of her husband in the move to organize a “new party,” told her constituents today what England needed in the present emergency was a government “with the guts to govern.” Speaking before nearly 4,000 persons in King’s Hall, Lady Cynthia described as “cheek and humbug” the recent demands of the Fenton and Longton labor parties that she resign her seat in parliament because she had withdrawn from labor's parliamentary party to help her husband, Sir Oswald Mosley, in organizing his “new party.” “Every pledge that I made in the last election I still stand for,” said Lady Cynthia, who is a daughter of the late Marquis Curzon and a granddaughter of Levi Leiter, Chicago merchant. “Isn't it time that you had a government with guts to govern? Isn't the situation in the country dangerous and critical? We are in bad times.”

London, March 8 (P) — A belated winter storm with snow and icy gales held Europe in its grip over the weekend. Surrounding waters were lashed to a fury with resultant damage to small shipping. Great Britain had the coldest weather of the year, with snow in many places. Eastern Scotland was covered with the deepest snow in years. Sheep-farmers there have lost half of the season’s yield in lambs. Northeastern England also experienced heavy snows and several villages were cut off. High tides and great waves pounded the coast and at some points cellars were filled with flood waters. In the North Sea the steamer Stern was sunk after a collision with the steamer City of Malines. Her crew of sixteen were saved. Fishing fleets were held in port and Atlantic liners were delayed. All Austria was under snow which fell for 46 hours without stopping.
