PARIS, Mar. 9. (W.P)—Japan was understood today to have asked for another delay in publication of the naval accord reached between the governments of France, Italy and Britain to bring France and Italy under limitations of the London naval treaty. The delay was said to have been asked to permit further study of the accord in an effort to determine whether the Japanese government will approve or object to “certain changes” necessary in the London treaty as a result of the Franco-Italian agreement. The fact that under terms of the accord France and Italy would be permitted to build at once two 23,333-ton cruisers was believed to be the chief point studied by Japan. The London treaty engaged the United States, Britain and Japan to suspend building of such craft until 1936, when another conference would be held. The French cruisers of 23,333 tons, as planned at present, will be “super” ships

MOSCOW, Mar. 9—(#)—The sixth biennial All-Union Soviet Congress was under way here today in the Grand opera house after a rousing inaugural by Vyacheslav Molotov, president of the Council of People’s Commissars. Molotov in his opening address assailed the United States and other capitalistic countries, thus providing a background against which to paint the progress of Russia under Soviet and communist rule. Sitting on the stage behind him during a long address were the Russian strong man, Joseph Stalin; the commissar of war, K. E. Voroshilov; Michael Kalinin and other communist chieftains. Stalin laughed and talked with Voroshilov and the others as Molotov spoke. Once the speaker alluded to Stalin, who is secretary general of the all-powerful communist party, and the hall, occupied by 1,479 delegates, went into an uproar of applause. Stalin rose but when the shouts and tumult did not die

Paris, March 9—Delay by the United States and Japan in approving the naval accord among Great Britain, France and Italy has given rise to an impression here that the agreement may be regarded officially as a regional arrangement among the three countries to run until 1986 without any modification of the London and Washington naval treaties. It is felt here that there is a tendency in Tokyo and Washington to avoid a new five-power conference to ratify the accord. Dispatches from Tokyo today were interpreted as indicating that the political opposition there was attempting to impede endorsement of the accord on the ground that the French submarine tonnage allocated in the agreement is not satisfactory to Japan.

TOKYO, March 9 (UP)—Japan was rocked early today by an earthquake which damaged 884 houses at Hachinohe and Aomori prefectures on the northern tip of the island of Honshu. Fissures were opened in the earth and strong shocks were felt from 150 miles north of Tokyo, where many houses collapsed.

MADRID, March 9.--(UP)--The Princess Christina underwent an operation for appendicitis at noon today in the Suburban Red Cross hospital, where she was trained to be a nurse. An official bulletin said the operation was successful and the princess was resting well. Princess Beatrice also was in the hospital.

TOKIO, March 0.—(UP)—Hundreds of men, women and children received burns on their faces, hands and clothes today while watching a serial pageant. Military planes were demonstrating methods of laying down a smoke screen by spraying chemicals into the air. Some of the chemicals fell on the crowds.

Paris, March 8. (P)—Sensitive ladies and bachelors as well as everybody else had to reveal their age today to an army of officials which combed France to take the quinquennial census. France counts her population in one day, but it will be four or five months before the 155 employees in the census office, working in two nine-hour shifts daily, complete their tabulation of the figures. It is not expected the population will show an increase beyond the unofficial 1929 count of 41,000,600.

TOKYO, March 9 (AP)—An earthquake today shook Hakodate, on the Island of Hokkaido, causing minor damage but no casualties. Two chimney stacks crashed into the streets and overhead telegraph and telephone wires to various sections of the city were broken and several houses were slightly damaged. The shock was felt slightly here causing a general tremor.

Tokio, March 9—(UP)—Japan was rocked early today by an earthquake which damaged 884 houses at Hacinoye, Aomori Prefecture, on the northern tip of the islands of Houshinu. Fissures were opened in the earth. Strong shocks were felt at Fukushima, some 60 miles north of Tokio, where many houses collapsed. Belgrade, Jugoslavia, March 9.—(UP)—The rough mountain country of Macedonia which overlaps the frontiers of Jugoslavia, Greece and Bulgaria has been widely devastated by three days of the most severe earthquakes which have occurred in many years in the Balkans. The full extent of the disaster was still uncertain today, although official advices from more than a score of towns in the three countries revealed vast damage and heavy loss of life. Shortly before noon an incomplete death toll of 43 was announced by the government, which said at least 700 had been injured. Nine villages, including

BERLIN —(#)— Charlie Chaplin set foot in Berlin today in a snowstorm reminiscent of the closing scenes in his picture the “Gold Rush,” and found a great crowd waiting to greet him. He came from London to attend the premiere of his new picture. When Chaplin first visited Berlin in 1922 he was so little known that he would have been denied a table at an evening club but for the accidental presence of Pola Negri. She recognized him. Today an enthusiastic crowd made a rush to meet Chaplin.

1 ROME, March 9.~-(4P)—This is the feast day of Santa Francesca, pious Roman widow, who died in 1440 and is the patron saint of motorists. They drive their cars to the church of Santa Maria Nova in the ancient forum and have them blessed and ask that they be preserved from accidents.

TOKYO, March 9.—(Monday)—More than 100 spectators of smoke screen maneuvers by army airplanes were burned on the hands and faces yesterday by chemicals which failed to vaporize when released by the planes. The chemicals descended like rain and also burned many of the spectators’ clothing. The accident occurred during air defense exercises at the Yoyogi parade grounds but the extent of casualties was not realized until victims began reporting their injuries to the war department.

1931-01-02.text: Cardiff, Wales, Jan. 1 (4)—There was little activity today in the great collieries of South Wales, where last night negotiations between miners, operators and government officials ended in a sort of combined strike and lockout. One hundred fifty thousand men are employed in the fields and most of them were idle today, although here and there small bodies of men went into the pits by special local agreements. As some workers already were idle because of industrial disputes, the number out of jobs in the area now ranges close to 230,000. The trouble results from a dispute over both hours and wages. At this the Miners’ Federation balked and ordered the 150,000 men not to report for work today. The owners countered with an edict that the mines should be locked to all who refused to accept their wage reduction offer.

Tring, Hertfordshire, England, Jan. 2. (P)—A little gray donkey has provided the biggest thrill of the English hunting season and furnished huntsmen with many hearty laughs. A pack of drag hounds was being exercised near here yesterday when a donkey straying from a farmyard suddenly trotted into their midst, brayed loudly and took off across the country at a gallop. Off went the hounds in pursuit, chasing the ass hard into a wood. There he turned and faced the dogs, who instead of attacking the strange quarry lay down around him and watched to see what he would do next. By coincidence a fox suddenly broke over nearby and the hounds, forgetting the donkey, immediately gave chase to the more natural game. Then to the amazement of the huntsmen the ass joined the hounds, and galloped after the fox, leaping hedges and ditches in grand style, apparently enjoying the chase as much as the dogs,

New York, Jan. 2, ()—Heads of the four eastern trunk line railroads who reached an agreement last week on the major points of a consolidation plan were in conference here again today. There was no announcement as to the subject of the discussion, but it was believed that ratification of the agreement's terms, which have not been made public officially, was being considered. It is known that the executives desire their proposals before the Interstate Commerce Commission as soon as possible, perhaps by the end of this month.

PARIS, Jan. 1.—Clinging to life with the astonishing vitality which has marked his 12 days of desperate illness, Marshal Joffre lay tonight in a coma from which he had not aroused since 11 o'clock in the morning. His doctors, nonplused by the vigor of this rugged old hero, expected death at any moment and all Paris which had been plunged into grief by a premature report of his death this morning, was prepared for the end. He sank into unconsciousness an hour before noon and it appeared for a moment his gallant life was over. Even those at the bedside thought he was dead and the report flashed across the world. But a few minutes later the feeble pulse fluttered, the heart was beating and the marshal of France breathed. — Quickly the premature report was denied, but the denial was a long time in catching up with the first report and not until late in the afternoon was France convinced “Pap

BERLIN, Jan. 2: (4)—Thirty-nine rocks were thrown last night at windows of the Berlin police headquarters in Alexanderplatz and each rock smashed a pane. Franz Heider, arrested as the culprit, said he did it because he was tired of life.

ESSEN, Germany, Jan. 2.—(#)— Workers in 20 collieries of the Ruhr valley coal mines laid down their tools today in a strike not authorized by the trade unions, but allegedly incited by jobless workers and communists. Dissatisfaction among the coal miners is great, due to notice of discharge received by about 306,000, effective as of Jan. 15. After that date they will be re-employed only at reduced wages.

ROME, Jan. 2-47, Benito Mussolini, Italian premier and “strong man,” spoke for 16 minutes into a microphone here last evening in English, to an audience of millions of Americans from Atlantic to Pacific coasts who listened to one of the most ambitious radio broadcasts ever attempted. Premier Mussolini, who is reputed not to have known a word of English when he rose to power eight years ago, took the occasion to wish America a Happy New Year, explain some of the tenets of Italy’s Fascist regime, and to declare that Italy never would start a war. Mussolini pointed out in his address that he himself had fought in the ranks and was severely wounded, and he asked how anyone with his experience as a man and a statesman could consider a future conflict without horror. He was emphatic in his assertion that neither he nor his people desire another conflict of arms. The training which Fascist yout

Berlin. Jan. 1. (4)—Germany looks to the rest of the world for a helping hand in her present economic difficulties, President Von Hindenburg told the diplomatic corps at the New Year's reception today, but she is doing all that she can to help herself out of the depression. “Our hope for lasting improvements,” he said, “rests upon circumstances over which we have no control. The German people anticipate that in this new year international cooperation will save Germany from further painful disappointment. There must be a reconciliation among all the world’s peoples if the obstacles to progress are to be surmounted. This is the great task of peace and Germany is determined to play her

1931-02-24.text: NEW DELHI, INDIA, Feb. 24—(?)— Behind the scenes of the present political drama in India is an English woman, Miss Madeline Slade, daughter of Sir Edmund Slade, for many years commander in chief of British naval forces in India. Renouncing all the pleasures, comforts and amenities of everyday existence, Miss Slade has embraced asceticism and the mysteries of Hindu life and has become the ardent disciple of Mahatma Gandhi, who took her to the Sacred City of Benares and after immersing her in the holy Ganges river, initiated her into the mysteries of the Hindu religion. She has shaved her head in monastic fashion, given all her money to the poor, goes barefooted, burned all her European attire and wears only the cheapest homespun Hindu garments. She has taken the Hindu name of “Mira Bai.” When asked by her British friends if she is “Miss Slade” she replied: “No. Miss Slade has been dead an

Sydney, Australia, Feb. 23—(7—- Mme, Nellie Melba, who died Sunday night in a hospital here, is to be buried on Thursday at Lilydale, Victoria. The funeral services will take place at the Scottish church where her father used to sing in the choir. Tuesday the body will be taken to Melbourne, the city from which Nellie Porter Mitchell fashioned the name by which the world knew one of the greatest sopranos of all time, and the people of her homeland will have their opportunity to do her honor.

New Delhi, India, Feb. 23. ()—In this ancient city in the heart of India, where successive empires of two thousand years have lived and died, one of the strangest dramas of modern times is being enacted. Lord Irwin and Mahatma Gandhi are the leading actors. Thin, ascetic, with a loin cloth his only dress and his shaven head a detail of his odd appearance, Gandhi calls Lord Irwin, viceroy of India, “my dear friend,” and gives passive battle to all the might of the British Empire in his fight for self-determination for India. No difference could be more vivid than that between these two men. Lord Irwin, tall, stately, dignified, surrounded by all the majesty of empire; Gandhi, shrunken, mystic, in the humble home of one of his disciples. Sitting, tailor-fashion, on a potato sack in the sun, he turns ceaselessly at his home-made spinning wheel like a child playing with a top. About him are

LONDON, Feb. 24—A momentous battle of wills in which the Mahatma M. K. Gandhi has pitted himself against the government of Great Britain entered its critical stage today with the future of the great subcontinent of India at stake. Whether the 320,000,000 Indians shall go forward peacefully toward the set goal of Federal Government or shall renew rebellion and bloodshed for complete independence from British rule will be decided by the outcome of conferences between the slight, bent man who is called “the great soul” and the tall, stately representative of King George, Viceroy Lord Irwin. Already stirred to tense feelings by fresh disorders and fighting in Bombay after almost a year of riots, battles and wholesale arrests growing out of the civil disobedience movement, the natives awaited a decision with great uncertainty. Lord Irwin has consulted the home government by telegraph as to fu

LONDON, Feb. 26--Sidney Chas. G. Dawes today set at rest reports that he intended to resign as ambassador to the Court of St. James and return to America, either in connection with the forthcoming world’s fair at Chicago or political work. The fair, he said, was a year ahead of itself so far as preparations were concerned and everything was progressing so very favorably that his presence at Chicago was not needed. “Unless some unforeseen circumstances arise,” he told the Associated Press, “I expect to serve my full term as ambassador. (This would mean another two years). “I see no reason now why I should have to leave here.” He paused and then added: “I am 65 years old. What more should I want to do?” The general made it clear, however, that there was a period last year when it seemed possible that he might have to resign to devote his energies to the fair. He said that more than $12,000

PARIS, Feb. 24.—France and Great Britain today reached an accord, in principle, on Naval Limitation. Foreign Minister Briand announced the accord which was merely verbal and will not become definite until after the British representatives have consulted Premier Benito Mussolini of Italy.

BERLIN, Feb. 24.—(UP)—An unemployed man who had been seeking financial aid in the palace of President Paul Von Hindenburg was arrested today when he pointed a loaded revolver at a detective in the reception room. The man, identified as Alois Broll, a clerk, entered the left wing of the palace about noon. He asked for financial help, and was told he would have to submit his request in writing. Then he drew his revolver and aimed it at the detective, but was overpowered, arrested, and handed over to police, who gave him a mental examination.
PARIS, Feb. 24 (AP) — Hawks, American speed flier, today was named America’s “premier aviator” for 1980 by the International League of Aviators.

PARIS, Feb. 24—(P)—An agreement between the French and British foreign ministers, Aristide Briand and Arthur Henderson, on the conditions under which France will adhere to the London naval treaty was virtually reached this afternoon. Mr. Henderson and A. V. Alexander, first lord of the admiralty, will probably leave for Rome tonight in an effort to obtain the adhesion of Italy to the accord. If they succeed, the London tripartite treaty between the United States, Great Britain and Japan will become a five-power treaty.

PISA, Italy, Feb. 24—-(AP)—The last sacraments were administered today to Cardinal Maffi, one of the most prominent of the college of cardinals, who is believed dying of influenza. The cardinal insisted on rising from his bed and kneeling at a little altar to receive the Host which was brought in a procession from the cathedral,

PARIS (Feb. 23.—(AP)—Arthur Henderson, British foreign secretary, and A. V. Alexander, first lord of the admiralty, came here tonight from London to take a hand in the Franco-Italian naval negotiations which hitherto have been carried on between R. L. Craigie, the British expert and Count Rene Massigli for France. They went into conference immediately with Aristide Briand and Charles Dumont, minister of the navy. Should France and Italy fail to reach an accord on their naval program, a building race between those countries might ensue, such a race, it is felt in naval circles, would imperil the London treaty and might oblige Great Britain to invoke its safeguard clause and build in proportion to Italy and France. Such a course on the part of Great Britain, it was said, might entail similar activity by the United States and Japan and thus destroy the whole London agreement. These possibil

PALERMO, Sicily, Feb. 24. (AP) — The violent storm which swept Sicily for two days and then subsided, raged again today. The fishing boat Vineinzina was swamped at Catania and three persons were drowned. The bridge over the St. Leonard River fell, killing a soldier. Palermo is practically without water as a consequence of breaking of the Scillato aqueduct. There is no electricity available.

Berlin. Feb. 24. (AP)—Telegraphic Union dispatches from Moscow today said the Soviet government had forbidden importation of Bibles and religious works in all languages under penalty of seizure and destruction.

Paris, Feb. 24,—(4')—Foreign Minister Aristide Briand and Charles Dumont, minister of the navy, announced today that France and Great Britain had reached a naval accord in principle, conditional upon ratification and participation by Italy. They added that the agreement would be held secret until its approval by Italy. Rome, Feb. 2 — Settlement of naval differences between France and Italy was regarded today in well-informed quarters as entirely possible under the arrangement reported to have been reached today at Paris between France and Great Britain. It was thought here that the presence of the British foreign secretary, Arthur Henderson, and A. V. Alexander, first lord of the admiralty, who are due here tomorrow night, would indicate that important progress has been made toward finding a formula acceptable to both France and Italy. 1931-03-22.text: GREENOCK, Scotland, March 21. —Aj—Two hundred passengers from the Canadian-Pacific liner Montclare, including 20 mothers and their children, were brought here tonight from the little island of Cambria after the Montclare ran hard aground on a reef in the Firth of Clyde. The crew stayed aboard and it was believed the Montclare might be floated tomorrow although her bows were badly damaged.

PUTNEY-ON-THAMES, England, March 21. ()—Cambridge defeats Oxford today in their 83rd annual eight oared boat race on the Thames. It was the contest's eighth straight victory in the historic event, which had been competed intermittently since 1829. Cambridge took a lead at the start, never relinquishing the advantage during the four and a quarter mile stretch from Putney to Mortlake. The victory gave Cambridge a margin of two races in the series, the light blue having triumphed 42 times to Oxford's 40 wins. The race of 1877 was a dead heat. The official time was 19 minutes and 26 seconds, almost a full minute behind the record set by Oxford in 1911 at 18 minutes 29 seconds. Cambridge’s margin of victory was two and one quarter lengths.

New Delhi, India. — (PF) — Mahatma Gandhi agreed today to participate in the second round table conference at London this fall if he succeeds in settling the Hindu-Moslem communal question. He told Viceroy Irwin today he believed this question could be solved by granting universal adult franchise. This and other important decisions were reached today at a miniature round table conference at the vice regal palace in which Lord Irwin, Gandhi and the congress of Indian princes participated. Attired only in his loin cloth, which cost about a shilling, he sat at a massive walnut table in the sumptuous viceroy's palace with blue blooded Indian princes clad in resplendent silk and gold robes, stunning turbans and glistening jewels around him. At his right sat Viceroy Irwin, who a year ago had him thrown in jail for his challenge to the British crown.

LONDON—A report from Dublin this afternoon stated that Timothy Healy, famous Irish statesman, was seriously ill at his home. He was the Irish Free State's first governor-general in 1922 and is one of the most notable figures in Irish-English political history in modern times.

LONDON, March 21.—Concern was felt today for Arnold Bennett, English author, reported in a critical condition. Bennett suffered complications after an illness of six weeks. He first was forced to go to bed with an attack of influenza.

Glasgow, Scotland, March 21—Two hundred passengers were landed safely on Little Cambrae island in the Firth of Clyde today after the Canadian Pacific liner Montelare, inward bound for Greenock, was grounded on a hidden reef on the northwestern side of the island today in a dense fog. The passengers were taken off the liner in lifeboats and were picked up by tugs which landed them on the island. They will be taken to the mainland late tonight or early tomorrow morning. The crew remained aboard the Montelare. Some was lying at a 45 degree list and was believed to have been badly stove in.

GLASGOW, Scotland, March 21.—(7)—The Canadian Pacific liner Montclare, with a bad hole in her bow, lay fast on a reef off the little island of Cambrai in the Firth of Clyde tonight while her 200 passengers crowded the island cottages waiting to be brought to the mainland. The liner struck the rocks in a dense fog today while she was bound in from Greenock. She settled to a 45 degree list and it was feared she had been badly stove in. The crew remained aboard. Tugs scuttled out to her assistance at the first word of her distress, but when it was found that she was hard aground the boats were put over and the passengers loaded in. The tugs convoyed them to the island where it seemed likely they would have to remain overnight. U. S. S. ARIZONA, March 21.—(®)—Cheers for President Hoover reverberated today from the throats of 800 gobs in white massed in the forecastle of the warship Arizona.

LONDON, March 21. (INS)—Arnold Bennett, distinguished English novelist, was gravely ill today following complications that developed after an attack of influenza. His condition gave rise to increasing anxiety. Straw was laid down in the street outside his house to deaden traffic noises. The writer contracted influenza some six weeks ago, and has been under physician’s care ever since. Attending physicians reported a slight rally by the patient toward noon.

BERLIN, March 21. ()—How he—a Hohenzollern prince and son of the former kaiser—was rudely clubbed by German policemen in Koenigsberg last night was related today by August Wilhelm, himself, fourth son of the ex-emperor on his arrival from East Prussia. He and Paul Goebbels, fascist aide, were beaten and bruised at the Koenigsberg railway station when police broke up a national socialist demonstration, after the two had been forbidden to speak at a rally of that party. Hit With Clubs “I was struck over the shoulder, then clubbed on the head and ears,” August Wilhelm said. “A lady who got in the way was also clubbed. I appealed to a police major who was standing near, but he merely signalled to another policeman who whacked me again.” National socialists asserted that several hundred of them were giving August Wilhelm and Goebbels a peaceful ovation at the railway station.

MADRID, Mar. 21, (®)—Court gossip today had it that there soon is to be a wedding in the Spanish royal family. The Infanta Beatriz, oldest daughter of King Alfonso, is said to have become affianced to her second cousin, Antonio Alvaro de Orleans, second son of Prince Alfonso de Orleans and Princess Beatrice. Beatriz is 21 years old and Antonio is 20. They have been seen together frequently and are said to be genuinely attached to one another. Young Antonio Alvaro probably will be made an infante shortly in anticipation of the formal engagement announcement.

BERLIN, March 27—UP—August Wilhelm, a prince of Hohenzollern and fourth son of the former kaiser, learned last night in Koenigsberg how it feels to stop the swing of a policeman’s club. The former kaiser’s son said on his arrival here today that he and Paul Goebbels, right-hand man of Adolf Hitler, National Socialist leader, were beaten at the Koenigsberg railway station last night when police broke up a National Socialist demonstration after the two had been forbidden to speak at a rally of that party. Koenigsberg police merely said that the prince was clubbed because he wouldn’t move on when requested to do so. “I was struck over the shoulders and then clubbed on the head and ears,” the prince said. “A lady who got in the way was also clubbed. I appealed to a police major, who was standing near, but he merely signaled to another policeman, who whacked me again.” Koenigsberg police expl

Berlin, March 21 (4)—The gesture from which Hermann Mueller’s political opponents never forgave him lived after him today as the Nationalists and Communists boycotted a Reichstag session paying tribute to the memory of the chancellor who signed the Versailles treaty. One Communist attended and he refused to rise with the other members as a token of respect for the statesman whose creed was conciliation: There was a near riot and members loyal to Mueller’s memory spat upon the offending Communists. Mueller’s body is to lie in state until next Thursday at the headquarters of his Social-Democratic party, and on Thursday afternoon will be cremated. The funeral has been tentatively set for March 29. The former chancellor, who was only 54, died on Friday night after a long illness, —
Hamburg, Germany, March 21—Ur)—One Communist was killed and Policeman was wounded tonight in a riot at funeral services for Ernst Henning, Communist leader who was assassinated here last Saturday.

1931-03-19.text: PISA (WP)—Col. Umberto Maddalena, famous Italian flier, was killed here Thursday when his seaplane crashed off Marina Di Pisa. Lieut. Fausto Cecconi, who was Maddalena’s companion on many distinguished flights, also was killed in the crash, as was another officer, whose name was not ascertained. It was understood they were testing their seaplane in preparation for a flight from Italy to the Panama Canal this summer. Col. Umberto Maddalena was one of the greatest of Italian fliers. He piloted the plane which first sighted the survivors of the dirigible Italia when it was wrecked on its north pole expedition and carried food to them.

SHANGHAI, March 18—(#)— The slaughter of 3,000 peasants in a Communist uprising along the Hupeh-Szechwan border was reported in Chinese dispatches today. Nationalist government military forces at Shasi, Hupeh province, were reported to have undertaken an expedition against the Reds. The scene of the uprising was designated as north of the Yangtse river in the border area mentioned. The area was said to have been pillaged. Communists and mutinous soldiers severed the Peiping-Hankow railway at the Hupeh-Henan border and ravaged the countryside. The disorders were said to be continuing there.

London, March 19—(UP)—The steamer, Chang Kiang, struck the rock off Heihan Island near Haimen Monday and sank with a loss of 14 lives, Lloyd’s was advised today from Shanghai. The vessel was a total loss. The French gunboat Marne was standing by taking the surviving crew and passengers on board.

The American beauty’s attorney said she repeated to the magistrate her story to police that she shot in self-defense when she slew the Philadelphia theatre owner and quoted her as saying to the judge: “I have led a dog’s life, but I will always regret I was in a position where I was forced to take human life.” Sobbing often in the course of the two hours and a half she was questioned, her counsel said, the young wife declared fright and terror caused her to keep firing at her husband and chasing him around the room after one bullet had taken effect. | Nice, France, March 18.—()— Mrs. Charlotte Nash Nixon-Nirdlinger must stand trial for killing her husband, Fred Nirdlinger, Magistrate Vachier admitted today after questioning the former St. Louis beauty queen, but he indicated the charge would not be murder in the first degree. Stylishly dressed, Mrs. Nixon-Nirdlinger was driven to the chambers of Magistrate Vachier today in a prison wagon and told her story, containing the details of how she shot her husband a week ago in their apartment. She told the judge: “IT have led a dog's life, but I will always regret I was in a position where I was forced to take human life.” In Terror She sobbed frequently during the questioning, which lasted two and a half hours, her counsel said, and declared that fright and terror caused her to keep firing at her husband and chasing him around the room after one bullet had taken effect.

TOKYO, March 19—(AP)—Eleven participants in an anti-government demonstration were injured in a clash with police and several policemen also were hurt when they attacked the demonstrators near the parliament buildings today. The demonstration was arranged by the seiyukai, or minority, party as a prelude to introduce in the diet tomorrow a motion of non-confidence in the minseito (majority) cabinet of Premier Hamaguchi. The demonstrators were attempting to reach the diet after marching through the streets carrying banners reading “Dissolve the corrupted diet,” and “Overthrow the reactionary Hamaguchi cabinet.” About 140 demonstrators were arrested. Simultaneously, the social-democratic and proletarian parties held mass meetings and parades and endeavored to march to the diet to present petitions but, like the seiyukai sympathizers, were unable to get within two blocks of the building, whic

NICE, France, Mar. 19.--The fixing of a date for the trial of Mrs. Charlotte Nash Nixon-Nirdlinger on charges of killing her husband was awaited today by her counsel. A magistrate decided yesterday that the former beauty queen should be tried, but on a lesser charge than that of first degree murder, for the slaying last week of her husband, Fred, Philadelphia theater owner. Her plea will be self-defense. Police Doctor Peaulelieu, who performed an autopsy on Mr. Nixon-Nirdlinger’s body, confirmed today that he found evidences of a cranial operation. It has been indicated the operation might have some bearing on the case.

1931-01-11.text: Windsor, England, Jan. 10. — King George stood with bowed head today before the scarlet and gold high altar in St. George’s chapel, Windsor castle, to bid a last farewell to his eldest sister, the princess royal, who died last Sunday. The service was simple and solemn, but the scene itself was one of color and pageantry. The coffin was borne from Albert memorial chapel, where it had rested overnight. It was carried between ranks of the Military Knights of Windsor, clad in blue capes and plumed hats, and the king’s life guards in scarlet uniforms and flashing breastplates. Two pipers playing a Scottish dirge preceded the coffin, and behind it walked the king, Queen Mary, the two daughters of the princess and other members of the royal family. It was laid at the foot of the altar during the brief service and then was lowered into the vault. While the ceremony at Windsor was in progress the

SHANGHAI, Jan. 10.—(#)—Sweeping down out of the barren steppes of Mongolia, a blizzard and sand storm that started Thursday had brought death and desolation to a wide area of North China tonight. Hundreds were reported to have died in the dust and snowstorm that raged southward as far as the Yangtse river. Temperatures suddenly dropped 40 degrees to an average of 15 below over the region most affected. Misery and suffering came to thousands of the poor people in the storm’s path. Peiping police gathered from the streets the bodies of 100 persons who perished in the last 24 hours. In outlying districts 18 more bodies were found in unheated shacks. Penniless, these victims were unable to buy fuel. Twenty froze to death in Tientsin. In both Peiping and Tientsin the Salvation Army and Chinese organizations set up gruel kitchens. They also built temporary shelters for many. The vast area from

LEBOURGET, France, Jan. 10.—(P)—All seaboard aviation posts from Biarritz to Nantes were instructed today to be on the watch tomorrow and thereafter for the monoplane Tradewind, which left Bermuda today on a flight to Paris by way of the Azores. The plane left Hamilton at 1:16 a.m. E.S.T. tomorrow. Should the pilots, Mrs. Beryl Wart and Lieutenant William S. MacLaren, push right on after refueling they should reach Paris some time after midnight Sunday. Authorities today made preparations at both Suresnes Fond, in the river Seine near Paris and at Enghien lake to receive the ship, which is equipped with pontoons for coming down on the water. The Montvalerien searchlight, near Suresnes, will flash intermittently as she comes and the river will be lighter if the weather is clear. Enghien lake will be lighted should it be foggy.

1931-03-05.text: New Delhi, India, March 5. ()-- Mahatma Gandhi and the all-India congress party today terminated the civil disobedience campaign, bringing a temporary halt, at least, to India’s political turmoil. The action was in accordance with the terms of an agreement reached yesterday by Gandhi and Lord Irwin, the viceroy. The principal provisions of the truce are: Abandonment of the civil disobedience campaign. Abandonment of the boycott as a political weapon. Release of prisoners. Release of prisoners held for non-violent offenses, Recognition of right of salt area residents to make their own salt. Picketing of non-aggressive nature to be permitted. Repressive ordinances issued during civil disobedience campaign to be withdrawn, Where property confiscated for taxes has been sold to a third party the transaction is to be regarded as final so far as the government is concerned. NEW DELHI, India, March 5 (UP)—Orders for all independence workers in India to observe the peace truce signed yesterday by Mahatma Gandhi and Lord Irwin were issued today by the All-India Congress Working Committee. The committee passed a resolution approving and endorsing the Gandhi-Irwin agreement and directing the All Congress Committee to act immediately in accordance with the pact.

(By The Associated Press) New Delhi, India, March 4—When India awoke this morning it found peace on its doorstep. Overnight, Mahatma Gandhi had led his invisible sleeping multitudes from the precipice of war to the path of peace. By agreeing to forget and forgive the past he won the confidence of Viceroy Lord Irwin, who less than a year ago jailed the mystic agitator for challenging the authority of the British Empire. An accord was reached which ended the year-old civil disobedience movement. Regarded as Triumph Nationalist circles naturally regard the truce as a triumph of Gandhi's doctrine of non-violence which, as Rabindranath Tagore said, introduced a new technique into international revolution. Now the truce will allow the Mahatma to return to his Ashram colony at Ahmedabad, which he left a year ago on his famous march to the sea for the making of salt, vowing he would never return

New Delhi, India, March 8.—(A. P.)—The text of the peace pact between Mahatma Gandhi and the viceroy of India, ending the nationalist civil disobedience campaign, was made public here today and placed before the British parliament in London and the council of the government of India as a basis for negotiations to be continued at a new round table conference. The Mahatma, speaking to newspaper correspondents, after the text had been distributed, addressed an appeal to his countrymen to support the agreement and give him a chance to attain his goal of Independence without violence. The essence of the agreement is a virtual cancellation of the civil disobedience campaign and boycott measures which have won for Gandhi and his nationalist followers a large measure of the demands they outlined a year ago at the outset of their protracted period of passive resistance. Bangalore, India, Mar. 5—(P)— Sixty-five football fans were injured today in a riot which began at a match between Hindu and Moslem teams and spread throughout the city. Police arrested 45 before quiet was restored. The teams had tied three times and there was heavy betting on today’s game which the Hindus won 3 to 0. As the final whistle blew the 3,000 spectators began fighting.

——— NEW DELHI, India, March 5.—(?) —The terms of the truce between Lord Irwin, viceroy, and Mahatma Gandhi, Nationalist leader, permitting abandonment of the civil disobedience campaign were published here today. The principal provisions are (1) Abandonment of the civil disobedience campaign. (2) Abandonment of the boycott as a political weapon. (3) Release of prisoners held for non-violent offenses. (4) Recognition of right of salt area residents to make their own salt. (5) Picketing of non-aggressive nature to be permitted. (6) Repressive ordinances issued during civil disobedience campaign to be withdrawn. (7) Where property confiscated for taxes has been sold to a third party the transaction is to be regarded as final so far as the government is concerned. (8) Sale and purchase of British goods is not to be interfered with. (9) Abandonment of Nationalist demands for an inquiry into a

ROME, March 4—(AP)—Italy gains practical parity of construction with France over the next five years under the terms of the British-Franco-Italian naval accord as disclosed unofficially here today, and in 1936 when the accord expires will be in a better position relative to France than she is today. The principle of parity which broke up the London conference so far as Italy and France were concerned is not settled by the new accord and is postponed until 1936. Meantime naval construction programs are put on a practical level and so harmonized as to guarantee each country against surprise and to permit accurate check on annual tonnage laid down. The annual programs are reduced from more than 40,000 tons to an average between 21,000 and 22,000. Italy made some sacrifices, the terms of the agreement show, but she believes they will not affect the national security and that they are balance

Berlin, March 5—(A.P.)—A Tele- graphic Union dispatch said word had come from Habarowsk in East Siberia of the arrest of General Bluecher, commanding the Soviet forces in the Far East. He was charged, the reports said, with conspiring with a Ukrainian national organization to foster an insurrection in the army and establish an anti-Soviet military dictatorship. It was stated also that the Soviet secret police have uncovered an elaborate conspiracy in the Soviet Ukraine which also involved General Kossak, commander of the red army officers school in Kharkov. Kossak was reported to have been arrested also with 90 Ukrainian students, 60 East Galician officers in Ukrainian regiments, and Prof. Lozynski, formerly an instructor in the Ukrainian university at Prague.

Lucca, Italy, March 5--A jury today acquitted Emilio Dinueci of charges of assassinating Augusto Besso in 1918. The acquittal was on the grounds that he was drunk at the time of the killing, which occurred at Reno, Nevada. Dinueci was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1925, but escaped from the Nevada state prison. He fled to Italy where he was arrested and tried upon the request of American authorities.

1931-01-09.text: LONDON, Jan. 9.—Airplanes dropped food, clothing, and fuel to 16 fishermen stranded in a small boat on an ice floe eight miles off Styrsudd lighthouse today while an ice breaker was en route to their rescue, a dispatch to the Exchange Telegraph Company from Helsingfors said. Seven fishermen and two women, adrift in the Baltic for 36 hours, had reached land after forcing their boat through thin ice. The fishermen were lost among drifting ice when they went to sea in an effort to save their nets, cut loose by a storm. Airplanes were sent from Helsingfors to look for them.

United Press Staff Correspondent. London, Jan. 9.— (UP) —George Bernard Shaw, materialistic and stalwart westerner, and Sir Rabindranath Tagore, dreamy and timid poet of the East, met in cosmopolitan London and agreed that politicians constitute a menace of some sort or other. Tagore, addressing the All Peoples Association, deplored the fact that nations are represented by politicians. "It is almost as bad as allowing a band of robbers to organize the police," the Indian said. Shaw greeted Tagore at a reception after his speech. "I have always been telling my people not to listen to politicians," he said, "I have tried to do this in my own writings, but you know what uphill work it is to try to convince people against their own will." The Irishman and the Indian then posed for their photographs. Shaw was the distinct loser so far as facial decoration was concerned, Sir Rabindranath’s flo

London, Jan. 9. (AP).—Captain Malcolm Campbell, British racing driver, will sail for America next Wednesday on the Homeric with a new “Bluebird,” said to be his most powerful racing machine. He will take the automobile to Daytona Beach where he will seek a speed above 231 miles an hour, the world’s record. His weird car has the center of balance off the center to the right. It was exhibited here this week beside a fleet of motors picked by the Prince of Wales for his South American trip.
On SUING Arbitration A abls. CARDIFF, Wales, Jan. 9. (F)— Negotiations looking to the settlement of the great South Wales coal strike collapsed this afternoon.

SALLY LAKE City, Jan, &— (AP)— Jean Dayle, 21, cabaret singer, held here for the murder of Sam Frank, jewelry auctioneer of Memphis, Tenn., several weeks ago, repudiated an alleged confession today. Police said the girl repeated that she drugged Frank, intending to rob him, but denied any connection with his death. She said her first story that two men killed Frank while she was preparing to leave was correct.

BY THE ASSOCIATED PRESS. Glasgow, Scotland, Jan. 8 — Sir Thomas Lipton today gave the city of Glasgow $50,000 for distribution among the poor mothers and children in his native city. He made the gift, he said, in memory of his mother, "the guiding star of my life," and in appreciation of the "many kindnesses" he had received from the city.

(By The Associated Press) | Rome, Jan. 8—The full power and authority of the Roman Catholic church were invoked by Pope Pius RI today to uphold the sanctity of Christian marriage and to stamp out the practices of birth control, “companionate” marriage and divorce. In the most sweeping exposition of the church's views on matrimony in many years he condemned the use of contraception, abortion, sterilization or any other means to prevent the fruitfulness of wedlock. His pronouncement came in the form of a long encyclical, the first of its kind in 50 years of ecclesiastical history. In it he enjoined his bishops to propagate the church's view that marriage is indissoluble except by death, and that the family, within the meaning of this sacrament, “is more sacred than the state.” Shameful, Vicious Deed Birth control is a deed “shameful and intrinsically vicious” and a “horrible crime,” the po

MADRID, Jan. 9—The Spanish Army Air Service was disbanded and plans for its reorganization were outlined in a decree published today. Officers and men of the service were given 15 days in which to apply for membership in the new air corps, or to return to the branches of the army with which they served originally. The decree had been expected in view of the attempted revolt at Cuatro Vientos Airdrome recently, led by Ramon France.
(By United Press.) BERLIN, Jan. 9.—Sixty persons were injured, many of them seriously, in a collision between a passenger train and a freight train near Vilnius Friday.

His plan for complete self-government with “disciplined rule from within” makes it possible for India to remain within the British empire, he said, “but our partnership with England must be on terms of absolute equality.” “Some of my associates believe British statesmen will never reconcile themselves to absolute equality for India,” he said. “I may be a visionary, but I hold differently. I see the day when New Delhi and not Downing Street will be the center of the Indian nation. Under Common Flag “When we achieve independence it will not be under the British flag but under a common flag. As a visionary, I see the day when there will be no armies, but it will not come during my lifetime. It may take ages before even the Indian nature accommodates itself to having no army. “I fear no invasion by the Bolsheviks. If

Lomion — () — Approbation, laughter and denunciation were visited upon Lady Cynthia Moseley Friday in the public's answer to her courageous speech last evening, setting her husband's “new party” on its way. Sir Oswald was ill abed with influenza, and could not address a great crowd which assembled at Farrington Hall to hear an outline of his principles, but his wife, a daughter of the late Marquis Curzon and a granddaughter of Levi Leiter, Chicago merchant, served ably in his stead. One section of her hearers cheered her statements but others obviously had come to heckle her. At one point after a series of unusual taunts she answered: “My God, if you had sat in the House of Commons for the last eighteen months you would be here on the platform beside me.” Her message was a warning of the “abnormal dangerous and desperate” national crisis facing Britain, for which she offered as a solutio

| TRURO, N. S., (P)—Twenty families have been huddled for more than a night and day in upper stories of their home on Devil’s Island while roaring waves, sweeping in from the sea through the hamlet’s streets, seethed below them. Word of the plight of the islanders came in telephone messages here during the night. The messages told of a 90-mile gale which sent the seas racing through the village, pounding structures and weakening their foundations. Blinding snow and sleet added to the discomfort of the marooned families. The growling wind and splashing waves ripped to pieces breakwaters and wharves. Only the lighthouse seemed able to withstand their onslaughts. Many tales of bravery among the fishermen were current here today. One concerned Ben Henneberry, lighthouse keeper, who was rescued by neighbors after he was washed out to sea by a giant wave while attempting to save his little boa

NEW DELHI, India, March 5.—The terms on which John Bull and Mother India will resume a speaking acquaintance were made public today, but the way to the altar was still fraught by bypaths to dissension. Mahatma Gandhi ordered the termination of the civil disobedience campaign, and Lord Irwin moved to revoke the statutes against those who waged it, pending the next turn of the wheel of India’s fate.

New Delhi, India, March 5 (Pi -- While he sipped his goat's milk from a battered can brought from his recent prison, Mahatma Gandhi gave a notable interview today based on the results of his agreement with Lord Irwin. He admitted that the settlement had given much to the nationalists, but served notice anew on Britain that complete independence is the goal of India. "That is the birthright of India as it is of every nation worthy of the name," he said. "If the All-India Congress has shown a readiness to participate in the second round table conference, it is because it seeks to make federation an Indian responsibility, with such safeguards and reservations as will promote the real growth of the country along political, social, economic and moral lines. "If the Congress succeeds in making its position acceptable to the conference then I claim the fruits of that effort will complete indepe

LONDON (U.P)—There are indications that the long-awaited trade boom will start here this spring. These indications are many. Leaders of industry and members of the government are said to be basing their plans on them. The federation of British industries, in its trade barometer just issued, says: “Spring should see some improvement. Chancellor of the Exchequer Philip Snowden is preparing his budget on the assumption that the trade returns will shortly show a substantial improvement and yield him increased revenue. The trade fair, which opens in the spring, and which is attended by buyers from all parts of the world, probably will provide big orders for British industry. Meanwhile, many huge contracts are being secured, often in the face of world competition. Further evidence of the approaching spring boom is to be found in the announcement that the Wellman Smith Owen Engineering corporat

By United Press AMSTERDAM, March 6—An earthquake at Tjoeklil, Java, killed several persons and destroyed many houses today, reports received here said. Thousands fled from their homes, which were flooded by the bursting of dykes in the River Tjitarcen.

MOSCOW.—(#)—N. Bagatsky, a locomotive engineer held responsible for a railroad wreck in eastern Siberia, Friday was sentenced to be shot and twelve members of his train crew were sent to prison for three to ten years. In the wreck inquiry, government investigators contended that this and numerous similar incidents in the past year were the result of sabotage.
By United Press P March 6. — The United States liner President Harding, en route from Hamburg to New York, radioed today that she had been damaged and was heading for Southampton for repairs.

1931-03-12.text: | LONDON, March 11—(AP)— Limitation of French and Italian naval programs until 1936 is definitely laid down in the terms of the British-Franco-Italian naval accord made public today. But even more important than its technical provisions, in the opinion of the three governments concerned, the agreement brings European peace measurably closer and provides a point of departure for the disarmament conference at Geneva next year. The accord covers building programs for battleships, cruisers, aircraft-carriers and submarines in substance as follows. Battleships—Both France and Italy are given the right to complete before December, 1936, two capital ships whose displacement shall not exceed 23,333 tons and whose gun calibre shall not exceed twelve inches. Cruisers—Both nations agree that after completion of the 1920 class they will build no more big cruisers with armament larger than six-inch g

LONDON, March 12 (UP)—A committee representing the United States, Britain, Japan, France and Italy will be formed to draft a new five power naval limitations agreement incorporating the new Franco-Italian accord, it was understood today in reliable American quarters. The committee would meet here possibly in April with Ambassador Charles G. Dawes as the probable United States representative. Dawes will visit the foreign office today regarding a matter separate from the naval accord, but probably will discuss the naval limitations question.

LONDON, Mar. 12. (4)—Winter still held most of Europe in a fierce, unrelenting grip today. Germany, France, Austria, Switzerland, Scandinavia, Holland and the British Isles suffered from storms which began last week and have continued with little pause since. The Zuyder Zee, Holland’s great inland sea, for the first time in several years, was frozen over and ferry service was suspended. Roads were either blocked by snowfall or made extremely dangerous for traffic in all the affected countries. Conditions in Great Britain were a trifle less severe than yesterday, although cold winds and frost continued. There was some anxiety in the Hill country at the prospect of melting drifts bringing floods.

CANBERRA, Mar. 12.—Abandonment of Canberra, Australia’s federal capital dream city which cost $66,000,000, is being urged by many leaders in public life and business men. Described by some politicians as “the nation’s symbol of unity,” and by others as “a running ulcer of finance,” it would be returned to the sheep which once grazed on its broad acres if a widespread movement prevails. It is isolated and its maintenance is costly. Its roads, gardens, public buildings, hotels and homes are among the best in Australia, but because the city was designed to eventually accommodate a big population, its buildings are scattered over 900 acres. There are no street cars and to buy a tube of toothpaste one has to walk a mile or more. Water supply, drainage, sewerage, and everything was designed on a grand scale and at a grand cost. A paper parliament house cost $3,000,000. Five hotels costing over

LONDON, UP, Snow, high winds and bitter cold weather impeded traffic on land and sea Wednesday night as the worst late winter storm of recent years continued to rage in many sections of Europe. Ships were delayed, automobiles were stalled in drifts and many trains were far behind schedule. The blanket of snow covered much of England, France, Germany, Austria and other countries. Numerous accidents were blamed on the storm. The icy streets in Berlin alone caused more than thirty injuries and sent a dozen persons to the hospital with broken bones. Paris faced the menace of flood, since the snow was causing the river Seine to reach a high stage. In Munich and Berlin, scores of snow plows made little progress against the drifts. The street cleaning personnel was augmented by hundreds of unemployed.

GLASGOW — Nearing 95, Charles Brown wonders where his 33 children are. His first wife bore him three, his second wife, 16, including three sets of twins and one of triplets, and his third wife 14. They have scattered to far countries.

Tipton, Ia., March 12.—Ray Handley, 35-year-old mail carrier, was found beaten into unconsciousness today after his kidnappers had set fire to his automobile. A motorist last night discovered the burning car on the Lincoln highway near Clare, and notified officials who identified it as belonging to Handley. An all-night search followed, which was terminated at dawn with the discovery of Handley’s unconscious form on the rear porch of a home here. Handley apparently had been beaten and thrown from the kidnappers’ car, and had crawled to the porch before losing consciousness. There was no known motive for the attack and police were unable to learn of any enemies of the mail carrier's. Handley’s wife is in a Davenport hospital.

SHANGHAI, March 12.—(UP)— The explosion of a small Yangtze river steamer with a loss of 225 lives became known today when the revenue cruiser Chuentao reached port with 119 survivors of the accident. The Chuentao also carried the bodies of seven victims of fire and blast aboard the steamer Pachi. The captain of the latter vessel said there was an unknown number missing. The accident occurred Wednesday night off Big Tree beacon, 60 miles from Shanghai. The captain of the Pachi said 100 soldiers boarded the ship at Woosung and virtually took possession. He asserted that cigarettes carelessly thrown by the soldiers started the fire and caused the resultant explosion. The captain said about 250 passengers were aboard the Pachi when the soldiers arrived. He feared 225 may have lost their lives on the vessel. The Pachi, known as a chicken boat, was owned by the Pata company.

Thousands of Homes Evacuated as Result of Floods and Freezing. PARIS, March 12.--(P)—Floods and freezing temperature spread suffering and death along almost every river in France today as storms which swept southward from the British Isles continued in Europe. Entire villages along the Seine, Loire, Rhone, Lot and Meuse valleys were evacuated and thousands of families were homeless.

NICE, France, March 11. (P— Mrs. Fred Nixon Nirdlinger was arrested tonight on charges of shooting and killing her husband, a Philadelphia theatrical agent, in their apartment here. She is 26 years old and her husband is 54. She said she shot in self-defense. Police said their inquiries indicated the shooting was the culmination of a violent quarrel said to have arisen from the behavior of the husband.

BERLIN, March 12 (AB)—Physicians to former Chancellor Hermann Mueller, who is suffering from a recurrence of an old gallstone ailment, said today that he was “very low.” ‘An erroneous report of his death this afternoon was quickly denied.

BERLIN, March 12—Among the many who contracted sore throat and cold in the head during last night's unseasonable storm was Charlie Chaplin. After a party he insisted upon taking a walk in the snow, for which his Hollywood routine hardly prepared him. As a consequence he had to remain in bed today and cancel his proposed visit to the Reichstag. It was uncertain when he would leave Berlin but his next jump will be to Nice or Vienna.
ISTANBUL, March 11. (AP).—A violent earthquake was felt at 10:00 last night at Smyrna. The population was terrified and rushed into the streets, cemeteries and other open spaces.

(By The Associated Press) ISTANBUL—City clerks should wear Prince Alberts when they perform marriage ceremonies for the women of modern Turkey, contends one of them. A new woman alderman, Rana Yaver Hanim, put the question to the city fathers in her first speech. They are deliberating.

BERLIN—A roving radio reporter, H. H. Hellmutt, is on his way to America to broadcast to the old world his impressions of the new. With his microphone under his arm he will tell of the skyscrapers of New York or the film lots of Hollywood. NBC will transmit by a short wave.

MADRID, March 11.—Reports of a movement toward a republic in the province of Catalonia were spread today, but tonight it appeared they were caused by the merger of two strong political parties which seek first administrative autonomy within the existing Spanish set-up. These parties, the Accion Catalana and the Accion Republicana, formed the "new Catalonian republican party" today. They favor the establishment of a Spanish republic eventually, but do not wish to separate from the remainder of Spain in the meantime, as advocated by some of the other republican factions. Hence their advocacy of administrative autonomy now. Leaders of the new party announced a general party assembly for March 22, principally to establish a slate for the April 12 municipal elections and to work out a platform. Paris dispatches from the Havas News Agency said an unsigned manifesto circulated along the French

1931-01-24.text: NEW DELHI, India, Jan. 23.—(”) Before another 24 hours have passed, Mahatma Gandhi, imprisoned leader of the Indian nationalists, probably will be a free man, it was predicted here today. The end of his eight months’ imprisonment appeared to be delayed only by a decision as to what other leaders of the congress party should be given their freedom with him. The viceroy and his council were discussing this matter today but it was believed they already had decided to restore Gandhi's freedom. His liberation and that of his associates is bound up with the issue of general amnesty for all India’s 60,000 or more political prisoners. At the close of the round table conference in London, Ramsay MacDonald said amnesty would be granted if order could be restored in India.

LONDON, Jan 24 (P)—A gale of fifty miles an hour velocity swept Western Europe and the British Isles during the night. There was an accompanying deluge of rain and thunder and lightning. High seas led to some anxiety for shipping. A Portuguese trawler was sunk in the mouth of the Tagus and two of its crew were drowned. The liner Vardulia, en route from St. John to London, damaged a rudder in the Bay of Biscay and broadcast a distress signal which brought the Dutch tug, Witte Zee, to her assistance. Two other tugs already had gone to her help so the Witte Zee returned. The Vardulia radioed her position to Lloyds as somewhat south of her course, indicating possibly she was being driven by the storm. She was not considered in any danger. No anxiety was felt for the British cruiser Canterbury en route from the Mediterranean although she was many hours overdue at Plymouth.

MADRAS, India, Jan. 24.— Ten miners were killed and fifty injured in a terrific fall of rock yesterday in the Kolar gold fields in the state of Mysore. Pit heads were shaken by the fall and the entire district was thrown into panic.

MANCHESTER, Eng. Jan, 24.— (UP)—A prolonged mill stoppage was foreseen in Lancashire today when the weavers voted against resuming negotiations for settlement of the present conflict which has put some 250,000 men out of work and threatens to make as many more idle. The vote was 90,770 to 44,990 against resuming negotiations. The cotton trouble grew out of efforts of employers to put the "more looms per weaver" system into effect. The workers objected.

MOSCOW (UP)—A statement issued Saturday under the signature of Josef V.Y. Stalin announced the beginning of “a decisive final drive” to eradicate the kulaks of Russia as a class. The drive against the kulaks (a term chiefly applied to rich peasants) will be carried out with the intention of eliminating the class within the present year. It was interpreted as meaning a new offensive in behalf of the collectiveization campaign which probably would exceed the intensive drive of 1939.

GENEVA, Jan. 4—(#)—The council of the League of Nations today formally invited the governments of the world to assemble for a general disarmament conference Feb. 2, 1932. The date was designated at the first Tuesday after the session of the council in January 1932, which will begin Jan. 25 and last about a week. Geneva was designated conditionally as the place for the conference.

GENEVA, Jan. 23 (4)—The nations of the world will gather once more, in the last week of January 1932, in a general conference for reduction of arms on land, on the sea and in the air. No decision was reached as to the man who will be chairman. During the public and private meetings of the council the name of Dr. Edward Benes, the Czechoslovakian, has been proposed, but the Germans objected to him and there was suggestion, so far purely informal, that Ambassador Charles Gates Dawes be asked to accept the post.

| Paris, Jan. 23.—— (4) —— Political observers were looking tonight to Aristide Briand as a likely candidate for the task of forming a new French government to replace that of Theodore Steeg, which fell by 16 votes in the chamber yesterday on the issue of price fixing for wheat. Students of politics are agreed that a stable government is impossible so long as the parties in the chamber are split up as they are at present.

PARIS, Jan. 24 (*) — President Doumergue today telephoned to Aristide Briand at Geneva offering him the premiership of France. Political experts had expected this development since the fall of the Steer cabinet on Thursday, but there was a general belief that Briand would decline the task. He has refused the post three times in the past 18 months in the belief that he is more valuable to the nation as foreign minister, continuing his task of building a permanent peace for Europe. Briand has been at Geneva for nearly two weeks, attending sessions of the League of Nations council and of representatives of 26 European nations examining his project for a ‘Pan-European federation. It was thought that if Briand would decline to become premier the president would turn to Pierre Fiandin, to Pierre Laval or to Louis Barthou. Emile Borel, an independent of the Left, told Doumergue that the chamber
iy The Associated Press} PARIS, JAN 24—IT WAS OFFICIALLY ANNOUNCED TONIGHT THAT ARISTIDE BRIAND HAD DEFINITELY DECLINED AN OFFER TO BECOME PREMIER OF FRANCE TENDERED BY PRESIDENT DOUMERGLE.

MADRID, Jan. 26—(4)—Rioting broke out again today among students at the University of Madrid and several were injured. The University remained closed under an order issued Saturday because of clashes between rival student groups. A heavy guard of soldiers and police remained at the University grounds.

GENEVA, Jan. 24. - The great and small powers of the world will assemble in the second month of next year for the most ambitious effort in history to prevent 'the next war.' The League of Nations council, in setting the date of February 2, 1932, for convening of the world disarmament conference, gave the military and naval powers a period of more than a year to settle the most vital controversies over comparative defensive needs of various nations or accept responsibility for endangering the success of the conference. Authorities were virtually unanimous that collapse of the 1932 conference, for which the League preparatory commission has been preparing for half a dozen years, would mean a setback of many years for the cause of disarmament and world peace.

Paris, Jan. 24,— Aristide Briand, veteran Foreign Minister and former Premier, was asked by President Gaston Doumergue today to form a new cabinet, succeeding the defeated government of Theodore Steeg. The request was contained in a telegram sent to Briand at Geneva, where he is attending the League of Nations Council meeting. Earlier Briand had told friends he did not desire to become Premier.

aves 6488 San tS. Moscow, Jan. 24. (AP)—Hostility to the selection of Charles Gates Dawes or Charles Evans Hughes as chairman of next year’s world disarmament conference was expressed today by the newspaper Izvestia in an editorial asserting that “international anti-soviet elements are intriguing” to elect a chairman from a country unfriendly to Russia.

1931-02-15.text: MADRID, Feb. 14.--The year-old cabinet of Premier Damaso Berenguer resigned today, forced to this action by countrywide opposition to its electoral program, and King Alfonso set about the difficult task of forming another ministry. He met with a serious obstacle, however, when the powerful constitutional party announced that it would not participate in any government that did not include all political factions. The king had at first planned a “concentration” ministry of royalist leaders. Thus, unless Alfonso agrees to a “nation” cabinet embracing Republicans, Socialists and other groups, he apparently faces a ministry composed largely of Liberal party leaders with perhaps some conservatives. This would leave the Socialists, Republicans and Constitutionalists as disgruntled as they were when Premier Berenguer was in power, according to political observers. Some military groups were even r

1931-03-25.text: WINDSOR, Eng., April 29. (AP)—The Prince of Wales and his brother George arrived here at one o'clock this afternoon from Le Bourget airport, ending an 18,000-mile tour to South America. Their plane, City of Glasgow, dropped down in Windsor Park near the ancient castle where King George and Queen Mary were awaiting them. They had come home in the same manner as they left, by air. Their arrival was informal and unostentatious, with scarcely a cheer from the waiting crowd. It was as though the heir to the British throne had just returned from one of those week-end hops to the continent instead of one of the most important missions he had performed.

LONDON, March 25.—David Lloyd George today was able to promise the labor government of Prime Minister MacDonald probably sufficient labor support to keep it in office indefinitely, provided it asks parliament to do nothing offensive to Liberal principles. The parliamentary liberal party, in an eight hour private meeting last night, voted 33 to 17 in endorsement of a statement of policy drawn up by Lloyd George which must become the keynote of labor legislative policy if labor is to remain in power. The 17 votes cast against the doughty Liberal leader, who many believe engaged in a fight to culminate his brilliant political career with another term as premier marked a highwater mark for the Sir John Simon opposition group, whose watchword has become “turn the rascals out.” The terms of the Liberal statement of policy were withheld for publication but they are understood to involve no depa

NELSON, B. C., Mar. 25. (AP) — With the arrival of spring, members of the Sons of Freedom, Doukhobors, a religious sect, have begun to discard their winter clothing. Reports of Doukhobors disrobing in the vicinity of Thrums, B. C., resulted in a police investigation today. Staff Sergeant Stephenson and two provincial constables discovered seven naked Doukhobor women perched on fences at Thrums near a highway and a railroad right-of-way. The police ordered the women to seek shelter and don their clothing but they refused. A melee ensued in which the officers dusted the women with itch powder. A male Doukhobor brought a garden hose for the women and they turned water on the officers. The women finally were driven into their homes.

LONDON, MAR. 25. (AP) -- Rallying after their recent defeat in attempting to introduce prohibition into Great Britain by act of parliament, the temperance forces today sought to curtail liquor advertisements which flare over town and country through the Isles. The Commons rejected the move by a vote of 127 to 112.

MADRID, Mar. 25 (—After a four hour battle in which one policeman was killed and a score of police and students were wounded, rebellious students of the San Carlos Medical school abandoned the fortified building today. Police made no effort to detain the students. Eight police were known to have been seriously wounded and perhaps 20 students. Two of the youths were in a critical condition, one with a bullet in the lung and the other with one in the stomach. The students had barricaded within the school building to repel the attacks of the authorities. The red banner of revolution floated openly above the school and its roofs teemed with students watching the fray. The streets were congested for blocks. Students outside the building threw stones at the police. The government was understood to be prepared to suppress further republican outbreaks. The republican leader, Niceto Alcala Zamora

PARIS, Mar. 25—(4)—The international reaction resulting from the Austro-German customs accord seemed to be eased today with the prospect that the matter would go before the council of the League of Nations, probably next May. The council will be asked, it was indicated, whether the Austro-German accord violates the Geneva protocol and the St. Germain treaty, as the French allege. The first hint of the possible submission of the question to the league council was suggested in a communique issued by the British embassy today. In it Arthur Henderson, British foreign minister, expressed strong hope that before the Austrian and German governments pursued their negotiations the league council, under whose auspices the Geneva protocol of 1922 was consummated, 'would be given an opportunity to assure itself that the proposals were not contrary to Austria’s engagements under the protocol.'

MADRID—Civil guards after four hours of student rioting at the University of Madrid Wednesday, forced the students to raise a white flag over the medical college buildings. The guards surrounded the medical college and fired into the air, terrorizing the entire university district. Police had battled unsuccessfully with the students for two hours before 160 picked men of the guards, fully armed, relieved them. Many persons were wounded and two were reported killed. The victims were said to be a civil guard from company 26 and an unidentified student.

Madrid, March 24.—(P—Bullets pattered in the streets of Madrid, Tuesday, as King Alfonso, returned only Tuesday morning from a visit to his mother-in-law in London, sat in his palace worrying over the rats which three days of liberty had brought to his capital. These were the highlights of an exciting day. Aleala Zamora, who proclaimed the republic last December, was released from prison under suspended sentence of six months and a day. Several of his companions in the December movement were liberated with him. Santiago Alba, powerful liberal leader, came home after eight years of self-imposed exile, placed himself at the head of the constitutionalists and in an uncompromising manifesto declared political war on Premier Aznar and called upon the king to take a vacation while a constitutional convention decides whether Spain shall remain a monarchy or become a republic. Madrid, March 25.—Students of the Medical College of the University of Madrid and police fought in the streets in front of the college again today, the third day of clashes in which numerous persons have been injured. A police captain and two students were wounded by gunfire this morning and eight policemen were injured by stones. Fighting began after a student carrying a large banner inscribed "Viva la Revolucion," shouted insults at the police and started throwing stones. Police fired several shots and armed students returned the fire. Several laborers and residents of the district aided the students. A police officer attempted to negotiate with the students and was told that they demanded immediate amnesty for all political prisoners. The officer transmitted the request to police headquarters, where it was refused. A motion picture cameraman named Luck was arrested for taking pictures

PARIS, March 24 (AP)—Renunciation of the commercial treaty with Germany and a decision to abstain from all financial aid constitute the possible policy of France toward Germany if she persists in carrying out an economic pact with Austria, the Associated Press was informed tonight in official quarters. Inquiry among diplomats accredited to France shows a prevalence of belief that the Austro-German move is one of the most important political developments since the war, embodying a possible attempt to form a central European bloc of powers just as the naval accord between France and Italy had given optimistic conviction that the war clouds of Europe had been dissipated. It is now admitted that the French representation to Vienna has taken the form of a resolute, though "friendly protest," and it was learned that at yesterday's meeting the French cabinet judged the affair so potentially gra

1931-03-16.text: LONDON, March 15.—(AP)— Victoria station was heavily guarded this evening when King Alfonso of Spain arrived to visit his mother-in-law, Princess Beatrice, who is recovering from a serious illness. The king left Paris at noon, after spending the night there. The credentials of all persons approaching the railroad platform were carefully examined. Those who were not traveling and had no business there were denied admittance to the station. The Duke of York, the Marquise of Carisbrooke, as well as the personnel of the Spanish embassy, welcomed the monarch at the station. The Spanish ambassador had met Alfonso on his arrival at Dover and accompanied him to London. Immediately after his arrival the king, who is staying at the west end hotel, drove to Kensington Palace to see Princess Beatrice, who is the aunt of King George.
