SYDNEY, N. S. W., Mar. 16. (AP) - Police today discovered an entire family of six wiped out at the lonely homestead of Denman, 90 miles from Newcastle. - John T. Marriott, the homestead owner, was found dead on his doorstep with a wound in his head. Inside the house were the charred bodies of Marriott's wife and four young children. - Police believed that he shot his family, fired the homestead, and then killed himself.

Heir To Silk Fortune Was One Of Wealthiest Men In Britain. London, March 16—Hugh Morrison, 62, one of the wealthiest men in all Britain, died here yesterday after a long illness. Morrison recently resigned his seat in parliament, which he held for Salisbury, Wiltshire, for thirteen years. He was a Unionist. Morrison's fortune was supposed to be several times the amount left him by his uncle in 1922—about $55,000,000. His own share of the huge family estate built upon the silk trade has been greatly enlarged by the addition of money left by others in the family.

LONDON, Mar. 16 (#)—King Alfonso of Spain had lunch with King George and Queen Mary at Buckingham Palace today after visiting his mother-in-law, the Princess Beatrice, whose illness brought him here, and paying formal calls at the home of Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and at the foreign office. The king drove to Kensington Palace immediately on his arrival yesterday to see the Princess Beatrice, aunt of King George, who has been ailing for some weeks. The Spanish king, who came from Madrid by way of Paris, was accompanied in all his movements by a heavy police guard.

London, Mar. 16—(A P)— The majority of the MacDonald government in the House of Commons shrank to ten today when an amendment by the Conservatives to the section of the electoral reform bill dealing with university constituencies was rejected 178 to ... The amendment provided that certain university constituencies should be excluded from the general abolition of university constituencies for which the bill calls. The government was declared by observers to face a possibility of defeat tonight in a final division of the house at the end of debate. The section under argument involves the representation in parliament of certain universities, including Oxford and Cambridge, whose graduates are now permitted to vote and send a member of their own to parliament. The bill calls for abolishing these constituencies. Certain liberals and the full strength of the conservative party are opposed to t

LONDON, March 16,—(UP)— King Alfonso of Spain, who arrived last night apparently in unusually good health and smiling broadly despite the recent threats to his throne, was the object of extraordinary police precautions today. Two inspectors, several sergeants and 30 uniformed police officers assembled in the luggage room and dozens of plain clothes detectives mingled with the crowd at Victoria station upon the arrival of the king, who came here to visit his mother-in-law, Queen Beatrice, who is ill:

Bombay, India, March 15.—(AP)—While Mahatma Gandhi at Sisroad today was disclaiming the supernatural attributes which some of his disciples see in him, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, influential congress party leader, exhorted a great audience here to be content with nothing short of complete independence. A tremendous crowd listened to him. Half a dozen men were hurt when the loudspeakers broke down and the mob stampeded toward the platform. The Pandit explained his version of complete independence as full! (Continued on Page 2)

Londen, Mar. 16. (AP)—Throughout Europe women are raising their eyes from their hearths to the political arena, some with hope, some with determination and a considerable number with actual ambition. Even Asia has begun to open its political gates to wives and mothers. The house of representatives in Turkey passed a bill granting women equal franchise rights with men in elections for city, town, and village autonomous assemblies. The women of England and Germany have secured a far firmer position in politics than most of their sisters in neighboring lands. Though only in the past few years have they emerged from their harems during their way to parliament. They made their political debut this year when the Kemalist government granted them the municipal vote, and those who know Kemal believe it well within the realm of possibility that during next November's general elections, he will giv

Tokyo, March 16. (4P)—Police credited a dog with having saved the life of a high Soviet official from an assassin here today. The intended victim, Paul Anikeieff, Soviet commercial counsellor here and chief of the trade delegation handling the Japan-Russian fisheries dispute, was wounded dangerously. He probably would have been shot to death, police asserted, had not a dog belonging to a Japanese neighbor interfered. Nobukatsu Sato, 34, later surrendered, declaring he was responsible for the shooting. Anikeieff was leaving his home when the assassin leaped to the running board of his automobile and opened fire with a small automatic pistol. Two bullets struck the Russian before the dog leaped at the assassin. The man swung on the dog, sending two shots into its body, then returned to Anikeieff. No charges have been brought against the former St. Louis girl, who contends she fired in self-defense last Tuesday night when she slew the Philadelphia theater owner. Her counsel, Louis Gassin, said witnesses were necessary to prove self-defense and that in this case there were none, since the 26-year-old wife and the husband twice her age were alone in their bedroom when the killing occurred. Yakovleff, union commissar of agriculture, providing for introduction of piece work systems in more than 85,000 collective farms. The standard of wages will be fixed in either money or commodities so that the man who works hard will earn more than the man who does not. Hitherto opposition to piece work has been one of the chief planks in the platforms of workers’ organizations. Yakovleff averred that the collective farm movement already was a success, and that the collectives had more than 9,000,000 peasant families as members. He added that there were numerous defects and unsolved problems. He pointed out that in the past some peasant families have contributed livestock and farm equipment to the common fund and then have done as little work as possible, the more industri

Tokyo, March 16 (Monday) (P).— Paul Anikeieff, Soviet commercial counsellor here was shot and seriously wounded today by an unidentified assailant. Anikeieff was in his automobile en route from his home to the Russian embassy when his assailant leaped on the running board and fired three effective shots from an automatic pistol. Anikeieff was wounded in the right arm, hip and right breast. Physicians said the breast wound was most dangerous. Anikeieff’s chances for recovery were termed good. He heads the Soviet trade delegation handling the Japan-Russian fisheries dispute which for months has been on the verge of rupture, the Soviets having taken a firm, uncompromising stand. Police said Anikeieff's assailant was a Japanese, aged about thirty. The assassin escaped.

TOKIO, Japan, March 16.-Nobukatu Sato surrendered voluntarily to police tonight and confessed that he had shot and seriously wounded Commercial Counsellor Anikeiff, of the Soviet embassy. Sato, who had lived in Russia for 20 years and was once connected with the fisheries in which Japanese participate off the Siberian coast, said the attack was not connected with a Japanese-Soviet fisheries controversy, despite his former connections. Anikeiff was attacked this morning while en route to the Soviet embassy. He was shot in the right thigh and left arm. At the Keio University Hospital, where he was taken, it was said that his wounds were severe but that his life was not in danger.

NICE, France, March 15.—(®—Char~ Joite Nixon-Nirdlinger, who killed her jealous husband after a quarrel in their home here last Wednesday night, probably will have to go back to the room in which she shot him and go through the tragedy in pantomime while the French police “reconstruct” the crime. This is the procedure usually followed in cases of the kind and it seemed likely today this prisoner would be no exception. She is not to be examined by the magistrate, however, until some time next week. During that procedure, her attorney has intimated, new arguments will be adduced to support her contention she shot in self-defense when she killed Pred G. Nixon-Nirdlinger, the Philadelphia theatrical magnate, whom she married after coming in second at an Atlantic City beauty contest. It consists of plans for reorganization of all collective farms in Soviet Russia along lines which seemingly resemble capitalistic methods but which are expected to achieve results in output far exceeding the five. As Anikeieff swung his automobile from his driveway toward the Russian embassy here Monday, an unidentified man leaped to the running board and fired at Anikeieff with an automatic pistol. Two shots entered the Russian’s body when the dog attacked the assassin. Thereupon his assailant turned his weapon on the dog, shooting twice. Then he returned to Anikeieff, sending his last bullet into the Russian’s chest. Police asserted Anikeieff would have been riddled with bullets but for the dog. The Russian also was wounded in the right arm and hip. Physicians said he was dangerously wounded but that his chances for recovery were good. The assassin was not captured. 1931-02-13.text: London, Feb. 13—(AP)—Bucharest society reports that Queen Helen, unable to hold the love of her handsome Prince, now King Carol, plans to marry a Rumanian officer, Colonel Skeletti, were published here today. Helen is said to have written Carol, whose friend in Paris, the red-headed Magda Lupescu, is understood to be lodged now near the royal quarters, that she will resist all his efforts to nullify the divorce she obtained from him in absentia in 1928. While the Holy Synod of the Rumanian Orthodox Church declared that divorce null and void shortly after Carol became king last June, it has been explained that this made it only morally non-existent, since legal annulment would have to come through the courts. “Such a marriage as is reported to be contemplated by Helen would be almost unheard of in European royal circles.

LONDON, Feb. 13—(4’)-—The House of Commons by a vote of 187 to 18 today rejected the bill introduced by Edwin Sorymgeour, prohibition member from Dundee, Scotland, which would have prohibited the use of alcoholic liquors as beverages throughout the United Kingdom. The vote came after a lengthy debate in which Lady Nancy Astor, Virginian born member of the house, played a leading role by her slashing attack on alcohol. ~ Rave and girls basketball
| MANCHESTER, Eng. Feb, H- gi. The long drawn out tie-up in the Lancashire cotton industry ended today, and 300,000 weavers who were locked out last month will return to work on Monday.

Melbourne, Feb. 13. - Violent earth shocks occurred in the Hawkes Bay region of North Island, New Zealand, today, where several towns were virtually destroyed and about 200 lives were lost in an earthquake a short time ago. Minor shocks were felt throughout the north and south islands. No casualties were reported. Communications with Napier, the center of the first earthquake, were re-established late today. Officials there, in charge of rehabilitating the ruined city, reported that the latest shocks were violent, but did little. Reports received here said that the earthquake was felt as far north as Hamilton, north of Hawkes Bay on North Island, and as far south as Invercargill, on the southern tip of South Island.

LONDON, Feb. 18—Lady Astor, American-born member of the House of Commons, brought a heated debate on prohibition to a climax today by reiterating her prohibition sentiments but stating that she would not support Edwin Scrymgeour’s anti-liquor bill because she believed in local option. The House of Commons, by a vote of 187 to 18, rejected the second reading of the prohibition bill. The rejection did not constitute a governmental defeat. “You might as well call it the ‘peerage’ as the peerage,” said Lady Astor, referring to the House of Lords. “That would be a very good name for it.” Scrymgeour previously had denounced titled members of parliament who are brewers as “engaged in producing national degradation.” The speaker intervened to halt Lady Astor’s remarks, reminding her of the rule against saying anything disrespectful. Lady Astor was not restrained, however, in her denunciation of

LONDON, Feb. 12 (4)—Harsh gales which have lashed the English channel and the Irish sea for 24 hours swept up to the north of England tonight, the fiercest storm of the season. The winds abated somewhat, however, in both the channel and the Irish sea, and ships prepared to resume the journeys that had been held up for two days. No casualties were reported to shipping, but tugs took in tow the British steamer Swiftway, which called for help while wallowing in the high seas off the southwest coast of Ireland.
Cadiz, Spain, Feb. 12. (4)--Heavy police patrols guarded the streets tonight after a series of disturbances in which four striking workmen were wounded when civil guards broke up a demonstration.

1931-02-12.text: London, Feb. 12. (47)—One of the most violent of gales of the winter blew over England and adjacent seas during the night. The wind reached a velocity of 50 and 60 miles frequently and occasionally blew more than 70 miles an hour. The channel was lashed into furious waves which seamen estimated to be 30 feet high. Channel steamers suffered some damage and many arrived at ports hours late. The Bemridge lifeboat searched for six hours last evening for a small unidentified vessel seen earlier drifting in the channel. It returned unsuccessful and it was feared that the small vessel was lost. Many trees were uprooted and chimneys and roofs damaged.

LONDON, Feb. 10—Shipping badly buffeted by a fierce gale which rose suddenly yesterday and continued to blow all day today with little diminished force. One steamer was reported in distress tonight. She was the British freighter Built Way, of 2,917 tons, which left Las Palmas, Canary Islands, Feb. 1 for Limerick, Ireland. Her steering gear was carried away and she was drifting helplessly in the vicinity of Southwest Ireland. Two tugs left Cobh (Queenstown) to assist her. High seas raged in the channel and drove all sorts of craft to shelter in various ports, a large number taking refuge in Plymouth Sound while a score of Welsh trawlers, fishing in Irish waters, sheltered in Battery Bay. A number of vessels reported more or less damage.

NAPIER, New Zealand, Feb. 12 (AP) —— Prolonged earth shocks rocked the ruins of this city and nearby town of Hastings today, but they seemed to be of different character from the destructive quake of last week and no further damage was reported. Considerable progress has been made here and at Hastings in clearing up the earthquake wreckage.

LONDON, Feb. 12 (AP) — A large question mark was written across Britain's immediate economic future today as businessmen and politicians alike asked what Philip Snowden referred to in the Commons yesterday when he spoke of impending ‘drastic and disagreeable measures’ to maintain the budget. Prime Minister MacDonald, triumphant by a 75-vote majority in repulsing a conservative motion of censure on a count of extravagance, turned to face grave differences in his own party growing out of the chancellor’s speech. The comment was heard in the lobbies that he had won ‘worse than a pyrrhic victory.’ Increased death duties, an increased supertax, delayed application of some measures involving large expenditures which have passed the House but have not yet been finally enacted, and reduction of interest on government loans were some of the measures which popular speculation credited Snowden with
LONDON, Feb. 12, (1A radio message received here today said that Sir Charles Parsons, inventor of the turbine steam engine, died last night while on a trip to the West Indies. He was 76 years old.

LONDON, Feb. 12.—A prolonged and severe earthquake shock was felt at Napier and Hastings, New Zealand, today, it was stated in an Exchange telegraph dispatch from Wellington.— These two cities were virtually wiped out by a series of earth temblors last week which took a toll of hundreds of dead and injured. Floods are menacing as a result of a heavy rainfall, the dispatch added.

D., a cousin of Mrs. Arnot... The sanity of Mrs. Arnot is being determined before a jury in district court in an effort to decide whether she is to face trial on a murder charge growing out of the death of her husband, J. E. Arnot, former Glasgow banker, from what the state contends was poisoning. The defense offered in evidence certified copies of the commitment of Margaret Levitre, sister of Mrs. Arnot, to the Fergus Falls institution and of the petition for inquiry into her sanity in Clay County, Minnesota. BERLIN, Feb. 12.— (UP) — The Reichstag, opening its campaign against the “war guilt lie,” adopted a resolution today asking the government to seek abolition of that part of the treaty of Versailles which places responsibility for the world conflict on Germany. Another resolution, protesting against the disarmament of Germany while other powers were failing to observe their armament agreements under the treaty, also was adopted. The resolutions were introduced by the peoples party and the Catholic party. The Reichstag adopted them with rising votes. The adoption of the protest measures came after the legislative body had rejected Communist and Fascist motions to discontinue the Young plan payments, withdraw from the League of Nations and create a frontier guard against Poland. The Reichstag adopted a motion, however, favoring opening of negotiations immediately with signatories of the You

BERLIN, Feb. 12. - A resolution introduced by the Centrist party attacking the “war guilt” and demanding an impartial commission of inquiry to determine the causes of the world war was approved by the Reichstag today against the opposition of the Communists. At the same time a Communist motion to cease all reparations payments was voted down, 314 to 58.

QR INQPBIVE INES Dat N ERR BERLIN, Feb. 12.—The Reichstag today by a vote of 314 to 58, with one abstention, defeated a Communist motion to discontinue the Young plan payments. The Reichstag subsequently, by a vote of 314 to 46, passed the Christian Socialists’ motion which favors opening of negotiations immediately with signatories of the Young plan in the hopes of obtaining a revision.

MADRID, Feb. 11—()—Troops were held under arms in their barracks today in case they should be needed to put down disorders as Republican groups celebrated the anniversary of the proclamation of the First Spanish Republic in 1873. Although a number of political agitators, strike promoters, and others were arrested during the day, the situation was reported calm tonight. At 5 p.m. the special confinement of the soldiers was terminated and the situation was left in the hands of police, who remained in large numbers on the streets.

Paris, Feb. 12.—(#)—Three hundred thousand persons are unemployed in France and 1,350,000 are working on part time it was learned today on high authority. The government considers the situation serious, though not grave, nor is preparing to relieve it by increasing allocations of state funds and development of public works.

1931-03-10.text: LONDON, March 10. (AP) — Sir Oswald Mosley was expelled from the Labour Party today for his “act of gross disloyalty” in launching a “new political party.”

Bedford, Eng., March 10—(A.P.)—Alfred Arthur Rouse, man of many loves who last November tried to “die by proxy” in an effort to escape the responsibilities of his amorous adventures, today was hanged for the murder of an unidentified man. He was the first person in 145 years to be executed for the murder of an unidentified victim. The body of the man he killed was kept unburied throughout his trial and subsequent incarceration in the hope that Rouse in a last minute confession would tell who he was. During the trial Rouse said the victim was a hitch-hiker, to whom he had given a lift and who had accidentally, perhaps in lighting a cigarette, set fire to his car while Rouse was outside the vehicle effecting temporary repairs. The case was marked by the unswerving loyalty of Rouse’s wife and one of the three women with whom he loved, the mother of his child. After his arrest the wife and t

BEDFORD, England, Mar. 1—Alfred Rouse, dapper, handsome, 36-year-old bigamist whose tangled love affairs held the attention of England for many days, was hanged today for the murder of an unknown man. Prosecution used circumstantial evidence, convincing a jury that Rouse deliberately killed a passenger in his car then set fire to the car so that he might wipe out his past life and start anew.

LONDON — (4) — Southern England was making up today for the lack of real winter weather during the past three months. A temperature of 22 degrees Fahrenheit prevailed in London this morning, and thousands of erstwhile unemployed were engaged in removing an estimated 9,000,000-ton fall of snow which came down yesterday, the heaviest precipitation in twenty years. The sky today was threatening and continued snow and colder weather were predicted. Roads all over the British Isles were piled high with snow or, more dangerous still, were encrusted with ice which made traffic difficult and hazardous. The railroads brought out their snow plows and train schedules were fairly well adhered to. Cross channel steamers and some air services continued to operate through snow storms. Airplane pilots described the experience as much like that of flying through a fog. Among incoming liners buffeted by t

LONDON, March 10.—(U. P.) — The greater part of Europe and its surrounding seas continued today under the lash of storms which were lessening in intensity but were still severe after four days of blizzards, high gales, floods and earthquakes. The known death toll in the European area was high—close to 200—and thousands were injured and homeless. The material damage was immense, but could not be estimated due to incomplete advices. Snow covered the British Isles from Scotland to Cornwall, and the most severe March snowstorm in 20 years took a toll of eight dead and hundreds injured. The steam trawler Locklong was wrecked off Fifeshire, sailors in the channel reported the blizzard so dense that they could not see from one end of their ships to the other; the Hempstead observatory recorded 13 degrees below freezing—the coldest since 1906—roads in many districts were impassable due to snow d

LONDON, March 9 (AP)—Riding down from Iceland on a bitter cold wind, a winter storm held most of Europe in its grasp tonight with frigid temperatures general except in the southernmost countries and with deep snow in many sections. It snowed all day in London and the heaviest fall in 20 years lay several inches deep, seriously impeding traffic. Along the British coast from the channel to the Orkneys high waves battered shipping and several small vessels ran aground. There was deep snow in the north, causing heavy losses to sheep farmers. Germany, Austria and France had snow. In many places it was the coldest day in years, and in France rising rivers caused considerable concern. The Seine was menacing Paris and continuing snow gave rise to fears of serious floods. Snowdrifts blocked the highways and delayed trains and the cold belt ran from Scandinavia to Spain, in Vienna snow fell for 48

Tipton, Ia, Mar. 10—A "passive resistance" campaign against Iowa bovine tuberculosis testing laws bore fruits of success today. State agents, supported by deputy sheriffs, attempted yesterday to read the tests made on a herd of cattle at the William Butterbrodt farm, near here, but when they encountered a crowd of nearly 1,000 farmers in the barn yard they staged an orderly retreat. The attempt to enforce the state testing law yesterday brought to light an extensive organization among the farmers of Cedar County so that all will band together to resist state enforcement agencies. The workings of this organization are similar to revolutionary times, when rapid relays were sent up to warn of the approach of an enemy. Moscow, March 9.—Fourteen menshevists on trial for “interventionist” activities against the Soviet government were found guilty today and sentenced to varying prison terms. Seven were given 10 years in prison, four eight years, and three five years. The fourteen members of the minority confessed their guilt as the defendants did in the first interventionist trial.

Moscow, March 9. (4)—Russia's second great counter-revolutionary trial in four months, with fourteen prominent mensheviks accused of anti-bolshevik activities, ended today with the defendants receiving sentences ranging from five to ten years in prison. Death sentences had been asked for seven of them and all confessed fully.

MOSCOW, March %.—(#)—Fourteen mensheviks on trial for treason since last Sunday today were sentenced to prison for terms running to 10 years. The men were charged with plotting to overthrow the soviet government. Death sentences had been asked for seven, two of whom declined yesterday during the summation to ask for leniency, saying they deserved to die. Most of the defendants had asked for brief sentences so that they might devote their lives to the service of the soviet government. The trial began two weeks ago yesterday. Interest in it had waned after the first few days.

Tokyo, March 10—7P—Japan’s reply to the British Franco-Italian naval accord has been sent to London, and while not published, is understood to express unreserved approval although appending a number of comments in the nature of desiderata. These notes direct attention to the large tonnage both of submarines and superannuated craft allowed to France. The fear is expressed that the proposal will allow both countries to exceed the limits of the Washington treaty in capital ships and thus entail re-ratification of the treaty in modified form which is considered waning.

Madrid, Mar. 8—The infanta Maria Cristian, third child of King Alfonso VIII, was operated upon today for appendicitis. All of the royal family and various government officials expressed satisfaction at what they say were happy results.

Moscow.—(A.P.)——Russia has celebrated “International Women’s Day” in honor of their emancipation from the kitchen stove. With 881,000 women now working outside the home—30 per cent of all employees—the government expects to have 600,000 more in industry by the end of the five-year plan. But parade bands still are composed of males.

By United Press TOKYO, March 10.—The second earthquake in two days shook Japan at 3:45 a.m., but was less severe than the shocks which damaged northern regions yesterday. The second quake caused residents of the Aomori district and of Hokkaido, on Hokkaido Island, to flee their homes again.

1931-03-14.text: London, March 14.—(/)—Dame Madge Kendall, famous actress of a generation and more ago, who will be 82 tomorrow, retains her belief in old fashioned girls, and thinks the maids of today are given their latch keys too early. “I was 68 before my husband gave me one,” she said today. “On my birthday I persuaded my husband to give me one. He brought me a little charm to hang it on, so I shouldn't lose it. I wish women would try to retain their old fashioned ways. We have made divorce so cheap marriage has become almost comical.” Old Folks to Gather Dame Madge will preside on her birthday night at a dinner of the Old Players’ club, a noted organization of first nighters.

SOUTHAMPTON, England— a pink bathroom for the Prince of Wales; a green one for Prince George. They were installed on the liner that will return them from Buenos Aires. An apple-green reception room was thrown in.

By The Associated Press. NICE, France, March 14.--Under no circumstances will Mrs. Fred G. Nixon-Nirdlinger, who killed her husband here last Wednesday night be released without a jury trial, the examining magistrate said today. She will be brought before the ordinary session of the court of assizes which does not meet until August, the magistrate said.

Nice, France, March 12.—(U.P.)—Mrs. Fred G. Nixon-Nirdlinger, 26, who was Charlotte Nash of St. Louis, won second honors in the 1924 international beauty pageant at Atlantic City, was held by police today on charges of killing her husband. Nixon-Nirdlinger, once a prominent figure in theatrical life in the United States, was killed during a quarrel at the villa of the couple on the fashionable promenade Des Anglais. Mrs. Nixon-Nirdlinger told police she fired two shots at her husband in self-defense when he threatened her with physical harm. Nixon-Nirdlinger died immediately, but the police investigation was hindered because of the inability of his wife to make herself clearly understood. It was understood that the Philadelphian had been married previously. He was 60. Police said the shooting occurred when Mrs. Nixon-Nirdlinger was studying Italian. Her husband was said to have been jeal

Nice, France, March 13. (&) — French authorities sent today to St. Louis and Philadelphia, former homes of Mrs. Charlotte Nash Nixon-Nirdlinger, for character evidence which may determine whether charges shall be brought against her for killing her husband. The young beauty clung, against all police efforts, to her story that she fired in self-defense Wednesday night when she killed the wealthy Philadelphia theatre man. "It was he or I," she repeated, "and something was bound to happen." Officials quit trying to shatter her version when they found in the Nixon-Nirdlinger apartment a revolver they said had been her husband’s. It tended, they conceded, to prove her contention that she was in fear of her life when her husband grasped her throat after accusing her of having an Italian lover. In the jail which shut her from friends with whom she lately frolicked along the Riviera, the 26-year

HAMBURG, Germany, March 14 (2P)—Professor Albert Einstein came back to Germany today after his American trip but went to great pains to outwit crowds which had gathered to welcome him. A large crowd gathered to greet him last night when the boat train from Cuxhaven arrived, but he was not aboard and some concern was felt. It developed today that he had spent the night aboard the Deutschland and disembarked here this morning when the boat docked at Hamburg.

BERLIN, March 14 () — Charlie Chaplin today found himself unwittingly enmeshed in German political discussion. The “Young Guard,” communist youth organ, quoted the movie actor as declaiming to its editor, “My greetings and all my sympathies are with the communist youth of Germany.” The conservative nationalist Boersenzeitung asserted that if the remark were true it constituted an unwarranted meddling with Germany's internal affairs. Chaplin denied having made any such statement. His secretary said he believed the incident to have arisen from the visit of a delegation representing German unemployed in the stage and film fields. The actor expressed profound sympathy with their lot but pointed out that 100,000 American film people also were unemployed. “The word communism was never mentioned,” the secretary said. “Charlie is no politician and never expresses political opinions.”

1931-01-25.text: London, Jan. 26...P)—Dame Nellie Melba, famous singer, is seriously ill at Sydney, an Exchange Telegraph dispatch said today. Dame Melba was too ill to go ashore when her ship reached Australia some weeks ago. She was said later to have been suffering from prickly heat, contracted during a voyage through the tropics.

PARIS, Jan. 24—Pierre Laval, youthful Independent-Socialist senator, and one of the leaders of the Left Center Moderates, tonight took up the task of forming a cabinet to succeed that headed by Senator Theodore Steeg, overthrown in the chamber of deputies on Thursday. He accepted the task at the hands of President Doumergue after Aristide Briand, veteran of many ministries, had declined the premiership for a fourth time in a year and a half. In two long conversations with President Doumergue by telephone from Geneva where he was attending the sessions of the council of the league of nations, M. Briand said he preferred to retain the post of foreign minister and the premiership should go to a younger man. Senator Laval attempted to form a government after the defeat of the Tardieu cabinet in December last year, but was prevented by what seemed an irreconcilable battle between the Right an

Geneva, Jan. 24. —-(#)—- The council of the League of Nations topped off a week of laborious sessions tonight by composing the inflammatory German-Polish minority question with a settlement hailed in Geneva as one of the most important decisions of the League in recent years. In effect the council unanimously condemned the activities of certain patriotic organizations in Poland which were charged with violent acts against the German minority and summoned the Polish government to break off all connections with these bodies. Must Report: Further, the Warsaw government was asked to report to the council before its session next May what measures had been taken to execute the league’s mandate.

1931-01-16.text: LONDON, Jan. 16. (AP).—The Prince of Wales got off to a flying start today on his tour to South America. With his brother, Prince George, he left Hendon airport in a plane bound for Paris on the first leg of a tour which will take them over 18,000 miles.

LONDON, Jan. 16.—A wave of influenza swept Europe today while Britain was in the midst of the worst epidemic of grippe, influenza, and colds experienced since 1927. France, Germany, Spain, and Portugal reported unusual suffering. Severe cold in Spain and Portugal added to the discomfort of thousands; the military college in Lisbon was closed due to the illness of 370 cadets. Reports from Berlin estimated that 10,000 persons in Germany were being treated for influenza and colds. One-third of the patients were in hospitals. Approximately 200 deaths in England during the last fortnight were attributed to influenza; recent cold, foggy weather and the neglect of colds were considered responsible. It was estimated that bad weather, and consequent illness, caused the loss of 7,000,000 weeks of work in Britain during 1930. The epidemic of grippe in Spain was reported intensified by continued exc

London — (— An influenza epidemic, covering a large part of Europe, especially in the cities and towns, has put thousands in their beds and hampered business and transportation services through reductions in staffs. In some cases schools have closed. In 107 large towns of England on whose returns the country's vital statistics are based there were 191 deaths from the disease last week compared with 60 deaths the previous week. Otherwise there have been no

(by Associated Press) KALGOORLIE, Western Australia, Jan. 15—A 17-year-old boy was reported today to have found at Larkinville a gold nugget weighing 78 pounds and worth 5,500 pounds (about $26,785). The nugget was said to measure 26 inches by 12 by 3.

By BRUCE CATTON, NEA Service Writer.* Eleven years after national prohibition became effective, a nationwide poll of approximately 1,500 daily newspapers in the United States with circulations totaling far into the millions shows: Three hundred and eighty-nine newspapers with a total circulation of 3,932,041 favor the prohibition amendment as it now stands. Three hundred and forty-five newspapers with a total circulation of 12,520,911 are opposed to the prohibition amendment as it now stands. HENDON AIRDROME, Bng., Jan. 16.--The Prince of Wales and Prince George began their South American trip officially when they left Hendon for Paris at 1 P. M. today. The royal brothers travel in a private biplane piloted by F. Fielden. They will spend the night in Paris and proceed to Santander, from where they will embark for South America tomorrow. The Prince of Wales will travel as the Earl of Chester, and will be known by this title throughout the trip. Prince George is traveling as the Duke of York.

BIRMINGHAM, England, Jan. 15 (®)—Former Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin is broke—and is proud of it. In recent years shares in the iron trade owned by the Conservative leader have depreciated in value from three pounds (about $14.60) in 1923 to 20 pence (40 cents) now, he revealed last night.

LONDON, Jan. 16 (AP) — Mrs. William McKechnie of Gaven told a magistrate that she had been whipped by her husband every day for the past 18 years and was growing tired of the procedure. Magistrate Campbell, doing a lightning calculation, figured she had been thrashed about 6,570 times and placed William on probation for 12 months, promising a jail sentence if he used his razor strop on his wife again.

LONDON, Jan. 15 (#)—The persistence of two government officials who refused to admit defeat when success seemed impossible tonight resulted in an agreement which probably will put 150,000 miners back at work in the South Wales coal fields Monday. The agreement stipulates the rate of pay will remain as heretofore and underground hours will be seven and one-half daily each day of the week.

Bombay, India, Jan. 16.—(P)—Henry Ford is building great plants at Bombay, Calcutta, Madras and Multan for the assembly of Ford cars and trucks to be shipped from Canada for distribution throughout India. The company has announced that it will “Indianize” its staff, a matter involving the technical training of a vast number of young Hindoos in assembly, servicing and selling the cars through the company’s 250 dealers in India. Construction of the plants coincides with a widespread boycott of automobiles made in England and an increasing demand for American cars. The latter constitute about 80 per cent of all automobiles used in India.

Harbin, Jan. 16—(A.P.)—Siberia, Mongolia, and North Manchuria were swept today by the severest cold of thirty years, Mongolia reporting a temperature of 65 below freezing. Seven men froze to death in the region of Manchuli. In Siberia it was 50 below freezing. Locomotives had difficulty keeping steam in their boilers. It was 45 below about Harbin. All schools were closed.

Geneva, Jan. 16—Europe has come to the belief that her nations must unite if they are to live, Aristide Briand today told delegates from European states gathered here under the auspices of the League of Nations to examine his plan for a pan-European federation. “We have a long road to travel,” he told the assembly as he opened its sessions, “and we must map it out. We must never be swerved from our purpose and in our task we will reject the co-operation of none.” Dr. Julius Curtius, Germany’s foreign minister, echoed the French chairman’s declaration, asserting that his nation, supporting any program of cooperation and peace, agrees that in these first meetings economic collaboration among the nations must be emphasized.

GENEVA, Jan. 16.—Aristide Briand, veteran French foreign minister and campaigner for world peace, told European statesmen that “the time has come when we must unite or die” when he convened a meeting of the European Union here today. “Never has the economic situation burdening Europe been so manifest,” Briand said. He urged the satisfactory inauguration of a United States of Europe before the second organization meeting of the proposed European Federation. German Foreign Minister Dr. Julius Curtius emphasized that Europe’s economic problems were uppermost in the interests of the Union. He suggested that organization work stress the problems arising from the uncompleted League of Nations economic conference and suggested that the admission of non-European members be considered, apparently referring to Turkey and Russia.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 14. (UP)—G W. Brophy, manager of the aviation department of the Le Gale Company, will attempt a Pacific flight from here to Manila next Sunday, he announced today. Brophy hopes to demonstrate the feasibility of a regular commercial air route between Shanghai and Manila, by way of Foochow and Canton. Using a plane called the Phoenix, Brophy plans to take off from Hungfno Aerodrome here. The aviator formerly maintained a flying school at Phoenix, Ariz. At one time he served as an instructor in the Mexican air force and later was a pilot for the Mexico-Guatemala Air Company.

1931-02-07.text: Oxford, England, Feb. 6 (P)—A city so ancient that its ruins show watermarks reputedly left by the Biblical flood has been discovered a few miles east of Babylon by the Oxford University Field Museum expedition in Mesopotamia. On top of it is the first well-preserved palace of the Sassanian dynasty of Persian kings ever found. And the discovery of the palace was largely accidental, Prof. Stephen Langdon, the American-born director of the expedition, explained it to the Associated Press today. The field director, he said, waiting to begin excavations on the main hill over the site of the ancient city, set his Arab workmen to leveling the mounds of earth nearby. They had not been at work for a week before one wall and two gateways of the Royal Persian Palace had been laid bare. Prof. Langdon estimates its date at about 360 A.D. Below it, in layers representing the various stages of civiliz

Birmingham, England, Feb 6. (P)—A letter recently arrived at the home of Tom Winshull, jr. It stated that the writer, who signed herself “Lilly,” regretted her hasty refusal on the previous evening and indicated that if Mr. Winshull would call that started a little research. He learned the letter was mailed in 1908 and was meant for his father, who died several years ago. “Lilly” also was dead, he learned. She never married.

(International News Service) LONDON, Feb. 7 - According to figures 160 bodies have been recovered from the ruins of the cities of Napier and Hastings, New Zealand, said an exchange telegraph company dispatch from Wellington today. Sixteen hundred persons injured in Tuesday's earthquake were treated in emergency hospitals erected in the two cities. Twelve thousand of Napier's 20,000 inhabitants, including most of the women and children, have been evacuated from Napier.

LONDON, Feb. 6 (4)—Sometimes Sinclair Lewis wonders whether he wasn't better off back in Sauk Center, Minnesota, before all this Nobel Prize business began. “It's no bed of roses,” he said today, “I'm still getting letters, and they all want money. I tell them I'm poor, too, but it doesn’t do any good. “There was a Gypsy sent me a letter in Berlin asking me to pay off the mortgage on his old homestead and when I said I couldn't do it he sent me five postal cards calling me some names I never heard of and saying he was praying every day at his mother’s grave that something terrible should happen to me and my wife.”

TOKYO, Feb. 6—(AP)—Bitterness over the London Naval treaty caused a free-for-all fight today in an ante room of the Diet, and a dozen persons, two of them members of the Diet, were injured. — The fight started when a member of the opposition party wielded a dagger during hot debate of Foreign Minister Shidehara’s explanation in the Diet that Emperor Hirohito, by approving the treaty, had proved it did not endanger the security of Japan. The explanation was regarded by government opponents as an effort to blame the emperor for any defeat in the treaty. Fifty men milled about the ante room wielding clubs and hurling anything they could get their hands on. Several were cut about heads and hands. Others were bruised and were cut by crashing glass. Baron Shidehara, acting head of the government since Premier Hamaguchi was shot and severely wounded in November by a fanatical patriot, was in an

By the Associated Press. | Rome, Italy, Feb. 6.—Michele Schirru, a naturalized American citizen born in Sardinia, must face trial before a special tribunal on a charge of planning to assassinate Premier Mussolini with a bomb. Under the law he may be executed. Today the police gave out the gist of a confession they said he had made yesterday in the hospital where he was taken after an unsuccessful attempt at suicide at the end of a battle in a police station. In the scuffle he wounded three policemen. The alleged confession admitted a plan for the assassination. Schirru said he had been an anarchist for years and had been plotting against Mussolini since last summer.
BERLIN, Feb 7 (UP).—The Reichstag rejected motions of no-confidence against the Bruening government, introduced by fascists and communists, by a vote of 293 to 221 today.

Berlin—(UP)—Overriding the opposition by decisive majorities, Chancellor Bruening won 2 distinct victories in the Reichstag today when the parliament voted down a series of obstructionist measures proposed by the Communists and the National Socialists. By 293 to 221 the members defeated a joint no-confidence motion by the two parties, 2 similar motions directed against Gottfried Treviranus, minister without portfolio, lest 312 to 206; and a National Socialist motion requesting President von Hindenburg to dissolve the parliament was voted down by 318 to 207. The majorities were interpreted as an indication that the government would succeed in pushing through its “Spartan” 1931 budget without having recourse to the “dictator clause” in the constitution which provides for suspension of the Reichstag and government by decree. After adopting the chancellery budget the Reichstag adjourned unti
ROME.—(/)—The American consulate was informed officially Saturday that Marcel Schirru, arrested for plotting an attempt on Premier Mussolini's life, did not have a United States passport.

1931-03-24.text: LONDON, Mar, 24—(#)—Continued co-operation between liberals and the labor government, but not an out and out pact for maintenance of the government in power, was reported in political circles today to be the probable outcome of present negotiations between the labor and liberal party leaders. Liberal circles buzzed with activity today as the liberal parliamentary party assembled for a meeting at which policies were to be outlined. Recommendations of the shadow cabinet, containing the leaders of the party, both pro and con Lloyd George, which met last night will be submitted to the parliamentary group meeting. It was understood today that the sense of the shadow cabinet’s deliberations was that the liberals should maintain their party entity although giving the government cooperation on such measures as come within the scope of broad liberal policy. In other words, the arrangement will co

MELBOURNE, Australia, March 23.—(AP)—The airliner Southern Cloud carrying a pilot and six passengers still was missing today in spite of the extensive search by land and air. Participating in the rescue are Wing Commander Charles Kingsford-Smith, managing director of National Airways, the owners of the plane, who was forced down near Holbrook, Victoria, in his plane Southern Sun. He broke the propeller which later was replaced by a spare. A girl pilot, Nancy Lyle, was flying with him at the time. The Southern Cloud was last seen at 3:30 p.m. Saturday at Wagaratta, 145 miles north of here.

Paris, March 24.--(4)--The economic union projected by Austria and Germany today stole the thunder of the “Pan-European committee meeting to consider further phases of Aristide Briand’s scheme for an economic un- ion of all Europe. Members of the Briand committee assembled in an atmosphere of some distrust of the proceedings at Berlin and Vienna, and of suspicion that the projected Austro-German accord is the first step toward a political union of the two countries in violation of the peace treaties and the Geneva protocol of 1922. The text of the accord, which is subject to ratification of the two parliaments, was made public in Berlin and telegraphed here. Its features are clauses which proclaim the equality and independence of the two nations and their willingness to have other nations join them in the union. As seen here the effect of the accord will be to give Germany free and favor

ISTANBUL, Turkey, March 24 (P)—Word was received here today that 14 Turkish longshoremen had been torn to pieces March 17 in Zonguldak harbor by the propeller of the German boat Mexico. The men had approached alongside the Mexico in a rowboat when the engines were unexpectedly started, the report said, tearing the occupants of the small boat limb from limb.

Nice, France, Mar. 24---(AP)---The situation of the two children of Mrs. Charlotte Nixon-Nirdlinger is becoming desperate for lack of funds, Magistrate Vachier, who is conducting the inquiry into the shooting of Mrs. Nirdlinger’s husband, said today. He said that there remained only money enough to provide food for the children until tomorrow noon. In her prison cell, Mrs. Nixon-Nirdlinger, who is being held for trial for the killing of her husband, maintained the same stolid indifference which characterized the first days of her imprisonment. She seems still to be unaware of her position. Magistrate Vachier, with Police Chief Curty and American Consul Honey, spent the entire morning today searching trunks in the Nirdlinger apartment in an effort to discover more cash, but nothing negotiable was found. As far as could be learned no money has been sent Mrs. Nixon-Nirdlinger from the Unite

Paris, March 23 (#)—Europe as a whole was doing a lot of worrying tonight over the Austro-German economic agreement which, it is felt here, may be the first move toward political union of Austria and Germany, thereby reopening war wounds which Europe has been striving to heal. News of the customs accord between the two countries comes just at a time when League of Nations forces are congregated in Paris for tomorrow's meeting which is expected to advance the project of Aristide Briand, French Foreign Minister, for a United States of Europe. Julius Curtius and Johann Schoeber, German and Austrian Foreign Ministers, respectively, are described as making a protocol which, while seeming to help out Briand’s idea of an economic union by getting rid of customs barriers, is considered really injurious to the project because it goes too far in one jump and is not done with the consent of other n

Berlin, March 23 (#)—Germany and Austria, under the proposed customs union between them, would retain complete independence, a protocol published by the German government today indicates. They would abolish customs levies on Austro-German traffic, and split their net customs receipts on a fixed scale. Both countries bind themselves to negotiate with any other nation which wants to enter a similar agreement, and each country is to bear the cost of its own customs administration. Both Germany and Austria are left free to conclude commercial treaties with other nations, but when such treaties are made Germany and Austria will conclude separate treaties, ratified documents concerning which would be exchanged simultaneously with the third power. Today's protocol characterizes the proposed customs union as initiating a new order in European economic conditions by means of regional treaties.

Istres, France, March 24. (?)— Joseph Lebrix, former flying partner of Dieudonné Coste, landed the airplane Hyphen here today at 2:45 p.m., smashing practically all French records for closed circuit flying with a heavy load. When he came down, he had been aloft 32 hours 17 minutes and 58 seconds. He thus evened the score with Coste who had previously broken the former’s records for distance over a closed circuit with a thousand kilo load and for endurance with a five hundred kilo burden.

1931-01-26.text: NEW DELHI, India, Jan. 25—(AP)—The unconditional release from prison of Mahatma Gandhi and other members of the nationalist congress working committee was ordered today by the Viceroy, Lord Irwin. Although no time was set in the release order, it is expected to take effect by tomorrow evening. Gandhi, leader of the nationalist movement, has been in jail at Poona since May 5. The Viceroy also issued an order establishing the lawfulness of the congress working committee. In his statement, the Viceroy said: “In order to provide an opportunity for consideration of the statement made by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald on January 19, my government, in consultation with the local government has thought it right that members of the congress working committee of the all-India congress should enjoy full liberty of discussion between themselves and with those who have acted as members of the commit

NEW DELHI, India, Jan. 26. (UP) — Millions of Indians awaited the release from prison today of their revered nationalist leader, Mahatma Gandhi. Unconditional freedom for past and present members of the All-India National Congress executive committee was ordered by Viceroy Lord Irwin. Orders which outlawed the working committee of the congress were cancelled. The release of such important native politicians as Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhai Patel, Mrs. Sarojini Naidu and Sen Gupta, was expected sometime today. The Indian civil disobedience leaders thus will have an opportunity to meet and discuss the proposals of the Indian round table conference. Upon his release, Gandhi will resume active command of the congress movement, which since he was imprisoned May 5, has had a score of leaders all of whom were arrested. Gandhi, a frail vegetarian, has been weakened by his long imprisonment

POONA, India, Jan. 26.—(CP)— Mahatma Gandhi, Indian Nationalist leader awaiting release from his prison quarters at Yeroda here this afternoon, signified to prison authorities that he would go to Bombay as soon as granted his liberty. The "holy one" was spending his day of silence and refused to utter a word when asked in writing where he wished to proceed, but taking a slip of paper wrote on it in English, "Bombay." Police and troops were in readiness here to prevent any demonstration when the prison’s gates should be opened to release the man who has led the Nationalists in their campaign of civil disobedience to secure Indian independence. Demonstrations Feared His decision to make Bombay his destination when leaving the prison aroused considerable anxiety among authorities, who feared demonstrations with possible bloodshed and rioting when he reaches the city where his popularity is

J Press Staff Correspondent, DON, Jan. 28, —Great Britain has taken the first step forward gaining the support of Mahatma Gandhi and his millions of Nationalist followers for the proposed Indian constitution framed at the round table conference, at which the Nationalists refused to participate. The government's decision to free more than a score of the principal All-India Congress leaders, including Gandhi, and to withdraw the outlawing of the committee, will be regarded here as a shrewd tactical move towards Gandhi's party and moderate elements, inasmuch as it forces the Nationalists' hands and impels them to make a decision soon on the proposed constitutional plan. Gandhi faces the most momentous decision in his career for whatever he decides to do is likely to split his followers into two camps. The great question now is whether Gandhi can control the movement that has started. He is

Mahadev Desai, general secretary of the All-Indian Congress and secretary to Mahatma Gandhi, was released from the Ahmedabad jail this morning. He was the first of prominent Indian politicians to be freed by order of the Viceroy, Lord Irwin. It was understood that delay in releasing Gandhi was due to the prison governor's waiting to receive signed instructions. Authorities said nothing regarding the time of his release. It was recalled that this was Gandhi's weekly day of silence, and that if he was released today he probably would say nothing.

Poona, India, Jan. 25 (/P)—Once again India’s future destiny appears to rest upon the caprice or determination of the frail and mystical ascetic known as Mahatma Gandhi. At New Delhi today Viceroy Lord Irwin decreed the unconditional release from prison of Gandhi and other members of the working committee of All India National Congress, to take effect probably tomorrow. But the question agitating the officials of Yeroda prison here tonight was: Will Gandhi accept? The bespectacled little leader was astonished today when informed of the plan to release him and already has made known that he would prefer to remain a prisoner unless all those whom he calls his “fellow martyrs” are liberated with him. These total around 50,000. If he definitely refuses to leave the prison, the British authorities will face the embarrassing obligation of evicting him. And if this occurs, so observers believe,

CAIRO, Jan. 26—U.P)—An ancient Egyptian tomb said to rival that of King Tut-Ankh-Amen in beauty and interest has been found by Prof. Selim Hassan, famous archaeologist, according to reports received here. The tomb was found in the enclosure of Ra-Wer, one of the most powerful of Egyptian high priests, near the Sphinx. It was sealed, and intact. It consisted of two chambers, one containing the queen's sarcophagus surmounted by a gold crown set with precious stones, and the other holding furniture, gold toilet requisites, and linens.

PARIS, Jan. 26.—(AP)—Senator Pierre Laval expressed confidence today that he would have a cabinet to replace that of Premier Theodore Steeg, which resigned Thursday, before tonight, and would be able to read his declaration of policy to the chamber of deputies Thursday. His optimism was in the face of a renewal of old antagonisms between the radical socialists, a powerful left group, and the rightist colleagues of Louis Marin. Yesterday the radicals voted to collaborate with their 135 chamber votes with the new premier designate, but their resolution was ambiguous and today it was understood that they maintained their old refusal of collaboration in any cabinet in which the Marinists were represented.

| SHANGHAI (UP)—Fear that G. W. Brophy, aviator flying from Foochow to Canton, may have met with disaster of some kind, was felt there when no word had been received of his whereabouts by 12:30 a. m. Monday, Brophy, forced down several days ago at Foochow, while flying from Shanghai to Canton, as the first leg of a flight to Manila, took off Monday at 7:15 a. m. Apprehension for the airman was felt when bad weather was reported along the coast route which Brophy was known to be following, and there were no reports that he had been sighted since shortly after the takeoff. It was even considered possible that he had lost his bearings in a heavy fog, and may have wandered out over the ocean.

PARIS, Jan. 25 —(#)—The formation of a cabinet by Pierre Laval, youthful Independent Socialist Senator, appeared assured tonight when the Radical Socialist party, controlling 125 votes in the Chamber of Deputies, voted its support. The Laval cabinet, it is expected will be composed of many elements of the former Steeg and Tardieu cabinets, dropping the Socialist support and seeking a majority in the center and moderate right elements. Tardieu is expected to be offered a portfolio.

Stendal, Germany, Jan. 26—(AP)—Fifteen persons were badly injured, some of them innocent passersby, when police clubbed and dispersed a band of communist demonstrators who had come here in fourteen automobiles during the night.

MENEMEN, Turkey, Jan. 25 (?) - Death sentences were demanded by the government last night for 5 Turks accused of plotting a holy war against the republic. The group is the first of several hundred persons to be tried before a military court for participation in a religious revolt last December 2. Sentences for the first group will be pronounced tomorrow.

‘By United Press ROME, Jan. 26.—Commandant Umberto Maddalena, famous Italian aviator who participated in the recent seaplane squadron flight from Italy to Brazil, will attempt a non-stop flight from Rome to Washington in a land airplane, it is reliably reported here. It is understood that the attempt will be made before General Italo Balbo, commander of the flight across the south Atlantic, leads 18 seaplanes from Lake Orbetello on a flight to New York, via Spain, Portugal, the Azores and Bermuda, in 1932. Maddalena piloted the airplane which first sighted survivors of the dirigible Itala, lost on a North Pole flight, and carried food to them. He has planned to attempt a non-stop flight to New York for several years. He holds several Italian aviation records.

ROME, Jan. 26.—(4) Italian Colonial troops routed a band of natives in severe fighting Saturday at Et Tag in the heart of the Cufra oasis region of Libya. The Colonial troops lost two officers and two native soldiers were killed. Sixteen native soldiers in the Italian forces were wounded. Twenty of the rebel tribesmen were killed and thirteen were taken prisoner. Hundreds of rifles and a quantity of ammunition also were seized. The oasis zone in Cufra has long been an objective of the Colonial authorities after the conquest of the Fezzan region. Operations began Jan. 1 over a front two columns of troops starting from Vialo with Sahara corps, and a squadron of armored cars with native soldiers from Uauel Chebir. They converged at Bir Zighen on Jan. 9. The rebels fought them bitterly and a decisive action which began Jan. 19 continued until the tribesmen, seeing themselves surrounded, fled

1931-01-10.text: BURNLEY, Eng. Jan, 10.—(P)— Twenty-five thousand weavers in the cotton textile industry were locked out this morning by ninety per cent of the mill owners, carrying out the owners’ threat that the mills would be closed unless 5,000 men who struck earlier in the week returned to their jobs by today. It seems a bit unlikely that any of the mills would reopen. The textile dispute arose from the weavers’ refusal to accept the mill owners’ demand that each man now operating four looms take over eight. There were fears that the difficulties with the weavers would spread throughout the industry, affecting about 250,000 weavers and as many spinners.

London, Jan. 9. (P)—Today’s developments in the labor disputes of two great British industries, coal and cotton, developed the gloomy probability of extended unemployment for about 650,000 workers, with resultant hardship for three or four times that number of their dependents. Hope for a settlement of the South Wales coal stoppage affecting 140,000 men, died when a “peace” meeting at Cardiff, Wales, broke up over interpretations of a single phrase. The mines will remain closed at least until next week. In the cotton dispute over the owners’ announced intention of introducing more looms per weaver, the central committee of the Cotton Spinners and Manufacturers associations at Manchester recommended that association members close their mills on January 17 if the dispute remains unsettled on that date. This action would throw about 250,000 weavers out of work, and also would suspend automa

[INTERNATIONAL NEWS SERVICE] LONDON, Jan. 10.—Three bodies have been recovered and many other persons were feared dead after a landslide at Lecco, Italy, according to reports today from Milan to the London News-Chronicle. Part of the town was demolished by the tons of earth and rocks that tumbled down, it was stated.

- Windsor, England, Jan. 10, WA— Funeral services for Lavise, the princess royal and sister of King George V., were held in the newly restored St. George’s chapel at Windsor Castle today. King George and Queen Mary, the Prince of Wales, the Duke and Duchess of York, other members of the royal family and several members of the government and diplomats attended. The coffin was placed in the royal tomb house holding the remains of King Edward and Queen Alexandra.

PARIS, Jan. 10 (AP)—The little town of Fleury Les Aubrais paid tribute today to the heroism of a Catholic nun, Sister Therese Augusta, who sacrificed her life yesterday to save the inmates of the Catholic hospital there from a fire which threatened to destroy the building. The flames broke out on a lower floor, cutting off escape by the stairways. Sister Therese made a rope of sheets and started to climb down so that she could summon firemen. Halfway down she was overcome by smoke, lost her hold on the improvised rope, fell to the ground and was killed. Neighbors, seeing the smoke and hearing the cries of the inmates, brought the firemen who extinguished the blaze after rescuing all the patients. Another nun, Sister Marie Patrice, died of a heart attack during the fire.

BRUSSELS — (P) — A pilot and mechanic, the only occupants of the night air mail plane from Brussels to Croydon, were killed when the plane crashed at midnight at Melle. Because of the fog the pilot decided to return to Brussels but, turning at too low a height, the wing tip struck the ground and the plane was wrecked.

(By United Press.) BERLIN, Jan. 10—Hostile demonstrations were renewed Saturday at various towns visited by Chancellor Heinrich Bruening, returning from his East Prussian tour. Communists and fascists maligned the chancellor as “death and hunger dictator” at Oppeln, Rosenberg and Beuthen. Stones were thrown at the automobiles of the Bruening party at Beuthen. At Beuthen, which is on the Polish frontier, strong police guards surrounded the chancellor's party but the hurling of stones could not be prevented. One stone smashed the window of an automobile in the chancellor's party. The walls of the palace of the archbishop of Breslau, where Bruening is due to halt Saturday night, were daubed with great streaks of red paint and the words: “Death and hunger dictator.”

ANTWERP, Belgium, Jan. 1 (P)—Nine Spanish army aviators who participated in the recent revolutionary movement there arrived from Portugal today and were permitted to enter Belgium. Among them was General Llano, who said he would become sales agent in France for an important Portuguese export firm. “The others were Commanders Miranda Cario and Gonzalez Gillies Artur, and six captains in the Spanish air corps.

By United Press TOKYO, Jan. 10.— The Osaka Asahi’s Paris correspondent says the aviator Cobos will arrive in Japan in March to attempt a non-stop flight from Japan to the Pacific Coast of the United States. Dieudonne Costes’ plane Question Mark, which has already flown the Atlantic, will be used. This will be the second attempt to span the Pacific from West to East. Harold Bromley, Seattle aviator, took off from Northern Japan last fall, but was forced back by stormy weather. Bromley announced that he plans to try again in the spring.
MOSCOW, Jan. 10—(7)—Amy Johnson, the British aviatrix, arrived here today by train from Warsaw and announced that she had given up her plans to fly to Peiping across Siberia, at least until!

1931-03-01.text: NEW DELHI, India, Feb. 28 (P)— Mahatma Gandhi is going to see the viceroy again tomorrow in one last effort to straighten out the tangled Indian political situation, but tonight it looked as though their efforts to reach an agreement would fall. This afternoon the working committee of the All India Congress Party voted to reject the viceroy’s terms of settlement and no one would say what the result would be. It was understood that the deadlock followed the government’s refusal to grant Gandhi's demands that Indians be given the right to make their own salt. On this issue the viceroy has said that the salt revenue law can be changed only by the legislature. Lord Irwin also was said to be determined not to yield the right to boycott British goods, arguing that it would be unthinkable to permit the Congress Party or any other Indian group to tear down the British commercial trade which was

LONDON.—(#)—Young Sir Oswald Mosley, who in his 35 years has sat in the House of Commons as a Conservative, an Independent and a Laborite, Saturday formally announced the launching of a new party to deal with the “grave national economic crisis.” That's the party's name—the “new party,” and it appeals, its sponsor said, “to youth and all those who have young ideas on government” to help merge the Liberal, Conservative and Labor parties into one great national force for the rehabilitation of Britain. There is a suspicion of the spirit of fascism and a dash of Soviet cabinet rule in his bold plan for turning the “talk shop” of Parliament into a “workshop” by means of what the press generally has termed a limited dictatorship by a small inner cabinet of five or six ministers without portfolio acting as the national executive. Challenging all existing parties, Sir Oswald plans to mobilize 40

ROME, Feb. 28. (P)—Italy and Great Britain today reached an agreement in principle for the settlement of naval problems left over by the London conference last year, and although the accord is subject to French approval, in official circles here there was a general feeling it is all but signed. Arthur Henderson, British foreign secretary who headed his nation's naval delegation at Paris and here, said tonight before he started back for the French capital, "we'll get an agreement in Paris if we do as well there as we did here." He added that the prospects were bright for such a result.

1931-02-08.text: Brisbane, Australia, Feb. 7—(P)—All available police were rushed to the south side of the city during the night to warn residents of an impending flood. Rains have ceased but an enormous quantity of flood water up country had to find its way seaward. Coastal districts within 100 miles north and south of Brisbane were flooded. Seventy miles south of this city an automobile collided with a motor boat which was traveling on the flooded main stream. More than 1,000 people in this city were homeless today as a result of the floods. When the ground floor of the telephone building was flooded out, a plucky girl operator dressed in a swimming suit climbed through an upper window of the exchange and kept the lines open for several hours.

Berlin, Feb. 7.--(#)--Three times today Chancellor Bruening turned back the opposition in the Reichstag and the government whose fate seemed to hang by a thread before the Christmas recess emerged in full control, firmly entrenched in power and with a substantial majority in the parliament. Political observers saw this coming last Thursday when the chancellor, in a quiet but firm exposition of the country’s economic situation, told the deputies he was opposed to invoking the ‘dictatorship clause’ of the constitution and that the Reichstag must assume full responsibility for adopting the 1931 budget as speedily as possible. The Vote Today’s three-fold defeat took the starch out of the Communists and the National Socialists. A joint no-conference motion by both parties was defeated by a vote of 293 to 22.

PARIS, Feb. 5—(UP)—Bare legs, bare feet and painted toes protruding from scant sandals, all part of Jean Worth’s evening gown ensemble, created a sensation in the Paris fashion world today. In contrast, Worth’s models also wore long suede gloves and huge fur collars in the same ensemble. Long afternoon and evening skirts were slashed at the knee, revealing the leg during the process of walking. The skirts were reminiscent of the “sheath” skirts popular in 1910. There was a scarcity of printed silks in the display. There was much wool, wool lace, tweeds, jersey tussors, crepes satin, georgette, chiffon and lace. Pastel colors predominated, in chartreuse, champagne, shell pink, almond, green, grape, black and white. Navy blue was favored for day wear.

Rome, Feb. 7, (4)—Thomas Tittoni, one of the most active of Italian statesmen in the pre-Mussolini era, died here today. Tommaso Tittoni was one of the most prominent exponents of the pre-Fascist regime in Italy to rally to the cause of Mussolini. Few of his contemporaries in the kingdom had the wealth of experience in foreign affairs possessed by Tittoni. He was four times foreign minister, premier for a brief period, ambassador to London and Paris and in addition president of the senate from 1919 to 1929. He also served as first president of the Royal. In the summer of 1922, Tittoni visited the United States, being Italy's spokesman at the Institute of Politics at Williams College, Williamstown, Mass. Upon the adjournment of the institute he gave a number of lectures in different (Continued on page two)

1931-02-25.text: By The Associated Press London, Feb 24--Gen Charles G. Dawes, America’s fiery ambassador to the Court of St. James, who has won his way to the hearts of the British people, plans to serve his full term of two more years here, he told the Associated Press today. The ambassador thus silenced rumors that he would return to the United States either for political work or in connection with the World Fair at Chicago. He and his brother made themselves responsible for the opening of the exposition on time. The general, who has a host of friends here, seems perfectly satisfied with his present job, although it was reported to be costing him $160,000 a year out of his own pocket. In announcing his intention to remain here for two more years, unless some unforeseen circumstance arises, he waived his famous under-slung pipe and said: “I am 65 years old. What more should I want to do?”
