As a newspaperman it was my business to watch the exciting scene with the utmost attention; as a human being I was absorbing in watching it quite aside from professional duty. Rewildering spectacle cast into the crucibles of an immense unprecedented experiment—a word communists dislike as applied to their revolution. It implies the possibility of failure and they do not admit such a possibility. When I arrived here in February 1928 certain processes were only beginning which since then have gathered speed and startled the world with their audacity and relentlessness. The revolution at that time had just passed through what Lenin

ROME, Feb. 24. (4)—Transformation of the London naval three power pact into a five power treaty, with Italy and France adhering, appeared a distinct probability tonight. Word that British minister Arthur Henderson and A. V. Alexander, first lord of the admiralty, had left for home to present a conditional accord reached in Paris was hailed with satisfaction in circles conversant with Italian official views.

Paris, F. D. 24, VAT) "VCS IR DaUON 25 the world’s premier aviator today was voted Dieudonne Coste, Paris-New York flier, by the awards committee of the International League of Aviators. Admiral Richard E. Byrd was awarded a gold plaque for his South Pole flight and plaques were voted also to Col. Charles A. Lindbergh and Brent Balchen. Ward Van Orman, of the United States, was awarded the spherical balloon trophy and Allam McCracken a plaquette of honor. Hugo Eckener was voted the world’s premier dirigible pilot and Charles Rosendahl, U. S. was awarded honorable mention like Dr. Eckener. Amy Johnson was voted the best of the women fliers and plaques were voted Mrs. Lindbergh, mg Victor Bruce and Maryse Bas- Captain Frank Hawks, noted American speed pilot, was designated as America’s premier aviator for

(by Associated Press) VIENNA, Feb. 24—Police and soldiery of numerous countries of central and southeastern Europe, including the Balkans, were mobilized tonight to prevent disorders tomorrow—variously designated as international, communist, unemployment and hunger day—with force of arms if necessary. From the nature of measures adopted and orders issued authorities appeared to anticipate stubborn resistance to orders issued in many countries forbidding demonstrations or indoor and outdoor meetings during the day. Austria, where the influence of the communists on Socialist unemployed is slight, is one of the few countries where such strict bans against public gatherings have not been issued. A public parade will be permitted here. In Berlin, where authorities have forbidden a demonstration called by the communists, the police tonight warned that their clubs would be used freely in breaki

1931-02-11.text: LONDON, Feb. 11—(#)—The Dole, it is officially estimated, cost the British taxpayer between $250,000,000 and $275,000,000 or even more during the financial year opening April 1, next. The figures are contained in a memorandum submitted by the British treasury to the royal commission on unemployment insurance. The memorandum drew attention to the gravity of the situation. “The increase of expenditure in 1930 over that of 1928 was $125,000,000," says the memorandum, “and the increase of 1931 over 1928 may amount to some $225,000,000. Even in the most favorable conditions so great an increase so swiftly incurred would overtax the budget. “In the present conditions it must be taken in conjunction with the other continuing liabilities of the state, both for the war debt and otherwise, and in these conditions it will not merely disturb but will entirely upset the equilibrium of the budget on t

LONDON, Feb. 11.—(U.P.)—The Stars and Stripes will float from many masts tomorrow and wreaths will be placed at the foot of a beloved statue in Parliament Square. In this simple, yet sincere way will United States citizens in London observe the 122nd anniversary of the birth of Abraham Lincoln. A handful of old, bent men, veterans of Civil War days, will place wreaths at the foot of Lincoln's statue which occupies a conspicuous place in Parliament Square just opposite Westminster Abbey.

SPF FORTE Sees YEW R OCT MT, LONDON, Feb. 11.—Three mysterious SOS signals intercepted by a channel steamer advising of a liner in distress 1,000 miles off the west Irish coast and carrying 300 passengers today puzzled maritime authorities. French and British wireless stations immediately sought to communicate with the stricken vessel, but were unable to establish contact. The operator of the cross-channel steamer Engadine, who intercepted the distress calls, was unable to catch the name of the vessel, distinguishing only the last two letters “us.”

Tokyo, Feb. 11.°-(AP)—Plans for a solo flight by Belja Yoshiwara across the Pacific via the Kurile and Aleutian islands were announced today by the vernacular newspaper ‘Hochi. The flight will be made in April. Yoshiwara plans nineteen stops, expecting to follow the route of the American army found the world fliers in 1924. The announcement said the flight was in the interest of Japanese-American friendship. The newspaper will sponsor the venture. Yoshiwara, 26 years old, studied aviation in Germany three years. He is known as “The Japanese Sea Gull.” He will use a light all-metal Junkers seaplane.

BERLIN, Feb. 11, (4)—The threat of a rump parliament was heard in Germany today from Fascist and Nationalist members of the Reichstag, but was not regarded seriously in government quarters. A spokesman for the two parties, whose Reichstag deputation marched out in a body yesterday shortly before an important address on foreign policy by Dr. Julius Curtius, said the Fascists might call an Opposition sitting at Weimar, birthplace of Germany's constitution. Rumors were current today that the Fascists, who recognize the leadership of Adolf Hitler, had taken night trains for Weimar but inquiry at their hotels brought the information that they were still registered. Even should the Fascists and Nationalists go through the motions of organizing a Reichstag at Weimar, government circles felt the organization would be more than a demonstration meeting. It was felt that the two parties, after thei

By The Associated Press: Berlin, Feb. 11--The opposition benches were empty this afternoon when the Reichstag convened to resume debate on foreign affairs. Apparently the national socialists and the nationalists were carrying out their threat, made yesterday, just before Foreign Minister Curtis began an outline of his policies, that they would stay out of the chamber until an important vote demanded their presence.

PARIS, (UP).—The French naval building program for 1931-32 has been completed for submission to the Chamber of Deputies late this week, asking for speedy construction of half a dozen formidable warships of the latest fighting type. The program, which totals 42,000 tons of projected ships, and definitely ends the “naval building truce” with Italy as a result of failure of negotiations between the two countries for a limitation agreement, was described to the United Press today as follows: One battle cruiser, a super-ship of 23,300 tons which will outclass the new “pocket battleship” type built by Germany. It will have a high speed and carry heavy armaments. A light cruiser of 7,000 tons. A light cruiser of 6,500 tons. A destroyer of the latest type, about 2,400 tons. A “super submarine” of the type of the great Surcouf, considered by French experts to be the most modern underwater craft e

KOBE, Japan, Feb 10—(P)—Boats searching the blizzard lashed waters of the Japanese coast last night picked up thirty persons counted as lost in the sinking of the Japanese steamer Kisusui Maru yesterday after a collision with the French steamer Porthos. Reports today from outlying ports said thirty rescued had been landed, leaving nineteen unaccounted for. The Kisusui Maru was bound for Shodo island in the Sea of Harima with Japanese returning to celebrate with their families the old style Japanese New Year when the collision with the Porthos occurred in the dense fog. The Kisusui Maru was sunk. The Porthos rescued twenty-five persons and landed them at Kobe today. Other vessels picked up additional survivors of Hyogo prefecture at the northern tip of Awaji island. The nineteen missing include women and children from factories of Okayama. The storm continued to rage with unabated fury se

TOKIO, — Twenty-one Japanese, missing since the Japanese ship Kikushui Maru sank near Kobe Monday night after a collision with the French liner Porthos, was given up Wednesday for lost. Twenty-one survivors of the Kikushui Maru were picked up Wednesday and 27 were rescued Tuesday out of 69 aboard when it sank.

BERLIN, Feb. 10.—(UP)—A sensational declaration that publication of certain documents held secret in official German archives would definitely disprove allegations of Germany's war guilt was made by Dr. Julius Curtius, foreign minister, during a tumultuous session of the Reichstag Tuesday... The declaration by Dr. Curtius came during his presentation of the government’s foreign policy, which included a statement that Germany did not intend to “destroy the Young Plan” for reparations payments. He decried the lack of disarmament among the powers allied during the World War, however, and insisted that arms limitations be made, as promised at the Treaty of Versailles. The foreign minister’s spectacular address was made to a “silent house,” strained or the irreconcilable fascists.

1931-01-20.text: LONDON, Jan. 20,—(/?)-—Partnership of India as a dominion with responsible self-government in the British commonwealth of nations was pledged Monday by Ramsay MacDonald as the great Indian round table conference in old St. James’s Palace came to a close. “You have opened a new chapter in the history of India,” was King George's message to the 100 or more delegates. MacDonald, in a long and earnest speech outlining British policy in India, extended the hand of dominion fellowship to the great Asian sub-continent where a fifth of the world's population dwells.

Vigo, Spain, Jan. 20.—(4)—The Prince of Wales and his youngest brother, Prince George, sailed from Spain today on their 18,000 mile tour of South America after a day of sightseeing along the northern Spanish coast. The Prince of Wales, saying farewell in Spanish, promised his hosts that when he returned he would speak their language more fluently. The two Princes left their ship at Corunna yesterday and motored along the coast to Santiago De Compostela and Vigo. They went back (Continued on Page 7)

GENEVA, Jan. 20. (4)—Discussion of disarmament began today in the League of Nations council but the delegates did not reach the point of fixing a date for a general disarmament conference. Aristide Briand, Arthur Henderson, Julius Curtius and Dino Grandi today joined in pledging their governments to cooperate in a program for limiting armament and agreed that the nations should assemble to frame a general treaty as soon as possible.

1931-02-27.text: LONDON, Feb. 27. (UP)—The resignation of Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's labor government was considered a possibility in some political quarters today after a Liberalist amendment to the trades disputes bill had taken most of the original flavor out of the measure. The bill, intended to legalize general strikes, in its amended form defines as illegal "any strike or walkout the effect of which at any time by reason of its extension or continuation endangers public health and safety by interfering with supplies or distribution of water, fuel, lights, medicine and sanitary service or other necessities of life." Trade unionists were particularly bitter regarding the amendment and said it violated the entire trade disputes bill.

LONDON, Feb. 27 (AP) — Queen Mary has broken her rule about wedding presents. Usually brides in the court receive from the queen a piece of jewelry set with the royal cipher. But to the Hon. Imogene Grenfell, who yesterday married Viscount Gage, a captain of the Coldstream Guards, she gave a beautiful dressing case. The bag was small, in a handbag design, of green crushed Morocco leather. The top is nearly covered by a circular plaque of white jade in a delicate pattern. Bottles and other fittings are done in a soft green enamel to match the leather.

PARIS.—Police Friday seized a high-powered grenade which had been placed in the automobile of Count Manzoni, the Italian ambassador to France. The explosive was discovered by the ambassador's chauffeur before Count Manzoni entered the automobile. A police investigation was started immediately.

MOSCOW, Feb. 27.—The Soviet Union prepared today for the trial of 14 men who had attained high positions in the economic workings of the government, indicted on charges of planning intervention and sabotage. The accused are members of the Menshevik minority. The state alleged that their backing came from France and Germany. The proceedings will start Sunday and were expected to be similar to the recent trial of eight prominent engineers and professors who were sentenced to prison for alleged intervention plots. As in the previous trial, the 14 men involved in the new process confessed and pleaded guilty. Their trial may be even more significant than that of Professor Leonid Ramzin and his comrades, for it will involve the correct application of Marxist doctrines to the problems of Communist government and may be the final round in the battle between Mensheviks (minority) and Bolshevik fa

PARIS, Feb. 27.—(UP)— The 16th anniversary of the death of Edward Mandelstone, of Chicago, first American killed in the World War, was observed today with a ceremony before the monument to Americans who died for France. American and French war veterans, many of them with an arm or leg missing, gathered before the monument and placed a wreath in memory of the first American blood spilt there. The ceremony was organized by Trench and Air, an association of American volunteer combatants in the French army, of which John G. Hopper, of San Francisco and Paris, is president.

| TOKIO, Feb. 27.—(AP)—An “interesting event” of paramount concern to the 90,000,000 subjects of the emperor of Japan is expected within a few days, for the birth of an infant that may become the sovereign of the empire should take place about March 10. The Empress Nagako is about to present her consort, Emperor Hirohito, with a child, and in the imperial palace preparations for the expected arrival have taken precedence over everything else. Even if the little mite of the blood imperial is a girl there will be nation-wide rejoicing for the safety of the empress and her baby, but the celebrations will not be so extensive as if it is a prince to be welcomed. In either case, however, there will be ceremonies to announce the birth in the three shrines of the imperial palace—the Kashikodokoro, or Holy of Holies, where the imperial mirror of the sun goddess is enshrined; the Korei-Den, dedica

MOSCOW, Feb. 27.—Fourteen prominent Russians will go to trial tomorrow for treason here March 1, charged with counter-revolutionary activities. The defendants, who are described in the indictments as friends of the recently condemned group of engineers led by Professor Leonid Ramsin, are headed by the widely known agronomist, Professor Groman. They are all members of the Menshevik (minority as opposed to Bolshevik, majority) faction of the Communist party.

Naples, Italy, Feb. 26.—(AP)—Cyclonic storms, which have battered southern Italy for almost a week, had abated tonight, leaving in their wake about 27 persons drowned and several million dollars damage. The storm which reached its most northern point here, wrought its worst damage on small vessels, sea-ports and country districts. The southern provinces were hardest hit in recent years. As reports trickled in from outlying towns the death toll climbed steadily.

1931-01-06.text: Plymouth, England, Jan. 5—(/P)— Thirty seamen of H. M. S. Lucia, submarine depot ship, were under arrest today, facing possible court martial for refusing to work when their week-end shore leave was cancelled. An official inquiry went forward into the affair, which was termed by Admiral Sir Hubert Bland, commander-in-chief of the Davenport area, as “not a mutiny.” The men were held in barracks ashore. All communication between the Lucia and the shore was cut.

Surat, British India—/—Lamd as Gandhi, son of Mahatma Gandhi, Tuesday was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment at hard labor. He was arrested last month for delivering a speech on civil disobedience.

Almost every day is inaugural day somewhere in the United States during the first weeks of the New Year as governors in 33 states take the oath of office as designated by their constitutions. The advent of new administrations in many states recalls the Democratic victories of the election in November with many Democrats replacing Republicans in state executive offices. Two names long prominent in American politics are listed in the roster of new governors. Philip Fox LaFollette was inaugurated in Wisconsin yesterday. Governor LaFollette is the second son of the late Senator Robert M. LaFollette and a brother of “Young Bob,” who now occupies his father's seat in the Senate. Like the other LaFolletes, he is a Progressive. He succeeds Walter J. Kohler, Conservative Republican. Charles W. Bryan, brother of the late William Jennings Bryan, will be inducted into office as governor of Nebraska

PARIS, Jan. 3. — (4) — Marshal Joseph Jacques Joffre, the “Defender of Paris,” as he will go down in history, lay in state today to receive an homage from the people of France that has rarely, perhaps never, been surpassed in his country’s annals. The crowd began to take form at dawn and slowly, as the day advanced, it grew until just before nightfall it became a vast multitude which at one moment got out of bounds and women were knocked and trampled upon before order was restored. At first a single line, the stream of those who filed through the portals of France's famous military school to pause for a moment beside the body of the old warrior, grew so deep and stretched from the entrance of the school nearly a quarter of a mile away across the Champ de Mars. There were many thousands of them and one of the most touching tributes was that of the hundreds of children who joined in the so

Berlin, Jan. 6—The Dornier works announced today that the big seaplane Do-X is scheduled to start her transatlantic flight to America on Jan. 20. The crew left for Lisbon, Portugal, to take over the plane last year.

PARIS—Foreign troops and distinguished visitors arrived today to participate in the state funeral services tomorrow for Marshal Joffre. A long line of Joffre’s countrymen meanwhile formed outside the Chapel of Saint Louis, several hours before the doors opened, and 20,600 walked past the camp cot where he lay during the morning. A detachment of The Glorious Contemptibles, survivors of the British Expeditionary Force that fought with Joffre at the Marne in 1914, were received enthusiastically by Parisians. Notre Dame Cathedral, where Joffre’s body will be taken tonight, was draped in black today. Post No. 2 of the American Legion in Paris will not participate in the funeral, it was announced today. It was recalled there was some adverse criticism to the Legion’s representation at the funeral of Marshal Ferdinand Foch.

Astrakaan, U. S. S. R., Jan. 6.—(P)—Rescue parties were mobilized today to save the lives of 50 fishermen and their horses who were carried out to the Caspian Sea yesterday when a huge mass of ice on which they were fishing broke loose from shore. A storm which was blowing at the time broke off the huge berg and carried it far from the shore upon the dangerous waters. Steamers and airplanes have been dispatched to aid them.

STUTTGART, Germany, Jan. 8.- Plans for drastic changes in the financial policy of Chancellor Heinrich Bruening and his cabinet, including abolishment of the government’s annual dole of three billion marks, were revealed today in a sensational speech delivered at a party conference here by Finance Minister Hermann Dietrich. The revelation came by a bombshell, astounding not only the delegates but all of Germany.

VIENNA, Jan. 5 (F)~Arson was added today to the measures taken by objectors to the American war film, "All Quiet On the Western Front", to prevent its being shown in Germany and Austria. A theater in which the film was to be exhibited tomorrow, was set on fire, but the flames were extinguished before they had spread beyond the projection room, a small portion of which was destroyed. The police arrested four national socialists.

1931-03-18.text: | DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Mar. '17.—(AP) Ireland today remembered her patron saint by the wearing of the green as thousands feasted and danced and attended religious and civic ceremonies on St. Patrick’s Day. Never before has the shamrock been worn so freely, many of the girls even wearing bunches on their dance frocks. Although the celebration was anew and quiet in Dublin, it was the gayest in years at Belfast. Schools and official offices were closed in Ulster, where the younger generation took the lead in the merrymaking. Impressive services in Irish were held in Catholic and Irish churches in Dublin and traditional Irish hymns were sung in Old as Patrick’s where the city’s joys and sorrows have been sanctified for a century. - Martial music stirred historic College Green at noon when 1,200 officers and men of the Free State Army took part in a parade. The general salute was taken b

London, Mar. 18--(A.P.)—Widespread stories today of new British party alignments, which would lead David Lloyd George to the labor fold, and Sir John Simon to the conservative standard greatly excited political circles. The reports, published in the Daily Sketch and a liberal organ, appeared to be the outgrowth of the defeat of the labor government Monday night by four votes on a minor clause of the electoral reform bill principally because Sir John and ten fellow Liberals refused to follow Lloyd George in voting with the populists.

By JAMES A. MILLS Bombay, India, March 17.—(AP) Two American women from New York state, Mrs. Hattie Belle Johnston, of New York, and Mrs. R. A. C. Clark, of Lockport, saw Mahatma Gandhi return to Bombay today an almost deified idol before an audience estimated at 250,000 people. Back from his triumphant peace conference with Lord Irwin, India’s viceroy, it was half an hour before the famous leader of India was able to speak above the terrific din and confusion of the tumultuous welcome from the forest of shouting, surging humanity. Mrs. Johnston and Mrs. Clark occupied seats as guests of Mrs. Gandhi, on the huge rostrum in the middle of the vast concourse of spectators. Mrs. Gandhi asked the American women many questions about the emancipation of women in the United States. “Keep the Truce!” When the Mahatma was finally able to make his voice heard over the ocean of brown, upturned, whit

GLASGOW, Scotland, March 18 - The steamer Citritie was wrecked Tuesday night in a fog. The ship sank immediately. Two members of the crew swam ashore. The other nine were reported drowned, the announcement said.

LONDON, March 17—(AP)— A miniature naval conference was held at the foreign office this afternoon after Ambassador Dawes had rushed Senator Dwight W. Morrow, who arrived on the Leviathan to Downing Street to expound to Foreign Minister Henderson and A. V. Alexander, First Lord of the Admiralty, the American attitude toward the new Anglo-French-Italian naval agreement. It was understood that the meeting was satisfactory to all concerned and with Downing Street now officially informed of the American view that the tripartite accord is a matter of European concern only, it is expected the work of formally drafting the new agreement will begin Thursday as planned.

London—()—United States Senator Dwight W. Morrow concluded his mission to London in connection with the tripartite-naval agreement today and prepared to continue with Mrs. Morrow on the European holiday which he interrupted to confer with British cabinet officials. The conversations in which Senator Morrow participated at the foreign office yesterday and today were considered from the British viewpoint to have had a satisfactory conclusion. The new Anglo-French-Italian naval agreement is to stand as a strictly European matter. Its formal drafting will be started tomorrow, but neither Mr. Morrow nor any other representative of the United States will be present officially or unofficially, and neither will Japan be represented.

'Lendon, Mar, 18—(P)—Wages of approximately 100,000 railway workmen throughout England will be reduced four and one-sixth per cent as the result of a settlement reached today between the railroad companies and the unions. A statement issued at the close of the conference, however, stated that the earnings of any adult male employee will not be reduced below 40 shillings a week. BERLIN, Mar. 18.—(AP)—The condition of former Chancellor Mueller was considerably worse this afternoon. He was in a coma most of the time.

1931-01-14.text: LONDON, Jan. 14 (AP)—British radio systems today paged Sir Francis Barrow, English baronet who mysteriously disappeared 18 years ago and has not since made his whereabouts known. A broadcast carried the urgent appeal of friends to come home immediately since his eldest son, Wilfred John Wilson Croker, heir to his title, is seriously ill. The broadcast was the first revelation to the general public that the baronet, who is the fourth of his line, was missing. Lady Barrow, his wife, and other members of the family declined to discuss the disappearance or other circumstances of the case. If still alive Sir Francis would be 68 years old.

LONDON (iUP).—Capt. Malcolm Campbell sails for the United States Wednesday, confident that the New Blue Bird speed automobile he will take to Daytona Beach will set a new world record of around 250 miles an hour. The New Blue Bird, which was shrouded with much secrecy during its construction, was described as more than half again as powerful as the famous Golden Arrow in which the late Sir Henry Segrave attained a speed of 231.447 miles an hour to set the present mark at Daytona in 1929. One of Campbell's chief aides during the trials which he will make in Florida probably will be R. J. Leech, who was on the giant British dirigible R-101 when it crashed in France three months ago. Leech was one of the few survivors of the disaster. He was invited by Campbell to assist in the noted driver’s attack on the speed record.

Paris, Jan. 13. (@)—The chamber of deputies reconvened after the Christmas recess in a fighting mood today and even in the purely formal opening there were indications of troubled waters ahead. The first came when many socialist deputies and all the Communists failed to join in the eulogy of Marshal Joffre pronounced by Maurice Sibille, dean of the house. The second manifested itself in the sudden opposition that developed to the re-election of Fernand Boulssot, veteran Socialist, as president of the chamber. His re-election had been expected to be merely a matter of form, but when the ballots were counted it was found that he had failed to obtain half the votes polled as was necessary to selection. He finally won on the second ballot by 261 votes to 220 for Maurice Rolliouxy-LaFont.

1931-01-15.text: London, Jan. 14.—-(AP)—-By the narrow margin of one seat in the Punjab provincial legislature, the Indian Round Table conference tonight failed to solve the Indian minorities problem, although Hindu and Moslem leaders reached a provisional accord which in itself may force a full agreement later. The evening session ended however, with the conference still deadlocked over deep racial and religious problems as they affect India’s political future under the proposed federal organization.

LIVERPOOL, Eng. Jan. 15-- (UP)—The steamer Oropesa, of which the Prince of Wales and Prince George will go to South America, departed today for La Rochelle-Pallice, France, carrying the luggage of the royal party. The Prince of Wales and his brother will proceed to Paris tomorrow, probably by airplane if conditions are favorable. They will go to Santander, Spain by train and board the ship there for the start of their 20,000 miles “salesmanship” trip through Latin America. The first halt on the trip will be at range on January-

SHANGHAI, Jan. 15—(UP)— Army bombing planes were concentrated today in the southern part of Kiangsi province in an attempt to rescue Khang Hu-Chan, nationalist government general, reported captured during the battle with communists. Hankow advices asserted General Chang was being held for 2,000,000 Mexican dollars ransom and that the 15th and 18th divisions, which he was commanding, had been routed. Other dispatches received from Changsha said a communist army numbering 2,000 had been defeated in an offensive drive against a division of government troops in the Hunan province. The repulsed communists, after heavy casualties, were believed withdrawing eastward.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 15, (P)—Fighting between government troops and marauding armies of Reds was reported from three south China provinces today. Amoy reported 200 Communist bandits had been slain at Yungting, southern Fukien province, when provincial forces drove the outlaws from that city. The Reds had held Yungting since Jan. 1. Reports from southern Kiangsi province said sharp fighting was in progress between Reds and the military near Ningtu, which Communists looted last December.

| PARIS, Jan. 15, (AP).—United States Ambassador Walter E. Edge told the American Club at Paris today that America’s “darkest age” of economic apathy and stunned business inertia was past. The ambassador, who was the guest of the club upon his return from the United States, said that the “dark age” followed “the most cataclysmic deflation of security markets in our history.” He added that it had been superseded by a period of courageous effort under the scientific leadership of President Hoover and Federal and State officials. Mr. Edge said that he had no desire to deny that American business, in common with world illness, was still ailing, but he declared that the crisis was past.

1931-04-01.text: LONDON, March 31.—Lord Stamfordham, private secretary to King George, died today, aged 81. Secretary to royalty for the last fifty years, Lord Stamfordham started in the Zulu Bush country and rose to a place unique in European court circles. He was possessed of more state secrets than any living man, it was said, acting as England's "Man behind the throne."

London, March 31, ().—Leaking gas bags and bad weather were held by a court of inquiry to have caused the crash of the giant dirigible on a hillside near Beauvais, France, on the early morning of October 5, with the loss of 48 lives. The conclusions, published today, closely agree with the opinion of Dr. Hugo Eckener, commander of the Graf Zeppelin, who testified at the inquiry.

Parla, March 31 (UP)--The 1931 budget was approved today after an all-night session, during which the chamber gave the government of Premier Pierre Laval a vote of confidence. The budget, which was approved yesterday by the Senate, was voted by the Chamber after the surplus had been reduced to 60,189,000 francs. The budget provides for receipts of 50,771,458,409 francs and expenditures of 50,711,358,800 francs.

1931-01-17.text: LONDON, Jan. 17 (AP) — A violent storm which raged over England during the night abated today. The gale ripped open the roof of the Claydonotyne chemical factory spilling 100 tons of sulfuric acid. Employees hurriedly neutralized the acid, preventing what would undoubtedly have been serious consequences as it spread through the neighborhood. Three persons were killed by falling chimneys and signs. Many signs were torn from their hangings but absence of pedestrians at the early hour kept the casualty list down.

LONDON, Jan. 17.—(OP)—Three persons were reported killed by falling chimneys and signs during a violent gale which swept over England. At Liverpool the Canadian liner Duchess of York, due to sail at 4:50 p.m. was pinned to her dock by the force of the wind, notwithstanding the efforts of tugs to get her into midstream.

London, Jan. 17.--(#)—The Daily Express says that, as a consequence of recent gunnery developments, naval experts now believe British ships to be immune from aircraft attacks at sea. This, it was claimed, is due to the mounting of eight inch guns in the latest battle cruisers in such a way that they can be raised and fired effectively at an elevation of from 75 to 80 degrees. At that elevation they could have an effective range of 27,000 feet, which is higher than any bombing airplane could fly. The guns could fire a curtain of shrapnel which it would be impossible for any airplane to penetrate. Low-flying ships would be guarded against by means of various types of guns which would put a wall of bursting shells around any ship.

By The Associated Press. Cardiff, Wales, Jan. 16.—All this day well into the night the coal miners of South Wales, who have been out of work for two weeks, trudged to their meeting halls and voted to accept terms reached by their representatives with the coal mine owners on the basis that work would be resumed Monday. After they had voted and as they trudged back home through grimy, muddy streets they sang the rhythmic songs of Wales, for from those homes and the women and children in them had been driven the grim specter of starvation.
London, i. 17—(AP)— David Lloyd George, leader of the British Liberal today observed his 68th birthday.

GENEVA, Jan. 17—(UP)—A sub-committee of eight, appointed to determine whether to invite Russia and Turkey to participate in Aristide Briand’s proposed European Federation, today recommended an immediate invitation be sent to them. Dino Grandi, Italian foreign minister, thereupon immediately proposed that sessions of the organization meetings be suspended until the arrival of the Russian and Turkish delegates.

Geneva, Jan. 16,—--(4?)-—-Twenty-six European foreign ministers met here today to talk about Aristide Briand’s project for a federation of European states, but a hitch developed at the very outset when the German and Italian representatives proposed that Turkey and Soviet Russia be invited to participate. Neither of these two countries is a member of the League of Nations, but Dino Grandi, Italy's bearded young foreign minister, asserted that any federation excluding them would merely divide Europe into two camps.

Paris, Jan. 16, (JP) - Two traveling salesmen from London spent this evening in comparative quiet at their hotel here, but they were the object of considerably more attention than is usually accorded a commercial traveler. They were the Prince of Wales and his brother, Prince George, but they were strictly incognito and there was none of the pomp which visiting royalty is usually pestered. The two young men, on their way to South America where the Prince of Wales is to open the British Trade Exposition next March, crossed the channel in the prince’s airplane, reaching Le Bourget field after two hours flying over threatening clouds and through fog. The Prince of Wales was a little deaf from the roar of the motors after they landed, but he recovered quickly. To Take Liner Tomorrow the brothers will get up early to catch a train for Santander, Spain, where they will board the liner Oropesa

The Hague, Jan. 17.—(AP)—Mineichiro Adachi, former Japanese ambassador to France, has been elected president of the permanent court of international justice, replacing Dionisio Anzilotti, Italian, who headed the so-called “world court.” The court is now composed of fifteen judges instead of eleven, among the new members being Frank B. Kellogg, former secretary of state of the United States.

Berlin, Germany, Jan. 17.—A storm of hurricane proportions swept parts of Germany last night and today, causing a train wreck, doing great damage to shipping, unroofing houses and blowing down trees. The engine of the wrecked train was blown off the tracks, killing the engineer.

| ISTRES, France, Jan. 17. Joseph Lebrix, French pilot, and his mechanic, Doret, abandoned their second attempt to break the world’s distance and endurance record over a closed circuit today at 5:32 a.m. Violent winds throughout the night hampered their flying.

Paris, Jan. 15— (UP)— The mayors of all the villages and towns in America which bear the name of Paris may visit France as guests of the municipal fathers of the one and only Paris, “City of Light”. The municipal council voted credits to bring the mayors of the American Parises, about 30 in all, to France next summer during the colonial exposition. The largest of the overseas Paris are in Texas, Kentucky, Illinois and Ohio.

GENEVA, Jan. 17—The European commission investigating possibilities of Aristide Briand’s scheme for a European confederation could not reach a decision this morning on the demand of Germany and Italy that invitations to participate in the commission’s work be extended to Russia and Turkey. Discussion will be resumed this afternoon. It was said the steering committee voted 6 to 2 in favor of inviting Russia and Turkey immediately, Great Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and Greece supporting the invitation and Belgium and Holland opposing. In the meeting of the commission as a whole it was understood the Norwegian and Rumanian members took a strong stand against the invitation also. Dino Grandi, Italian foreign minister, insisted that the invitation be sent immediately and that the commission recess until Moscow and Angora are heard.

1931-03-31.text: LONDON, March 31.—The disaster to the dirigible R-101, which stunned the world when it came down in flames on a hillside near Beauvais, France, last October, killing 48 men, was attributed today to mechanical causes, and not to human failure. The report of the Simon commission, which made a long study of the disaster, made public this evening, attributed the disaster mainly to ‘a substantial loss of gas in very bumpy weather.’ The report considered it probable that the forepart of the ship's envelope was ripped. “Something of this sort happened on a previous occasion and no amount of care could assure that it would not happen again,” the report said, emphasizing the possibility of mechanical failure in dirigibles as at present constructed. PARIS, March 31, (AP) - The government of Pierre Laval was sustained by a vote of 347 to 318 on a motion in the chamber of deputies to refer the pension phase of the budget to a committee for a detailed study, which would require a month. A proposal has been made to put all pensions granted prior to 1914 on the same basis as those granted now. Laval was firm in seeking further study of the measure. He said it would add almost $23,000,000 to the budget.

MUNICH, Ger., March 31.—(UP) Adolph Hitler, leader of the Fascist party, will file suit in the supreme court challenging the constitutionality of the dictatorial decree issued Saturday by President Paul Von Hindenburg for suppression of political violence in Germany, it was announced today. The suit will be filed “to demonstrate the legality” of the Fascist movement, which was seriously handicapped by terms of the decree. Meanwhile, Hitler ordered his brown shirts to avoid violation of the decree under threat of expulsion from the party. The decree prevents them from meeting.

MUNICH, Germany, March 31.—(I, N.S.) —Adolf Hitler, militant leader of the German Fascists, announced today he would institute suit in the constitutional court against the dictatorial decree promulgated by President Von Hindenburg to curb radical activities. At the same time Hitler ordered members of the Fascist party to obey scrupulously all restrictive measures imposed by the government while awaiting the expected judicial review.

ROME, March 31—An official announcement today admitted that a bomb had been found near the Royal Palace at Turin, the residence of Crown Prince Umberto and Crown Princess Marie Jose. Three policemen discovered the bomb, wrapped in paper, Sunday near a square adjoining the Royal Palace, the announcement said. The bomb consisted of a number of cartridges charged with black powder. The bomb was exploded without damage to person or property, according to the announcement. Officials yesterday denied reports of a bomb explosion near the Royal Palace.
(By The Associated Press) PARIS, March 30.—Charlie Chaplin, film comedian, left Paris for Nice today to bask in the sun along the Riviera.

1931-03-28.text: (By The Associated Press) LONDON, March 27. — The thunder of hoofs at Aintree echoed like golden music to the little Italian village of Isola, where live forty relatives of Emilio Scala, winner of the first prize of $1,772,720 in the Irish hospital sweepstakes at the Grand National today. Scala, who came to London thirty years ago and wheeled an ice cream barrow until he was able to buy the little coffee shop he owns, managed to purchase a $2.50 ticket in the sweepstakes and then offered to let his hometown relatives buy pieces of it. They all sent Emilio something, although they are poor and a few cents was all they could afford. Scala sold half of his ticket to a syndicate for $50,000. He retained a small share himself and his wife has a quarter share. The second prize, amounting to $886,360, was also a family affair, although there were not so many participants. C. C. Woods, of Buffal

1931-03-15.text: NICE, France, March 14.—Charlotte Nixon-Nirdlinger, who killed her husband last Wednesday night at the end of a bitter quarrel, is the calmest person the jail warden here ever saw. "She hasn't asked to see her children since the night they brought her here," he said. "She doesn't want to exercise, she won't read books, but spends her time manicuring her nails. It seems to me there is something unnatural about her." The examining magistrate today set at rest reports that she would be liberated without a trial by announcing that she would go before the court of assizes which reconvenes next August.
